docs.title: Section 10.3: Solving Two-Step Equations (ax + b = c) (Workbook pp. 99–100)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 7, Sections 3.3–3.5 (Solving Two-Step Equations) (CCSS.MATH.7.EE.B.4a) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: Two-Step Inverse Operations | Way 2: Balance Scale / Bar Model Unwrapping • Block Kit: PLACE-01 (Place Value Studio)

Key Vocabulary: two-step equation (ax + b = c) • reverse order of operations • undo addition/subtraction first • undo multiplication/division second

A two-step equation contains two operations. To isolate the variable, undo the operations in the REVERSE order of operations: Step 1 undo addition or subtraction first to isolate the variable term (ax), and Step 2 undo multiplication or division second to isolate the variable x.

⚠️ WATCH OUT: In two-step equations (ax + b = c), undo addition/subtraction FIRST, then undo multiplication/division SECOND!

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (PLACE-01: Place Value Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Two-Step Algorithm (ax + b = c): 1. Undo addition or subtraction FIRST to isolate the variable term ax. 2. Undo multiplication or division SECOND to isolate x.
  2. Textbook Verification: Substitute your solution x back into the original two-step equation and follow PEMDAS to confirm Left Side = Right Side.
  3. Block Reinforcement (PLACE-01): For 3x + 7 = 28, subtract 7 from both sides first (3x = 21), then split 21 equally into 3 sockets so each holds a [7] Digit Block.

docs.title: Authentic Textbook Worked Examples (Learn & Solve by Hand First in 1 Way +10 pts or 2 Ways +20 pts)
docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.99) Solve 3x + 7 = 28 and check your solution. WAY 1: Two-Step Inverse Operations (Reverse PEMDAS): In 3x + 7 = 28: Step 1: Subtract 7 from both sides -> 3x = 21. Step 2: Divide both sides by 3 -> x = 7. WAY 2: Balance Scale / Part-Whole Bar Model (With Blocks): A bar of 28 splits into three x-parts and a 7-part. Take away 7 (leaves 21 for the three x-parts), then divide 21 ÷ 3 = 7. x = 7 (Step 1: 3x = 21) Practice B (p.100) The temperature is 14°F and drops 3°F each hour. After how many hours will the temperature reach 2°F? WAY 1: Write & Solve -3x + 14 = 2 Using Inverse Operations: Step 1: Subtract 14 from both sides: -3x = 2 - 14 = -12. Step 2: Divide both sides by -3: x = (-12) ÷ (-3) = 4 hours.Two-Step Solution: 30x + 35 = 155 -> subtract 35 (30x = 120) -> divide by 30 (x = 4 hours). WAY 2: Total Change ÷ Rate of Change (or Countdown Table): Total drop = 14°F to 2°F = 12°F drop. At 3°F per hour, 12 ÷ 3 = 4 hours (14° -> 11° -> 8° -> 5° -> 2°).Substitution Check: 30(4) + 35 = 120 + 35 = $155 (matches total bill!). 4 hours

docs.title: Practice B (p. 100): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
At the go-kart track, admission was $8 plus $6 per lap r, and Leo had $38 to spend (6r + 8 = 38). At first he tried dividing 38 by 6 right away, got a messy fraction, and felt stuck. Then Maya reminded him of how you get dressed in the morning versus how you undress at night: you put your socks on first and your shoes on second, so to undo it you have to take your shoes off FIRST and your socks off SECOND! In 6r + 8 = 38, r was multiplied by $6 first and $8 was added second—so subtracting the $8 admission fee first (6r = 30) and dividing by $6 second gave a clean 5 laps.

docs.title: Section 10.4: Theoretical Probability, Combinations & Permutations (Workbook pp. 101–102)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 7, Chapter 7 (Probability) & SC-6 Graduation Finale (CCSS.MATH.7.SP.C.5) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: Probability Ratio & Complement Rule | Way 2: Tree Diagram / Outcome List | Way 3: Fundamental Counting Principle • Block Kit: FRAC-01 (84mm Fraction Studio)

Key Vocabulary: experiment • outcomes • event • sample space • theoretical probability P(E) • complement P(not E) • tree diagram • Fundamental Counting Principle

Theoretical probability is the ratio of favorable outcomes to total equally likely outcomes: P(event) = Favorable ÷ Total, written as a simplified fraction, decimal, or percent. The probability of an event NOT occurring is the complement: P(not E) = 1 - P(E). For counting arrangements: n! counts ways to order all n items; nPr counts ordered permutations; and nCr counts unordered combinations.

⚠️ WATCH OUT: Ask 'Does order matter?' — awarding 1st/2nd/3rd medals is a Permutation (nPr); choosing a group/team is a Combination (nCr)!

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (FRAC-01: 84mm Fraction Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Theoretical Probability: P(event) = Favorable Outcomes ÷ Total Outcomes (from 0 to 1, or 0% to 100%), and P(not E) = 1 - P(E).
  2. Textbook Counting & Permutations vs. Combinations: Fundamental Counting Principle multiplies choices; Permutations nPr (order matters) vs. Combinations nCr (order doesn't matter).
  3. Test Strategy: Ask 'Does order matter?' — awarding 1st/2nd/3rd medals is a Permutation (nPr); choosing a 3-person committee is a Combination (nCr = nPr ÷ r!)!

docs.title: Authentic Textbook Worked Examples (Learn & Solve by Hand First in 1 Way +10 pts or 2 Ways +20 pts)
docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.101) A 10-sector spinner has 4 Blue, 3 Gold, and 3 Red sectors. Find P(Blue) as a fraction, decimal, and percent, and find how many ways 5 trophies can be arranged in a row (5!). WAY 1: Theoretical Probability Ratio P(E) = Favorable / Total: Spinner (4 Blue, 3 Gold, 3 Red = 10 sectors): P(Blue) = 4/10 = 2/5 = 40%. P(not Blue) = (3 + 3)/10 = 6/10 = 3/5 = 60%. WAY 2: Complement Rule P(not E) = 1 - P(E): Subtract P(Blue) from 1 whole (100%): P(not Blue) = 1 - 2/5 = 3/5 (or 100% - 40% = 60%).WAY 3: Fundamental Counting Principle (5 Trophies in a Row): Multiply choices for each spot: 5 choices for 1st × 4 for 2nd × 3 for 3rd × 2 for 4th × 1 for 5th = 120 arrangements. P(Blue) = 2/5 = 0.4 = 40%; 5! = 120 ways Practice B (p.102) Compare awarding 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place ribbons to 10 runners (order matters) with choosing a 3-person relay crew from 10 runners (order does not matter). WAY 1: Fundamental Counting Principle (Order Matters): For 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place ribbons, multiply choices: 10 choices for 1st × 9 for 2nd × 8 for 3rd = 720 ordered ways.Ordered Podium (Permutation): 10 × 9 × 8 = 720 ways. WAY 2: Divide Out Duplicate Orders When Order Does Not Matter: Any 3 chosen runners can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 orders. Divide 720 ordered ways by 6: 720 ÷ 6 = 120 relay crews.Unordered Trio (Combination): Divide 720 by 3! = 6 rearrangements -> 720 ÷ 6 = 120 trios. 720 ordered podiums; 120 unordered 3-runner crews

docs.title: Practice B (p. 102): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
When Maya's coach needed to pick 3 players from 7 teammates, Maya couldn't understand why picking a 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place batting order had 210 possibilities while picking a 3-person cleanup crew from the same 7 kids had only 35! She wrote out three players—Ali, Ben, and Cam—and suddenly saw why: in a batting order, Ali-Ben-Cam and Ben-Ali-Cam are different lineups (6 different orders for the same 3 kids!), whereas on a cleanup crew, Ali, Ben, and Cam are the exact same group of 3 people no matter whose name is called first. Dividing 210 by those 6 duplicate orders (3! = 6) explained why combinations (35) are six times smaller than permutations (210).

# Modeling Real Life Application Prompt Tutor Setup & SC-6 Check Final Answer B1 20-Sided Die: You roll a fair 20-sided die numbered 1 to 20. What is the theoretical probability of rolling a multiple of 5? Write your answer as a simplified fraction, a decimal, and a percent. Setup: Simp(4/20) | SC-6: [.] 4 [.] 20 [g][SIMP] [FDISP] 4/20 = 1/5 = 0.20 = 20% B2 Complementary Event: The weather forecast says there is a 35% chance of rain tomorrow. What is the probability that it does not rain tomorrow? Setup: 100 - 35 | SC-6: 100 [ENTER] 35 [-] 65% (13/20 = 0.65) B3 Kea Parrot Token Jar: Researchers show a kea parrot a jar containing 6 black (reward) tokens, 5 green tokens, and 4 white tokens. What is P(black) and what is P(not white) in simplest form? Setup: Simp(6/15) | SC-6: [.] 6 [.] 15 [g][SIMP] P(black) = 2/5; P(not white) = 11/15 B4 Custom Skateboard Choices: A skate shop offers 5 deck designs, 4 truck colors, and 6 wheel sets. In how many different orders can all 5 songs be played without repeating? Setup: 5! | SC-6: 5 [x!] 5! = 120 orders B6 Batting Order: A softball coach chooses 3 players from a group of 7 to bat 1st, 2nd, and 3rd. How many different 3-batter orders are possible? docs.title: RPN Elementary Power Guide
4-Stack XYZT, Skip-Counting [REP], LastX Verification & Integer Division
docs.text:
RPN PEDAGOGY // ELEMENTARY FOUNDATIONS (GRADES K–6) ● DEFAULT 4-STACK XYZT • CLASSROOM PROVEN 📖 Master Guide 📗 SC-6 Companion Workbook (253 Problems) 📘 SC-32 Companion Casebook (339 Problems) 🚀 Big Ideas 45-Day Catch-Up (SC-6) ⚡ RPN Power Guide 📝 120 Station Worksheets 🎯 Standards Matrix 🧑‍🏫 Teacher Guide 🏆 UIL Competition

Traditional elementary calculators force children into an algebraic syntax that creates unnecessary cognitive barriers: students struggle with hidden memory registers (M+), syntax errors caused by nested parentheses, and decimal answers when they are learning division with remainders.

In the latest system revisions, the StackCalc SC-6 Elementary Calculator standardizes on a default 4-stack XYZT live operational display for general arithmetic, while providing a toggleable 2-stack mode (\(Y, X\)) for early elementary instruction when focusing on two-row Place Value trays (PLACE-01). This guide explains the mathematical and pedagogical rationale behind this architecture, and provides classroom-ready teaching modules for core RPN elementary capabilities:

  1. The 4-Stack XYZT Visual Model & 2-Stack Manipulative Modes: Visual permanence for multi-step arithmetic, with focused 2-line views for paired entry.
  2. Integer Division with Remainders ([÷R]): Simultaneous quotient (\(X\)) and remainder (\(Y\)) display.
  3. Instant Inverse Verification ([LASTX]): Concrete student self-checking without teacher intervention.
  4. Rhythmic Skip-Counting ([REP]): Auditory and tactile reinforcement of multiplication facts.

docs.title: 1. Why 4-Stack XYZT is the Default in Elementary Math
docs.text:
In early prototype testing, a 2-line display was considered for simplicity. However, empirical classroom trials across Grades 3–6 revealed that a 4-level XYZT stack is dramatically more intuitive for young learners for three fundamental reasons:

+-------------------------------------------------------+
|  HIGH-CONTRAST MONOCHROME LCD (TERMINUS PIXEL FONT)   |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
|  T:        12.0000   <-- Top / Overflow Memory Level  |
|  Z:        35.0000   <-- Suspended Subtotal Level     |
|  Y:         3.0000   <-- Active Remainder / Operand 1 |
|  X:         5.0000   <-- Active Input / Quotient      |
+-------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 1.1 Cognitive Load & Visual Permanence
docs.text:
On a standard calculator, intermediate calculations vanish. In a problem like: $\((4 \times 8) + (15 \div 3)\)$ a student evaluating \(4 \times 8 = 32\) must either write \(32\) down on scratch paper, memorize it in short-term memory, or master obscure memory keys (STO, RCL, M+).

On the SC-6, evaluating 4 [ENTER] 8 [×] leaves 32 sitting visibly in the stack. When the student types 15 [ENTER] 3 [÷], 32 gently slides up to Register \(Y\), while 5 appears in Register \(X\). Both numbers remain simultaneously visible on the screen. Pressing [+] (full sequence: 4 [ENTER] 8 [×] 15 [ENTER] 3 [÷] [+]) combines them to yield 37. Zero writing, zero memory keys, zero working memory fatigue.

docs.title: 1.2 Zero Parentheses Syntax Errors
docs.text:
Elementary students have not mastered algebraic formal syntax. On standard in-fix calculators, entering: $\(2 + 3 \times 4\)$ yields either 20 (on cheap non-precedence calculators) or 14 (on algebraic hierarchy machines), creating profound confusion about what the machine is actually doing. In RPN, there is strictly no ambiguity and no parentheses keys: * If you mean add first: 2 [ENTER] 3 [+] 4 [×] = 20 * If you mean multiply first: 3 [ENTER] 4 [×] 2 [+] = 14

The student controls the order of operations explicitly, mirroring the natural mental decomposition taught in Singapore Math and Bridges.

docs.title: 1.3 Uniformity Across the K–12 Continuum
docs.text: By standardizing on a 4-stack XYZT display from Grade 1, students develop an intuitive spatial mental model of the stack that carries forward seamlessly to the flagship SC-32 Scientific Calculator in middle school, high school AP Physics, and collegiate engineering. There is zero unlearning.

docs.title: 1.4 Two-Stack Mode (\(Y, X\)) & Stack Depth Configuration Rubric
docs.text: While the 4-stack XYZT architecture is the default for general multi-step arithmetic, early elementary teachers can focus young learners on just the two active registers (Waiting Shelf Y and Workbench X): * Two-Row Place Value & Part-Whole Modeling (PLACE-01): On the Place Value Studio 6×2 tray, Row 1 (upper row) maps directly to Register \(Y\) and Row 0 (lower row) maps to Register \(X\). Focusing on \(Y\) and \(X\) creates an exact 1:1 spatial correspondence between the physical rows on the tray and the screen without the distraction of upper registers (\(Z, T\)). * Returning to Standard 4-Stack Number Mode: Pressing [NUM] (Whole Number Mode key at Row 3 Col 4) or [FDISP] immediately restores the default 4-stack XYZT operational display. * Manual Stack Depth Switching ([FLAGS] Key Rubric): Kindergarten and early Grade 1 teachers who want to keep cognitive load minimal across all arithmetic operations can manually switch the SC-6 into 2-stack mode at any time using the hardware configuration rubric: 1. Press [g] [FLAGS] to open the system configuration matrix. 2. Press digit [5] (5:DEP) to cycle stack depth between 4-LV (4-level XYZT) and 2-LV (2-level \(Y, X\)). 3. Press [C] (or [g] [FLAGS]) to dismiss the flags matrix and resume calculations with the chosen stack depth. (In the desktop and companion apps, clicking the LCD stack depth badge or opening the Flags menu provides the same direct toggle.)

docs.title: 2. Curricular Module 1: Integer Division with Remainders ([÷R])
docs.text: // STANDARDS ALIGNMENT CCSS-M: 4.OA.A.3, 4.NBT.B.6, 5.NBT.B.6 • TEKS: 4.4E, 4.4F, 5.3C • Singapore: Primary 3A Ch 3, Primary 4A Ch 2

docs.title: The Elementary Division Dilemma
docs.text:
In Grades 3 through 5, division is introduced as fair sharing with leftovers (quotient and remainder): $\(23 \div 4 = 5 \text{ R } 3\)$ When an elementary student enters \(23 \div 4\) on a standard smartphone or cheap school calculator, the screen displays: $\(5.75\)$ For a 9-year-old who has not yet learned decimal place value or fraction-to-decimal conversion, \(5.75\) is actively counter-productive. It fails to answer: * "How many full boxes of 4 can we pack?" (5 boxes) * "How many items are left over?" (3 items, not 0.75 items!)

Because of this, teachers routinely ban calculators during division units.

docs.title: The SC-6 Solution: The [÷R] Integer Division Key
docs.text:
The SC-6 provides a dedicated Integer Division with Remainder operator located at [g] [÷R] (legend ÷R):

        DIVIDEND                 DIVISOR                     OPERATION
   [2] [3] [ENTER]                 [4]                   [g] [÷R]  (÷R)
          |                         |                          |
          v                         v                          v
+-----------------+       +-----------------+        +-----------------+
| T:         0    |       | T:         0    |        | T:         0    |
| Z:         0    |       | Z:         0    |        | Z:         0    |
| Y:        23    |       | Y:        23    |        | Y:         3  <-- REMAINDER
| X:        23    |       | X:         4    |        | X:         5  <-- QUOTIENT
+-----------------+       +-----------------+        +-----------------+

docs.title: Keystroke Protocol & Display State
docs.text:
1. Enter Dividend: Type 23, press [ENTER].
  2. Enter Divisor: Type 4.
  3. Execute Integer Division: Press [g] [÷R] (full sequence: 23 [ENTER] 4 [g] [÷R]).
  4. Immediate Result:
  5. Register X displays the Quotient (5).
  6. Register Y displays the Remainder (3).
  7. Both values are visible at the same moment on the 4-line display!

docs.title: Swapping Quotient and Remainder ([x⇄y])
docs.text: If a follow-up calculation requires the remainder, the student does not need to retype it. Simply press [x⇄y] (the primary swap key): * X becomes 3 (Remainder ready for computation) * Y becomes 5 (Quotient preserved in stack)

docs.title: Classroom Investigation: Spool Slicing & Filament Leftovers
docs.text:
Scenario: A 5th-grade maker lab has a 1,000-gram spool of Sunlu Midnight Navy PLA filament. Each 3D-printed calculator housing requires exactly 82 grams. 1. How many complete calculator housings can the class 3D print? 2. How many grams of filament remain on the spool for calibration test chips?

  • Verified Keystroke Sequence: 1000 [ENTER] 82 [g] [÷R]
  • Verified Quotient (\(X\)): 12 complete calculator chassis printed!
  • Verified Remainder (\(Y\)): 16 grams of scrap / test filament remaining (T: 0 | Z: 0 | Y: 16 | X: 12).

docs.title: 3. Curricular Module 2: Instant Inverse Verification with [LASTX]
docs.text: // STANDARDS FOR MATHEMATICAL PRACTICE CCSS.MATH.PRACTICE.MP1: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them. CCSS.MATH.PRACTICE.MP3: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others. CCSS.MATH.PRACTICE.MP6: Attend to precision.

docs.title: The Misconception: "I Got an Answer, So I'm Done"
docs.text:
A persistent struggle in elementary math is teaching students to check their work using inverse operations: $\(\text{If } A + B = C \implies C - B = A\)$ $\(\text{If } A \times B = C \implies C \div B = A\)$

On standard calculators, as soon as the user presses =, the input operands vanish into the ether. Checking the answer requires re-entering the entire problem from scratch, which students find tedious and resist doing.

docs.title: The SC-6 Solution: The [LASTX] Key
docs.text:
The SC-6 maintains a hardware memory register called LASTX. Whenever an arithmetic operation (+, -, ×, ÷, ÷R, MOD) is executed, the calculator automatically copies the value that was in Register \(X\) right before the calculation into LASTX.

Pressing [f] [LASTX] pushes that saved operand back into Register \(X\), lifting the answer into Register \(Y\)!

docs.title: Recipe 1: Self-Checking Multi-Digit Addition
docs.text:
Student Task: Solve \(487 + 265\) and verify using inverse subtraction (487 [ENTER] 265 [+] [f] [LASTX] [-] → 487).

PHASE 1: SOLVE THE ADDITION
1. [4] [8] [7] [ENTER]    --> Y: 487 | X: 487
2. [2] [6] [5]            --> Y: 487 | X: 265
3. [+]                    --> X: 752  (Sum)
   [Calculator quietly stores 265 in LASTX]

PHASE 2: VERIFY WITH INVERSE SUBTRACTION (ONE KEYSTROKE!)
4. [f] [LASTX]            --> Y: 752 | X: 265  (Original addend retrieved!)
5. [-]                    --> X: 487  (Original starting number restored!)

Teacher Facilitation Prompt: "Did your screen return to 487? If yes, your addition is mathematically guaranteed to be correct. You proved it yourself without asking the teacher!"

docs.title: Recipe 2: The Complete Division Proof (\(Q \times D + R = \text{Dividend}\))
docs.text:
Student Task: Divide \(79 \div 8\) using [g] [÷R], then prove the result using [f] [LASTX] (79 [ENTER] 8 [g] [÷R] [f] [LASTX] [×] [+] → 79).

PHASE 1: INTEGER DIVISION
1. [7] [9] [ENTER] [8] [g] [÷R]
   SCREEN READOUT:
   Y: 7  (Remainder R)
   X: 9  (Quotient Q)
   [LASTX automatically holds the Divisor: 8]

PHASE 2: THE 3-KEYSTROKE PROOF
2. [f] [LASTX]            --> Z: 7 (R) | Y: 9 (Q) | X: 8 (Divisor D)
3. [×]                    --> Y: 7 (R) | X: 72 (Q × D)
4. [+]                    --> X: 79  (Original Dividend restored!)

This 3-keystroke verification sequence ([f] [LASTX] → [×] → [+]) concretizes the Division Algorithm identity: $\(\text{Dividend} = (\text{Quotient} \times \text{Divisor}) + \text{Remainder}\)$ Students actively experience how multiplication and addition undo division and subtraction.

docs.title: Recipe 3: Recovering from a Keystroke Slip
docs.text:
Elementary students frequently press the wrong operator by mistake (e.g., hitting [-] instead of [+]). On traditional calculators, they must press CLEAR and start over. On the SC-6 (150 [ENTER] 25 [-] [f] [LASTX] [+] [f] [LASTX] [+] → 175):

  • Problem: Student wants \(150 + 25\).
  • Mistake: They enter 150 [ENTER] 25 [-] and get 125.
  • Recovery:
  • Press [f] [LASTX] → 25 returns to \(X\), 125 lifts to \(Y\).
  • Press [+] → 150 (Starting base restored!).
  • Press [f] [LASTX] → 25 returns to \(X\), 150 lifts to \(Y\).
  • Press [+] → 175 (Correct sum reached without re-typing 150 or 25!).

docs.title: 4. Curricular Module 3: Rhythmic Skip-Counting with [REP]
docs.text: // STANDARDS ALIGNMENT CCSS-M: 2.OA.C.4, 3.OA.A.1, 3.OA.A.7 • Bridges: Grade 2 Unit 1, Grade 3 Unit 2 • Singapore: Primary 2A Ch 4, Primary 3A Ch 3

docs.title: Why Kinesthetic Rhythm Matters
docs.text:
Multiplication is fundamentally equal groups of items. Before children can memorize \(7 \times 6 = 42\), they must feel and hear the cadence of the sequence: $\(7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42\)$

The SC-6 features a dedicated Replication Key [REP] located at [g] [REP]. Pressing [g] [REP] populates every level of the 4-level stack with the active number: $\(T = K, \quad Z = K, \quad Y = K, \quad X = K\)$

Because an RPN 4-stack duplicates the \(T\) register when the stack drops during dyadic addition, pressing [+] repeatedly adds the constant indefinitely!

                     HOW [REP] CREATES AN INFINITE FACT LADDER

1. [7] [g] [REP]           2. PRESS [+]              3. PRESS [+] AGAIN
+---------------------+    +---------------------+    +---------------------+
| T:         7        |    | T:         7        |    | T:         7        |
| Z:         7        |    | Z:         7        |    | Z:         7        |
| Y:         7        |    | Y:         7        |    | Y:         7        |
| X:         7        |    | X:        14  (7×2) |    | X:        21  (7×3) |
+---------------------+    +---------------------+    +---------------------+
                                 (T duplicates on drop!)    (T duplicates on drop!)

docs.title: Classroom Activity: The Rhythm of Multiples
docs.text:
1. Teacher Prompt: "Let's build the 6-times multiplication ladder up to 60."
  2. Setup: Student types 6 [g] [REP]. All 4 stack registers are now primed with 6.
  3. Execution: The student chants aloud with each tactile snap:
  4. Press [+] → "6 times 2 is 12!" (Screen: 12)
  5. Press [+] → "6 times 3 is 18!" (Screen: 18)
  6. Press [+] → "6 times 4 is 24!" (Screen: 24)
  7. Press [+] → "6 times 5 is 30!" (Screen: 30)
  8. Press [+] → "6 times 6 is 36!" (Screen: 36)
  9. Press [+] → "6 times 7 is 42!" (Screen: 42)
  10. Press [+] → "6 times 8 is 48!" (Screen: 48)
  11. Press [+] → "6 times 9 is 54!" (Screen: 54)
  12. Press [+] → "6 times 10 is 60!" (Screen: 60)

The 400-gram snap-dome keys deliver an audible acoustic "click" and physical tactile feedback that anchors the auditory chant to muscle memory.

docs.title: Advanced Skip-Counting Explorations
Exploration A: Backwards Countdown Ladders (Subtracting Constantly)
docs.text: Task: Start at 100, skip-count backwards by 8. 1. Enter starting point: 100 [ENTER]. 2. Prime the subtrahend: 8 [g] [REP]. 3. Press [-] repeatedly: * Press [-] → 92 * Press [-] → 84 * Press [-] → 76 * Press [-] → 68 ... down to 4 (the remainder of \(100 \div 8\)!).

docs.title: Exploration B: Geometric Exponential Doubling (Powers of 2)
docs.text: Task: Discover exponential growth (doubling lily pads on a pond). 1. Prime the base: 2 [g] [REP]. 2. Press [×] repeatedly: * Press [×] → 4 (\(2^2\)) * Press [×] → 8 (\(2^3\)) * Press [×] → 16 (\(2^4\)) * Press [×] → 32 (\(2^5\)) * Press [×] → 64 (\(2^6\)) * Press [×] → 128 (\(2^7\)) ... up to 1024 (\(2^{10}\))!

docs.title: 5. Curricular Module 4: Order of Operations without Parentheses
docs.text: // STANDARDS ALIGNMENT CCSS-M: 5.OA.A.1, 6.EE.A.2 • Big Ideas Math: Grade 5 Ch 1, Grade 6 Ch 3

docs.title: Multi-Term Word Problem Example
docs.text:
Scenario: A school STEM club buys: * 3 microcontrollers at $4.50 each * 2 battery holders at $1.25 each * 4 LED packs at $0.75 each

What is the total cost of the order? $\(\text{Total} = (3 \times 4.50) + (2 \times 1.25) + (4 \times 0.75)\)$

docs.title: How Infix vs. SC-6 4-Stack Handles the Problem (3 [ENTER] 4.5 [×] 2 [ENTER] 1.25 [×] [+] 4 [ENTER] 0.75 [×] [+] → 19)
docs.text:
Step Traditional Infix Calculator SC-6 4-Stack XYZT (RPN) Stack Registers (\(T, Z, Y, X\)) 1 Press ( 3 × 4.50 ) + (Must remember parentheses!) 3 [ENTER] 4.5 [×] \(X: 13.50\) 2 Press ( 2 × 1.25 ) + (Hope parentheses don't nest wrong!) 2 [ENTER] 1.25 [×] \(Y: 13.50, \quad X: 2.50\) 3 Press ( 4 × 0.75 ) = [+] \(X: 16.00\) (Running total!) 4 Hope order-of-operations evaluated correctly 4 [ENTER] 0.75 [×] \(Y: 16.00, \quad X: 3.00\) 5 — [+] \(X: 19\) (Final total verified!)

The Pedagogical Difference: On the SC-6, students never type a parenthesis. Every sub-calculation is evaluated immediately, and the intermediate products wait patiently on the screen. The child can pause at Step 2 and see both $13.50 and $2.50 resting on the screen.

docs.title: 5.5 Curricular Module 5: SC-6 Tutorial Mode (?) & Two-Method Verification
docs.text:
// TWO-METHOD VERIFICATION & WORKBOOK INTEGRATION Published Block Studios: PLACE-01, FRAC-01, PRIME-01 • Tutorial Keycap: [↰] [C] (Question Mark in a Circle ?)

Many upper-elementary and middle-school learners resist solving the same problem in multiple ways because traditional worksheets punish extra strategies with twice the handwriting. The 114-Page Big Ideas Math Daily Supplement turns multi-method verification into a structured two-step habit:

  • 1st Way (+10 pts): Solve Question \(N\) using your primary method (Big Ideas textbook method, physical block kit—PLACE-01, FRAC-01, or PRIME-01—or SC-6 RPN) and record +10 pts in the worksheet scoring box.
  • 2nd Way (+20 pts Double Points): Verify the exact same question using a second method (checking your block/paper work on the SC-6 stack or in SC-6 Tutorial Mode [↰] [C]) to earn +20 pts.

docs.title: 7. Station Challenge Cards (Reproducible Classroom Prompts)
Challenge Card 1: The Cookie Bakery Box Packing (Grades 3–4)
docs.text: Prompt: A baker bakes 58 chocolate chip cookies. Each gift box holds 6 cookies. 1. Use [g] [÷R] on your SC-6 to find how many full gift boxes she can pack. 2. How many cookies are left over for the baker to eat? 3. Press [f] [LASTX] [×] [+] to prove your answer matches 58! Expected Keystrokes: 58 [ENTER] 6 [g] [÷R] ==> X: 9 boxes, Y: 4 leftover cookies. Proof: 58 [ENTER] 6 [g] [÷R] [f] [LASTX] [×] [+] ==> 58 cookies.

docs.title: Challenge Card 2: The Multiplication Table 7s Race (Grades 2–3)
docs.text: Prompt: Load 7 into your SC-6 using [g] [REP]. 1. Press [+] four times. What multiple of 7 is on the screen? (\(7 \times 5 = 35\)) 2. Press [+] three more times. What is \(7 \times 8\)? (\(56\)) 3. Can you reach 70 without making an error? Expected Keystrokes: 7 [g] [REP] [+] [+] [+] [+] ==> 35. [+] [+] [+] ==> 56.

docs.title: Challenge Card 3: The Detective Proof Station (Grades 4–5)
docs.text: Prompt: A student calculated \(345 + 189 = 534\). 1. Enter 345 [ENTER] 189 [+] on your SC-6. 2. Use [f] [LASTX] to recall the second addend. 3. Press [-] to perform the inverse operation (345 [ENTER] 189 [+] [f] [LASTX] [-]). Did you get 345? 4. Write an explanation: Why does LASTX guarantee the answer is correct?

docs.title: Summary: Empowering Young Mathematicians
docs.text: The transition to a default 4-stack XYZT display in the SC-6 transforms the calculator from a passive answer generator into an active, transparent laboratory instrument. With [÷R], [LASTX], and [REP], young students explore the fundamental structures of arithmetic—quotients, remainders, inverses, and multiples—with tactile certainty and joy.

docs.title: Executive Warm-Up Problems (25 Cross-Disciplinary RPN Table Exercises)
docs.text: These 25 worked scientific and engineering warm-up problems complement the 5 signature showcase problems in the Preface of Thinking in the Stack, providing complete 4-register (\(T, Z, Y, X\)) stack trace tables across mechanics, thermodynamics, optics, acoustics, and electrochemistry.

docs.title: Warm-Up Problem 0.1: Hypotenuse and Vector Magnitude
docs.text:
When a bridge pin joint experiences simultaneous horizontal shear \(F_x = 24.5\text{ kN}\) and vertical bearing load \(F_y = 18.2\text{ kN}\), structural sizing requires the resultant force magnitude \(F_R\). Rather than opening an outer square-root bracket and nesting squared terms inside parentheses as on an infix calculator, we work from the inside out: squaring \(F_x\) in place, keying \(F_y\) (which automatically lifts \(F_x^2\) into Register \(Y\)) and squaring it, adding the two squares in a single stroke, and extracting the square root:

\[F_R = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} = \sqrt{24.5^2 + 18.2^2} \quad \text{[kN]}\]

Keystroke Sequence: 24.5 [↰] [x²] 18.2 [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] \(\to \mathbf{30.520321099\text{ kN}}\).

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 24.5 \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(24.5000\) Load \(F_x\) [↰] [x²] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(600.2500\) Square \(F_x\) in \(X\) 18.2 [↰] [x²] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(600.2500\) \(331.2400\) Lift \(600.25\) to \(Y\) and square \(F_y\) [+] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(931.4900\) Sum of squares: \(600.25 + 331.24\) [√x] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(30.5203\) Resultant force \(F_R \approx 30.5203\text{ kN}\)

docs.title: Warm-Up Problem 0.2: Kinetic Energy Calculation
docs.text:
When sizing automotive braking rotors, engineers must determine the translational kinetic energy stored in a vehicle of mass \(m = 1450\text{ kg}\) cruising at highway velocity \(v = 28\text{ m/s}\) (\(100.8\text{ km/h}\)). Pushing mass \(m\) into Register \(Y\) first allows you to square velocity \(v\) in place in Register \(X\) via [↰] [x²], multiply by mass, and halve the product in a linear left-to-right flow:

\[E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \quad (m = 1450\text{ kg},\; v = 28\text{ m/s})\]

Keystrokes: 1450 [ENTER] 28 [↰] [x²] [×] 2 [÷] \(\to \mathbf{568400\text{ J}} = 568.4\text{ kJ}\).

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 1450 [ENTER] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(1450.0000\) \(1450.0000\) Push vehicle mass \(m\) 28 [↰] [x²] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(1450.0000\) \(784.0000\) Velocity squared \(v^2\) in \(X\) [×] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(1136800.00\) Product \(m v^2\) 2 [÷] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(568400.00\) Divide by 2: \(568.4\text{ kJ}\)

docs.title: Warm-Up Problem 0.3: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
docs.text:
Astrodynamics calculations span 35 orders of magnitude, where a single misplaced parenthesis in scientific notation corrupts the exponent by \(10^{16}\). To compute the gravitational attraction between Earth (\(M_E = 5.972 \times 10^{24}\text{ kg}\)) and the Moon (\(M_M = 7.342 \times 10^{22}\text{ kg}\)) at mean orbital separation \(r = 3.844 \times 10^8\text{ m}\), we use the dedicated exponent key [E] to chain the numerator \(G M_E M_M\) in Register \(Y\), square \(r\) in place in Register \(X\), and divide:

\[F = G \frac{M_E M_M}{r^2} \quad (G = 6.6743 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2)\]

Keystrokes: 6.6743 [E] 11 [+/-] [ENTER] 5.972 [E] 24 [×] 7.342 [E] 22 [×] 3.844 [E] 8 [↰] [x²] [÷] \(\to \mathbf{1.980492E20\text{ N}}\).

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 6.6743 [E] 11 [+/-] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(6.6743 \times 10^{-11}\) Universal gravitational constant \(G\) [ENTER] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(6.6743 \times 10^{-11}\) \(6.6743 \times 10^{-11}\) Stack lift: pushes \(G\) into \(Y\) 5.972 [E] 24 \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(6.6743 \times 10^{-11}\) \(5.9720 \times 10^{24}\) Earth mass \(M_E\) in \(X\) [×] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(3.9859 \times 10^{14}\) Gravitational parameter \(\mu_E = G M_E\) 7.342 [E] 22 \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(3.9859 \times 10^{14}\) \(7.3420 \times 10^{22}\) Moon mass \(M_M\) in \(X\) [×] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(2.9264 \times 10^{37}\) Force numerator \(G M_E M_M\) 3.844 [E] 8 \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(2.9264 \times 10^{37}\) \(3.8440 \times 10^{8}\) Lunar orbital distance \(r\) [↰] [x²] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(2.9264 \times 10^{37}\) \(1.4776 \times 10^{17}\) Square orbital radius \(r^2\) in \(X\) [÷] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(1.9805 \times 10^{20}\) Mutual orbital attraction force in Newtons

docs.title: Warm-Up Problem 0.4: Ideal Gas Law Pressure
docs.text:
A high-pressure welding cylinder with internal volume \(V = 0.045\text{ m}^3\) contains \(n = 3.5\text{ moles}\) of inert Argon gas heated to \(T = 315\text{ K}\). Using the Ideal Gas Law, we chain the thermal energy product \(n R T\) sequentially in Register \(X\) before dividing by cylinder volume \(V\):

\[P = \frac{n R T}{V} \quad (R = 8.31446\text{ J/mol}\cdot\text{K})\]

Keystrokes: 3.5 [ENTER] 8.31446 [×] 315 [×] 0.045 [÷] \(\to \mathbf{203704.27\text{ Pa}} \approx 203.70\text{ kPa}\).

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 3.5 [ENTER] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(3.5000\) \(3.5000\) Molar substance quantity \(n\) in \(Y\) 8.31446 [×] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(29.1006\) Molar gas scale factor \(n R\) 315 [×] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(9166.6922\) Thermal kinetic product \(n R T\) 0.045 [÷] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(203704.27\) Static pressure \(P\) in Pascals (\(203.70\text{ kPa}\))

docs.title: Warm-Up Problem 0.5: Quadratic Discriminant & Root Characterization
docs.text:
Before extracting the roots of the quadratic equation \(3.2 x^2 + 8.5 x - 4.1 = 0\), evaluating the discriminant \(\Delta = b^2 - 4ac\) immediately reveals whether the roots are real or complex conjugates. By squaring \(b = 8.5\) first, the RPN stack holds \(b^2 = 72.25\) safely in Register \(Z\) and then \(Y\) while we form the signed product \(4(3.2)(-4.1) = -52.48\) in Register \(X\):

\[\Delta = b^2 - 4ac = (8.5)^2 - 4(3.2)(-4.1)\]

Keystrokes: 8.5 [↰] [x²] 4 [ENTER] 3.2 [×] 4.1 [+/-] [×] [-] \(\rightarrow\) 124.73

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 8.5 [↰] [x²] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(72.2500\) \(b^2 = 8.5^2 = 72.25\) 4 [ENTER] \(0.0000\) \(72.2500\) \(4.0000\) \(4.0000\) Load coefficient factor 4 3.2 [×] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(72.2500\) \(12.8000\) Form \(4a = 4 \times 3.2 = 12.8\) 4.1 [+/-] \(0.0000\) \(72.2500\) \(12.8000\) \(-4.1000\) Constant \(c = -4.1\) loaded to \(X\) [×] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(72.2500\) \(-52.4800\) Form \(4ac = 12.8 \times (-4.1)\) [-] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(124.7300\) \(\Delta = 72.25 - (-52.48) = 124.73\)

Because 8.5 [↰] [x²] (\(\mathbf{72.25}\)) sits in Register \(Y\) while 4 [ENTER] 3.2 [×] (\(\mathbf{12.8}\)) is multiplied by \(c = -4.1\) in Register \(X\), a single subtraction confirms \(\Delta = 124.73 > 0\) (two distinct real roots).

docs.title: Warm-Up Problem 0.6: Compound Interest & Exponential Growth
docs.text:
An endowment principal of \(P = \$15,000\) is invested at an annual nominal rate \(r = 6.5\%\) compounded monthly (\(n = 12\)) over \(t = 8\text{ years}\) (\(96\text{ months}\)). Instead of keying Principal first and opening nested parentheses, we evaluate the innermost periodic rate \(r/12\) first, add \(1\), raise the base in place to the \(96\text{th}\) power via [yˣ], and scale by \(15,000\):

\[A = P \left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} = 15000 \left(1 + \frac{0.065}{12}\right)^{96}\]

docs.text:
Escape velocity from Mars (\(M = 6.4171 \times 10^{23}\text{ kg}\), \(R = 3.3895 \times 10^6\text{ m}\)):

\[v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}} \quad (G = 6.6743 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2)\]

Keystrokes: 2 [ENTER] 6.6743 [E] 11 [+/-] [×] 6.4171 [E] 23 [×] 3.3895 [E] 6 [÷] [√x] \(\to \mathbf{5,027.122221\text{ m/s}} \approx 5.027\text{ km/s}\).

Multiply kinetic scaling by gravitational parameter \(2GM\), divide by planetary radius, and apply square root directly in place without parentheses (Munroe, 2014; HP, 1982).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 1.1: Transflective LCD Photometric Contrast Ratio
docs.text:
Unlike emissive OLED screens that wash out under bright ambient room lighting and drain tens of milliamperes, the SC-32's STN liquid-crystal display uses a rear transflective polarizer that reflects ambient light back through the liquid-crystal twist cell. A spot photometer measures luminance from an unactivated reflective background pixel (\(L_{\text{white}} = 142.0\text{ cd/m}^2\)) and an absorptive black segment (\(L_{\text{black}} = 9.35\text{ cd/m}^2\)): $\(C_R = \frac{L_{\text{white}}}{L_{\text{black}}}\)$

Keystrokes: 142 [ENTER] 9.35 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 15.1872 \(\approx 15.2:1\).

Dividing background reflectance (\(L_{\text{white}} = 142.0\text{ cd/m}^2\) in \(Y\)) by dark-state luminance (\(L_{\text{black}} = 9.35\text{ cd/m}^2\) in \(X\)) yields the photopic contrast ratio \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{15.1872})\)—exceeding ISO 9241-303 Class 1 legibility requirements without drawing a single microampere of backlight current.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 1.2: Low-Dropout Linear Regulator (LDO) Power Dissipation
docs.text:
During factory tethered diagnostics, an external bench supply feeds \(V_{\text{in}} = 5.80\text{ V}\) into the CMOS low-dropout linear regulator supplying \(V_{\text{out}} = 3.30\text{ V}\) at full dual-core active current \(I = 18.2\text{ mA}\). Because a linear pass transistor regulates by dropping excess voltage as Joule heat, its thermal dissipation is governed by the voltage headroom product: $\(P_{\text{diss}} = (V_{\text{in}} - V_{\text{out}}) \cdot I\)$

Keystrokes: 5.80 [ENTER] 3.30 [-] 0.0182 [×] 1000 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 45.5000\(\text{ mW}\).

Evaluating the pass-element voltage drop first (5.80 [ENTER] 3.30 [-]) places \(\Delta V = 2.50\text{ V}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.5000)\) with zero parentheses. Scaling by active load current and milliwatt normalization (0.0182 [×] 1000 [×]) yields package heat dissipation \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{45.5000}\text{ mW})\)—confirming that in a SOT-23-5 package (\(\theta_{JA} \approx 220^\circ\text{C/W}\)), junction temperature rises by less than \(10^\circ\text{C}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 1.3: Flash Sector Wear Endurance Under Extreme Daily Editing
docs.text:
Non-volatile NOR flash memory cells degrade via Fowler-Nordheim tunneling oxide stress after \(100,000\) program/erase cycles per sector. By alternating writes between two ping-pong sectors and committing state only on sleep transitions or explicit edits (\(45\text{ writes/day}\)), the SC-32's wear-leveling supervisor extends flash longevity to: $\(t_{\text{years}} = \frac{2 \times 100,000}{45 \times 365.25}\)$

Keystrokes: 200000 [ENTER] 45 [ENTER] 365.25 [×] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 12.1683\(\text{ years}\).

Loading the dual-sector endurance budget (\(200,000\text{ cycles}\)) and computing annual write demand (200000 [ENTER] 45 [ENTER] 365.25 [×]) leaves \(Y = 200,000\) poised above \(X = 16,436.25\text{ writes/yr}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 200000.0000, X: 16436.2500)\). A single [÷] stroke resolves the guaranteed sector lifetime \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{12.1682}\text{ years})\)—and rotating the ring across 16 sectors multiplies endurance beyond 97 years.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 1.4: Quiescent Sleep Power Consumption Over 18 Months
docs.text:
In deep retention sleep, the high-speed \(150\text{ MHz}\) PLL powers down and the system idles at \(I = 11.8\,\mu\text{A}\) on the \(V = 3.0\text{ V}\) lithium rail. Over an 18-month warehouse or desk-drawer storage interval (\(547.5\text{ days} = 13,140\text{ hours}\)), total chemical energy drawn from the cell in Joules is: $\(E = V \cdot I \cdot t\)$

Keystrokes: 3.0 [ENTER] 11.8 [E] 6 [+/-] [×] 13140 [×] 3600 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 1,674.5616\(\text{ Joules}\).

Multiplying cell potential by quiescent sleep current (3.0 [ENTER] 11.8 [E] 6 [+/-] [×]) establishes the continuous standby power floor of \(35.4\,\mu\text{W}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 3.5400 \times 10^{-5})\). Chaining storage hours and seconds (13140 [×] 3600 [×]) accumulates the 18-month energy budget \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{1674.5616}\text{ Joules})\)—consuming less than \(69\%\) of a single CR2032 cell's \(2,430\text{ J}\) (\(225\text{ mAh} \times 3.0\text{ V} \times 3600\text{ s/h}\)) reserve.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 1.5: Microcontroller Core Clock PLL Lock Phase Margin
docs.text:
When waking from deep sleep upon a keypress edge, Core 0's phase-locked loop (PLL) must lock onto the \(12\text{ MHz}\) quartz reference and ramp to \(150\text{ MHz}\) before user-perceptible latency (\(> 10\text{ ms}\)) occurs. With a critically damped second-order loop filter (\(\zeta = 0.707\)) and natural loop bandwidth \(\omega_n = 2.40 \times 10^6\text{ rad/s}\), the \(1\%\) phase-error settling time (\(e^{-\zeta \omega_n t_{\text{lock}}} = 0.01 \implies \zeta\omega_n t_{\text{lock}} \approx 4.6\)) is: $\(t_{\text{lock}} \approx \frac{4.6}{\zeta \omega_n}\)$

Keystrokes: 4.6 [ENTER] 0.707 [ENTER] 2.40 [E] 6 [×] [÷] 1 [E] 6 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 2.7109853843\(\,\mu\text{s}\).

Entering the four-decade settling constant (\(4.6\)) and dividing by the product \(\zeta\omega_n\) (4.6 [ENTER] 0.707 [ENTER] 2.40 [E] 6 [×] [÷]) yields \(t_{\text{lock}} = 2.7110 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.7110 \times 10^{-6})\). Scaling by \(10^6\) (1 [E] 6 [×]) confirms that the PLL locks in \(2.71\,\mu\text{s}\)—over a thousand times faster than human tactile perception.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 1.6: Keypad Matrix Phantom Key Sneak Current Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose a fast RPN operator rolls three fingers across keys at row-column coordinates \((R_1, C_1)\), \((R_1, C_2)\), and \((R_2, C_1)\). In a naive matrix lacking series diodes, those three closed switches form a conductive bridge that pulls row \(R_2\) low when column \(C_2\) is strobed, registering a false fourth "phantom" key at \((R_2, C_2)\) with sneak current (\(R_{\text{pu}} = 10\text{ k}\Omega\) to \(V_{\text{cc}} = 3.3\text{ V}\)): $\(I_{\text{sneak}} = \frac{V_{\text{cc}}}{R_{\text{pu}} + 3 R_{\text{contact}}} \approx \frac{3.3}{10000} = 0.33\text{ mA}\)$ Because the SC-32 places a discrete Schottky diode in series with all 43 switches, the third switch in that loop is reverse-biased and blocks sneak current completely (\(I_{\text{leak}} < 0.1\,\mu\text{A}\)), guaranteeing true \(N\)-key rollover.

Dividing supply rail voltage by row pull-up resistance (3.3 [ENTER] 10000 [÷]) resolves the unmitigated sneak current \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{3.3000 \times 10^{-4}}\text{ A} = 0.33\text{ mA})\) in Register \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 1.7: Ambient Light Sensor ADC Resolution and Lux Mapping
docs.text:
To calibrate display contrast under laboratory and outdoor lighting, a PIN photodiode generates \(I_{\text{photo}} = 0.25\,\mu\text{A}\) per \(100\text{ lux}\) through a \(R_f = 2.4\text{ M}\Omega\) transimpedance amplifier into a 12-bit successive-approximation ADC (\(2^{12} = 4096\text{ counts}\) across \(V_{\text{ref}} = 3.30\text{ V}\)): $\(V_{\text{out}} = I_{\text{photo}} \cdot R_f = \left(\frac{0.25 \times 10^{-6}\text{ A}}{100\text{ lux}}\right) \times 2.4 \times 10^6\,\Omega = 0.0060\text{ V/lux} = 6.0\text{ mV/lux}\)$ $\(V_{\text{LSB}} = \frac{3.30\text{ V}}{4096} \approx 0.80566\text{ mV}, \qquad \text{Resolution} = \frac{V_{\text{LSB}}}{0.0060\text{ V/lux}} \approx \mathbf{0.1343\text{ lux/count}}\)$

Evaluating the 12-bit quantization step (3.3 [ENTER] 4096 [÷]) places \(V_{\text{LSB}} = 8.0566 \times 10^{-4}\text{ V}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 8.0566 \times 10^{-4})\). Dividing directly by the transimpedance gain (0.006 [÷]) resolves photometric quantization resolution \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.1343}\text{ lux/count})\) without intermediate rounding.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 1.8: Chassis Thermal Equilibrium Temperature Rise
docs.text:
Under sustained \(150\text{ MHz}\) dual-core numerical quadrature, the microcontroller and regulator dissipate \(P = 60.0\text{ mW} = 0.060\text{ W}\). Across a total enclosure surface area \(A = 0.024\text{ m}^2\) with natural still-air convection coefficient \(h_c = 6.5\text{ W/m}^2\text{K}\), Newton's law of cooling determines the steady-state surface temperature rise above ambient: $\(\Delta T = \frac{P}{h_c \cdot A}\)$

Keystrokes: 0.060 [ENTER] 6.5 [ENTER] 0.024 [×] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 0.3846\(\text{ K} \approx 0.38^\circ\text{C}\).

Loading thermal dissipation (\(0.060\text{ W}\)) and forming the convective conductance product \(h_c A\) (0.060 [ENTER] 6.5 [ENTER] 0.024 [×]) leaves \(Y = 0.0600\text{ W}\) and \(X = 0.1560\text{ W/K}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0600, X: 0.1560)\). Pressing [÷] resolves the equilibrium temperature rise \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.3846}\text{ K} \approx 0.38^\circ\text{C})\)—confirming that the SC-32 operates isothermally in the hand, immune to thermal drift or clock throttling.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.1: Right Triangle Polar Resolution
docs.text:
In geodetic surveying, converting orthogonal Cartesian offsets—eastward departure \(x = 42.5\text{ m}\) and northward latitude \(y = 68.2\text{ m}\)—into radial sightline distance \(r\) and bearing angle \(\theta\) is a daily field operation. Because the SC-32 maps 2D Cartesian space directly onto the register pair \((Y: y,\; X: x)\), polar conversion requires neither inverse trigonometric menus nor manual squaring:

Keystrokes: 68.2 [ENTER] 42.5 [↰] [▸θ,r] \(\rightarrow\) 80.3685.

Loading northward latitude into Register \(Y\) (68.2 [ENTER], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 68.2000, X: 68.2000\)) and eastward departure into Register \(X\) (42.5, \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 68.2000, X: 42.5000\)) aligns the coordinate vector on the stack. Pressing [↰] [▸θ,r] executes a simultaneous two-register hardware rotation: - Register \(X\) receives the Euclidean hypotenuse \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \mathbf{80.3685\text{ m}}\). - Register \(Y\) receives the four-quadrant angle \(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x) = \mathbf{58.0772^\circ}\). Tapping [x⇄y] swaps the registers to inspect \(\theta = \mathbf{58.0772^\circ}\) in Register \(X\) while retaining \(r = \mathbf{80.3685\text{ m}}\) in Register \(Y\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.2: 3D Vector Norm without Variable Registers
docs.text:
A structural tie-back anchor resists a spatial tension vector \(\vec{T} = (14.2, -8.7, 21.5\text{ kN})\) across three orthogonal axes. Computing the 3D Euclidean norm requires accumulating three squared components under a single radical:

\[|\vec{T}| = \sqrt{14.2^2 + (-8.7)^2 + 21.5^2}\]

Keystrokes: 14.2 [↰] [x²] 8.7 [↰] [x²] [+] 21.5 [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] \(\to \mathbf{27.1895\text{ kN}}\).

Because squaring a real component is always non-negative (\(|-8.7|^2 = (+8.7)^2\)), the negative sign on \(T_y\) can be omitted entirely during entry. Squaring the \(x\)-component in place (14.2 [↰] [x²]) deposits \(201.6400\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 201.6400)\). Entering and squaring the \(y\)-component (8.7 [↰] [x²]) auto-lifts \(T_x^2\) to \(Y\) while forming \(75.6900\) in \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 201.6400, X: 75.6900)\), and [+] collapses the planar norm squared to \(277.3300\) in \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 277.3300)\). Squaring the \(z\)-component (21.5 [↰] [x²]) lifts \(277.3300\) to \(Y\) and forms \(462.2500\) in \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 277.3300, X: 462.2500)\); pressing [+] [√x] collapses all three spatial dimensions into the resultant cable tension \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{27.1952}\text{ kN})\) while never occupying more than two stack registers.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.3: Four-Bar Linkage Coordinate Reduction
docs.text:
In planar mechanism kinematics, the coupler link of a four-bar linkage connects crank pin \(A(48.2, 110.3\text{ mm})\) to follower pin \(B(125.4, 85.0\text{ mm})\). Evaluating the Euclidean link length \(\ell = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\) showcases how Register \(Z\) acts as an automatic holding bay while the second coordinate difference is computed:

Keystrokes: 125.4 [ENTER] 48.2 [-] [↰] [x²] 85.0 [ENTER] 110.3 [-] [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] \(\to \mathbf{81.2393\text{ mm}}\).

Evaluating the horizontal span first (125.4 [ENTER] 48.2 [-]) forms \(\Delta x = 77.2\text{ mm}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 77.2000)\), and [↰] [x²] squares it in place to \(\Delta x^2 = 5959.8400\text{ mm}^2\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 5959.8400)\). When the vertical pin coordinates are entered and subtracted (85.0 [ENTER] 110.3 [-]), \(\Delta x^2\) rides up to Register \(Z\) and then drops back to Register \(Y\) as \(\Delta y = -25.3\text{ mm}\) forms in \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 5959.8400, X: -25.3000)\). Squaring \(\Delta y\) in place ([↰] [x²]) yields \(640.0900\text{ mm}^2\) in \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 5959.8400, X: 640.0900)\), and [+] [√x] sums the orthogonal squares (\(6599.9300\text{ mm}^2\)) to extract the rigid coupler length \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{81.2400}\text{ mm})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.4: Finite Geometric Series Summation
docs.text:
In digital signal processing and financial annuity valuation, the partial sum of \(n = 8\) geometric terms with initial amplitude \(a = 12.0\) and common decay ratio \(r = 0.75\) collapses via the closed-form identity:

\[S_8 = 12 \frac{1 - 0.75^8}{1 - 0.75} = 12 \frac{1 - 0.100113}{0.25} = 12 \times 3.599548 = 43.194576\]

Keystrokes: 0.75 [ENTER] 8 [yˣ] 1 [-] [+/-] 0.25 [÷] 12 [×] \(\to \mathbf{43.194576}\).

Evaluating the exponential attenuation term \(r^8\) first (0.75 [ENTER] 8 [yˣ]) places \(0.100113\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.1001)\). Rather than swapping registers to compute \(1 - r^8\), subtracting \(1\) and negating in place (1 [-] [+/-]) yields the complement \(1 - r^8 \approx 0.899887\) without lifting the stack \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.8999)\). Dividing by \(1 - r = 0.25\) (0.25 [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 3.5995\)) and scaling by the leading amplitude (12 [×]) resolves the 8-stage sum \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{43.1946})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.5: Thermodynamic Otto Cycle Thermal Efficiency
docs.text:
In an idealized spark-ignition internal combustion engine with volumetric compression ratio \(r_c = V_{\max}/V_{\min} = 9.5\) and diatomic air specific-heat ratio \(\gamma = C_p/C_v = 1.40\), the Nikolaus Otto cycle efficiency is governed by isentropic temperature scaling:

\[\eta = 1 - r_c^{1 - \gamma} = 1 - 9.5^{-0.40}\]

Keystrokes: 9.5 [ENTER] 0.40 [+/-] [yˣ] 1 [-] [+/-] \(\to \mathbf{0.5936} = 59.36\%\).

Loading the compression ratio (9.5 [ENTER], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 9.5000, X: 9.5000\)) and the isentropic exponent (0.40 [+/-], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 9.5000, X: -0.4000\)) prepares the power evaluation. Pressing [yˣ] computes the fraction of heat rejected to the cold sink, \(T_{\text{low}}/T_{\text{high}} = 9.5^{-0.40} \approx 0.4064\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.4064)\). Applying the subtraction-and-negation idiom (1 [-] [+/-]) converts heat rejection into net work efficiency \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.5936} = 59.36\%)\) without lifting the stack.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.6: Wheatstone Bridge Out-of-Balance Voltage
docs.text:
In strain-gauge and resistance-thermometer (RTD) instrumentation, a quarter-bridge Wheatstone network driven by \(V_s = 10.0\text{ V}\) compares a reference half-bridge (\(R_1 = R_2 = 1000\,\Omega \implies V_{\text{ref}} = 0.5 V_s\)) against a sensing divider (\(R_3 = 1000\,\Omega\), active element \(R_x = 1025\,\Omega\)):

\[V_o = V_s \left(\frac{R_x}{R_3 + R_x} - 0.5\right)\]

Keystrokes: 1025 [ENTER] 2025 [÷] 0.5 [-] 10.0 [×] \(\to \mathbf{0.061728\text{ V}} = 61.73\text{ mV}\).

Evaluating the active divider ratio (1025 [ENTER] 2025 [÷]) places \(R_x / (R_3 + R_x) \approx 0.5062\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.5062)\). Subtracting the balanced null point (0.5 [-], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0062\)) and scaling by the bridge excitation (10.0 [×]) isolates the differential millivolt signal \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.0617}\text{ V} \approx 61.73\text{ mV})\). Notice that if \(R_3\) and \(R_x\) are arbitrary resistances, keying 1025 [ENTER] [ENTER] 1000 [+] [÷] forms \(R_x / (R_x + R_3)\) while typing \(R_x = 1025\) only once!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.7: Harmonic Mean of Four Speed Trials
docs.text:
When a test vehicle traverses four equal-distance proving-ground laps at speeds \(v = [45.0, 52.0, 58.0, 64.0\text{ mph}]\), the true average speed over the total distance is the harmonic mean—not the arithmetic mean (\(54.75\text{ mph}\)), because more time is spent on slower laps:

\[v_h = \frac{4}{\sum_{i=1}^4 \frac{1}{v_i}}\]

Keystrokes: 45 [1/x] 52 [1/x] [+] 58 [1/x] [+] 64 [1/x] [+] 4 [x⇄y] [÷]\(\to \mathbf{53.8184\text{ mph}}\).

Inverting the first lap speed (45 [1/x]) places its slowness \(1/v_1 \approx 0.0222\text{ h/mi}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0222)\). Each subsequent lap is inverted in place and added to the running slowness accumulator: 52 [1/x] [+] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0415)\), 58 [1/x] [+] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0587)\), and 64 [1/x] [+], accumulating \(\sum 1/v_i \approx 0.0743\text{ h/mi}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0743)\). Keying 4 [x⇄y] [÷] divides the 4-lap distance by total elapsed time, resolving the true harmonic mean speed \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{53.8184}\text{ mph})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.8: Bending Moment on Overhanging Crane Beam
docs.text:
An overhead shop crane applies a concentrated hoist load \(P = 35\text{ kN}\) at an overhang distance \(a = 1.8\text{ m}\) beyond its support column on a wide-flange steel I-beam of elastic section modulus \(S = 4.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3\):

\[M = P \cdot a = 35 \times 1.8 = 63.0\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{M}{S}\]

Keystrokes: 35000 [ENTER] 1.8 [×] 4.5 [E] 4 [+/-] [÷] 1 [E] 6 [÷]\(\to \mathbf{140\text{ MPa}}\).

Forming the root bending moment (35000 [ENTER] 1.8 [×]) establishes \(M = 63,000\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 63000.0000)\). Dividing by the elastic section modulus (4.5 [E] 4 [+/-] [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.4000 \times 10^8\)) and normalizing to megapascals (1 [E] 6 [÷]) yields peak outer-fiber bending stress \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{140.0000}\text{ MPa})\)—confirming a safety factor of \(1.79\) against A36 structural steel yield (\(250\text{ MPa}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.9: Sound Attenuation Over Distance
docs.text:
Because acoustic wave energy from an isotropic point source spreads over a spherical wavefront of area \(4\pi r^2\), sound pressure amplitude decays as \(1/r\) (\(20\text{ dB}\) per distance decade). From a near-field machinery noise reading of \(L_1 = 92.0\text{ dB}\) at \(r_1 = 5.0\text{ m}\), the sound pressure level at the plant boundary \(r_2 = 45.0\text{ m}\) is:

\[L_2 = L_1 - 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)\]

Keystrokes: 45 [ENTER] 5 [÷] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×] 92.0 [x⇄y] [-]\(\to \mathbf{72.9151\text{ dB}}\).

Evaluating the radial expansion ratio first (45 [ENTER] 5 [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 9.0000\)), taking the base-10 logarithm ([↰] [LOG], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.9542\)), and scaling by \(20\) (20 [×]) isolates the spherical spreading attenuation of \(19.0849\text{ dB}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 19.0849)\). Entering the reference level and swapping operands (92.0 [x⇄y] [-]) resolves the far-field sound level \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{72.9151}\text{ dB})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.10: Doppler Radar Velocity Extraction
docs.text:
A pulse-Doppler X-band weather/traffic radar transmitting at \(f_0 = 10.0\text{ GHz} = 1.0 \times 10^{10}\text{ Hz}\) measures a two-way beat frequency shift \(f_d = 4,850\text{ Hz}\) (\(c = 2.99792 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\)). Because the electromagnetic wave experiences a Doppler shift both arriving at the moving target and reflecting back to the dish, the denominator carries a factor of \(2\): $\(v = \frac{f_d \cdot c}{2 f_0}\)$

Keystrokes: 4850 [ENTER] 2.99792 [E] 8 [×] 2 [÷] 1 [E] 10 [÷]\(\to \mathbf{72.69956\text{ m/s}} = 261.7\text{ km/h}\).

Loading the beat frequency (4850 [ENTER], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 4850.0000, X: 4850.0000\)) and multiplying by the speed of light (2.99792 [E] 8 [×]) forms \(f_d c = 1.4540 \times 10^{12}\text{ m/s}^2\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.4540 \times 10^{12})\). Dividing by the round-trip factor \(2\) (2 [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 7.2699 \times 10^{11}\)) and by the carrier frequency (1 [E] 10 [÷]) yields radial target speed \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{72.6996}\text{ m/s})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.11: Centripetal Acceleration in Elliptical Orbit Periapsis
docs.text:
At the perigee of a low-Earth transfer orbit (\(r_p = 6,800\text{ km} = 6.80 \times 10^6\text{ m}\)), a spacecraft moving at tangential speed \(v_p = 8,200\text{ m/s}\) experiences radial centripetal acceleration:

\[a_c = \frac{v_p^2}{r_p}\]

Keystrokes: 8200 [↰] [x²] 6.80 [E] 6 [÷]\(\to \mathbf{9.8882352941\text{ m/s}^2}\).

Squaring periapsis speed in place (8200 [↰] [x²]) places specific kinetic energy \(v_p^2 = 6.7240 \times 10^7\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 6.7240 \times 10^7)\), and dividing by orbital radius (6.80 [E] 6 [÷]) yields radial acceleration \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{9.8882}\text{ m/s}^2)\). Because local gravitational acceleration at \(r_p = 6,800\text{ km}\) is \(g_p = \mu/r_p^2 \approx 8.620\text{ m/s}^2 < a_c\), the excess centripetal requirement (\(9.8882 > 8.620\text{ m/s}^2\)) confirms the spacecraft is at the perigee of an elliptical orbit ascending toward a higher apogee.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.12: Aerodynamic Vehicle Drag Power at \(120\text{ km/h}\)
docs.text:
While aerodynamic drag force scales with the square of velocity (\(F_d = \frac{1}{2}\rho C_d A v^2\)), the mechanical power required to overcome air resistance (\(P = F_d \cdot v\)) scales with the cube of velocity—explaining why doubling highway speed octuples aerodynamic fuel consumption. At \(v = 120\text{ km/h} = 33.3333\text{ m/s}\) (\(\rho = 1.20\text{ kg/m}^3,\; C_d = 0.28,\; A = 2.20\text{ m}^2\)): $\(P = \frac{1}{2} \rho C_d A v^3\)$

Keystrokes: 120 [ENTER] 3.6 [÷] 3 [yˣ] 0.5 [×] 1.20 [×] 0.28 [×] 2.20 [×] 1000 [÷]\(\to \mathbf{13.6889\text{ kW}}\).

Converting highway speed to meters per second (120 [ENTER] 3.6 [÷]) places \(v = 33.3333\text{ m/s}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 33.3333)\), and cubing ([ENTER] 3 [yˣ]) forms \(v^3 = 37,037.0370\text{ m}^3/\text{s}^3\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 37037.0370)\). Streaming the aerodynamic coefficients (0.5 [×] 1.20 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 22222.2222\), then 0.28 [×] 2.20 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 13688.8889\)) and dividing by \(1000\) (1000 [÷]) resolves road-load drag power \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{13.6889}\text{ kW})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.13: Hydraulic Pump Output Fluid Power
docs.text:
A positive-displacement axial-piston pump delivering \(Q = 45.0\text{ L/min} = 7.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) across a manifold pressure rise \(\Delta P = 180\text{ bar} = 1.80 \times 10^7\text{ Pa}\) imparts fluid power \(P_{\text{hyd}}\) equal to the product of volumetric flow and pressure head: $\(P_{\text{hyd}} = Q \cdot \Delta P\)$

Keystrokes: 45 [ENTER] 60 [÷] 1000 [÷] 1.80 [E] 7 [×] 1000 [÷]\(\to \mathbf{13.5\text{ kW}}\).

Normalizing liters per minute into SI cubic meters per second (45 [ENTER] 60 [÷] 1000 [÷]) places \(Q = 7.50 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 7.5000 \times 10^{-4})\). Multiplying by Pascal pressure (1.80 [E] 7 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 13500.0000\)) and dividing by \(1000\) (1000 [÷]) yields net fluid power \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{13.5000}\text{ kW})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.14: Solar Array Solar Irradiance Incident on Tilted Panel
docs.text:
To maximize photovoltaic yield on a roof tilted at \(\beta = 35.0^\circ\) when the sun is at altitude \(\alpha = 48.0^\circ\) and azimuth offset \(\Delta\gamma = 15.0^\circ\) from the panel normal (\(I_0 = 980\text{ W/m}^2\)), the spherical dot product between the solar ray vector and panel normal determines the cosine projection factor: $\(\cos\theta = \sin\alpha \cos\beta + \cos\alpha \sin\beta \cos(\Delta\gamma), \qquad I_{\text{incident}} = I_0 \cos\theta\)$

Keystrokes: 48 [SIN] 35 [COS] [×] 48 [COS] 35 [SIN] [×] 15 [COS] [×] [+] 980 [×] \(\to \mathbf{959.87919595\text{ W/m}^2}\).

Evaluating the vertical projection product (48 [SIN] 35 [COS] [×]) places \(\sin 48^\circ \cos 35^\circ \approx 0.6088\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.6088)\). Forming the horizontal azimuth projection (48 [COS] 35 [SIN] [×] 15 [COS] [×]) lifts \(0.6088\) to Register \(Y\) while placing \(0.3707\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.6088, X: 0.3707)\). Summing the two projections ([+], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.9795\)) shows the panel captures \(97.95\%\) of direct normal irradiance, and 980 [×] resolves the incident flux \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{959.8792}\text{ W/m}^2)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.15: Automotive Emergency Braking Stopping Distance
docs.text:
Equating kinetic energy \(\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2\) to tire-pavement frictional work \(\mu m g d\) for a vehicle traveling at \(v_0 = 100\text{ km/h} = 27.7778\text{ m/s}\) on wet asphalt (\(\mu = 0.65,\; g = 9.80665\text{ m/s}^2\)) reveals that stopping distance is independent of vehicle mass and grows quadratically with speed:

\[d = \frac{v_0^2}{2 \mu g}\]

Keystrokes: 100 [ENTER] 3.6 [÷] [↰] [x²] 2 [ENTER] 0.65 [×] 9.80665 [×] [÷]\(\to \mathbf{60.5517\text{ m}}\).

Converting kilometers per hour to meters per second and squaring in place (100 [ENTER] 3.6 [÷] [↰] [x²]) places specific kinetic energy \(v_0^2 \approx 771.6049\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 771.6049)\). Forming the deceleration denominator (2 [ENTER] 0.65 [×] 9.80665 [×]) holds \(v_0^2\) in Register \(Y\) while computing \(2\mu g = 12.7486\text{ m/s}^2\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 771.6049, X: 12.7486)\), and [÷] resolves the minimum stopping distance \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{60.5245}\text{ m})\).

docs.title: Chapter 03: Algebra, Transcendentals & Display Formatting — Extended Engineering & Competition Problems
docs.text: Accompanies Chapter 03 of Thinking in the Stack (22 Worked Engineering Problems)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.1: Blood Bicarbonate Buffer System pH
docs.text:
Human arterial blood plasma maintains homeostasis within a narrow pH window (\(7.35\text{--}7.45\)) through the coupled carbonic acid–bicarbonate equilibrium (\(\text{pK}_a = 6.10\) at \(37^\circ\text{C}\)), governed by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. When clinical blood-gas analysis reports renal bicarbonate \([\text{HCO}_3^-] = 24.0\text{ mEq/L}\) and dissolved pulmonary carbon dioxide \([\text{CO}_2] = 1.20\text{ mEq/L}\): $\(\text{pH} = \text{pK}_a + \log_{10}\left(\frac{[\text{HCO}_3^-]}{[\text{CO}_2]}\right) = 6.10 + \log_{10}\left(\frac{24.0}{1.20}\right)\)$

Keystrokes: 24.0 [ENTER] 1.20 [÷] [↰] [LOG] 6.10 [+] \(\rightarrow\) 7.4000.

Dividing metabolic base by respiratory acid (24.0 [ENTER] 1.20 [÷]) isolates the classic \(20:1\) physiological buffer ratio in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 20.0000)\). Applying the common base-10 logarithm and adding the dissociation constant ([↰] [LOG] 6.10 [+]) yields arterial pH \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{7.4010})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.2: Fiber Optic Cable Total Attenuation & Output Power
docs.text:
In long-haul optical telecommunications at the \(1550\text{ nm}\) silica transparency window, Rayleigh scattering limits attenuation to \(\alpha = 0.22\text{ dB/km}\). When a DFB laser launches \(P_{\text{in}} = 15.0\text{ mW}\) into a \(L = 65.0\text{ km}\) unamplified span, the logarithmic decibel loss converts back to linear optical power via base-10 exponentiation: $\(\text{Loss}_{\text{dB}} = \alpha \cdot L = 0.22 \times 65.0 = 14.30\text{ dB}, \qquad P_{\text{out}} = P_{\text{in}} \cdot 10^{-\text{Loss}_{\text{dB}} / 10} = 15.0 \cdot 10^{-1.430}\)$

Keystrokes: 0.22 [ENTER] 65 [×] 10 [÷] [+/-] [↰] [10ˣ] 15 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 0.5567\(\text{ mW} = 557.3\,\mu\text{W}\).

Computing total span loss in bels and negating (0.22 [ENTER] 65 [×] 10 [÷] [+/-]) places the decade exponent \(-1.4300\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -1.4300)\). Evaluating the antilogarithm and scaling by launch power ([↰] [10ˣ] 15 [×]) resolves the received photodiode power \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.5573}\text{ mW})\) (\(557.3\,\mu\text{W}\), or \(-2.54\text{ dBm}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.3: Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation Burnout Velocity
docs.text:
Derived by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in 1897 by integrating momentum conservation \(m\,dv = -v_e\,dm\), the ideal rocket equation proves that a launch vehicle's velocity increment \(\Delta v\) grows logarithmically with its wet-to-dry mass ratio \(m_0 / m_f = 9.20\) and linearly with effective exhaust velocity \(v_e = 3,150\text{ m/s}\): $\(\Delta v = v_e \ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)\)$

Keystrokes: 9.20 [LN] 3150 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 6989.78\(\text{ m/s} \approx 6.99\text{ km/s}\).

Taking the natural logarithm of the mass ratio (9.20 [LN]) places \(\ln(9.20) \approx 2.2192\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.2192)\), and multiplying by exhaust velocity (3150 [×]) resolves burnout velocity \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{6990.4910}\text{ m/s})\) (\(\approx 6.99\text{ km/s}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.4: Richter Earthquake Seismic Energy Ratio
docs.text:
In seismology, Beno Gutenberg and Charles Richter established that while surface-wave amplitude scales by \(10^M\), total radiated elastic wave energy scales as \(10^{1.5 M}\) (\(\approx 31.62\times\) per magnitude unit, and \(1,000\times\) per two magnitude units). Comparing a major \(M_2 = 7.8\) earthquake to a moderate \(M_1 = 5.2\) tremor:

\[\frac{E_2}{E_1} = 10^{1.5 (M_2 - M_1)}\]

Keystrokes: 7.8 [ENTER] 5.2 [-] 1.5 [×] [↰] [10ˣ] \(\rightarrow\) 7943.28.

Evaluating the magnitude span and scaling by \(1.5\) (7.8 [ENTER] 5.2 [-] 1.5 [×]) forms the decade exponent \(3.9000\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 3.9000)\). Pressing [↰] [10ˣ] resolves the seismic energy ratio \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{7943.2823})\)—demonstrating that a \(2.6\)-unit increase on the Richter scale releases nearly 8,000 times more strain energy.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.5: Barometric Altitude Determination from Pressure
docs.text:
In an isothermal hydrostatically balanced atmosphere with scale height \(H_s = \frac{R T_0}{M g} = 8,434\text{ meters}\) and sea-level reference pressure \(P_0 = 1013.25\text{ hPa}\), an aircraft static port measuring \(P = 725.0\text{ hPa}\) determines pressure altitude by inverting the exponential barometric law:

\[h = - H_s \ln\left(\frac{P}{P_0}\right)\]

Keystrokes: 725 [ENTER] 1013.25 [÷] [LN] 8434 [×] [+/-] \(\rightarrow\) 2826.96\(\text{ meters} \approx 9,263\text{ ft}\).

Forming the static pressure ratio and taking the natural logarithm (725 [ENTER] 1013.25 [÷] [LN]) places \(\ln(P/P_0) \approx -0.3347\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -0.3347)\). Scaling by atmospheric scale height and negating (8434 [×] [+/-]) resolves pressure altitude \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{2823.2529}\text{ m})\) (\(\approx 9,263\text{ ft}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.6: Astronomical Apparent Magnitude and Stellar Luminosity
docs.text:
Norman Pogson formalized Hipparchus's ancient stellar magnitude scale in 1856 by defining a 5-magnitude difference as a \(100:1\) flux ratio (\(100^{1/5} = 10^{0.4} \approx 2.5119\) per magnitude). Comparing the night sky's brightest star, Sirius (\(m_1 = -1.46\)), against the North Star, Polaris (\(m_2 = +1.98\)):

\[\frac{L_1}{L_2} = 10^{0.4 (m_2 - m_1)}\]

Keystrokes: 1.98 [ENTER] 1.46 [+/-] [-] 0.4 [×] [↰] [10ˣ] \(\rightarrow\) 23.7684.

Computing the magnitude span \(\Delta m = 1.98 - (-1.46) = 3.44\) and multiplying by Pogson's \(0.4\) coefficient (1.98 [ENTER] 1.46 [+/-] [-] 0.4 [×]) places \(1.3760\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.3760)\). Pressing [↰] [10ˣ] resolves the apparent flux ratio \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{23.7684})\)—confirming Sirius delivers \(23.8\times\) more photon flux to an earthbound telescope aperture than Polaris.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.7: Permeability and Darcy Fluid Flow in Porous Sandstone
docs.text:
In petroleum reservoir characterization, Henry Darcy's law relates volumetric flow \(Q = 1.8 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) of crude oil (viscosity \(\mu = 0.035\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}\)) through a sandstone core plug (\(L = 0.050\text{ m}\), cross-sectional area \(A = 0.00125\text{ m}^2\)) under differential pressure \(\Delta P = 250\text{ kPa} = 250,000\text{ Pa}\) to intrinsic rock permeability \(k\) (\(1\text{ Darcy} = 9.86923 \times 10^{-13}\text{ m}^2\)): $\(k = \frac{Q \cdot \mu \cdot L}{A \cdot \Delta P}\)$

Keystrokes: 1.8 [E] 7 [+/-] [ENTER] 0.035 [×] 0.050 [×] 0.00125 [ENTER] 250000 [×] [÷] 9.86923 [E] 13 [+/-] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 1.021356276\(\text{ Darcy}\).

Chaining the viscous numerator product (1.8 [E] 7 [+/-] [ENTER] 0.035 [×] 0.050 [×]) places \(Q \mu L = 3.15 \times 10^{-10}\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 3.1500 \times 10^{-10})\). Forming the pressure-force denominator and dividing (0.00125 [ENTER] 250000 [×] [÷]) isolates SI permeability \(1.0080 \times 10^{-12}\text{ m}^2\) in \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.0080 \times 10^{-12})\), and dividing by the Darcy conversion constant (9.86923 [E] 13 [+/-] [÷]) yields \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{1.0214}\text{ Darcy})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.8: Shannon-Hartley Information Capacity Limit
docs.text:
Claude Shannon's 1948 noisy-channel coding theorem establishes the absolute upper bound on error-free bit rate \(C\) across an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel of bandwidth \(B = 20.0\text{ MHz} = 2.0 \times 10^7\text{ Hz}\) and signal-to-noise ratio \(\text{SNR} = 30.0\text{ dB}\) (\(\text{SNR}_{\text{linear}} = 10^{30/10} = 1,000\)): $\(C = B \log_2(1 + \text{SNR}) = B \frac{\ln(1 + \text{SNR})}{\ln 2}\)$

Keystrokes: 1001 [LN] 2 [LN] [÷] 20 [E] 6 [×] 1 [E] 6 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 199.34452518\(\text{ Mbps}\).

By the change-of-base identity \(\log_2(x) = \ln(x)/\ln(2)\), keying 1001 [LN] 2 [LN] [÷] evaluates spectral efficiency \(\log_2(1001) \approx 9.9672\text{ bits/s/Hz}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 9.9672)\). Scaling by the \(20\text{ MHz}\) channel bandwidth (20 [E] 6 [×] 1 [E] 6 [÷]) resolves maximum theoretical throughput \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{199.3445}\text{ Mbps})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.9: Chemical Reaction Equilibrium Constant from \(\Delta G^\circ\)
docs.text:
In chemical thermodynamics, a negative standard Gibbs free energy change \(\Delta G^\circ = -33.3\text{ kJ/mol} = -33,300\text{ J/mol}\) at \(T = 298.15\text{ K}\) drives the reaction equilibrium constant \(K\) exponentially above unity:

\[K = \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{R T}\right)\]

Keystrokes: 33300 [ENTER] 8.31446 [ENTER] 298.15 [×] [÷] [eˣ] \(\rightarrow\) 6.8220E5.

Loading the magnitude \(-\Delta G^\circ = 33,300\text{ J/mol}\) (33300 [ENTER], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 33300.0000, X: 33300.0000\)) and dividing by the molar thermal energy \(RT\) (8.31446 [ENTER] 298.15 [×] [÷]) isolates the dimensionless thermodynamic driving force \(-\Delta G^\circ / (RT) = 13.4331\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 13.4331)\). Pressing [eˣ] exponentiates in place to yield the equilibrium constant \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{6.8220 \times 10^5})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.10: Beam Elastic Curve Cubic Deflection
docs.text:
Along a simply supported girder of span \(L = 6.0\text{ m}\) and flexural rigidity \(E I = 1.2 \times 10^7\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2\) carrying uniform load \(w = 8.5\text{ kN/m} = 8,500\text{ N/m}\), the vertical deflection \(\delta(x)\) at station \(x = 2.0\text{ m}\) is governed by the fourth-order Euler-Bernoulli elastic curve: $\(\delta(x) = \frac{w x}{24 E I} (L^3 - 2 L x^2 + x^3)\)$

Keystrokes: 6 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] 2 [ENTER] 6 [×] 2 [↰] [x²] [×] [-] 2 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [+] 8500 [ENTER] 2 [×] [×] 24 [ENTER] 1.2 [E] 7 [×] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 0.0103888889\(\text{ m}\).

Evaluating the cubic span polynomial \((L^3 - 2Lx^2 + x^3)\) first collapses the geometry into a single scalar before scaling by load and stiffness: 6 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] forms \(L^3 = 216.0000\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 216.0000)\), 2 [ENTER] 6 [×] 2 [↰] [x²] [×] [-] subtracts \(2 L x^2 = 48.0000\) to leave \(168.0000\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 168.0000)\), and 2 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [+] adds \(x^3 = 8.0000\) to complete the geometric factor \(176.0000\text{ m}^3\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 176.0000)\). Scaling by \(w x\) (8500 [ENTER] 2 [×] [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.9920 \times 10^6\)) and dividing by \(24 E I\) (24 [ENTER] 1.2 [E] 7 [×] [÷]) resolves the vertical sag \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.0104}\text{ m} \approx 10.39\text{ mm})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.11: Radiative Cooling Time of Molten Metal Droplet
docs.text:
In space-based shot-tower manufacturing, a spherical droplet of molten iron (\(\rho = 7,800\text{ kg/m}^3,\; c_p = 450\text{ J/kg}\cdot\text{K},\; r = 0.0015\text{ m},\; \varepsilon = 0.80,\; \sigma = 5.67037 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W/m}^2\text{K}^4\)) cools strictly by Stefan-Boltzmann radiation \(-m c_p \frac{dT}{dt} = 4\pi r^2 \varepsilon\sigma T^4\). Integrating \(T^{-4}\,dT\) from \(T_1 = 1,500\text{ K}\) to \(T_2 = 1,000\text{ K}\) yields an inverse-cube law:

\[t = \frac{\rho \cdot c_p \cdot r}{3 \varepsilon \sigma} \left(\frac{1}{T_2^3} - \frac{1}{T_1^3}\right)\]

Keystrokes: 1000 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [1/x] 1500 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [1/x] [-] 7800 [ENTER] 450 [×] 0.0015 [×] [×] 3 [ENTER] 0.80 [×] 5.67037 [E] 8 [+/-] [×] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 27.224854815\(\text{ seconds}\).

Forming the inverse-cube thermal interval (1000 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [1/x] 1500 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [1/x] [-]) places \((1/T_2^3 - 1/T_1^3) \approx 7.0370 \times 10^{-10}\text{ K}^{-3}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 7.0370 \times 10^{-10})\). Scaling by volumetric heat capacity per unit area (7800 [ENTER] 450 [×] 0.0015 [×] [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 3.7050 \times 10^{-6}\)) and dividing by \(3\varepsilon\sigma\) (3 [ENTER] 0.80 [×] 5.67037 [E] 8 [+/-] [×] [÷]) resolves the vacuum cooling time \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{27.2249}\text{ s})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.12: Dynamic Range and Theoretical SNR of 24-Bit Digital Audio
docs.text:
In uniform linear pulse-code modulation (PCM) quantization with \(N = 24\text{ bits}\), each additional bit halves the RMS quantization step size (\(20\log_{10} 2 = 6.0206\text{ dB/bit}\)), while the ratio of a full-scale sine wave to a uniform triangular quantization error distribution adds \(10\log_{10}(3/2) = 1.7609\text{ dB}\):

\[\text{SNR}_{\text{dB}} = 6.0206 N + 1.7609\text{ dB}\]

Keystrokes: 6.0206 [ENTER] 24 [×] 1.7609 [+] \(\rightarrow\) 146.2553\(\text{ dB}\).

Multiplying the per-bit gain by bit depth (6.0206 [ENTER] 24 [×]) forms the raw dynamic range of \(144.4944\text{ dB}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 144.4944)\), and adding the crest-to-quantization correction (1.7609 [+]) yields the ideal 24-bit SNR ceiling \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{146.2553}\text{ dB})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.13: Fermi-Dirac Semiconductor Electron Distribution
docs.text:
Because electrons are spin-\(1/2\) fermions obeying the Pauli exclusion principle, their thermal occupancy probability at energy \(\Delta E = E - E_F = 0.050\text{ eV}\) above the Fermi level at room temperature \(T = 300\text{ K}\) (\(k T = 0.025852\text{ eV}\)) follows Enrico Fermi and Paul Dirac's quantum distribution:

\[f(E) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(\frac{E - E_F}{k T}\right)}\]

Keystrokes: 0.050 [ENTER] 0.025852 [÷] [eˣ] 1 [+] [1/x] \(\rightarrow\) 0.126315 (\(12.63\%\)).

Normalizing the energy offset by thermal energy (0.050 [ENTER] 0.025852 [÷]) places \((E - E_F)/(kT) \approx 1.9341\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.9341)\). Chaining the three monadic/dyadic operations ([eˣ] 1 [+] [1/x]) evaluates the denominator \(1 + e^{1.9341} \approx 7.9177\) and inverts it in place to obtain the quantum state occupancy \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.1263} = 12.63\%)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.14: Viscous Pressure Drop in Poiseuille Laminar Capillary Flow
docs.text:
Jean Léonard Marie Poiseuille and Gotthilf Hagen discovered that laminar viscous pressure drop \(\Delta P\) in a cylindrical micro-capillary (\(\mu = 0.0025\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}\), length \(L = 0.20\text{ m}\), flow rate \(Q = 1.5 \times 10^{-8}\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)) is inversely proportional to the fourth power of inner radius \(R = 0.0005\text{ m}\) (\(0.5\text{ mm}\))—meaning a \(50\%\) plaque or fouling constriction increases required pumping pressure sixteen-fold: $\(\Delta P = \frac{8 \mu L Q}{\pi R^4}\)$

Keystrokes: 8 [ENTER] 0.0025 [×] 0.20 [×] 1.5 [E] 8 [+/-] [×] [↱] [π] [÷] 0.0005 [ENTER] 4 [yˣ] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 305.57749074\(\text{ Pa}\).

Streaming the viscous numerator (8 [ENTER] 0.0025 [×] 0.20 [×] 1.5 [E] 8 [+/-] [×]) places \(8 \mu L Q = 6.0000 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 6.0000 \times 10^{-11})\).
