docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.1: Elliptical Pressure Vessel Manway Area & Perimeter
docs.text:
A vessel inspection hatch is elliptical with semimajor axis \(a = 250.0\text{ mm}\) and semiminor axis \(b = 150.0\text{ mm}\). 1. Area \(A = \pi a b = \pi \times 250 \times 150 = 37,500\pi \approx \mathbf{117,809.72\text{ mm}^2}\) 2. Ramanujan's approximate perimeter \(P \approx \pi [3(a+b) - \sqrt{(3a+b)(a+3b)}]\): \(h = \frac{(a-b)^2}{(a+b)^2} = \frac{100^2}{400^2} = 0.0625 \implies P \approx \pi(a+b)(1 + \frac{3h}{10 + \sqrt{4 - 3h}}) \approx \mathbf{1,276.26\text{ mm}}\)

Keystrokes (Area): 250 [ENTER] 150 [×] [↱] [π] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 117,809.7245

Boiler inspection manways are made elliptical so the cover plate can be rotated \(90^\circ\), slipped edgewise through its own opening, and seated against the inside rim so internal boiler pressure seals the gasket automatically! While the area \(A = \pi ab\) is an exact affine scaling of a circle, the perimeter requires a complete elliptic integral of the second kind (approximated to \(10^{-9}\) accuracy by Srinivasa Ramanujan's rational \(h\)-formula). Push semimajor axis \(a = 250\) via 250 [ENTER], multiply by semiminor axis \(b = 150\) via 150 [×] to obtain planar product \(37,500.0\), and apply [↱] [π] [×] to resolve exact manway opening area at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 117809.7245)\), confirming \(117,809.72\text{ mm}^2\) (\(1,178.10\text{ cm}^2\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.2: Torus Volume and Surface Area (Hydraulic O-Ring)
docs.text:
An elastomer O-ring has major mean radius \(R = 45.0\text{ mm}\) and cross-sectional circular radius \(r = 3.5\text{ mm}\). 1. Volume \(V = 2\pi^2 R r^2 = 2 \pi^2 (45) (3.5^2) = 2 \pi^2 (45) (12.25) \approx \mathbf{10,880.89\text{ mm}^3}\) 2. Surface Area \(A = 4\pi^2 R r = 4 \pi^2 (45) (3.5) \approx \mathbf{6,217.85\text{ mm}^2}\)

Keystrokes (Volume): [↱] [π] [↰] [x²] 2 [×] 45 [×] 3.5 [↰] [x²] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 10,881.23885

By Pappus's centroid theorems, sweeping a circle of area \(\pi r^2\) and circumference \(2\pi r\) along a circular centerline of length \(2\pi R\) generates volume \(V = (\pi r^2)(2\pi R) = 2\pi^2 R r^2\) and surface area \(A = (2\pi r)(2\pi R) = 4\pi^2 R r\)—exactly the same as an unwrapped cylinder of length \(2\pi R\)! Evaluate \(2\pi^2\) via [↱] [π] [↰] [x²] 2 [×], scale by major centerline radius \(R = 45\text{ mm}\) via 45 [×], and multiply by cross-sectional radius squared \(r^2 = 3.5^2\) via 3.5 [↰] [x²] [×], establishing torus body volume at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 10880.8872)\).

Keystrokes (Surface Area): [↱] [π] [↰] [x²] 4 [×] 45 [×] 3.5 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 6217.6500

Notice that \(A / V = 2 / r\): if you already have \(V = 10,880.89\text{ mm}^3\) in Register \(X\), keying 2 [×] 3.5 [÷] yields \(A = 6,217.85\text{ mm}^2\) in three keystrokes! Or from scratch, compute the \(4\pi^2\) envelope constant via [↱] [π] [↰] [x²] 4 [×], then chain major and minor radii via 45 [×] 3.5 [×] to yield total contact surface area at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 6217.8508)\), confirming \(V = 10,880.89\text{ mm}^3\), \(A = 6,217.85\text{ mm}^2\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.3: Truncated Pyramidal Monument Volume
docs.text:
A stone pedestal is a truncated square pyramid: lower base side \(a = 3.20\text{ m}\), upper base side \(b = 1.80\text{ m}\), height \(h = 4.50\text{ m}\). Base areas: \(A_1 = 3.2^2 = 10.24\text{ m}^2\), \(A_2 = 1.8^2 = 3.24\text{ m}^2\): $\(V = \frac{h}{3} (A_1 + A_2 + \sqrt{A_1 A_2}) = \frac{4.5}{3} (10.24 + 3.24 + \sqrt{33.1776}) = 1.5 \times (13.48 + 5.76) = 1.5 \times 19.24 = \mathbf{28.86\text{ m}^3}\)$

Keystrokes: 3.2 [↰] [x²] [STO] 1 1.8 [↰] [x²] [STO] 2 [+] [RCL] 1 [RCL] 2 [×] [√x] [+] 4.5 [×] 3 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 28.86

Recorded in the 1850 BCE Egyptian Moscow Mathematical Papyrus (Problem 14), the truncated square pyramid formula \(V = \frac{h}{3}(a^2 + ab + b^2) = \frac{h}{3}(A_1 + A_2 + \sqrt{A_1 A_2})\) is one of the oldest jewels of solid geometry. Store lower base \(A_1 = 10.24\) into Register 1 via 3.2 [↰] [x²] [STO] 1, and upper base \(A_2 = 3.24\) into Register 2 via 1.8 [↰] [x²] [STO] 2. Add them via [+] for sum \(13.48\). Compute geometric mean \(\sqrt{A_1 A_2} = 5.76\) via [RCL] 1 [RCL] 2 [×] [√x], sum with base areas via [+], and multiply by \(h/3\) via 4.5 [×] 3 [÷], yielding pedestal volume at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 28.8600)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.4: Regular Icosahedron Dice Volume and Area
docs.text:
A 20-sided gaming die has edge length \(a = 18.0\text{ mm}\). 1. Surface Area \(A = 5\sqrt{3} a^2 = 5 \sqrt{3} (18^2) = 5\sqrt{3}(324) \approx \mathbf{2,805.9223\text{ mm}^2}\) 2. Volume \(V = \frac{5(3 + \sqrt{5})}{12} a^3 = \frac{5(5.236068)}{12} (5832) \approx \mathbf{12,723.65\text{ mm}^3}\)

Keystrokes (Volume): 5 [√x] 3 [+] 5 [×] 12 [÷] 18 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 12,723.64519

The vertices of a regular icosahedron lie on three mutually orthogonal golden rectangles of aspect ratio \(\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2\), so its volume constant \(\frac{5(3+\sqrt{5})}{12} = \frac{5\varphi^2}{6}\) is governed directly by the square of the golden ratio! Evaluate icosahedral volume factor \(\frac{5(3+\sqrt{5})}{12} \approx 2.181695\) via 5 [√x] 3 [+] 5 [×] 12 [÷]. Cube die edge \(a = 18\text{ mm}\) via 18 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] and multiply via [×], arriving at total polyhedron volume at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 12723.6452)\), confirming \(V = 12,723.65\text{ mm}^3\), \(A = 2,805.92\text{ mm}^2\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.5: Regular Dodecahedron Volume
docs.text:
12-sided solid with edge \(a = 12.0\text{ mm}\):

\[V = \frac{15 + 7\sqrt{5}}{4} a^3 \approx \frac{15 + 15.652476}{4} (1728) = 7.663119 \times 1728 = \mathbf{13,241.87\text{ mm}^3}\]

Keystrokes: 5 [√x] 7 [×] 15 [+] 4 [÷] 12 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 13,241.86956

Dual to the icosahedron, the regular dodecahedron can be constructed by erecting roof-like "tents" on the six faces of an inscribed cube of edge \(\varphi a\), giving volume constant \(\frac{15+7\sqrt{5}}{4} \approx 7.663119\). Compute this constant via 5 [√x] 7 [×] 15 [+] 4 [÷], cube facet edge \(a = 12\text{ mm}\) via 12 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ], and multiply with [×], yielding \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 13241.8694)\), confirming \(13,241.87\text{ mm}^3\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.6: 3D Euclidean Distance Between Aerospace Telemetry Nodes
docs.text:
Station \(A\) at coordinates \((1250, -420, 850)\text{ m}\), Station \(B\) at \((2100, 680, 1400)\text{ m}\):

\[\Delta x = 2100 - 1250 = 850\text{ m}, \quad \Delta y = 680 - (-420) = 1100\text{ m}, \quad \Delta z = 1400 - 850 = 550\text{ m}$$ $$d = \sqrt{850^2 + 1100^2 + 550^2} = \sqrt{722500 + 1210000 + 302500} = \sqrt{2235000} \approx \mathbf{1,494.9916\text{ meters}}\]

Keystrokes: 2100 [ENTER] 1250 [-] [↰] [x²] 680 [ENTER] 420 [+/-] [-] [↰] [x²] [+] 1400 [ENTER] 850 [-] [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] \(\rightarrow\) 1,494.991639

Computing a 3D Euclidean norm \(\sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2}\) on the stack never requires more than two active registers when each coordinate difference is squared and added immediately to the running sum of squares in Register \(Y\). Evaluate \(\Delta x^2 = 850^2 = 722,500\) via 2100 [ENTER] 1250 [-] [↰] [x²], accumulate \(\Delta y^2 = 1100^2 = 1,210,000\) with 680 [ENTER] 420 [+/-] [-] [↰] [x²] [+], and add \(\Delta z^2 = 550^2 = 302,500\) via 1400 [ENTER] 850 [-] [↰] [x²] [+]. Extract the square root via [√x] to resolve 3D spatial separation at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1494.9916)\), confirming \(1,494.99\text{ meters}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.7: Vector Cross Product in 3-Space (\(\vec{A} \times \vec{B}\))
docs.text:
\(\vec{A} = (3, -2, 4)\), \(\vec{B} = (1, 5, -2)\):

\[\vec{C} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} = (A_y B_z - A_z B_y)\hat{i} + (A_z B_x - A_x B_z)\hat{j} + (A_x B_y - A_y B_x)\hat{k}$$ * $C_x = (-2)(-2) - (4)(5) = 4 - 20 = \mathbf{-16}$ * $C_y = (4)(1) - (3)(-2) = 4 - (-6) = \mathbf{10}$ * $C_z = (3)(5) - (-2)(1) = 15 - (-2) = \mathbf{17}$ $$\vec{C} = (-16, 10, 17) \implies |\vec{C}| = \sqrt{256 + 100 + 289} = \sqrt{645} \approx \mathbf{25.3969}\]

Keystrokes (Magnitude): 16 [↰] [x²] 10 [↰] [x²] [+] 17 [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] \(\rightarrow\) 25.396850198

Geometrically, the cross product \(\vec{C} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B}\) is normal to the plane spanned by \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\), and its Euclidean magnitude \(|\vec{C}| = |\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\sin\theta = \sqrt{645}\) equals the area of the 3D parallelogram formed by the two vectors (and half of \(|\vec{C}|\) is the area of the spatial triangle). Square each Cartesian cross-product component sequentially: 16 [↰] [x²] 10 [↰] [x²] [+] 17 [↰] [x²] [+] produces sum of squares \(645.0\) in Register \(X\). Taking the square root via [√x] delivers vector magnitude \(|\vec{C}|\) at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 25.3969)\), confirming \(\vec{C} = (-16, 10, 17), |\vec{C}| = 25.40\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.8: Dihedral Angle Between Two Intersecting Planes
docs.text:
Plane 1: \(2x + y - 2z = 5 \implies \vec{n}_1 = (2, 1, -2)\). Plane 2: \(x - 2y + 2z = 3 \implies \vec{n}_2 = (1, -2, 2)\):

\[\cos\theta = \frac{|\vec{n}_1 \cdot \vec{n}_2|}{|\vec{n}_1| |\vec{n}_2|} = \frac{|(2)(1) + (1)(-2) + (-2)(2)|}{\sqrt{4+1+4} \sqrt{1+4+4}} = \frac{|2 - 2 - 4|}{3 \times 3} = \frac{4}{9} \approx 0.444444$$ $$\theta = \arccos(4/9) \approx \mathbf{63.6122^\circ}\]

Keystrokes: 4 [ENTER] 9 [÷] [↰] [ACOS] \(\rightarrow\) 63.612200039

The acute dihedral fold angle \(\theta\) between two intersecting sheet-metal or roof planes equals the angle between their outward surface normals \(\vec{n}_1\) and \(\vec{n}_2\) (which here are both Pythagorean triples of length \(\sqrt{2^2 + 1^2 + 2^2} = 3\)). Evaluate cosine quotient \(4/9 \approx 0.444444\) via 4 [ENTER] 9 [÷]. Taking inverse cosine via [↰] [ACOS] extracts the dihedral intersection angle in degrees, settling the stack at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 63.6122)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.9: Radius of Gyration (\(k\)) of Rotating Turbine Disk
docs.text:
Rotor disk with moment of inertia \(I = 14.8\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\) and mass \(M = 42.0\text{ kg}\):

\[k = \sqrt{\frac{I}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{14.8}{42.0}} = \sqrt{0.352381} = \mathbf{0.593617\text{ meters}} = 593.6\text{ mm}\]

Keystrokes: 14.8 [ENTER] 42 [÷] [√x] \(\rightarrow\) 0.5936168397

The radius of gyration \(k = \sqrt{I/M}\) is the radial distance at which the entire mass \(M\) of a complex profiled turbine rotor could be concentrated into an infinitesimally thin hoop (\(I = M k^2\)) without altering its rotational kinetic energy \(\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2\). Divide moment of inertia \(I = 14.8\) by mass \(M = 42.0\) via 14.8 [ENTER] 42 [÷] to form \(k^2 = 0.352381\text{ m}^2\). Extracting the square root via [√x] gives radius of gyration \(k\) in meters at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.593617)\), confirming \(k = 0.5936\text{ m}\) (\(593.6\text{ mm}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.10: Parabolic Solar Reflector Surface Area
docs.text:
Deep parabolic dish \(z = \frac{x^2 + y^2}{4f}\) with focal length \(f = 1.20\text{ m}\) and rim radius \(R = 2.0\text{ m}\). Surface area of revolution:

\[A = \frac{8\pi f^2}{3} \left[ \left(1 + \frac{R^2}{4f^2}\right)^{3/2} - 1 \right]$$ For $f = 1.2, R = 2.0$: $\frac{R^2}{4f^2} = \frac{4}{4(1.44)} = \frac{1}{1.44} \approx 0.694444$. $1 + 0.694444 = 1.694444 \implies (1.694444)^{1.5} \approx 2.205739$: $$A = \frac{8\pi(1.44)}{3} [2.205739 - 1] = 3.84\pi \times 1.205739 \approx \mathbf{14.5458\text{ m}^2}\]

Integrating the surface-of-revolution element \(2\pi r\sqrt{1 + (dz/dr)^2}\,dr\) for a paraboloid \(z = r^2/(4f)\) yields an exact \(u\)-substitution in \(u = 1 + r^2/(4f^2)\) that requires no elliptic integrals. Evaluate base factor \(1 + R^2/(4f^2) \approx 1.694444\) via 2 [↰] [x²] 4 [÷] 1.2 [↰] [x²] [÷] 1 [+]. Raise to power \(1.5\) and subtract unity via 1.5 [yˣ] 1 [-] to obtain \(1.205739\). Form leading coefficient \(\frac{8\pi f^2}{3} \approx 12.063716\) via 8 [↱] [π] [×] 1.2 [↰] [x²] [×] 3 [÷] and multiply via [×] to resolve reflector mirror area at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 14.5458)\) (compared to flat aperture \(\pi R^2 = 12.5664\text{ m}^2\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.11: Hydraulic Mean Depth & Wetted Perimeter
docs.text:
Trapezoidal irrigation canal: bottom width \(b = 4.0\text{ m}\), water depth \(y = 1.8\text{ m}\), side slope \(z = 1.5\) (\(1.5\text{ H} : 1\text{ V}\)): * Flow area \(A = (b + z y) y = (4.0 + 1.5 \times 1.8) \times 1.8 = (4.0 + 2.7) \times 1.8 = 6.7 \times 1.8 = \mathbf{12.06\text{ m}^2}\) * Wetted perimeter \(P = b + 2 y \sqrt{1 + z^2} = 4.0 + 2(1.8)\sqrt{1 + 2.25} = 4.0 + 3.6\sqrt{3.25} \approx 4.0 + 6.49 = \mathbf{10.4892\text{ m}}\) * Hydraulic radius \(R_h = A / P = 12.06 / 10.4892 = \mathbf{1.1498\text{ meters}}\)

In open-channel hydraulics, the hydraulic radius \(R_h = A/P\) measures the ratio of gravity-driven cross-sectional flow area \(A\) to boundary-shear wetted perimeter \(P\), driving Manning's velocity \(V = \frac{1}{n} R_h^{2/3} S^{1/2}\). Evaluate flow area \(A = (b+zy)y = 12.06\text{ m}^2\) with 1.5 [ENTER] 1.8 [×] 4 [+] 1.8 [×], then compute wetted perimeter \(P = b + 2y\sqrt{1+z^2} \approx 10.4892\text{ m}\) inside-out via 1.5 [↰] [x²] 1 [+] [√x] 2 [×] 1.8 [×] 4 [+], using only two active stack registers so \(A = 12.06\) stays safely in Register \(Y\) while \(P\) forms in Register \(X\). Pressing [÷] divides the two directly to establish hydraulic radius at \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.1498)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.12: Circular Segment Area (Partially Filled Pipe)
docs.text:
Storm sewer diameter \(D = 1.20\text{ m}\) (\(r = 0.60\text{ m}\)). Water depth \(d = 0.40\text{ m}\). Subtended angle:

\[\theta = 2 \arccos\left(\frac{r - d}{r}\right) = 2 \arccos\left(\frac{0.2}{0.6}\right) = 2 \arccos(0.333333) = 2(70.5288^\circ) = 141.0575^\circ = 2.461914\text{ rad}$$ $$\text{Area } A = \frac{1}{2} r^2 (\theta - \sin\theta) = 0.5(0.36)(2.461914 - \sin(141.0575^\circ)) = 0.18(2.461914 - 0.628539) = 0.18(1.833375) = \mathbf{0.330008\text{ m}^2}\]

Notice how stack duplication eliminates re-typing the pipe radius \(r = 0.60\text{ m}\) and subtended angle \(\theta\): duplicating \(r = 0.60\) via 0.6 [ENTER] [ENTER] 0.4 [-] [x⇄y] [÷] [↰] [ACOS] 2 [×] determines subtended angle \(\theta = 141.0576^\circ\) while typing \(0.6\) once (or work directly in [RAD] mode where \(\theta - \sin\theta\) requires no \(\pi/180\) conversion!). In [DEG] mode, duplicate \(\theta\) into Register \(Y\) and convert Register \(X\) to radians via [ENTER] [↱] [π] [×] 180 [÷], subtract \(\sin\theta\) via [x⇄y] [SIN] [-] to obtain the chord-segment factor \(1.833375\), and scale by \(r^2/2\) via 0.6 [↰] [x²] [×] 2 [÷] to deliver the wetted flow area at \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.3300)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.13: Slosh Baffle Circular Perforation Net Area
docs.text:
Circular baffle plate \(R = 400.0\text{ mm}\) perforated with 48 circular holes of diameter \(d = 35.0\text{ mm}\) (\(r_h = 17.5\text{ mm}\)): * Solid plate area: \(\pi(400^2) = 160,000\pi \approx 502,654.82\text{ mm}^2\) * Perforations total: \(48 \times \pi(17.5^2) = 48 \times 306.25\pi = 14,700\pi \approx 46,181.41\text{ mm}^2\) * Net remaining solid area: \((160,000 - 14,700)\pi = 145,300\pi \approx \mathbf{456,473.41\text{ mm}^2}\)

In liquid-propellant rocket tanks, perforated anti-slosh ring baffles damp propellant sloshing modes via orifice vortex shedding while minimizing structural mass. Evaluating gross solid plate area \(\pi R^2 \approx 502,654.82\text{ mm}^2\) with 400 [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×] and subtracting the 48 perforation holes \(48 \times \pi r_h^2 \approx 46,181.41\text{ mm}^2\) via 17.5 [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×] 48 [×] [-] leaves net solid baffle area at \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 456473.4126)\), confirming \(456,473.41\text{ mm}^2\) (a \(9.19\%\) open-area porosity ratio)—or factor \(\pi\) out to the end via 400 [↰] [x²] 17.5 [↰] [x²] 48 [×] [-] [↱] [π] [×] to save two keystrokes!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.14: Inscribed and Circumscribed Spheres of Regular Octahedron
docs.text:
Octahedron with edge length \(a = 40.0\text{ mm}\): * Circumscribed radius: \(R = \frac{a}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{40}{\sqrt{2}} \approx \mathbf{28.2843\text{ mm}}\) * Inscribed radius: \(r = \frac{a}{\sqrt{6}} = \frac{40}{\sqrt{6}} \approx \mathbf{16.3299\text{ mm}}\) Ratio \(R/r = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732051\).

Keystrokes: 40 [ENTER] 2 [√x] [÷] 40 [ENTER] 6 [√x] [÷] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 1.7321

In any regular octahedron (and in its dual, the cube!), the ratio of the circumscribed sphere radius \(R\) (passing through the 6 vertices) to the inscribed sphere radius \(r\) (tangent to the 8 equilateral-triangle faces) is the scale-invariant constant \(R/r = \sqrt{6}/\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{3}\). Evaluate circumradius \(R = a/\sqrt{2} \approx 28.2843\text{ mm}\) via 40 [ENTER] 2 [√x] [÷], then inradius \(r = a/\sqrt{6} \approx 16.3299\text{ mm}\) via 40 [ENTER] 6 [√x] [÷] (leaving both radii visible in \(Y\) and \(X\)). Dividing the two via [÷] yields exact sphere ratio \(R/r = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.7321\) at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1.7321)\), and squaring via [↰] [x²] confirms the dimension-free surface-area ratio \((R/r)^2 = 3.0000\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.15: Prolate Spheroid Volume and Eccentricity
docs.text:
Streamlined airship envelope with semimajor axis \(a = 60.0\text{ m}\), equatorial radius \(b = 15.0\text{ m}\):

\[V = \frac{4}{3} \pi a b^2 = \frac{4}{3} \pi (60)(15^2) = 80 \pi (225) = 18,000\pi \approx \mathbf{56,548.67\text{ m}^3}$$ $$e = \sqrt{1 - \frac{b^2}{a^2}} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{225}{3600}} = \sqrt{1 - 0.0625} = \sqrt{0.9375} \approx \mathbf{0.968246}\]

Keystrokes: 4 [ENTER] 3 [÷] [↱] [π] [×] 60 [×] 15 [↰] [x²] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 56548.6678; 15 [↰] [x²] 60 [↰] [x²] [÷] 1 [x⇄y] [-] [√x] \(\rightarrow\) 0.9682

A prolate spheroid of fineness ratio \(a/b = 60/15 = 4:1\) approaches the ideal low-drag Prandtl-Glauert hull shape for subsonic airships and submarine hulls. Evaluate volume constant \(\frac{4\pi}{3} \approx 4.188790\) via 4 [ENTER] 3 [÷] [↱] [π] [×] and multiply by \(a \cdot b^2 = 60 \times 15^2\) via 60 [×] 15 [↰] [x²] [×], establishing envelope volume \(56,548.67\text{ m}^3\) in Register \(X\). For eccentricity, form squared ratio \(b^2/a^2 = 0.0625\) with 15 [↰] [x²] 60 [↰] [x²] [÷], subtract from unity, and extract the square root via 1 [x⇄y] [-] [√x] to settle prolate eccentricity at \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 56548.6678, X: 0.9682)\).

docs.title: Chapter 07: Polynomials, Brent-Dekker Solver & Root Finding — Extended Engineering & Competition Problems
docs.text: Accompanies Chapter 07 of Thinking in the Stack (26 Worked Engineering Problems)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.1: Structural Column Buckling Transcendental Mode
docs.text:
For a slender elastic column of length \(L\) and flexural rigidity \(EI\) clamped at its base and pinned against lateral sway at its top, enforcing zero bending moment at the pinned support on the fourth-order Euler-Bernoulli beam-column differential equation \(EI w'''' + P w'' = 0\) (with wavenumber \(k = \sqrt{P/EI}\)) yields the transcendental buckling eigenvalue equation:

\[\tan(x) - x = 0 \quad (\text{with } x = k L)\]

Set the angular baseline mode to [RAD] and program the characteristic equation into [↱] [EQN] under label BUCK: X [TAN] X [-].

Keying 4.5 [STO] X loads the initial trial eigenvalue estimate \(x_0 = 4.5000\text{ rad}\) (just below the vertical asymptote at \(3\pi/2 \approx 4.7124\)) into variable \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 4.5000)\). Striking [↱] [SOLVE] X executes Brent's hybrid root solver, evaluating \(\tan(x) - x\) and rapidly contracting the interval via inverse quadratic interpolation to isolate the first non-trivial buckling root \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 4.5000, X: \mathbf{4.493409})\) in Register \(X\) (\(\approx 1.4303\pi\), corresponding to an effective column length factor \(K = \pi / x = 0.69916\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.2: Blackbody Planck Peak Wavelength (Wien's Law Derivation)
docs.text:
Differentiating Max Planck's (1900) quantum blackbody spectral radiance \(B_\lambda(\lambda, T) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5 (e^{hc/\lambda k_B T} - 1)}\) with respect to wavelength \(\lambda\) and setting \(\partial B_\lambda / \partial \lambda = 0\) under the dimensionless photon-energy substitution \(x = \frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}\) yields the universal transcendental root governing Wien's displacement law:

\[5(1 - e^{-x}) - x = 0 \quad (\text{where } x = h c / (\lambda k_B T))\]

Program the equation into [↱] [EQN] under label WIEN: 1 X [+/-] [eˣ] [-] 5 [×] X [-].

Entering 5.0 [STO] X stores initial estimate \(x_0 = 5.0\) (the high-energy Wien asymptotic limit where \(e^{-x} \ll 1\)) into variable \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 5.0000)\). Striking [↱] [SOLVE] X executes Brent's solver; within 6 iterations of guarded inverse quadratic interpolation, the root converges to \(10^{-12}\) precision \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 5.0000, X: \mathbf{4.965114})\) in Register \(X\), establishing Wien's displacement constant \(b = \frac{hc}{x k_B} = 2.897772 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\cdot\text{K}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.3: Adiabatic Flame Temperature Equilibrium
docs.text:
During constant-pressure adiabatic combustion of methane in air, integrating the temperature-dependent molar heat capacity \(C_p(T) = c_0 + c_1 T\) of the flue gas products (\(\text{CO}_2, \text{H}_2\text{O}, \text{N}_2\)) against the lower heating value enthalpy release yields a quadratic first-law energy balance:

\[H_{\text{prod}}(T) - H_{\text{react}} = 0 \implies 0.05 T^2 + 120 T - 280,000 = 0\]

Keystrokes: [↱] [POLY] 0.05 [A] 120 [B] 280000 [+/-] [C] 0 [D] [XEQ] [RCL] 3 \(\rightarrow\) 1,453.299832

In [↱] [POLY], keying 0.05 [A] 120 [B] registers enthalpy temperature coefficients \(A\) and \(B\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0500, X: 120.0000)\). Entering 280000 [+/-] [C] 0 [D] loads enthalpy release \(C = -280,000\) and depressed constant \(D = 0.0\) \((T: 0.0500, Z: 120.0000, Y: -280000.0000, X: 0.0000)\). Pressing [XEQ] computes Cardano roots; keying [RCL] 5 extracts the physical positive adiabatic flame temperature \((T: 120.0000, Z: -3853.3000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{1453.299832}\text{ K})\) in Register \(X\) (with unphysical negative rebound root \(-3,853.30\text{ K}\) stored in variable 1), confirming \(T_{\text{flame}} = 1,453.30\text{ Kelvin}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.4: Bungee Jumper Maximum Cord Stretch
docs.text:
A jumper of mass \(m = 75\text{ kg}\) steps from a bridge tethered to an elastic bungee cord of unstretched length \(L = 30\text{ m}\) and Hookean spring stiffness \(k = 40\text{ N/m}\). At the instant of maximum dynamic arrest, kinetic energy vanishes and total lost gravitational potential energy \(mg(L + x)\) equals stored elastic strain energy \(\frac{1}{2}kx^2\):

\[20 x^2 - 735.75 x - 22,072.5 = 0\]

Keystrokes: [↱] [POLY] 20 [A] 735.75 [+/-] [B] 22072.5 [+/-] [C] 0 [D] [XEQ] [RCL] 5 \(\rightarrow\) 56.366833086

In [↱] [POLY], keying 20 [A] 735.75 [+/-] [B] loads quadratic coefficient \(A = 20.0\) and linear coefficient \(B = -735.75\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 20.0000, X: -735.7500)\). Entering 22072.5 [+/-] [C] stores constant term \(C = -22,072.5\) (with cubic constant \(D\) defaulting to \(0.0\) automatically for depressed quadratic solving, or explicitly keyed as 0 [D]) \((T: 20.0000, Z: -735.7500, Y: -22072.5000, X: 0.0000)\). Striking [XEQ] computes Cardano roots; keying [RCL] 5 extracts the physical positive maximum dynamic cord elongation \((T: -735.7500, Z: -19.579333, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{56.366833}\text{ m})\) in Register \(X\) (with unphysical negative rebound root \(-19.5793\text{ m}\) stored in variable 1), confirming \(x = 56.3668\text{ meters}\) (total fall distance \(L + x = 86.37\text{ m}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.5: Chemical Equilibrium Dissociation Constant (\(K_c\))
docs.text:
Dinitrogen tetroxide dissociates endothermically into nitrogen dioxide gas (\(N_2 O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2 NO_2\)) in a sealed reactor with molar equilibrium constant \(K_c = 0.040\) and initial concentration \([N_2 O_4]_0 = 0.50\text{ M}\). By the Guldberg-Waage Law of Mass Action, an ICE (Initial-Change-Equilibrium) reaction extent \(x\) yields \([NO_2] = 2x\) and \([N_2 O_4] = 0.50 - x\), satisfying the quadratic equilibrium relation \(\frac{(2x)^2}{0.50 - x} = K_c\):

\[4 x^2 + 0.040 x - 0.020 = 0\]

Keystrokes: [↱] [POLY] 4 [A] 0.04 [B] 0.02 [+/-] [C] 0 [D] [XEQ] [RCL] 5 \(\rightarrow\) 0.0658872344

In [↱] [POLY], entering 4 [A] 0.040 [B] loads stoichiometry coefficients \(A\) and \(B\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 4.0000, X: 0.0400)\). Entering 0.020 [+/-] [C] loads constant \(C = -0.020\) (with \(D\) defaulting to \(0.0\) automatically for depressed quadratic embedding, or explicitly keyed as 0 [D]) \((T: 4.0000, Z: 0.0400, Y: -0.0200, X: 0.0000)\). Striking [XEQ] evaluates quadratic roots; keying [RCL] 5 isolates the positive dissociated equilibrium extent \((T: 0.0400, Z: -0.075887, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.065887}\text{ M})\) in Register \(X\) (\(65.89\text{ mM}\), corresponding to \([NO_2] = 2x = 0.1318\text{ M}\) and \(13.18\%\) dissociation).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.6: Cantilever Beam Deflection Under Distributed Load
docs.text:
For a statically indeterminate propped cantilever beam of span \(L = 10\text{ m}\) carrying a uniform distributed load, integrating the Euler-Bernoulli elastic curve \(EI v''(x) = M(x)\) yields a cubic compatibility polynomial whose root confirms zero deflection and slope at the clamped support:

\[2 x^3 - 3 L x^2 + L^3 = 0 \implies \text{for } L = 10\text{ m}: \quad 2 x^3 - 30 x^2 + 1000 = 0\]

Keystrokes: [↱] [POLY] 2 [A] 30 [+/-] [B] 0 [C] 1000 [D] [XEQ] [RCL] 3 \(\rightarrow\) 10

In [↱] [POLY], keying 2 [A] 30 [+/-] [B] registers cubic and quadratic flexural coefficients \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 2.0000, X: -30.0000)\). Entering 0 [C] 1000 [D] sets linear coefficient \(C = 0.0\) and boundary constant \(D = 1000\) \((T: 2.0000, Z: -30.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1000.0000)\). Striking [XEQ] runs Cardano's closed-form cubic resolvent, factoring \(2(x+5)(x-10)^2 = 0\); keying [RCL] 3 extracts the physical clamped-support double root \((T: -30.0000, Z: -5.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{10.000000}\text{ m})\) in Register \(X\), where the repeated multiplicity confirms both \(v(L) = 0\) and \(v'(L) = 0\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.7: Rocket Staging Mass Ratio Optimization
docs.text:
A two-stage orbital launch vehicle with payload \(m_p = 500\text{ kg}\) and stage structural mass fractions \(\epsilon = 0.10\) must maximize total Tsiolkovsky burnout velocity \(\Delta v = c_1 \ln R_1 + c_2 \ln R_2\) under a fixed gross liftoff mass constraint. Applying Lagrange multipliers to the coupled stage mass ratios yields a symmetric quadratic optimality condition:

\[\lambda^2 - 2 \mu \lambda + \mu = 0 \implies \lambda^2 - 4.828427 \lambda + 2.414214 = 0\]

Keystrokes: [↱] [POLY] 1 [A] 4.828427 [+/-] [B] 2.414214 [C] 0 [D] [XEQ] [RCL] 5 \(\rightarrow\) 4.2619723651

In [↱] [POLY], entering 1 [A] 4.828427 [+/-] [B] enters unit quadratic and negative coupling term \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.0000, X: -4.828427)\). Entering 2.414214 [C] sets structural constant \(C = 2.414214\) (with \(D\) defaulting to \(0.0\) automatically for quadratic solving, or keyed as 0 [D]) \((T: 1.0000, Z: -4.828427, Y: 2.414214, X: 0.0000)\). Striking [XEQ] evaluates Cardano roots; keying [RCL] 5 yields the optimal stage mass ratio \((T: -4.828427, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{4.261972})\) in Register \(X\) (with secondary reciprocal root \(\lambda_2 = 0.566455\) in variable 3), confirming \(\lambda = 4.261972\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.8: Economic Production Lot Size with Quadratic Storage Congestion
docs.text:
In a high-density distribution warehouse where floor congestion imposes a quadratic marginal holding cost (\(h_2 = \$0.05/\text{unit}^2\cdot\text{yr}\)) atop the classical Ford W. Harris (1913) linear inventory holding rate (\(h_1 = \$7.35/\text{unit}\cdot\text{yr}\)) and annualized setup-demand product (\(5,000\text{ units}^2/\text{yr}\)), differentiating total annual cost \(\text{TC}(Q) = \frac{K D}{Q} + \frac{h_1 Q}{2} + \frac{h_2 Q^2}{4}\) with respect to lot size \(Q\) yields the quadratic equilibrium condition: $\(0.05 Q^2 + 7.35 Q - 5,000 = 0\)$

In [↱] [POLY], keying 0.05 [A] 7.35 [B] loads quadratic congestion coefficient \(A = 0.05\) and linear holding coefficient \(B = 7.35\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0500, X: 7.3500)\). Entering 5000 [+/-] [C] [XEQ] loads setup constant \(C = -5,000.0\) (with \(D = 0.0\) by default) and computes the Cardano roots \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0500, Y: -398.1571, X: 0.0000)\). Keying [RCL] 5 recalls the positive optimal production lot size \((T: 0.0500, Z: -398.1571, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{251.157127}\text{ units})\) into Register \(X\), yielding \(Q^* = 251.16\text{ units}\) (smaller than the congestion-free Wilson EOQ of \(\sqrt{2(5000)/7.35} = 368.86\text{ units}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.9: Laser Resonator Cavity Gaussian Beam Waist Quadratic
docs.text:
A thermal lens with focal parameter \(f = 350\text{ mm}\) inside a flat-flat laser resonator cavity of length \(L = 600\text{ mm}\) establishes a confocal Rayleigh range squared \(z_0^2 = L(2f - L) = 600(700 - 600) = 60,000\text{ mm}^2\) (\(z_0 = 244.9490\text{ mm}\)). By Kogelnik's \(ABCD\) complex beam parameter transformation, the intracavity TEM\(_{00}\) beam waist positions \(z\) satisfy the quadratic resonator stability equation: $\(z^2 - L z + z_0^2 = 0 \implies z^2 - 600 z + 60,000 = 0\)$

In [↱] [POLY], keying 1 [A] 600 [+/-] [B] loads quadratic coefficient \(A = 1.0\) and cavity span \(B = -600.0\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.0000, X: -600.0000)\). Entering 60000 [C] [XEQ] sets \(C = 60,000.0\) and solves the quadratic \((T: 0.0000, Z: 1.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0000)\). Keying [RCL] 3 extracts the primary intracavity waist position \((T: 1.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{126.794919}\text{ mm})\), and keying [RCL] 5 recalls the conjugate symmetric waist location \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 126.7949, X: \mathbf{473.205081}\text{ mm})\) (with \(z_1 + z_2 = L = 600.0\text{ mm}\) by Viète's sum of roots).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.10: Centrifugal Pump and Piping System Operating Point Quadratic
docs.text:
A centrifugal pump with backward-curved impeller blades exhibits manometric head curve \(H_p(Q) = 60 + 0.15 Q - 0.002 Q^2\), while the pipeline system resistance (static lift plus Darcy-Weisbach friction loss) is \(H_s(Q) = 15 + 0.005 Q^2\). Equating pump supply head to pipeline demand head determines the steady-state hydraulic operating point: $\(60 + 0.15 Q - 0.002 Q^2 = 15 + 0.005 Q^2 \implies 0.007 Q^2 - 0.15 Q - 45 = 0\)$

In [↱] [POLY], entering 0.007 [A] 0.15 [+/-] [B] loads combined hydraulic resistance \(A = 0.0070\) and linear Euler swirl coefficient \(B = -0.1500\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0070, X: -0.1500)\). Keying 45 [+/-] [C] [XEQ] sets static head differential \(C = -45.0\) and solves for the roots \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0070, Y: -70.1768, X: 0.0000)\). Pressing [RCL] 5 isolates the physical positive operating discharge \((T: 0.0070, Z: -70.1768, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{91.605369}\text{ m}^3/\text{hr})\), yielding \(Q = 91.61\text{ m}^3/\text{hr}\) at operating head \(H = 56.97\text{ m}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.11: Combined Stokes-Newton Aerodynamic Drag Equilibrium
docs.text:
A spherical meteorological drop-sonde descending through the atmosphere experiences both linear Stokes viscous shear drag (\(c_1 v = 6\pi\mu r v\), with \(c_1 = 0.27\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}\)) and quadratic Newton pressure-wake drag (\(c_2 v^2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho C_D A v^2\), with \(c_2 = 0.018\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}^2/\text{m}^2\)) balancing its net buoyant weight \(W = 31.5\text{ N}\): $\(c_2 v^2 + c_1 v - W = 0 \implies 0.018 v^2 + 0.27 v - 31.5 = 0\)$

In [↱] [POLY], loading 0.018 [A] 0.27 [B] enters quadratic pressure-drag coefficient \(A = 0.0180\) and linear viscous coefficient \(B = 0.2700\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0180, X: 0.2700)\). Keying 31.5 [+/-] [C] [XEQ] loads net weight \(C = -31.5\) and solves the quadratic \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0180, Y: -50.0000, X: 0.0000)\). Pressing [RCL] 5 recalls the positive terminal equilibrium velocity \((T: 0.0180, Z: -50.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{35.000000}\text{ m/s})\), yielding \(v = 35.00\text{ m/s}\) (\(126.0\text{ km/h}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.12: Non-Linear Torsional Pendulum Oscillation Frequency
docs.text:
A hardening Duffing-type torsional suspension exhibits cubic nonlinear restoring torque \(\tau(\theta) = -k \theta - \alpha \theta^3\) under static external torque \(\tau_{\text{ext}} = 5.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\). For linear stiffness \(k = 10\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}\) and strain-hardening coefficient \(\alpha = 2\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/rad}^3\), static angular deflection \(\theta\) satisfies a naturally depressed cubic polynomial (\(B = 0\)):

\[2 \theta^3 + 10 \theta - 5 = 0\]

Keystrokes: [↱] [POLY] 2 [A] 0 [B] 10 [C] 5 [+/-] [D] [XEQ] [x⇄y] \(\rightarrow\) 0.478138005

In [↱] [POLY], entering 2 [A] loads non-linear cubic coefficient \(A = 2.0\) (with quadratic coefficient \(B\) defaulting to \(0.0\) automatically, or explicitly keyed as 0 [B]) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 2.0000, X: 0.0000)\). Entering 10 [C] 5 [+/-] [D] loads linear restoring torque \(C = 10.0\) and external load \(D = -5.0\) \((T: 2.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 10.0000, X: -5.0000)\). Striking [XEQ] computes Cardano roots; because \(p = C/A = 5 > 0\), the cubic is strictly monotonic and the unique real equilibrium deflection angle emerges in Register \(Y\) \((T: 2.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: \mathbf{0.478138}, X: 0.000000)\) with the complex conjugate pair stored in variables 3–6, or recalled directly via [RCL] 1, confirming \(\theta = 0.478138\text{ radians}\) (\(27.40^\circ\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.13: Annular Clutch Cubic Torque Allocation Root
docs.text:
For a uniform-wear annular friction clutch of outer radius \(R = 150.0\text{ mm}\) where axial contact pressure varies inversely with radius (\(p(r) \propto 1/r\)), normalizing the inner radius \(x = r_i / R \in (0, 1)\) produces normalized frictional torque capacity \(T(x) \propto x(1 - x^2)\), which peaks at \(x^* = 1/\sqrt{3} \approx 0.57735\). Sizing an annular lining to deliver a specified fraction of theoretical capacity requires solving the depressed cubic polynomial (\(\Delta < 0\), casus irreducibilis with three distinct real roots): $\(x^3 - 3 x + 1.5 = 0\)$

In [↱] [POLY], keying 1 [A] 0 [B] sets leading cubic coefficient \(A = 1.0\) and depressed quadratic coefficient \(B = 0.0\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.0000, X: 0.0000)\). Entering 3 [+/-] [C] 1.5 [D] [XEQ] loads \(C = -3.0, D = 1.5\) and executes François Viète's trigonometric trisection \((T: 1.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: -1.9422, X: 0.0000)\). Keying [RCL] 3 150 [×] recalls the unique physical inner-to-outer radius ratio \(x = 0.557875 \in (0, 1)\) and scales by \(R = 150.0\text{ mm}\) \((T: -1.9422, Z: -1.9422, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{83.681205}\text{ mm})\), yielding \(r_i = 83.68\text{ mm}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.14: Hydraulic Jump Conjugate Depth Quadratic (Bélanger Equation)
docs.text:
A supercritical open-channel spillway flow with upstream depth \(y_1 = 0.40\text{ m}\) and Froude number \(\text{Fr}_1 = 4.5\) (\(\text{Fr}_1^2 = 20.25\)) undergoes a turbulent stationary shock—a hydraulic jump—into tranquil subcritical flow. Although mechanical energy is dissipated across the turbulent roller, Jean-Baptiste Ch. Bélanger (1838) showed that specific momentum flux \(\frac{1}{2}y^2 + \frac{q^2}{gy}\) is conserved across the jump, yielding the Bélanger quadratic equation for downstream conjugate (sequent) depth \(y_2\): $\(y_2^2 + y_1 y_2 - 2 y_1^2 \text{Fr}_1^2 = 0 \implies y_2^2 + 0.40 y_2 - 6.48 = 0 \implies y_2 = \mathbf{2.353429\text{ meters}}\)$

In [↱] [POLY], entering 1 [A] 0.40 [B] loads unit quadratic coefficient \(A = 1.0\) and upstream depth \(B = 0.40\text{ m}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.0000, X: 0.4000)\). Keying 6.48 [+/-] [C] [XEQ] loads momentum constant \(C = -2(0.40)^2(20.25) = -6.48\) and extracts the roots \((T: 0.0000, Z: 1.0000, Y: -2.7534, X: 0.0000)\). Pressing [RCL] 5 recalls the positive subcritical conjugate depth \((T: 1.0000, Z: -2.7534, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{2.353429}\text{ m})\), yielding \(y_2 = 2.3534\text{ meters}\) (a \(5.88\times\) depth jump dissipating \(\Delta E = \frac{(y_2 - y_1)^3}{4 y_1 y_2} = 1.98\text{ m}\) of hydraulic head).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.15: Acoustical Helmholtz Resonator Neck-Radius Quadratic
docs.text:
An acoustic Helmholtz absorber chamber of volume \(V = 1.93793 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3\) and physical neck length \(L = 50.0\text{ mm}\) (\(c = 343\text{ m/s}\)) is tuned to attenuate a \(f_0 = 120\text{ Hz}\) tonal resonance. Because the oscillating air plug in the neck radiates piston-like acoustic inertia into both the cavity and free space, Lord Rayleigh's flanged end-correction extends the effective inertial length to \(L' = L + 1.7a\), coupling neck radius \(a\) (in \(\text{mm}\)) into both numerator area \(A = \pi a^2\) and denominator mass length inside \(f_0 = \frac{c}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{\pi a^2}{V(L + 1.7a)}}\): $\(a^2 - \left(\frac{6.8\pi f_0^2 V}{c^2}\right) a - \left(\frac{4\pi f_0^2 V L}{c^2}\right) = 0 \implies a^2 - 5.066225 a - 149.006625 = 0\)$

In [↱] [POLY], keying 1 [A] 5.066225 [+/-] [B] loads \(A = 1.0\) and Rayleigh end-correction coefficient \(B = -5.066225\text{ mm}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.0000, X: -5.066225)\). Entering 149.006625 [+/-] [C] [XEQ] sets cavity constant \(C = -149.006625\text{ mm}^2\) and solves the quadratic \((T: 0.0000, Z: 1.0000, Y: -9.9338, X: 0.0000)\). Striking [RCL] 5 isolates the physical positive neck radius \((T: 1.0000, Z: -9.9338, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{15.000000}\text{ mm})\), giving \(a = 15.00\text{ mm}\) (neck diameter \(d = 2a = 30.00\text{ mm}\) and effective acoustic neck length \(L' = 50.0 + 1.7(15.0) = 75.50\text{ mm}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.16: Relativistic Proton Kinetic Energy Quadratic
docs.text:
A synchrotron proton (\(m_0 c^2 = 938.272\text{ MeV}\)) circulates with relativistic momentum \(p c = 2,500.0\text{ MeV}\). Substituting total relativistic energy \(E = K + m_0 c^2\) into Einstein's Lorentz-invariant energy-momentum four-vector norm \(E^2 - (pc)^2 - (m_0 c^2)^2 = 0\) eliminates the rest-mass square and yields a quadratic equation directly in kinetic energy \(K\): $\(K^2 + 2(m_0 c^2) K - (pc)^2 = 0 \implies K^2 + 1876.544 K - 6,250,000 = 0 \implies K = \mathbf{1,732.0003\text{ MeV}}\)$

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.17: Heat Exchanger Implicit Terminal Temperature Root (LMTD)

Because \(\Delta T_2 = X\) appears simultaneously in the linear numerator difference and the logarithmic denominator ratio of \(\text{LMTD} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}\), isolating the cold-end terminal temperature approach requires solving the implicit transcendental LMTD equation: $\(f(X) = \frac{65 - X}{\ln(65 / X)} - 41.8624 = 0 \implies X = \Delta T_2 = \mathbf{25.0000^\circ\text{C}}\)$

Striking [↱] [SOLVE] X executes Brent's hybrid solver to isolate the cold-end terminal temperature difference \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 30.0000, X: \mathbf{25.000000}^\circ\text{C})\), yielding \(\Delta T_2 = 25.00^\circ\text{C}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.19: Planetary Escaping Orbit Hyperbolic Excess Velocity Quadratic

During a Trans-Mars injection burn at low-Earth parking radius \(r = 6,671\text{ km}\) (\(\mu_E = 398,600\text{ km}^3/\text{s}^2\), local parabolic escape energy \(\frac{2\mu_E}{r} = 119.5023\text{ km}^2/\text{s}^2\)), a spacecraft reaches geocentric burnout speed \(v = 11.45\text{ km/s}\). Conservation of specific orbital mechanical energy \(\mathcal{E} = \frac{v^2}{2} - \frac{\mu_E}{r} = \frac{v_\infty^2}{2}\) yields the vis-viva quadratic for the asymptotic hyperbolic excess velocity \(v_\infty\) (and characteristic injection energy \(C_3 = v_\infty^2\)): $\(v_\infty^2 - v^2 + \frac{2\mu_E}{r} = 0 \implies v_\infty = \sqrt{11.45^2 - \frac{2(398600)}{6671}} = \sqrt{131.1025 - 119.5023} = \sqrt{11.6002} = \mathbf{3.4059\text{ km/s}}\)$

Keying 2 [ENTER] 398600 [×] 6671 [÷] [-] evaluates local gravitational escape energy \(2\mu_E / r = 119.5023\text{ km}^2/\text{s}^2\) and subtracts to isolate \(C_3 = v_\infty^2 = 11.6002\text{ km}^2/\text{s}^2\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 11.6002)\). Striking [√x] extracts the positive quadratic root in place, resolving asymptotic interplanetary departure velocity \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{3.405903}\text{ km/s})\), yielding \(v_\infty = 3.4059\text{ km/s}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.20: Planar Couette-Poiseuille Channel Velocity Profile Root
docs.text:
Incompressible Newtonian fluid (\(\mu = 0.10\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}\), \(\nu = 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}\)) flows between a stationary lower wall (\(y = 0\)) and a parallel upper wall at \(h = 0.050\text{ m}\) translating at \(U = 2.0\text{ m/s}\) (\(\text{Re} = U h / \nu = 1,000.0\)) against an adverse stream-wise pressure gradient \(dp/dx = +120\text{ Pa/m}\). Integrating the Navier-Stokes momentum balance \(\mu \frac{d^2 u}{dy^2} = \frac{dp}{dx}\) superimposes linear Couette shear and parabolic Poiseuille backflow into \(u(y) = 600 y^2 + 10 y\). Find the channel elevation \(y\) where local velocity reaches \(u(y) = 1.00\text{ m/s}\): $\(600 y^2 + 10 y - 1.00 = 0 \implies y = \mathbf{0.033333\text{ meters}}\)$

In [↱] [POLY], loading 600 [A] 10 [B] enters pressure-gradient curvature \(A = \frac{1}{2\mu}\frac{dp}{dx} = 600.0\) and wall-shear gradient \(B = 10.0\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 600.0000, X: 10.0000)\). Keying 1 [+/-] [C] [XEQ] loads target velocity offset \(C = -1.00\) and solves the quadratic \((T: 0.0000, Z: 600.0000, Y: -0.0500, X: 0.0000)\). Pressing [RCL] 5 isolates the physical channel elevation \((T: 600.0000, Z: -0.0500, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.033333}\text{ m})\), yielding \(y = 33.33\text{ mm}\) (\(2/3\) of the channel gap \(h\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.21: Electromagnetic Skin-Depth Attenuation Wavenumber Root

At industrial plasma RF excitation frequency \(f = 13.56\text{ MHz}\) in an aluminum conductor (\(\sigma = 3.5 \times 10^7\text{ S/m}\), \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m}\)), Maxwell's curl equations in a good conductor (\(\sigma \gg \omega\varepsilon\)) reduce to the magnetic diffusion wave equation \(\nabla^2 \mathbf{E} = j\omega\mu_0\sigma \mathbf{E}\), whose attenuation wavenumber \(k = 1/\delta\) satisfies \(k^2 - \pi f \mu_0 \sigma = 0\): $\(\delta = \frac{1}{k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f \mu_0 \sigma}} = \mathbf{2.311 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}} = 23.11\,\mu\text{m}\)$

Keying 4 [↱] [π] [×] 1 [E] 7 [+/-] [×] [×] multiplies by permeability \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m}\), yielding \(53.5327\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 53.5327)\). docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.22: Standard-Atmosphere Cubic Barometric Polynomial via Horner's Method

Striking [×] 101.325 [+] multiplies by the fresh copy of \(8.4350\) in Register \(Y\) and adds sea-level standard pressure \(101.325\text{ kPa}\), resolving static pressure at \(h = 8.435\text{ km}\) \((T: 8.4350, Z: 8.4350, Y: 8.4350, X: \mathbf{52.693171}\text{ kPa})\) without ever re-keying \(h\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.23: Thick-Walled Pressure Vessel Lamé Wall-Thickness Quadratic
docs.text:
A high-pressure cylindrical autoclave of outer radius \(R_o = 200\text{ mm}\) (\(D = 400\text{ mm}\)) containing internal pressure \(P = 45.0\text{ MPa}\) must limit maximum inner-bore circumferential (hoop) stress—governed by Gabriel Lamé's (1852) thick-shell elasticity solution \(\sigma_\theta(R_i) = P \frac{R_o^2 + (R_o - t)^2}{R_o^2 - (R_o - t)^2}\)—to allowable working stress \(\sigma_{\text{allow}} = 125.0\text{ MPa}\), yielding the wall-thickness quadratic: $\(17 t^2 - 6,800 t + 360,000 = 0 \implies t = \mathbf{62.801132\text{ mm}}\)$

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.1: Exponential Distribution CDF Integral
docs.text:
In reliability engineering, the memoryless exponential distribution models the survival of electronic components subjected to random Poisson failure shocks. The cumulative probability that a component with unit hazard rate \(\lambda = 1\) fails before normalized time \(t = 1\) is \(F(1) = \int_0^1 e^{-x} dx\):

\[\int_0^1 e^{-x} \, dx = 1 - e^{-1} \approx 1 - 0.3678794 = \mathbf{0.632120559}\]

Program the hazard density into [↱] [EQN] as X [+/-] [eˣ]. Staging the unit lifetime interval 0 [ENTER] 1 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 1.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.0000)\) and invoking [↱] [∫] X constructs the Romberg tableau across the concave decay curve, depositing the certified Richardson truncation bound \(4.82 \times 10^{-12}\) into Register \(Y\) and the canonical \(1 - e^{-1} \approx \mathbf{0.632120559}\) (\(63.21\%\) one-time-constant failure probability) into Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 1.0000, Y: 4.82\times 10^{-12}, X: 0.632120559)\).

Analytical Stack Verification: 1 [ENTER] 1 [+/-] [eˣ] [-] \(\implies \mathbf{0.632121}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.2: Uniform Distribution Probability Integral
docs.text:
A quantizer or phase-locked loop whose phase error is uniformly distributed across \([0, 10]\) has constant density \(f(x) = 0.10\). Integrating over the half-span \([0, 5]\) provides an immediate diagnostic baseline for zero-curvature quadrature:

\[\int_0^5 0.10 \, dx = 0.10 \times 5 = \mathbf{0.500000}\]

Program the constant density 0.1 into [↱] [EQN], stage the interval 0 [ENTER] 5 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.1000, Y: 0.0000, X: 5.0000)\), and execute [↱] [∫] X. Because all higher derivatives \(f^{(2m)}(x)\) vanish identically in the Euler-Maclaurin expansion, the very first trapezoidal panel \(R(0,0)\) is exact, returning an identically zero truncation error bound \(0.0000\) in Register \(Y\) and \(\mathbf{0.500000000}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.1000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.500000000)\).

Analytical Stack Verification: 0.1 [ENTER] 5 [×] \(\implies \mathbf{0.500000}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.3: Gaussian Normal 1-Sigma Confidence Interval (\(68.27\%\))
docs.text:
The Gaussian density \(\phi(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}\) possesses no elementary antiderivative—a theorem proved by Joseph Liouville in 1835. Integrating across the central inflection points from \(z = -1.0\) to \(z = +1.0\) establishes the \(1\sigma\) metrological confidence band:

\[P(-1 \le Z \le 1) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-1}^1 e^{-x^2 / 2} \, dx \approx \mathbf{0.682689492}\]

With the standard normal curve NORM active, staging the symmetric \(1\sigma\) bounds via 1 [+/-] [ENTER] 1 (or 1 [+/-] [ENTER] [+/-]) \((T: -1.0000, Z: 1.0000, Y: -1.0000, X: 1.0000)\) and pressing [↱] [∫] X eliminates the inflection curvature through Richardson extrapolation, returning error bound \(1.85 \times 10^{-11}\) in Register \(Y\) and the \(68.27\%\) confidence probability \(\mathbf{0.682689492}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: -1.0000, Z: 1.0000, Y: 1.85\times 10^{-11}, X: 0.682689492)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.4: Gaussian Normal 2-Sigma Confidence Interval (\(95.45\%\))
docs.text:

\[P(-2 \le Z \le 2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-2}^2 e^{-x^2 / 2} \, dx \approx \mathbf{0.954499736}\]

Using the same NORM equation, stage the \(2\sigma\) limits 2 [+/-] [ENTER] 2 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: -2.0000, X: 2.0000)\) and invoke [↱] [∫] X. The Romberg tableau resolves the inflection transition with error bound \(3.14 \times 10^{-11}\) in \(Y\) and deposits the two-sided \(95.45\%\) confidence integral \(\mathbf{0.954499736}\) into Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 3.14\times 10^{-11}, X: 0.954499736)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.5: Gaussian Normal 3-Sigma Confidence Interval (\(99.73\%\))
docs.text:
In statistical process control (Walter Shewhart's \(\pm 3\sigma\) control limits), integrating from \(z = -3.0\) to \(z = +3.0\) captures all but \(0.27\%\) (\(2,700\text{ ppm}\)) of random variation:

\[P(-3 \le Z \le 3) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-3}^3 e^{-x^2 / 2} \, dx \approx \mathbf{0.997300204}\]

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.6: Polytropic Gas Expansion Work: \(P V^{1.4} = C\)
docs.text:
An ideal diatomic gas expands reversibly in an insulated cylinder from \(V_1 = 0.02\text{ m}^3\) to \(V_2 = 0.08\text{ m}^3\). Initial chamber pressure \(P_1 = 600.0\text{ kPa} = 600,000\text{ Pa}\). Polytropic index \(n = 1.4\). State constant \(C = P_1 V_1^{1.4} = 600,000 \times (0.02)^{1.4} \approx 2,492.357\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{m}^{4.2}\). Boundary expansion work \(W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P(V) \, dV\): $\(W = C \int_{0.02}^{0.08} V^{-1.4} \, dV = \frac{P_1 V_1 \left[ 1 - (V_1/V_2)^{0.4} \right]}{0.4} = \frac{12,000 \left[ 1 - (0.25)^{0.4} \right]}{0.4}\)$ $\((0.25)^{0.4} \approx 0.57434918 \implies 1 - 0.57434918 = 0.42565082\)$ $\(W = \frac{12,000 \times 0.42565082}{0.4} = 30,000 \times 0.42565082 = \mathbf{12,769.52\text{ Joules}} = \mathbf{12.7695\text{ kJ}}\)$

Program the adiabatic pressure law V 1.4 [+/-] [yˣ] 2492.357 [×] into [↱] [EQN]. Stage the expansion volume bounds 0.02 [ENTER] 0.08 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0200, X: 0.0800)\) and press [↱] [∫] V \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 2.18\times 10^{-10}, X: 12769.5248)\). Romberg quadrature integrates the steep inverse-power pressure decay across the \(4:1\) expansion ratio, placing error bound \(2.18 \times 10^{-10}\) in Register \(Y\) and mechanical boundary work \(12,769.5248\text{ J}\) in Register \(X\), which 1000 [÷] scales to kilojoules \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 2.18\times 10^{-10}, X: 12.7695)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.7: Surface Area of Paraboloid Radar Dish of Revolution
docs.text:
A parabolic satellite reflector dish is generated by revolving \(y = 0.25 x^2\) about the vertical \(y\)-axis from center \(x = 0\) to outer rim radius \(R = 2.0\text{ m}\). Surface area of revolution formula: $\(A = 2\pi \int_0^R x \sqrt{1 + [y'(x)]^2} \, dx = 2\pi \int_0^2 x \sqrt{1 + (0.5 x)^2} \, dx = 2\pi \int_0^2 x \sqrt{1 + 0.25 x^2} \, dx\)$ Analytical evaluation via \(u = 1 + 0.25 x^2, du = 0.5 x dx \implies x dx = 2 du\): $\(A = 4\pi \int_1^2 u^{1/2} \, du = \frac{8\pi}{3} \left[ u^{3/2} \right]_1^2 = \frac{8\pi}{3} (2\sqrt{2} - 1) = \frac{8\pi}{3}(1.8284271) \approx \mathbf{15.317764\text{ m}^2}\)$

Program the surface-element integrand X 0.5 [×] [↰] [x²] 1 [+] [√x] X [×] 2 [×] [↱] [π] [×] into [↱] [EQN]. Staging the aperture radial bounds 0 [ENTER] 2 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.0000)\) and pressing [↱] [∫] X integrates the curved paraboloid shell—which exceeds the flat aperture disc area \(\pi R^2 = 12.5664\text{ m}^2\) by \(21.9\%\)—returning error bound \(2.14 \times 10^{-10}\) in Register \(Y\) and surface area \(\mathbf{15.317764\text{ m}^2}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 2.14\times 10^{-10}, X: 15.317764)\) (\(A = 15.3178\text{ m}^2\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.8: Thermal Heat Conduction Across Temperature-Dependent Wall
docs.text:
High-temperature furnace wall of thickness \(L = 0.20\text{ m}\) and cross-sectional area \(A = 10.0\text{ m}^2\). Material thermal conductivity is temperature-dependent: \(k(T) = 0.50 + 0.002 T\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}\). Internal hot face \(T_1 = 800.0\text{ K}\), exterior cold face \(T_2 = 300.0\text{ K}\). One-dimensional steady heat flow rate \(q\) via Fourier's Law: $\(q = \frac{A}{L} \int_{300}^{800} k(T) \, dT = \frac{10.0}{0.20} \int_{300}^{800} (0.50 + 0.002 T) \, dT = 50.0 \left[ 0.50 T + 0.001 T^2 \right]_{300}^{800}\)$ $\(q = 50.0 \left[ 0.50(500) + 0.001(800^2 - 300^2) \right] = 50.0 [250 + 0.001(640,000 - 90,000)] = 50.0 [250 + 550]\)$ $\(q = 50.0 \times 800 = \mathbf{40,000.0\text{ Watts}} = \mathbf{40.000\text{ kW}}\)$

Program Kirchhoff's integral transform T 0.002 [×] 0.5 [+] 50 [×] into [↱] [EQN]. Staging the cold-to-hot wall boundary temperatures 300 [ENTER] 800 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 25.0000, Y: 300.0000, X: 800.0000)\) and pressing [↱] [∫] T \((T: 0.0000, Z: 25.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 40000.0000)\) integrates the temperature-dependent refractory conductivity with zero truncation error (\(0.0000\) in \(Y\), since Trapezoidal/Simpson quadrature is exact on linear and cubic polynomials), yielding \(40,000.0\text{ W}\) in \(X\) before 1000 [÷] scales the flux to kilowatts \((T: 25.0000, Z: 25.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 40.0000)\) (\(q = 40.000\text{ kW}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.9: Fresnel Sine Integral in Diffraction Optics (\(S(x)\))
docs.text:
When coherent light passes across a sharp razor edge, Augustin-Jean Fresnel (1818) showed that the near-field diffraction fringes are governed by the non-elementary Fresnel sine integral:

$\(S(x) = \int_0^x \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} t^2\right) dt\)$ Evaluate \(S(2.0)\) at normalized aperture coordinate \(x = 2.0\).

With radian mode engaged ([RAD]), program the quadratic-phase chirp integrand T [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×] 2 [÷] [SIN] into [↱] [EQN]. Staging 0 [ENTER] 2 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.0000)\) and pressing [↱] [∫] T resolves the accelerating phase oscillations across two full half-cycles, returning certified error bound \(1.48 \times 10^{-10}\) in Register \(Y\) and the Fresnel sine coordinate \(S(2.0) = \mathbf{0.343416}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.48\times 10^{-10}, X: 0.343416)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.10: Fresnel Cosine Integral (\(C(x)\))
docs.text:
The companion Fresnel cosine integral defines the horizontal coordinate of Marie Alfred Cornu's clothoid spiral (1874), whose arc length equals \(x\) and whose curvature grows linearly with arc length (\(\kappa = \pi x\)):

\[C(x) = \int_0^x \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} t^2\right) dt$$ Evaluate $C(2.0)$ at $x = 2.0$. Together with $S(2.0) = 0.343416$ stored in Register `A` from Workbook Problem 8.9, this defines the Cornu spiral phasor position: $$r = \sqrt{C^2(2) + S^2(2)} = \sqrt{0.488253^2 + 0.343416^2} = \sqrt{0.238391 + 0.117935} = \sqrt{0.356326} \approx \mathbf{0.596930}\]

In radian mode ([RAD]), with the companion cosine integrand T [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×] 2 [÷] [COS] in [↱] [EQN], first store \(S(2.0)\) in Register A, then integrate \(C(2.0)\) and combine both components on the stack without re-typing intermediate floats:

Store the Fresnel sine component 0 [ENTER] 2 [↱] [∫] T [STO] A \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.48\times 10^{-10}, X: 0.343416)\), then set integration limits 0 [ENTER] 2 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.3434, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.0000)\) and press [↱] [∫] T \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.3434, Y: 2.22\times 10^{-10}, X: 0.488253)\) to evaluate the Fresnel cosine integral \(C(2.0) = 0.488253\) with error bound \(2.22 \times 10^{-10}\) in Register \(Y\). Squaring, recalling \(S(2.0)\) from Register A to square and add, and taking the square root ([↰] [x²] [RCL] A [↰] [x²] [+] [√x]) yields the Cornu spiral phasor amplitude \(\mathbf{0.596930}\) \((T: 0.3434, Z: 0.3434, Y: 2.22\times 10^{-10}, X: 0.596930)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.11: Gravitational Attraction of Thin Rod on End Particle
docs.text:
A slender spacecraft boom of length \(L = 5.0\text{ m}\) and uniform mass \(M = 100.0\text{ kg}\) is positioned along the \(x\)-axis from \(x = 1.0\text{ m}\) to \(x = 6.0\text{ m}\). A sensor payload of mass \(m = 2.0\text{ kg}\) is positioned at the origin \(x = 0\). Linear mass density \(\lambda = M/L = 100.0 / 5.0 = 20.0\text{ kg/m}\). Gravitational constant \(G = 6.6743 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2\). Newtonian attraction force \(F\): $\(F = G m \lambda \int_1^6 \frac{dx}{x^2} = (6.6743 \times 10^{-11}) \times 2.0 \times 20.0 \left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_1^6 = 2.66972 \times 10^{-9} \left[ 1 - \frac{1}{6} \right]\)$ $\(F = 2.66972 \times 10^{-9} \times \frac{5}{6} = \mathbf{2.224767 \times 10^{-9}\text{ Newtons}} = \mathbf{2.224767\text{ nN}}\)$

Program the Newtonian differential attraction X [↰] [x²] [1/x] 2.66972 [E] 9 [+/-] [×] into [↱] [EQN]. Staging the boom span limits 1 [ENTER] 6 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.0000, X: 6.0000)\) and pressing [↱] [∫] X \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.15\times 10^{-16}, X: 2.224767\times 10^{-9})\) integrates the inverse-square field—demonstrating why distributed-mass gravity cannot be approximated at the geometric midpoint \(x = 3.5\text{ m}\), but acts at the harmonic mean distance \(\sqrt{x_1 x_2} = \sqrt{6} \approx 2.449\text{ m}\). Multiplying by \(10^9\) (1 [E] 9 [×]) scales the self-gravity perturbation to nanonewtons \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.15\times 10^{-16}, X: 2.224767)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.12: Fourier Series 1st Harmonic Sine Coefficient (\(b_1\))
docs.text:
An odd square wave of fundamental period \(2\pi\) has value \(+1\) on \((0, \pi)\) and \(-1\) on \((-\pi, 0)\). The fundamental Fourier harmonic sine coefficient \(b_1\) is: $\(b_1 = \frac{2}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \sin(x) \, dx = \frac{2}{\pi} \left[ -\cos(x) \right]_0^\pi = \frac{2}{\pi} (1 - (-1)) = \frac{4}{\pi} \approx \mathbf{1.273240}\)$

With radian mode engaged ([RAD]), program the orthogonal harmonic projection X [SIN] into [↱] [EQN]. Staging the half-period interval 0 [↱] [π] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 3.141593)\) and pressing [↱] [∫] X \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.82\times 10^{-11}, X: 2.000000)\) evaluates the sine arch area to \(2.000000\) with error bound \(1.82 \times 10^{-11}\) in \(Y\). Normalizing by 2 [×] [↱] [π] [÷] resolves the fundamental Fourier amplitude \(b_1 = 4/\pi \approx \mathbf{1.273240}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.82\times 10^{-11}, X: 1.273240)\)—explaining why the first harmonic of a unit square wave overshoots the flat \(\pm 1\) plateau by \(27.3\%\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.13: Sound Exposure Level (SEL) from Transient Flyover Noise
docs.text:
An aircraft flyover noise pulse at an airfield boundary is modeled by acoustic pressure \(p(t) = p_0 e^{-t^2 / 20}\text{ Pa}\) with peak pressure \(p_0 = 2.00\text{ Pa}\) over \(t \in [-15, +15]\text{ s}\). Reference acoustic pressure \(p_{\text{ref}} = 20\,\mu\text{Pa} = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Pa}\), reference time \(t_0 = 1.0\text{ s}\). Sound exposure integral \(E = \int_{-15}^{15} p^2(t) \, dt = \int_{-15}^{15} 4.0 e^{-t^2 / 10} \, dt\): $\(E \approx 4.0 \sqrt{10\pi} = 4.0 \times 5.604991 = \mathbf{22.41996\text{ Pa}^2\cdot\text{s}}\)$ $\(\text{SEL} = 10 \log_{10}\left( \frac{E}{p_{\text{ref}}^2 \cdot t_0} \right) = 10 \log_{10}\left( \frac{22.41996}{4.0 \times 10^{-10}} \right) = 10 \log_{10}(5.604991 \times 10^{10}) = \mathbf{107.4857\text{ dBA}}\)$

Because certification standards compress an entire transient acoustic event into a 1-second equivalent energy dose, entering the squared-pressure envelope T [↰] [x²] 10 [÷] [+/-] [eˣ] 4 [×] into [↱] [EQN] and sweeping across the 30-second flyover window 15 [+/-] [ENTER] 15 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 4.0000, Y: -15.0000, X: 15.0000)\) via [↱] [∫] T \((T: 0.0000, Z: 4.0000, Y: 4.88\times 10^{-11}, X: 22.419964)\) integrates total sound exposure \(E = 22.419964\text{ Pa}^2\cdot\text{s}\) in Register \(X\) (with quadrature uncertainty \(4.88 \times 10^{-11}\) in \(Y\)). Normalizing against the human auditory threshold \(p_{\text{ref}}^2 t_0 = 4.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ Pa}^2\cdot\text{s}\) and mapping to the decibel scale (4 [E] 10 [+/-] [÷] [↰] [LOG] 10 [×]) establishes the certified Sound Exposure Level \(\mathbf{107.4857\text{ dBA}}\) \((T: 4.0000, Z: 4.0000, Y: 4.88\times 10^{-11}, X: 107.485743)\) (\(\text{SEL} = 107.49\text{ dBA}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.14: Aerodynamic Circulation Line Integral & Prandtl Elliptic Spanwise Lift
docs.text:
An aircraft wing of span \(b = 12.0\text{ m}\) (\(y \in [-6, +6]\text{ m}\)) flying at freestream airspeed \(V_\infty = 60.0\text{ m/s}\) in air of density \(\rho_\infty = 1.225\text{ kg/m}^3\) exhibits Prandtl's minimum-induced-drag elliptic bound circulation distribution with root vortex circulation \(\Gamma_0 = 45.0\text{ m}^2/\text{s}\):

$\(\Gamma(y) = \Gamma_0 \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{2y}{b}\right)^2} = 45.0 \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{y}{6}\right)^2}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}\)$ By the Kutta-Joukowski theorem, sectional lift is \(L'(y) = \rho_\infty V_\infty \Gamma(y)\) (peaking at \(L'_0 = 1.225 \times 60.0 \times 45.0 = 3,307.50\text{ N/m}\) at the wing root), and total wing lift is the spanwise integral: $\(L = \rho_\infty V_\infty \int_{-6}^{6} 45.0 \sqrt{1 - (y/6)^2} \, dy = (1.225)(60.0)(45.0)\left(6\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 73.50 \times 424.1150 = \mathbf{31,172.45\text{ N}} = \mathbf{31.17\text{ kN}}\)$ Equivalent sustained aircraft mass: \(M = L / g = 31,172.45 / 9.80665 = \mathbf{3,178.71\text{ kg}} \approx \mathbf{3.18\text{ metric tonnes}}\).

In Ludwig Prandtl's lifting-line theory, an elliptical spanwise circulation profile produces uniform downwash across the trailing vortex sheet and minimizes induced drag. Defining Y 6 [÷] [↰] [x²] 1 [x⇄y] [-] [√x] 45 [×] in [↱] [EQN] and integrating from wingtip to wingtip 6 [+/-] [ENTER] 6 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 45.0000, Y: -6.0000, X: 6.0000)\) via [↱] [∫] Y \((T: 0.0000, Z: 45.0000, Y: 3.84\times 10^{-10}, X: 424.1150)\) yields the integrated vortex volume \(\int_{-6}^6 \Gamma(y)\,dy = 135\pi \approx 424.1150\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\). Scaling by the Kutta-Joukowski momentum flux \(\rho_\infty V_\infty\) (1.225 [×] 60 [×], \((T: 45.0000, Z: 45.0000, Y: 3.84\times 10^{-10}, X: 31172.4525)\)) gives total aerodynamic lift \(L = \mathbf{31,172.45\text{ N}}\) (\(\mathbf{31.17\text{ kN}}\)), which supports a steady-flight aircraft gross mass of \(\mathbf{3.18\text{ tonnes}}\) (9.80665 [÷] 1000 [÷], \((T: 45.0000, Z: 45.0000, Y: 3.84\times 10^{-10}, X: 3.1787)\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.15: Damped Harmonic Oscillator Energy Dissipated Per Cycle
docs.text:
Viscous dashpot damper force \(F_d = c \dot{x}\) with damping coefficient \(c = 15.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{s/m}\). Natural frequency \(\omega = 20.0\text{ rad/s}\), harmonic displacement amplitude \(X_0 = 0.020\text{ m}\) (\(20\text{ mm}\)). Velocity \(v(t) = -\omega X_0 \sin(\omega t) = -0.40 \sin(20 t)\text{ m/s}\). Oscillation period \(T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{\pi}{10} \approx 0.314159\text{ s}\). Energy dissipated per steady-state cycle: $\(\Delta E = \int_0^T c v^2(t) \, dt = 15.0 \int_0^{\pi/10} [ -0.40 \sin(20 t) ]^2 dt = 2.40 \int_0^{\pi/10} \sin^2(20 t) \, dt\)$ $\(\Delta E = 2.40 \times \left( \frac{T}{2} \right) = 2.40 \times \frac{\pi}{20} = 0.12 \pi \approx \mathbf{0.376991\text{ Joules}}\)$

Under steady-state harmonic excitation, the area enclosed by the elliptical force-displacement hysteresis loop equals the viscous thermal dissipation over one full period \(T = \pi/10\text{ s}\). With radian mode ([RAD]) active and the instantaneous power dissipation T 20 [×] [SIN] [↰] [x²] 2.4 [×] entered into [↱] [EQN], staging the single-cycle bounds 0 [↱] [π] 10 [÷] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.314159)\) and pressing [↱] [∫] T integrates the \(\sin^2(\omega t)\) waveform to an error bound of \(1.12 \times 10^{-11}\) in \(Y\) and per-cycle thermal loss \(\mathbf{0.376991\text{ Joules}}\) in \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.12\times 10^{-11}, X: 0.376991)\) (\(\Delta E = 0.3770\text{ Joules}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.16: Continuous Present Value of Perpetual Cash Flow Stream
docs.text:
Continuous discount rate \(r = 0.06\), cash flow intensity \(C(t) = 50,000 e^{-0.02 t}\):

\[PV = \int_0^{30} 50000 e^{-0.08 t} \, dt = \frac{50000}{0.08} [1 - e^{-2.4}] = 625,000 [1 - 0.090718] = \mathbf{\$568,301.25}\]

For a depleting petroleum reservoir or royalty trust whose production decays exponentially at \(2\%/\text{yr}\) while capital is discounted continuously at \(6\%/\text{yr}\), the net present value is governed by the combined hazard rate \(\lambda + r = 0.08\text{ yr}^{-1}\). Programming T 0.08 [×] [+/-] [eˣ] 50000 [×] into [↱] [EQN] and integrating over the 30-year concession horizon 0 [ENTER] 30 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 50000.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 30.0000)\) via [↱] [∫] T resolves the continuous valuation \(\mathbf{\$568,301.25}\) in Register \(X\) with quadrature error \(4.12 \times 10^{-11}\) in Register \(Y\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 50000.0000, Y: 4.12\times 10^{-11}, X: 568301.25)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.17: Second Moment of Area of Structural I-Beam Web (\(I_{xx}\))
docs.text:
For a vertical steel web of height \(h = 300\text{ mm}\) (\(y \in [-150, +150]\text{ mm}\)) and thickness \(t = 10\text{ mm}\), the flexural bending stiffness depends on the second moment of area \(I_{xx}\): $\(I_{xx} = \int_{-150}^{150} t y^2 \, dy = 10 \left[ \frac{y^3}{3} \right]_{-150}^{150} = \frac{20}{3}(3,375,000) = \mathbf{22,500,000\text{ mm}^4} = 2.25 \times 10^7\text{ mm}^4\)$

In Euler-Bernoulli beam bending, fibers farthest from the neutral axis carry linearly increasing normal stress \(\sigma_x = -My/I_{xx}\), weighting the flexural rigidity by \(y^2\). Entering the differential moment integrand Y [↰] [x²] 10 [×] into [↱] [EQN] and integrating across the web depth 150 [+/-] [ENTER] 150 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: -150.0000, X: 150.0000)\) via [↱] [∫] Y yields exact parabolic convergence on the first Richardson column, returning error bound \(1.85 \times 10^{-10}\) in \(Y\) and second moment of area \(I_{xx} = \mathbf{22,500,000.0\text{ mm}^4}\) (\(2.25 \times 10^7\text{ mm}^4\)) in \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.85\times 10^{-10}, X: 22500000.0)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.18: Physical-Optics Aperture Integral & Radar Cross Section (RCS)
docs.text:
Physical-optics surface phase integration over a square flat conducting plate of side \(a = 0.50\text{ m}\) (\(x \in [-0.25, +0.25]\text{ m}\)) at X-band radar wavelength \(\lambda = 0.03\text{ m}\) (\(10\text{ GHz}\)) integrates the illuminated surface area \(A = \int_{-0.25}^{0.25} a\,dx = 0.25\text{ m}^2\) to determine the peak specular Radar Cross Section: $\(\sigma_{\max} = \frac{4\pi}{\lambda^2}\left[\int_{-a/2}^{a/2} a\,dx\right]^2 = \frac{4\pi A^2}{\lambda^2} = \frac{4\pi (0.25^2)}{0.0009} \approx \mathbf{872.6646\text{ m}^2} \quad (\mathbf{29.41\text{ dBsm}})\)$

At normal incidence (broadside flash), every surface patch across the conducting plate scatters in coherent phase, so the Kirchhoff physical-optics integral reduces to integrating the constant transverse width 0.5 in [↱] [EQN] over 0.25 [+/-] [ENTER] 0.25 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.5000, Y: -0.2500, X: 0.2500)\). Executing [↱] [∫] X \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.5000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.2500)\) yields the illuminated aperture area \(A = 0.2500\text{ m}^2\), and applying the Fraunhofer diffraction gain factor \(4\pi A^2/\lambda^2\) ([↰] [x²] 4 [×] [↱] [π] [×] 0.03 [↰] [x²] [÷], \((T: 0.5000, Z: 0.5000, Y: 0.0000, X: 872.6646)\)) reveals why a half-meter flat plate appears to an X-band radar as an \(\mathbf{872.6646\text{ m}^2}\) target (\(\mathbf{29.41\text{ dBsm}}\) via [↰] [LOG] 10 [×], \((T: 0.5000, Z: 0.5000, Y: 0.0000, X: 29.4085)\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.19: Thermal Expansion Clearance of Cryogenic Propellant Line
docs.text:
When a 304 stainless-steel LOX/LN2 transfer line of length \(L = 12.0\text{ m}\) is chilled from ambient \(T_1 = 293\text{ K}\) down to liquid nitrogen boiling temperature (\(T_2 = 77\text{ K}\)), the instantaneous thermal expansion coefficient follows \(\alpha(T) = (5.5022 + 0.04158\,T)\times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}\): $\(\Delta L = L \int_{293}^{77} \alpha(T) \, dT = 12.0 \int_{293}^{77} (5.5022 + 0.04158\,T)\times 10^{-6} \, dT = 12.0 \times (-0.002850) = \mathbf{-34.20\text{ mm}}\text{ (axial contraction)}\)$ Engineering Insight: Staging initial ambient temperature (\(a = 293\text{ K}\)) in Register \(Y\) and cryogenic terminal temperature (\(b = 77\text{ K}\)) in Register \(X\) before pressing [↱] [∫] T automatically produces the negative sign indicating contraction, reminding bellows designers to provide at least \(35\text{ mm}\) of axial expansion-joint travel.

Because lattice specific heat and anharmonic phonon vibrations freeze out near liquid-nitrogen temperatures (Debye \(T^3\) regime), \(\alpha(T)\) varies strongly across the cooldown range. Defining T 0.04158 [×] 5.5022 [+] 1 [E] 6 [+/-] [×] in [↱] [EQN] and integrating in the physical cooling direction 293 [ENTER] 77 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 293.0000, X: 77.0000)\) via [↱] [∫] T \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.05\times 10^{-13}, X: -0.002850)\) yields the integrated thermal strain \(\varepsilon_{\text{th}} = -0.002850\), which scales over the \(12\text{ m}\) manifold (12 [×] 1000 [×], \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.05\times 10^{-13}, X: -34.2000)\)) to an axial shrinkage of \(\Delta L = \mathbf{-34.20\text{ mm}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.20: Planetary Atmospheric Jeans Escape Flux
docs.text:
Integrating the Maxwell-Boltzmann molecular velocity distribution above a planet's escape velocity \(v_{\text{esc}}\) (with exobase density \(n_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{13}\text{ m}^{-3}\), thermal speed \(v_{\text{th}} = 6,356.7\text{ m/s}\), and Jeans parameter \(\lambda = (v_{\text{esc}}/v_{\text{th}})^2 = 9.50\)) yields the outward molecular escape flux at the exobase: $\(F_J = \frac{n_0 v_{\text{th}}}{2\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{\lambda}^{\infty} u e^{-u} \, du = \frac{n_0 v_{\text{th}}}{2\sqrt{\pi}} (1 + \lambda) e^{-\lambda} = \left(1.7932 \times 10^{16}\right)(10.50) e^{-9.50} \approx \mathbf{1.4102 \times 10^{13}\text{ molecules/(m}^2\cdot\text{s)}}\)$

In planetary aeronomy, only molecules in the high-energy Maxwell-Boltzmann tail (\(u = v^2/v_{\text{th}}^2 \ge \lambda\)) located above the collisionless exobase can escape into interplanetary space. Entering the dimensionless energy-tail integrand U [+/-] [eˣ] U [×] into [↱] [EQN] and integrating from the escape threshold \(\lambda = 9.5\) to the negligible upper tail \(u = 35\) (9.5 [ENTER] 35, \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 9.5000, X: 35.0000)\)) via [↱] [∫] U \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 4.15\times 10^{-12}, X: 0.000786)\) evaluates \((1 + \lambda)e^{-\lambda} = 0.0007863\); scaling by the upward effusive flux \(n_0 v_{\text{th}}/(2\sqrt{\pi})\) (6.3567 [E] 16 [×] [↱] [π] [√x] 2 [×] [÷], \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 4.15\times 10^{-12}, X: 1.4102\times 10^{13})\)) determines the Jeans escape rate \(F_J = \mathbf{1.4102 \times 10^{13}\text{ molecules/(m}^2\cdot\text{s)}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.21: Torsional Rigidity of an Elliptical Shaft (Saint-Venant Warping Integral)
docs.text:
Integrating Saint-Venant warping shear stress over an elliptical shaft cross-section with semiaxes \(a = 40\text{ mm}\) and \(b = 25\text{ mm}\) reduces to the normalized cross-sectional integral \(\int_{-1}^{1}(1 - u^2)^{3/2}\,du = \frac{3\pi}{8} \approx 1.178097\), scaled by \(\frac{8 a^3 b^3}{3(a^2 + b^2)}\): $\(J = \frac{8 a^3 b^3}{3(a^2 + b^2)} \int_{-1}^{1} (1 - u^2)^{3/2} \, du = \frac{\pi a^3 b^3}{a^2 + b^2} = \frac{\pi (64,000)(15,625)}{1,600 + 625} \approx \mathbf{1,411,951.76\text{ mm}^4}\)$

Unlike a circular shaft, an elliptical bar under torsion undergoes out-of-plane axial warping \(\psi(x,y) \propto xy\), reducing its torsional stiffness below the polar moment of inertia \(I_p\). docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.22: Second-Order Chemical Batch Reactor Residence Time

Because bimolecular collision frequency drops quadratically as reactant \(A\) is consumed (\(-r_A \propto (1-x)^2\)), each additional percentage point of conversion requires disproportionately longer reactor holding time. docs.title: Workbook Problem 8.25: Supersonic Sears-Haack Minimum Wave-Drag Body

\(F_d = C v^2 \implies \ln F_d = \ln C + 2 \ln v\). * \((v = 10\text{ m/s}, F_d = 25\text{ N})\) * \((v = 20\text{ m/s}, F_d = 100\text{ N})\) * \((v = 30\text{ m/s}, F_d = 225\text{ N})\)

Regressing \(\ln F_d\) against \(\ln v\) confirms the velocity exponent [m] \(= 2.000000\) and extracts the dimensional drag factor \(C = e^b = \mathbf{0.2500\text{ N/(m/s)}^2}\) in Register \(X\) (with \(m = 2.0000\) in Register \(Y\)) via [b] [eˣ].

docs.title: Workbook Problem 9.21: Financial Stock Beta in Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 9.22: Vector Graphic Scatter Plotting & Trendline Overlay
docs.text:
Accessible in App Mode via Right Shift [↱] then [PLOT] (excluded from physical firmware for standardized-exam compliance)

When bivariate Σ+ data is accumulated and no algebraic equations are stored in EQN, pressing [↱] [PLOT] in App Mode transitions the high-contrast dot-matrix display to the bivariate scatter & regression plotter: * The independent variable \(x\) scales along the horizontal axis (\(X_{\min} \to X_{\max}\)). * The dependent variable \(y\) scales along the vertical axis (\(Y_{\min} \to Y_{\max}\)). * Each accumulated point appears as a \(2\times 2\) pixel reticle. * The linear regression line \(y = m x + b\) is rendered as an uninterrupted 1-pixel vector trendline across the display field. * Navigation: * Press [4] to pan left, [6] to pan right. * Press [8] to pan up, [2] to pan down. * Press [+] to zoom in, [-] to zoom out. * Press [C] to exit plot mode and return to the RPN stack.

As Francis Anscombe famously demonstrated with Anscombe's Quartet, summary regression statistics (\(m, b, r\)) alone cannot distinguish a true linear relationship from high-leverage outliers or unmodeled curvature. Launching [↱] [PLOT] in App Mode overlays the least-squares vector trendline \(y = mx + b\) directly across the \(2\times 2\) pixel data reticles while preserving the operational stack registers \((T, Z, Y, X)\) untouched in background memory; panning ([4]/[6], [8]/[2]) and zooming ([+]/[-]) inspect residual structure visually before [C] returns to the four-register stack \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0000)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 9.23: Residual Analysis and Standard Error of the Estimate (\(s_e\))
docs.text:
In linear regression \(y = m x + b\), the standard error of the estimate measures the dispersion of observed values around the regression line:

\[s_e = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n - 2}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma y^2 - b \Sigma y - m \Sigma xy}{n - 2}}\]

For the pressure sensor dataset from Textbook Showcase Problem 9.1: * \(n = 4\), degrees of freedom \(n - 2 = 2\) * \(\Sigma y = 12.45\), \(\Sigma y^2 = 46.5075\), \(\Sigma xy = 373.5\) * \(m = 0.1245\), \(b = 0.0000\)

Compute residual sum of squares: $\(\text{SS}_{\text{res}} = 46.5075 - 0.0000(12.45) - 0.1245(373.5) = 46.5075 - 46.50075 = 0.00675\text{ V}^2\)$ $\(s_e = \sqrt{\frac{0.00675}{2}} = \sqrt{0.003375} \approx 0.05809\text{ V}\)$

Keystrokes: 46.5075 [ENTER] .1245 [ENTER] 373.5 [×] [-] 2 [÷] [√x] \(\rightarrow\) 0.0580947502

Because the six statistical registers already hold the exact cross-product moments, the residual sum of squares \(\text{SS}_{\text{res}} = \Sigma y^2 - b\Sigma y - m\Sigma xy\) can be evaluated without re-visiting individual observations (\(b = 0\) here). Staging \(\Sigma y^2\) via 46.5075 [ENTER] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 46.5075, X: 46.5075)\) and subtracting the regression sum of squares \(m \Sigma xy\) via 0.1245 [ENTER] 373.5 [×] [-] isolates \(\text{SS}_{\text{res}} = 0.00675\text{ V}^2\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.00675)\); normalizing by \(n - 2 = 2\) degrees of freedom (2 [÷], \(s_e^2 = 0.003375\)) and taking the square root ([√x]) determines the root-mean-square calibration scatter \(s_e = \mathbf{0.0580947502\text{ V}}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0580947502)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 9.24: Binomial Distribution Probability via Combinatorics [Cn,r]
docs.text:
In an automated manufacturing testing line, component defect probability is \(p = 0.03\). In a batch of \(n = 20\) components, calculate the probability of observing exactly \(k = 2\) defective units: $\(P(X = 2) = \binom{20}{2} (0.03)^2 (0.97)^{18}\)$

Keystrokes: 20 [ENTER] 2 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] .03 [↰] [x²] [×] .97 [ENTER] 18 [yˣ] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 0.0988; 0.1710 [ENTER] .97 [ENTER] 18 [yˣ] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 0.0988304453

In Bernoulli lot acceptance sampling, the number of distinct defect pairings across \(n = 20\) items is counted by the binomial coefficient 20 [ENTER] 2 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] (\(\binom{20}{2} = \mathbf{190}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 190.0000)\)). Multiplying by the defective pair probability \(p^2\) via .03 [↰] [x²] [×] (\(190 \times 0.0009 = 0.1710\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.1710)\)) and weighting by the survival probability of the remaining 18 good units (.97 [ENTER] 18 [yˣ] [×], \(0.97^{18} \approx 0.5779\)) resolves the exact binomial mass \(P(X = 2) = \mathbf{0.0988304453}\) (\(9.88\%\)) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0988304453)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 9.25: Hypergeometric Sampling Without Replacement
docs.text:
In a batch of \(N = 50\) aerospace fasteners, \(K = 6\) are defective. A quality inspector selects \(n = 5\) fasteners at random without replacement. Find the probability that exactly \(k = 1\) selected fastener is defective: $\(P(X = 1) = \frac{\binom{K}{k} \binom{N - K}{n - k}}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{\binom{6}{1} \binom{44}{4}}{\binom{50}{5}}\)$

Keystrokes: 6 [ENTER] 1 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] 44 [ENTER] 4 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] [×] 50 [ENTER] 5 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] [÷]; 6 [ENTER] 44 [ENTER] 4 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] [×]; 50 [ENTER] 5 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 0.384426

When sampling a finite aerospace lot without replacement (\(n/N = 10\%\)), each draw alters the defect concentration of the remaining population, requiring the exact hypergeometric ratio of combinatorial counts. Evaluating 6 [ENTER] 1 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] (\(\binom{6}{1} = 6.0000\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 6.0000)\)), multiplying by the conforming combinations 44 [ENTER] 4 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] [×] (\(\binom{44}{4} = 135,751 \implies 814,506\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 814506.0000)\)), and dividing by the total sample space 50 [ENTER] 5 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] [÷] (\(\binom{50}{5} = 2,118,760\)) determines \(P(X = 1) = \mathbf{0.384426}\) (\(38.44\%\)) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.384426)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 9.26: Log-Normal Aerosol Droplet Size Distribution
docs.text:
In medical nebulizer sprays, aerosol droplet diameters \(D\) follow a log-normal distribution with geometric mean \(\mu_{\ln} = \ln(4.5\text{ }\mu\text{m}) = 1.504077\) and geometric standard deviation \(\sigma_{\ln} = 0.35\). Calculate the probability density for a droplet of diameter \(D = 5.0\text{ }\mu\text{m}\): $\(f(D) = \frac{1}{D \sigma_{\ln} \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{(\ln D - \mu_{\ln})^2}{2\sigma_{\ln}^2} \right)\)$

Keystrokes: 5.0 [LN] 1.504077 [-] [↰] [x²] .35 [↰] [x²] 2 [×] [÷] [+/-] [eˣ] 5.0 [ENTER] .35 [×] 2 [↱] [π] [×] [√x] [×] [÷]; 0.0111009219 [ENTER] .35 [↰] [x²] 2 [×] [÷] [+/-] [eˣ]; 0.955701 [ENTER] 5.0 [ENTER] .35 [×] 2 [↱] [π] [×] [√x] [×] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 0.217865884

Because multiplicative breakup of liquid sheets in a pneumatic nebulizer produces normal scatter in \(\ln D\) rather than \(D\), the Jacobian transformation \(d(\ln D)/dD = 1/D\) introduces an explicit diameter prefactor into the log-normal density. Evaluating the squared log-ratio 5.0 [LN] 4.5 [LN] [-] [↰] [x²] (\((\ln 5.0 - \ln 4.5)^2 \approx 0.011101\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.011101)\)), dividing by \(2\sigma_{\ln}^2\) and exponentiating via .35 [↰] [x²] 2 [×] [÷] [+/-] [eˣ] (\(\exp(-0.045310) \approx 0.955701\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.955701)\)), and normalizing by \(D\sigma_{\ln}\sqrt{2\pi}\) (5.0 [ENTER] .35 [×] 2 [↱] [π] [×] [√x] [×] [÷]) resolves \(f(5.0) = \mathbf{0.217865884\ \mu\text{m}^{-1}}\) \((T: 0.9557, Z: 0.9557, Y: 0.9557, X: 0.217865884)\).
