docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.1: IPv4 CIDR /27 Subnet (30 Usable Hosts)
docs.text:
A server has IP 10.20.30.142 /27. * \(10 = \text{0Ah}, 20 = \text{14h}, 30 = \text{1Eh}, 142 = \text{8Eh} \implies \text{0A141E8Eh}\). * Subnet Mask /27: \(27\) ones, \(5\) zeros \(\implies\) block size \(2^5 = 32_{10} = \text{20h}\) (\(255.255.255.224\)).

Octet 4 Representation Upper 3 Subnet Bits Lower 5 Host Bits Hex / Decimal Value Host Octet 4 100 01110 8Eh (\(142_{10}\)) Subnet Mask (/27) 111 00000 E0h (\(224_{10}\)) Network Base (÷R 20h × 20h) 100 00000 80h (\(128_{10}\)) Broadcast (+ 1Fh) 100 11111 9Fh (\(159_{10}\))

Keystrokes in [HEX] Mode: 1. 0A141E8E [ENTER] 20 [↱] [÷R] 20 [×] \(\rightarrow\) A141E80h (10.20.30.128) 2. Wildcard mask: \(32 - 27 = 5\) bits \(\implies 2^5 - 1 = 31_{10} = \text{1Fh}\). 3. Broadcast: 0A141E80 [ENTER] 1F [+] \(\rightarrow\) A141E9Fh (10.20.30.159) 4. Usable host range: 10.20.30.129 through 10.20.30.158 (\(30\) usable hosts).

In CIDR block allocation, a /27 prefix reserves 27 upper network bits and leaves \(32 - 27 = 5\) host bits, partitioning each /24 into eight 32-address (20h) blocks. Staging the packed address 0A141E8E [ENTER] (10.20.30.142) in [HEX] mode \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: \text{A141E8Eh}, X: \text{A141E8Eh})\) and dividing by the block stride 20 [↱] [÷R] splits the 27-bit network prefix quotient \(\text{50A0F4h}\) into Register \(X\) and the 5-bit host index \(\text{Eh}\) (\(14_{10}\)) into Register \(Y\) \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: \text{Eh}, X: \text{50A0F4h})\). Multiplying by the stride 20 [×] aligns the network base A141E80h (10.20.30.128), and adding the 5-bit wildcard mask 1F [+] (\(2^5 - 1 = 31_{10}\)) establishes the directed broadcast address \(\mathbf{\text{A141E9Fh}}\) (10.20.30.159).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.2: IPv4 Point-to-Point /30 Subnet (WAN Link)
docs.text:
A WAN router serial link connects two routers using 172.16.5.9 /30. * \(172 = \text{ACh}, 16 = \text{10h}, 5 = \text{05h}, 9 = \text{09h} \implies \text{AC100509h}\). * Subnet Mask /30: \(30\) ones, \(2\) zeros \(\implies\) block size \(2^2 = 4_{10} = \text{4h}\) (\(255.255.255.252\)).

Keystrokes in [HEX] Mode: 1. AC100509 [ENTER] 4 [↱] [÷R] 4 [×] \(\rightarrow\) AC100508h (172.16.5.8) 2. Wildcard: \(2^2 - 1 = 3 = \text{03h}\). 3. Broadcast: AC100508 [ENTER] 3 [+] \(\rightarrow\) AC10050Bh (172.16.5.11) 4. Router A interface: 172.16.5.9, Router B interface: 172.16.5.10 (\(2\) usable hosts).

Point-to-point WAN links traditionally use /30 prefixes (stride \(2^2 = 4\text{h}\)) to conserve IPv4 address space while providing exactly two routable endpoints between network and broadcast boundaries. Entering AC100509 [ENTER] in [HEX] mode and partitioning with 4 [↱] [÷R] separates host offset \(1\text{h}\) in Register \(Y\) from the 30-bit prefix quotient \(\text{2B040142h}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: 1\text{h}, X: \text{2B040142h})\); scaling back by 4 [×] recovers the wire network ID \(\mathbf{\text{AC100508h}}\) (172.16.5.8), and adding the 2-bit wildcard 3 [+] determines the link broadcast address \(\mathbf{\text{AC10050Bh}}\) (172.16.5.11).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.3: IPv4 Host Route (/32) and Loopback
docs.text:
A BGP loopback interface is assigned 198.51.100.1 /32. * In Hex: IP is C6336401h, Mask is FFFFFFFFh (\(255.255.255.255\)). * Network ID = Host IP = Broadcast = 198.51.100.1 (C6336401h). * Usable hosts: \(2^{32-32} = 2^0 = \mathbf{1\text{ host}}\).

Keystrokes in [HEX] & [DEC] Modes: 1. Load Host IP: C6336401 [ENTER] \(\rightarrow\) C6336401h 2. Wildcard mask: FFFFFFFF [ENTER] FFFFFFFF [-] \(\rightarrow\) 0h (0.0.0.0) 3. Broadcast Address: [+] \(\rightarrow\) C6336401h (198.51.100.1) 4. Host Capacity: Switch to [DEC], 2 [ENTER] 0 [yˣ] \(\rightarrow\) 1.

Autonomous system border routers advertise /32 loopback interfaces into BGP and OSPF so routing tables track a virtual node that never goes down when a single physical port flaps. With C6336401 [ENTER] staged on the stack \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: \text{C6336401h}, X: \text{C6336401h})\), complementing the 32-bit host mask (FFFFFFFF [ENTER] FFFFFFFF [-]) yields a zero wildcard offset 0h, confirming via [+] that network, host, and broadcast collapse into the single address \(\mathbf{\text{C6336401h}}\) (\(2^0 = \mathbf{1}\) via [↰] [BASE] [DEC] 2 [ENTER] 0 [yˣ]).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.4: CIDR Route Aggregation (Supernetting)
docs.text:
An ISP wants to summarize four contiguous subnets into a single route: * Subnet 1: 192.168.16.0 /24 (C0A81000h) * Subnet 2: 192.168.17.0 /24 (C0A81100h) * Subnet 3: 192.168.18.0 /24 (C0A81200h) * Subnet 4: 192.168.19.0 /24 (C0A81300h)

Inspect the third octet: \(16 = 00010000_2\), \(17 = 00010001_2\), \(18 = 00010010_2\), \(19 = 00010011_2\). The upper 6 bits (\(000100_2\)) are identical across all four routes! New network mask length: \(16 + 6 = \mathbf{22\text{ bits}}\) (/22). Supernet Mask: 255.255.252.0 (FFFFFC00h). Summarized Route: 192.168.16.0 /22.

Keystrokes in [HEX] Mode: 1. Base Network ID: C0A81000 [ENTER] \(\rightarrow\) C0A81000h (192.168.16.0) 2. Supernet block span: 4 [ENTER] 100 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 400h (\(1024_{10}\) addresses) 3. Wildcard Mask: 1 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 3FFh (0.0.3.255) 4. Broadcast Address: [+] \(\rightarrow\) C0A813FFh (192.168.19.255) 5. Usable Hosts: 3FF [ENTER] 1 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 3FEh (\(1022_{10}\) hosts).

CIDR route aggregation (RFC 4632) prevents global routing-table explosion by folding contiguous power-of-two /24 blocks into a shorter prefix. Staging the aligned base network C0A81000 [ENTER] and evaluating the 4-block span 4 [ENTER] 100 [×] (400h \(= 1024_{10}\) addresses, \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: \text{C0A81000h}, Y: 4\text{h}, X: 400\text{h})\)) followed by 1 [-] derives the 10-bit supernet wildcard mask 3FFh (0.0.3.255). Adding the wildcard to the waiting base address via [+] resolves the summarized broadcast boundary \(\mathbf{\text{C0A813FFh}}\) (192.168.19.255), while 3FF [ENTER] 1 [-] confirms \(\mathbf{\text{3FEh}}\) (\(1022_{10}\)) usable host addresses.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.5: Wildcard Mask Generation via 32-Bit Complement Subtraction
docs.text:
In Cisco ACLs, calculate the wildcard mask for /26 (\(255.255.255.192\)): 1. In [HEX]: Mask is FFFFFFC0h. 2. Subtract from the 32-bit all-ones mask FFFFFFFFh: key FFFFFFFF [ENTER] FFFFFFC0 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 3Fh. 3. In [DEC]: 3Fh = 63. 4. Dotted decimal wildcard: 0.0.0.63.

Because a bitwise one's complement on an \(N\)-bit unsigned word is algebraically identical to subtracting from \(2^N - 1\), subtracting the /26 netmask FFFFFFC0h from the 32-bit all-ones constant FFFFFFFF [ENTER] \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: \text{FFFFFFFFh}, X: \text{FFFFFFFFh})\) via FFFFFFC0 [-] \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: 0\text{h}, X: \text{3Fh})\) isolates the inverted access-control wildcard 3Fh, which [↰] [BASE] [DEC] displays as \(\mathbf{63}\) (0.0.0.63).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.6: Embedded GPIO Pin Bit-Clearing (-)
docs.text:
Clear Bit 11 (Disable motor enable line, currently \(1\)) in register holding 0x00002F80. Bit 11 weight: \(2^{11} = 2048_{10} = \text{800h}\).

Keystrokes in [HEX] Mode: 2F80 [ENTER] 800 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 2780h

When a target bit \(k\) is known to be asserted (\(1\)), subtracting its positional weight \(2^k\) executes a borrow-free bitwise clear (R & ~(1 << k)). Staging 2F80 [ENTER] in [HEX] mode and subtracting Bit 11's weight \(2^{11} = \text{800h}\) via 800 [-] clears the motor-enable bit cleanly without disturbing adjacent flags, leaving \(\mathbf{\text{2780h}}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: 0\text{h}, X: \text{2780h})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.7: Multi-Bit Field Insertion (Read-Modify-Write)
docs.text:
In a peripheral timer control register currently holding 0x4521, update the 4-bit prescaler field at bits [11:8] (currently 5h) with value 0xA (\(10_{10}\)), without altering any of the surrounding configuration bits.

Insertion Stage Binary Nibbles (Bits 15–0) Hexadecimal Value Original Timer Register 0100 0101 0010 0001 4521h Subtract Old Field (- 500h) 0100 0000 0010 0001 4021h Shifted New Field (A × 100h) 0000 1010 0000 0000 0A00h Updated Register (+) 0100 1010 0010 0001 4A21h

Keystrokes in [HEX] Mode: 1. Clear existing field: 4521 [ENTER] 500 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 4021h 2. Prepare shifted new field: A [ENTER] 100 [×] \(\rightarrow\) A00h 3. Merge fields: [+] \(\rightarrow\) 4A21h

Firmware read-modify-write sequences (R = (R & ~MASK) | (VAL << SHIFT)) translate cleanly onto the hexadecimal stack: subtracting the old field 4521 [ENTER] 500 [-] zeroes bits [11:8] to leave the masked register 4021h in Register \(X\) \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: 0\text{h}, X: \text{4021h})\), left-shifting the new nibble via A [ENTER] 100 [×] forms A00h in \(X\) while 4021h waits in \(Y\) \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: \text{4021h}, X: \text{A00h})\), and pressing [+] merges the updated control word \(\mathbf{\text{4A21h}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.8: RGB565 to RGB888 Color Unpacking & Expansion
docs.text:
Given packed RGB565 word 0xE5B2, extract individual color channels using [÷] and [↱] [÷R] and expand them to standard 8-bit values (\(0 \dots 255\)): * Red channel (bits 15–11): divide by \(2^{11} = \text{800h}\) * Green channel (bits 10–5): take remainder modulo \(\text{800h}\) via [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y], then divide by \(2^5 = \text{20h}\) * Blue channel (bits 4–0): take remainder modulo \(\text{20h}\) via [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]

Keystrokes in [HEX] & [DEC] Modes: 1. Extract Red: E5B2 [ENTER] 800 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 1Ch (\(28_{10}\)) * Expand in [DEC]: 28 [ENTER] 255 [×] 31 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 230.32258065 2. Extract Green: E5B2 [ENTER] 800 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 20 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 2Dh (\(45_{10}\)) * Expand in [DEC]: 45 [ENTER] 255 [×] 63 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 182.14285714 3. Extract Blue: E5B2 [ENTER] 20 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] \(\rightarrow\) 12h (\(18_{10}\)) * Expand in [DEC]: 18 [ENTER] 255 [×] 31 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 148.06451613 * Unpacked TrueColor: RGB(230, 182, 148) (#E6B694).

Because [↱] [÷R] simultaneously returns the upper bitfield quotient in Register \(X\) and the lower bitfield remainder in Register \(Y\), a 16-bit RGB565 pixel can be unpacked either channel-by-channel (E5B2 [ENTER] 800 [÷] \(\rightarrow \mathbf{\text{1Ch}} = 28_{10} \implies R = \mathbf{230}\); E5B2 [ENTER] 800 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 20 [÷] \(\rightarrow \mathbf{\text{2Dh}} = 45_{10} \implies G = \mathbf{182}\); E5B2 [ENTER] 20 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] \(\rightarrow \mathbf{\text{12h}} = 18_{10} \implies B = \mathbf{148}\)) or in a single-entry cascade: keying E5B2 [ENTER] 800 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 20 [↱] [÷R] unpacks all three channels onto the stack at once (Z: 1Ch Red, Y: 12h Blue, X: 2Dh Green) with E5B2 typed only once!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.9: RGBA4444 16-Bit Texture Color Packing
docs.text:
In embedded OpenGL ES graphics engines, 16-bit RGBA4444 allocates 4 bits per channel: Pack channels \(R=14\) (Eh), \(G=9\) (9h), \(B=3\) (3h), \(A=15\) (Fh): $\((R \times \text{1000h}) + (G \times \text{100h}) + (B \times \text{10h}) + A\)$

Keystrokes in [HEX] Mode: E [ENTER] 1000 [×] 9 [ENTER] 100 [×] [+] 3 [ENTER] 10 [×] [+] F [+] \(\rightarrow\) E93Fh

In 4-bit-per-channel RGBA4444 sprite textures, each channel aligns with a single hexadecimal digit weight (\(16^3, 16^2, 16^1, 16^0\)). Shifting Red via E [ENTER] 1000 [×] (\(\text{E000h}\), \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: 0\text{h}, X: \text{E000h})\)) and accumulating Green (9 [ENTER] 100 [×] [+] \(\rightarrow \text{E900h}\)), Blue (3 [ENTER] 10 [×] [+] \(\rightarrow \text{E930h}\)), and Alpha (F [+]) assembles the packed 16-bit texel \(\mathbf{\text{E93Fh}}\) in Register \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.10: Two's Complement Negation Proof (\((2^{36} - 1 - X) + 1\))
docs.text:
Verify that subtracting \(X\) from all ones (FFFFFFFFFh, 9 hex digits for 36 bits) and adding \(1\) produces the exact mathematical two's complement negation [+/-]: * Key in \(42\) in [DEC] mode and press [+/-]: produces -42. * Switch to [↰] [BASE] [HEX]: displays as FFFFFFFD6h (\(36\)-bit two's complement representation, \(2^{36} - 42\)). * Verify by one's complement subtraction: FFFFFFFFF [ENTER] 2A [-] 1 [+] \(\rightarrow\) FFFFFFFD6h (-42 in [DEC]).

In an \(N\)-bit two's complement ALU (\(N = 36\) on the SC-32), additive inverse is defined modulo \(2^{36}\) via \(-X \equiv (2^{36} - 1 - X) + 1 \pmod{2^{36}}\). Negating 42 [+/-] in [DEC] mode yields \(\mathbf{-42}\), whose underlying 36-bit word appears in [↰] [BASE] [HEX] as \(\mathbf{\text{FFFFFFFD6h}}\)—identical to forming the 9-nibble one's complement FFFFFFFFF [ENTER] 2A [-] (\(\text{FFFFFFFD5h}\)) and incrementing by the carry-in 1 [+].

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.11: Arithmetic Right Shift via Signed Integer Division
docs.text:
For signed negative integer \(-64\): * In [DEC]: 64 [+/-] [ENTER] 4 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) -16 (Exact arithmetic right shift by 2 bits, sign-extended).

Whereas a logical right shift (>>) pads vacated upper bits with zeros, an arithmetic right shift (>>> or ASR) replicates the sign bit (Bit 35) to preserve negative two's complement magnitudes. Staging 64 [+/-] [ENTER] in [DEC] mode and dividing by \(2^2 = 4\) via 4 [÷] yields \(\mathbf{-16}\) \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: -16)\), which [↰] [BASE] [HEX] confirms as the sign-extended 36-bit word \(\mathbf{\text{FFFFFFFFF0h}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.12: Parity Bit Generation
docs.text:
Data byte 0x3B (\(00111011_2\), five ones \(\implies\) odd parity). For even parity, the MSB parity bit (Bit 7, weight \(2^7 = 128_{10} = \text{80h}\)) must be set to \(1\): 3B [ENTER] 80 [+] \(\rightarrow\) BBh.

Because the 7-bit ASCII payload 3Bh (\(00111011_2\)) contains an odd population count of five 1 bits, asserting the MSB parity bit (\(2^7 = \text{80h}\)) via 3B [ENTER] 80 [+] brings total population weight to six 1 bits, forming the even-parity UART frame byte \(\mathbf{\text{BBh}}\) (\(10111011_2\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.13: Longitudinal Redundancy Check (LRC)
docs.text:
Calculate LRC across message bytes 0x02, 0x41, 0x42.

2 [ENTER] 41 [+] 42 [+] \(\rightarrow\) 85h.

LRC = \((256 - \text{Sum}) \bmod 256\): 100 [ENTER] 85 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 7Bh.

In Intel HEX and Modbus ASCII serial framing, the Longitudinal Redundancy Check (LRC) byte is the two's complement of the modulo-256 payload sum, ensuring that the sum of payload plus LRC equals 00h \((\bmod\text{ 100h})\) at the receiver. Summing the three frame bytes 2 [ENTER] 41 [+] 42 [+] yields 85h \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: 0\text{h}, X: \text{85h})\), and subtracting from 100h (100 [ENTER] 85 [-], or 100 [x⇄y] [-] without re-typing 85) generates the transmitted LRC byte \(\mathbf{\text{7Bh}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.14: Ethernet FCS 32-Bit Inversion & Frame Check Sequence Post-Conditioning
docs.text:
In IEEE 802.3 Ethernet frame transmission, the final 32-bit CRC remainder (Frame Check Sequence, FCS) is post-conditioned prior to transmission by inverting all 32 bits (one's complement). Given an Ethernet polynomial check state of 0xEDB88320: 1. Invert the 32-bit word by subtracting from the all-ones mask FFFFFFFFh: $\(FFFFFFFF_{16} - EDB88320_{16} = \mathbf{12477CDF}_{16} \ (306,678,751_{10})\)$

Keystrokes in [HEX] Mode: 1. Load 32-bit inversion mask: FFFFFFFF [ENTER] \(\rightarrow\) FFFFFFFFh 2. Subtract Ethernet generator polynomial: EDB88320 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 12477CDFh 3. Switch radix to inspect in decimal: [↰] [BASE] [DEC] \(\rightarrow\) 306678751.

In IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 hardware, post-inverting the shift-register state against FFFFFFFFh ensures that appending trailing zero bytes to a valid frame alters its CRC. Subtracting the reversed generator polynomial EDB88320h from FFFFFFFF [ENTER] via EDB88320 [-] produces the one's-complement word \(\mathbf{\text{12477CDFh}}\), which [↰] [BASE] [DEC] renders losslessly as \(\mathbf{306,678,751}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.15: SPI Clock Prescaler Selection
docs.text:
A SPI peripheral runs from a \(75.0\text{ MHz}\) bus clock. The connected flash memory specifies a maximum operating frequency of \(10.0\text{ MHz}\). The SPI prescaler offers powers of two: \(2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128\). Determine the optimal prescaler divider and actual SPI operating frequency.

Keystrokes: 75 [ENTER] 10 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) \(7.5\).

Dividing the \(75.0\text{ MHz}\) peripheral bus clock by the \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) NOR-flash ceiling yields the minimum divider ratio \(7.5000\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 7.5000)\). Rounding up to the next binary prescaler tap \(2^{\lceil \log_2 7.5 \rceil} = \mathbf{8}\) (8 [ENTER]) and dividing the bus clock via 75 [ENTER] 8 [÷] establishes the safe operating SPI clock \(f_{\text{SPI}} = \mathbf{9.375\text{ Hz}}\) (\(9.375\text{ MHz}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.16: I2C Fast-Mode Plus SCL Timing Register Calculations
docs.text:
Target I2C clock frequency \(f_{\text{SCL}} = 1.0\text{ MHz}\) (\(1000\text{ ns}\) cycle time) derived from a \(150.0\text{ MHz}\) core clock period (\(T_{\text{clk}} = \frac{1}{150\times 10^6} \approx 6.6667\text{ ns}\)). Total clocks per SCL period: \(150\text{ cycles}\). In Fast-Mode Plus, asymmetric duty cycle allocates \(t_{\text{LOW}} \ge 500\text{ ns}\) and \(t_{\text{HIGH}} \ge 260\text{ ns}\). Allocating \(\frac{1}{3}\) high and \(\frac{2}{3}\) low: * \(t_{\text{HIGH}} = 50\text{ cycles} \times 6.6667\text{ ns} = \mathbf{333.3\text{ ns}}\) (\(> 260\text{ ns}\)) * \(t_{\text{LOW}} = 100\text{ cycles} \times 6.6667\text{ ns} = \mathbf{666.7\text{ ns}}\) (\(> 500\text{ ns}\)).

Keystrokes: 1. Total cycles: 150 [ENTER] 1 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) \(150\) cycles 2. High phase clocks: 3 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) \(50\) cycles 3. Timing durations: 1000 [ENTER] 3 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 333.3 ns (\(t_{\text{HIGH}}\)); 2 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 666.7 ns (\(t_{\text{LOW}}\)).

Open-drain I2C buses require an asymmetric 1:2 high-to-low clock ratio at \(1\text{ MHz}\) (Fast-Mode Plus) so active pull-down transistors hold SCL low long enough (\(t_{\text{LOW}} \ge 500\text{ ns}\)) after passive pull-up RC rise times. Dividing the \(150\text{-cycle}\) period (150 [ENTER] 1 [÷]) by 3 [÷] assigns \(50\text{ cycles}\) to SCLL_H and \(100\text{ cycles}\) to SCLL_L; partitioning the \(1000\text{ ns}\) bit period (1000 [ENTER] 3 [÷]) confirms \(t_{\text{HIGH}} = \mathbf{333.3\text{ ns}} > 260\text{ ns}\) and 2 [×] confirms \(t_{\text{LOW}} = \mathbf{666.7\text{ ns}} > 500\text{ ns}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.17: Fixed-Point Q16.16 Arithmetic Multiplication
docs.text:
In digital signal processing without FPU acceleration, numbers are formatted as signed Q16.16 (16 integer bits, 16 fractional bits, scaling factor \(2^{16} = 65,536\)). Multiply \(A = 3.5\) and \(B = 2.25\): * \(A = 3.5 \times 65536 = 229,376 = \text{38000h}\) * \(B = 2.25 \times 65536 = 147,456 = \text{24000h}\) * Product formula: \(C = (A \times B) \gg 16 = (A \times B) / 65536\).

Keystrokes in [HEX] Mode: 38000 [ENTER] 24000 [×] 10000 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 7E000h

Because multiplying two Q16.16 fixed-point numbers \((A \cdot 2^{16})(B \cdot 2^{16}) = AB \cdot 2^{32}\) doubles the binary-point scaling to Q32.32, a 32-bit ALU would overflow on the intermediate product \(\text{38000h} \times \text{24000h} = \text{7E0000000h}\). The SC-32's 36-bit integer datapath accommodates the full 35-bit intermediate product (38000 [ENTER] 24000 [×]) without truncation, and right-shifting by 16 bits (10000 [÷]) normalizes the result back to Q16.16 word \(\mathbf{\text{7E000h}}\) (\(516,096_{10} / 65,536 = \mathbf{7.875}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.18: Permutations (\(nPr\)) in Cryptography S-Box Design
docs.text:
Calculate the total number of ways to construct an ordered 4-element substitution key from a pool of 16 distinct nibbles:

\[P(16, 4) = \frac{16!}{(16 - 4)!} = 16 \times 15 \times 14 \times 13 = \mathbf{43,680}\]

Keystrokes: 16 [ENTER] 4 [↱] [PROB] [Pn,r] \(\rightarrow\) 43,680

In block-cipher substitution-box (S-Box) construction, selecting an ordered sequence of \(r = 4\) distinct 4-bit nibbles without replacement from the 16-element hexadecimal alphabet spans the falling factorial \(16^{\underline{4}} = P(16, 4)\). Keying 16 [ENTER] 4 [↱] [PROB] [Pn,r] evaluates the exact keyspace cardinality \(P(16, 4) = \mathbf{43,680}\) (\(43,680\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.19: Combinations (\(nCr\)) and Hamming Sphere
docs.text:
In a \([7, 4]\) Hamming code, calculate the number of possible 2-bit error patterns:

\[\binom{7}{2} = \frac{7!}{2! \times 5!} = \mathbf{21}\]

Keystrokes: 7 [ENTER] 2 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] \(\rightarrow\) 21

In Richard Hamming's \([7, 4]\) single-error-correcting block code, the surface area of the Hamming sphere of radius \(t = 2\) around any 7-bit codeword counts all unordered pairs of corrupted bit positions. Evaluating 7 [ENTER] 2 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r] returns \(\binom{7}{2} = \mathbf{21}\) (\(21\) distinct double-bit error patterns).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.20: Factorials and Stirling's Approximation Comparison
docs.text:
Calculate \(15!\): Exact: 15 [↱] [PROB] [↰] [x!] \(\rightarrow\) 1,307,674,368,000.

Stirling's approximation: \(\sqrt{2\pi n} (n/e)^n \approx 1.3004 \times 10^{12}\) (Error \(< 0.6\%\)).

Evaluating 15 [↱] [PROB] [↰] [x!] computes the exact permutation count of a 15-element array, \(\mathbf{1,307,674,368,000}\) (\(1,307,674,368,000\)), whereas James Stirling's asymptotic leading term \(\sqrt{2\pi n}(n/e)^n \approx 1.30043 \times 10^{12}\) underestimates the exact factorial by the series correction factor \(e^{-1/(12n)} \approx 1 - \frac{1}{180}\) (\(0.55\%\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.21: Pseudo-Random Number Generation (RAND)
docs.text:
Generate 3 uniform random floats: [↱] [PROB] [RAND] \(\rightarrow\) \(0.724194\) [↱] [PROB] [RAND] \(\rightarrow\) \(0.183022\) [↱] [PROB] [RAND] \(\rightarrow\) \(0.941581\).

Because [↱] [PROB] [RAND] is a non-consuming generator that enables stack lift before pushing each uniform variate \(U_k \in [0, 1)\) into Register \(X\), three consecutive invocations populate a 3-dimensional Monte Carlo sample vector directly across Registers \(Z, Y,\) and \(X\): the first press generates \(U_1 = \mathbf{0.724194}\) in \(X\), the second lifts \(U_1 \to Y\) while placing \(U_2 = \mathbf{0.183022}\) in \(X\), and the third lifts \(U_1 \to Z, U_2 \to Y\) while placing \(U_3 = \mathbf{0.941581}\) in \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.22: Pseudo-Random Die Roll Simulation
docs.text:
Simulate a standard 6-sided die roll: [↱] [PROB] [RAND] 6 [×] 1 [+] [↱] [PARTS] [IP] \(\rightarrow\) Integer in \(1 \dots 6\).

Mapping a continuous uniform variate \(U \in [0, 1)\) ([↱] [PROB] [RAND], e.g., \(0.724194\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.724194)\)) onto a discrete equiprobable integer set \(\{1, \dots, 6\}\) uses the affine floor transformation \(\lfloor 6U + 1 \rfloor\): scaling by the cardinality 6 [×] (\(4.345164 \in [0, 6)\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 4.345164)\)), shifting the origin 1 [+] (\(5.345164 \in [1, 7)\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 5.345164)\)), and truncating via [↱] [PARTS] [IP] yields the unbiased die face \(\mathbf{5}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 5.0000)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.23: Decimal to Binary Conversion & Bit Inspection
docs.text:
Convert decimal 13 into its 4-bit binary representation and verify its bit weights (\(8 + 4 + 0 + 1\)): Keystrokes: 13 [ENTER] [↰] [BASE] [BIN] \(\rightarrow\) 1101b (\(1101_2\)).

Entering 13 [ENTER] in [DEC] mode and switching radix via [↰] [BASE] [BIN] formats the underlying integer as \(\mathbf{1101b}\) (\(1101_2 = 2^3 + 2^2 + 2^0 = 8 + 4 + 1\)), demonstrating that radix switching is a pure display projection that leaves all four stack registers unaltered.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 10.24: Binary to Hexadecimal & Decimal Reconstruction
docs.text:
Convert binary 1101b back to decimal (13) and hexadecimal (Dh) via [↰] [BASE] [DEC] and [↰] [BASE] [HEX], confirming lossless radix conversion across all stack registers.

Staging the binary nibble 1101 [ENTER] in [BIN] mode \((T: 0\text{b}, Z: 0\text{b}, Y: 1101\text{b}, X: 1101\text{b})\) and cycling through [↰] [BASE] [HEX] \((T: 0\text{h}, Z: 0\text{h}, Y: \text{Dh}, X: \mathbf{Dh})\) and [↰] [BASE] [DEC] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 13, X: \mathbf{13})\) verifies bijective, lossless radix projection across all four operational registers.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Financial Mathematics, Executive Analytics & TVM — Extended Engineering & Competition Problems
docs.text: Accompanies Chapter 11 of Thinking in the Stack (31 Worked Engineering Problems)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.1: Annual Revenue Acceleration (%CHG)
docs.text:
Revenues grew from \(\$42.50\text{M}\) in fiscal year 2024 to \(\$51.85\text{M}\) in fiscal year 2025. Calculate the annual percentage growth rate:

\[\%CHG = \frac{51.85 - 42.50}{42.50} \times 100 = \mathbf{+22.00\%}\]

Keystrokes: 42.50 [ENTER] 51.85 [↱] [%CHG] \(\rightarrow\) 22.

Staging prior-year revenue in Register \(Y\) and current-year revenue in Register \(X\) via 42.50 [ENTER] 51.85 \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 42.50, X: 51.85)\) and pressing [↱] [%CHG] evaluates \((X - Y)/Y \times 100\) in place, reporting top-line growth \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 42.50, X: \mathbf{22.00\%})\) while preserving the \(\$42.50\text{M}\) baseline in Register \(Y\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.2: EBITDA Margin Expansion in Basis Points
docs.text: A manufacturing firm expands revenue from \(\$240.0\text{M}\) to \(\$310.0\text{M}\). During the same period, EBITDA rises from \(\$36.0\text{M}\) to \(\$55.8\text{M}\). Determine the EBITDA margin expansion in basis points (\(1\text{ bp} = 0.01\%\)). Evaluating the current-year operating margin via 55.8 [ENTER] 310 [÷] 100 [×] places \(18.00\%\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 18.00)\), and evaluating the prior-year margin via 36 [ENTER] 240 [÷] 100 [×] places \(15.00\%\) in \(X\) while lifting \(18.00\%\) into \(Y\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 18.00, X: 15.00)\). Subtracting and scaling to basis points ([-] 100 [×]) isolates the operating leverage gain of \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{300.00}\text{ bps})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.3: 15-Year Mortgage Acceleration Comparison
docs.text:
Compare the \(\$350,000.00\) mortgage on a 15-year term (\(N = 180\)) at \(6.25\%\) interest (\(i = 6.25 / 12 = 0.520833\%\)): * Payment: 180 [N] 6.25 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%] 350000 [PV] 0 [FV] [PMT] \(\rightarrow\) -3,000.98003

Halving the amortization horizon to \(N = 180\text{ months}\) (180 [N], \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 180.00)\)) at a \(50\text{-bp}\) lower rate (6.25 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%] \(= 0.520833\%/\text{mo}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 180.00, X: 0.52)\)) on the same \(\$350,000\) principal (350000 [PV] 0 [FV], \((T: 180.00, Z: 0.52, Y: 350000.00, X: 0.00)\)) increases the monthly debt service [PMT] by only \(\$730.89/\text{mo}\) to \((T: 180.00, Z: 0.52, Y: 350000.00, X: \mathbf{-3000.98})\), while cutting total lifetime outlays (180 [×], \((T: 0.52, Z: 0.52, Y: 350000.00, X: \mathbf{-540176.41})\)) by \(\$277,057.19\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.4: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)
docs.text:
Equity capital \(\$60.0\text{M}\) (\(60\%\)) at required equity return \(K_e = 12.0\%\); Debt capital \(\$40.0\text{M}\) (\(40\%\)) at pre-tax interest rate \(K_d = 6.0\%\); Corporate income tax rate \(t = 25\%\): $\(\text{WACC} = \left(\frac{E}{V}\right) K_e + \left(\frac{D}{V}\right) K_d (1 - t)\)$

Under Modigliani-Miller corporate tax-shield accounting, interest expense is tax-deductible, reducing the effective cost of debt by \((1 - t)\). Computing the tax-shielded debt rate via 6 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER] 0.25 [-] [×] (\(4.50\%\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 4.50)\)) and weighting by the \(40\%\) debt share (.40 [×] \(= 1.80\%\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 1.80)\)), then evaluating the \(60\%\) equity component via 60 [ENTER] 100 [÷] 12 [×] (\(7.20\%\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 1.80, X: 7.20)\)) and summing with [+] establishes the blended corporate hurdle rate \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{9.00\%})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.5: Rule of 72 Doubling Time Precision
docs.text:
An investment yields \(8.0\%\) annually. Compare the Rule of 72 mental estimate with exact compound TVM: * Rule of 72 estimate: \(72 / 8 = \mathbf{9.00\text{ years}}\). * Exact TVM Doubling: 8 [I%] 1 [+/-] [PV] 0 [PMT] 2 [FV] [N] \(\rightarrow\) 9.01 years. * Error is under \(0.11\%\).

Luca Pacioli's classic Rule of 72 (72 [ENTER] 8 [÷] \(= 9.00\text{ years}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 9.00)\)) approximates \(N = \ln(2)/\ln(1+i) \approx 69.31/i + 0.35\), making \(72/i\) remarkably accurate near \(i = 8\%\). Programming 8 [I%] 1 [+/-] [PV] 0 [PMT] 2 [FV] \((T: 8.00, Z: -1.00, Y: 0.00, X: 2.00)\) and solving [N] yields the exact doubling horizon \(\ln(2)/\ln(1.08) = \mathbf{9.0065\text{ years}}\) \((T: 8.00, Z: -1.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{9.01}\text{ years})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.6: Continuous Compounding (\(A = P e^{rt}\))
docs.text:
Deposit \(\$10,000.00\) in a treasury note yielding \(5.50\%\) compounded continuously for 10 years:

\[A = 10,000 \times e^{0.055 \times 10} = 10,000 \times e^{0.55}\]

Keystrokes: .055 [ENTER] 10 [×] [eˣ] 10000 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 17,332.53018.

In the continuous compounding limit \(\lim_{m \to \infty}(1 + r/m)^{mt} = e^{rt}\), evaluating the dimensionless yield-time exponent .055 [ENTER] 10 [×] (\(rt = 0.55\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 0.55)\)), exponentiating via [eˣ] (\(e^{0.55} \approx 1.733253\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 1.73)\)), and scaling by initial principal 10000 [×] determines the terminal value \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{\$17332.53})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.7: Effective Annual Rate (EAR) from Nominal APR
docs.text:
A revolving credit line charges nominal \(21.99\%\) APR compounded daily (\(m = 365\)):

\[\text{EAR} = \left(1 + \frac{0.2199}{365}\right)^{365} - 1\]

Keystrokes: .2199 [ENTER] 365 [÷] 1 [+] 365 [yˣ] 1 [-] 100 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 24.586963176.

Converting a nominal APR into its true Effective Annual Rate (APY) reveals the compounding drag of daily interest accrual: dividing the nominal rate by the compounding frequency .2199 [ENTER] 365 [÷] 1 [+] forms the daily growth factor \(1 + r/365 = 1.00060247\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 1.000602)\), raising to the 365th power via 365 [yˣ] yields \(1.245870\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 1.25)\), and 1 [-] 100 [×] isolates the effective annual rate \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{24.59\%})\). (Single-Entry Compounding Choreography: Because 1 [+] overwrites LASTX with 1, you can avoid typing the compounding frequency 365 twice by duplicating it into Register \(Y\) upfront: 365 [ENTER] .2199 [x⇄y] [÷] 1 [+] [x⇄y] [yˣ] 1 [-] 100 [×] keeps 365 waiting in Register \(Y\) while forming \(1 + 0.2199/365\), so 365 is entered only once!)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.8: Auto Loan Financing with Trade-In
docs.text:
New vehicle price \(\$38,500.00\). Trade-in allowance \(\$8,500.00\). Net loan principal \(PV = \$30,000.00\). Financing: 60 months (\(N=60\)) at \(4.90\%\) APR (\(i = 4.90 / 12 = 0.408333\%\)): Keystrokes: 60 [N] 4.9 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%] 30000 [PV] 0 [FV] [PMT] \(\rightarrow\) -564.76.

Deducting the \(\$8,500\) trade-in credit leaves a net financed principal of \(\$30,000.00\): storing 60 [N] \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 60.00)\), converting the \(4.90\%\) APR to a monthly rate via 4.9 [ENTER] 12 [÷] [I%] (\(0.408333\%/\text{mo}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 60.00, X: 0.41)\)), and entering 30000 [PV] 0 [FV] \((T: 60.00, Z: 0.41, Y: 30000.00, X: 0.00)\) allows [PMT] to resolve the monthly installment \((T: 60.00, Z: 0.41, Y: 30000.00, X: \mathbf{-564.76})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.9: Equipment Lease vs. Buy Analysis
docs.text: An industrial CNC milling machine can be leased for \(\$12,000.00/\text{year}\) for 5 years at an \(8.00\%\) hurdle discount rate. Outright purchase price is \(\$52,000.00\): $\(\text{PV of Lease} = 12,000 \times \left[\frac{1 - 1.08^{-5}}{0.08}\right] = \mathbf{\$47,912.52}\)$ Leasing saves \(\$4,087.48\) in present value terms compared to outright purchase. Programming the 5-year lease obligation 5 [N] 8 [I%] 12000 [+/-] [PMT] 0 [FV] \((T: 5.00, Z: 8.00, Y: -12000.00, X: 0.00)\) and solving [PV] discounts the lease stream to \((T: 5.00, Z: 8.00, Y: -12000.00, X: \mathbf{47912.52})\), which compares directly against the \(\$52,000\) purchase price via 52000 [x⇄y] [-] to quantify the net present value advantage of leasing \((T: 5.00, Z: 8.00, Y: 52000.00, X: \mathbf{\$4087.48})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.10: Dining Bill with 8.25% Tax and 20% Tip
docs.text: Food and beverage subtotal: \(\$164.50\), regional tax \(8.25\%\) (164.50 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%] \(\rightarrow \$13.57\)), and \(20.0\%\) tip on the pre-tax subtotal (164.50 [ENTER] 20 [↱] [%] \(\rightarrow \$32.90\)). Because proper hospitality etiquette calculates gratuity on the pre-tax subtotal rather than the taxed total, duplicating the subtotal via 164.50 [ENTER] [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%] [+] forms the taxed bill \((\$178.07)\) in Register \(X\) while keeping a second copy of the pre-tax base \((\$164.50)\) in Register \(Y\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 164.50, X: 178.07)\). Swapping via [x⇄y] 20 [↱] [%] computes the \(20\%\) pre-tax gratuity \((\$32.90)\) in \(X\) while the taxed bill waits in \(Z\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 178.07, Y: 164.50, X: 32.90)\), or even more compactly, keying 164.50 [ENTER] 8.25 [ENTER] 20 [+] [↱] [%] [+] combines the two pre-tax rates (\(28.25\%\)) in a single percentage operation to reach \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{\$210.97})\) with 164.50 typed only once!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.11: 4-Way Bill Split via Stack Roll [R↓]
docs.text: Grand total \(\$210.97\) split equally among 4 dinner guests: key 210.97 [ENTER] 4 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 52.74 \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{\$52.74})\), establishing the per-person share directly in Register \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.12: Culinary Recipe Scaling with Fractions
docs.text: A cake recipe yields 8 servings and calls for \(2\text{-}1/2\text{ cups}\) of flour (\(2.5\text{ cups}\)). To scale the recipe to serve 14 guests, compute the scaling factor 14 [ENTER] 8 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 1.75 and multiply by the base flour requirement 2.5 [ENTER] 1.75 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 4.375 (\(4\text{-}3/8\text{ cups}\)). On a continuous stack, keying 14 [ENTER] 8 [÷] establishes the \(1.75\times\) multiplier in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 1.75)\), and 2.5 [×] scales the base flour directly to \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{4.38}\text{ cups})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.13: Kitchen Unit Volume Conversions
docs.text: Convert \(3.5\text{ fluid ounces}\) to tablespoons (\(1\text{ fl oz} = 2\text{ tbsp}\)), then to teaspoons (\(1\text{ tbsp} = 3\text{ tsp}\)): 3.5 [ENTER] 2 [×] 3 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 21.00. Chaining the dimensional factors on the stack (3.5 [ENTER] 2 [×] \(\rightarrow (T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{7.00}\text{ tbsp})\), followed by 3 [×] \(\rightarrow (T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{21.00}\text{ tsp})\)) converts across US customary volume tiers without intermediate re-entry.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.14: Bookshelf Bay Spacing with Dividers
docs.text:
Alcove width \(47\text{-}5/8^{\prime\prime}\) (\(47.625^{\prime\prime}\)). Two \(3/4^{\prime\prime}\) (\(0.75^{\prime\prime}\)) upright dividers create 3 equal bays: 47.625 [ENTER] .75 [ENTER] 2 [×] [-] 3 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 15.375.

In architectural millwork layout, deducting the combined thickness of all interior partitions before dividing by the bay count prevents cumulative layout drift: keying 47.625 [ENTER] .75 [ENTER] 2 [×] [-] subtracts the two \(0.75^{\prime\prime}\) dividers (\(1.50^{\prime\prime}\)) from the \(47.625^{\prime\prime}\) alcove opening to isolate the net clear span \(46.125^{\prime\prime}\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 46.13)\), and 3 [÷] partitions it into three equal bays of \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{15.38^{\prime\prime}})\) (\(15\text{-}3/8^{\prime\prime}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.15: Woodworking Saw Kerf Accumulation
docs.text:
Cut 5 identical table legs of length \(28\text{-}1/4^{\prime\prime}\) (\(28.25^{\prime\prime}\)) from a single board. The miter saw blade has a kerf thickness of \(1/8^{\prime\prime}\) (\(0.125^{\prime\prime}\)). There are 4 intermediate cuts: 28.25 [ENTER] 5 [×] .125 [ENTER] 4 [×] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 141.75.

Parting \(n = 5\) workpieces from a single blank requires \(n - 1 = 4\) internal kerf cuts: evaluating finished workpiece length 28.25 [ENTER] 5 [×] (\(141.25^{\prime\prime}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 141.25)\)), computing cumulative blade kerf loss .125 [ENTER] 4 [×] (\(0.50^{\prime\prime}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 141.25, X: 0.50)\)), and summing with [+] determines the minimum rough-mill board length \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{141.75^{\prime\prime}})\) (\(11\text{ ft } 9\text{-}3/4^{\prime\prime}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.16: Staircase Riser and Tread Layout
docs.text: Total vertical rise from finished basement floor to main level is \(108\text{ inches}\) (\(9\text{ ft}\)), and building code requires individual riser height \(h \le 7\text{-}3/4^{\prime\prime}\) (\(7.75^{\prime\prime}\)). Keying 108 [ENTER] 7.75 [÷] estimates the minimum riser count (\(13.935\)) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 13.94)\), which rounds up to 14 risers. Keying 108 [ENTER] 14 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 7.7142857143 evaluates the exact unit riser height \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 13.94, X: \mathbf{7.71^{\prime\prime}})\) (\(7\text{-}23/32^{\prime\prime}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.17: Blueprint Scale Conversion (\(1/4^{\prime\prime} = 1^{\prime}\text{-}0^{\prime\prime}\))
docs.text:
Wall on drawing measures \(5\text{-}3/8^{\prime\prime}\) (\(5.375^{\prime\prime}\)). Real length (\(4\text{ ft/in}\)).

5.375 [ENTER] 4 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 21.5.

On standard \(1/4^{\prime\prime} = 1^{\prime}\text{-}0^{\prime\prime}\) architectural plans (1:48 scale), each inch on paper represents \(4\text{ feet}\) in the field, so multiplying 5.375 [ENTER] 4 [×] converts the blueprint span directly to \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{21.50}\text{ ft})\) (\(21^{\prime}\text{-}6^{\prime\prime}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.18: Model Railroading HO Scale (1:87.1)
docs.text:
Real locomotive length is \(72\text{ feet}\) (\(864\text{ inches}\)). In HO scale.

864 [ENTER] 87.1 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 9.9196326062.

NMRA HO scale (\(3.5\text{ mm} = 1\text{ ft}\)) corresponds to a linear reduction ratio of \(304.8 / 3.5 = 87.086 \approx 87.1\): dividing the prototype length 864 [ENTER] 87.1 [÷] determines the scale chassis length \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{9.92^{\prime\prime}})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.19: Fuel Economy MPG to L/100km Conversion
docs.text:
Formula: \(\text{L/100km} = \frac{235.214583}{\text{MPG}}\). Convert \(32.0\text{ MPG}\).

235.215 [ENTER] 32 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 7.35046875.

Because US fuel economy measures distance per volume (\(\text{mi/gal}\)) whereas metric consumption measures volume per \(100\text{ km}\), the relationship is reciprocally proportional through the constant \(\frac{100 \times 3.785411784}{1.609344} = 235.214583\): keying 235.215 [ENTER] 32 [÷] yields \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{7.35}\text{ L/100km})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.20: Foreign Currency Exchange Fee and Spread
docs.text:
Traveler converts \(\$2,000\text{ USD}\) to Euros. Interbank rate is \(1.085\text{ EUR/USD}\). Bank charges a \(2.5\%\) FX spread fee.

2000 [ENTER] 2.5 [↱] [%] [-] 1.085 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 2,115.75.

Deducting the retail foreign-exchange spread via 2000 [ENTER] 2.5 [↱] [%] [-] leaves \(\$1,950.00\) of net convertible principal in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 1950.00)\), which converts at the interbank spot rate (1.085 [×]) to \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{2115.75}\text{ EUR})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.21: Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC)
docs.text:
Days Inventory Outstanding \(DIO = 45\text{ days}\); Days Sales Outstanding \(DSO = 38\text{ days}\); Days Payables Outstanding \(DPO = 52\text{ days}\):

\[\text{CCC} = DIO + DSO - DPO = 45 + 38 - 52 = \mathbf{31\text{ days}}\]

In working-capital treasury management, the Cash Conversion Cycle measures how many days cash remains tied up in inventory and customer receivables beyond trade supplier credit terms: 45 [ENTER] 38 [+] 52 [-] resolves \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{31}\text{ days})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.22: Enterprise Value (EV) Calculation
docs.text:
Market capitalization \(\$450\text{M}\), total debt \(\$120\text{M}\), cash and equivalents \(\$35\text{M}\):

\[\text{EV} = \text{Market Cap} + \text{Debt} - \text{Cash} = 450 + 120 - 35 = \mathbf{\$535.00M}\]

In mergers-and-acquisitions valuation, Enterprise Value represents the net takeover price of the operating business—acquiring all equity plus assuming gross debt, less liquid cash on the balance sheet (450 [ENTER] 120 [+] 35 [-] \(\rightarrow (T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{\$535.00M})\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.23: Sinking Fund Future Savings Goal
docs.text:
Save \(\$50,000\) in 5 years (\(N=60\text{ months}\)) at \(6.0\%\) APR (\(i = 0.5\%/\text{mo}\)): Keystrokes: 60 [N] .5 [I%] 0 [PV] 50000 [FV] [PMT]\(\rightarrow\) -716.64.

Programming the sinking-fund parameters 60 [N] .5 [I%] 0 [PV] 50000 [FV] \((T: 60.00, Z: 0.50, Y: 0.00, X: 50000.00)\) and solving [PMT] determines the required monthly deposit \((T: 60.00, Z: 0.50, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{-716.64})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.24: College Education Fund Present Value
docs.text:
Annual tuition \(\$35,000\) for 4 years (\(N=4\), beginning of year BEGIN mode) at \(5\%\) investment return: Toggled to BEGIN mode: 4 [N] 5 [I%] 35000 [PMT] 0 [FV] [PV] \(\rightarrow\) -$130,417.84.

Because university bursars collect tuition at the start of each academic year (an annuity due), toggling BEGIN mode and storing 4 [N] 5 [I%] 35000 [PMT] 0 [FV] \((T: 4.00, Z: 5.00, Y: 35000.00, X: 0.00)\) before pressing [PV] discounts only the three subsequent installments, yielding the required freshman-day endowment \((T: 4.00, Z: 5.00, Y: 35000.00, X: \mathbf{-\$130417.84})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.25: Net Present Value (NPV) Comparison of Capital Projects
docs.text:
A company evaluates two mutually exclusive industrial automation projects with a \(12.0\%\) hurdle rate: Project Alpha: Initial Cost \(\$80,000.00\); Inflows: \(\$35,000/\text{yr}\) for 3 years. Project Beta: Initial Cost \(\$120,000.00\); Inflows: \(\$52,000/\text{yr}\) for 3 years:

$\(\text{PV Annuity Factor} = \frac{1 - (1.12)^{-3}}{0.12} = \frac{1 - 0.71178}{0.12} \approx 2.40183\)$ * Project Alpha: \(35,000 \times 2.40183 - 80,000 = \$84,064.10 - \$80,000 = \mathbf{+\$4,064.10}\). * Project Beta: \(52,000 \times 2.40183 - 120,000 = \$124,895.22 - \$120,000 = \mathbf{+\$4,895.22}\). Project Beta delivers \(\$831.12\) more net present value to shareholders.

Because N, I%, and FV remain persistent across TVM evaluations, discounting Project Alpha (3 [N] 12 [I%] 35000 [+/-] [PMT] 0 [FV] [PV] \(\rightarrow \$84,064.10\), \((T: 3.00, Z: 12.00, Y: -35000.00, X: 84064.10)\), less 80000 [-] \(\rightarrow (T: 3.00, Z: 12.00, Y: -35000.00, X: \mathbf{+\$4064.10})\)) requires only updating PMT for Project Beta (52000 [+/-] [PMT] [PV] \(\rightarrow \$124,895.22\), \((T: 12.00, Z: -35000.00, Y: 4064.09, X: 124895.22)\), less 120000 [-] \(\rightarrow (T: 3.00, Z: 12.00, Y: -52000.00, X: \mathbf{+\$4895.22})\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.26: Capital Budgeting Profitability Index (PI)
docs.text:
Using the present value of inflows from Workbook Problem 11.25:

$\(\text{Profitability Index (PI)} = \frac{\text{PV of Future Inflows}}{\text{Initial Investment}}\)$ * Project Alpha: \(84,064.10 \div 80,000.00 = \mathbf{1.0508}\) (\(1.05\text{x}\)) * Project Beta: \(124,895.22 \div 120,000.00 = \mathbf{1.0408}\) (\(1.04\text{x}\)) Although Project Beta has higher absolute NPV, Project Alpha delivers higher capital efficiency per dollar invested!

When capital rationing constrains total CapEx budget, ranking projects by Profitability Index \(\text{PI} = \text{PV}_{\text{inflows}}/I_0\) (84064.10 [ENTER] 80000 [÷] \(\rightarrow (T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{1.0508}\text{x})\) for Alpha versus 124895.22 [ENTER] 120000 [÷] \(\rightarrow (T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 1.05, X: \mathbf{1.0408}\text{x})\) for Beta) identifies which project generates more present value per dollar of scarce capital.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.27: MACRS 5-Year Depreciation Schedule
docs.text:
A technology enterprise purchases \(\$250,000.00\) of server hardware depreciated under IRS 5-Year MACRS (\(20.0\%, 32.0\%, 19.2\%, 11.52\%, 11.52\%, 5.76\%\)): * Year 1 Deduction: 250000 [ENTER] 20 [↱] [%] \(\rightarrow\) 50,000 (Remaining basis: [-] \(\rightarrow\) \(\$200,000.00\)).

Under the IRS 200%-declining-balance half-year convention (250000 [ENTER] 20 [↱] [%]), Register \(X\) displays the Year-1 tax depreciation write-off \((\$50,000.00)\) while Register \(Y\) retains the \(\$250,000.00\) original cost basis \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 250000.00, X: 50000.00)\), so pressing [-] immediately resolves the adjusted Year-1 book value \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{\$200000.00})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.28: Staircase Stringer Layout with 1/16" Carpentry Cuts
docs.text:
Total vertical rise is \(105\text{-}1/2^{\prime\prime}\) (\(105.5^{\prime\prime}\)). Target riser height is \(7\text{-}1/4^{\prime\prime}\) (\(7.25^{\prime\prime}\)): 1. Riser count: 105.5 [ENTER] 7.25 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) \(14.55 \implies\) Round to 15 risers. 2. Exact riser height: 105.5 [ENTER] 15 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 7.0333333333. 3. Decompose to nearest \(1/16^{\prime\prime}\): Fractional part: 7 [-] 16 [×] \(\rightarrow\) \(0.5333 \approx 1/16^{\prime\prime} \implies\) Cut stringers at 7-1/16" (exact rise \(7.0625^{\prime\prime} \times 15 = 105.94^{\prime\prime}\), adjusted on bottom tread).

Dividing total floor-to-floor rise by the target riser height (105.5 [ENTER] 7.25 [÷] \(= 14.55\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 14.55)\)) indicates 15 risers; dividing 105.5 [ENTER] 15 [÷] yields the exact unit rise \(7.0333^{\prime\prime}\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 14.55, X: 7.03)\), and converting the fractional part to sixteenths (7 [-] 16 [×] \(= 0.5333/16^{\prime\prime}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 14.55, X: 0.53)\)) specifies a 7-1/16" stringer gauge layout.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.29: SaaS Unit Economics — LTV : CAC Ratio in One Chain
docs.text:
A B2B software enterprise generates Average Revenue Per User \(\text{ARPU} = \$250.00/\text{month}\) at an \(80.0\%\) gross margin, with monthly revenue churn \(c = 2.5\%\) (\(0.025\)) and Customer Acquisition Cost \(\text{CAC} = \$1,600.00\): $\(\text{LTV} = \frac{\text{ARPU} \times \text{GM}\%}{\text{Churn}} = \frac{250 \times 0.80}{0.025} = \$8,000.00, \qquad \frac{\text{LTV}}{\text{CAC}} = \frac{8000}{1600} = \mathbf{5.00\text{x}}\)$ Boardroom RPN Keystrokes: 250 [ENTER] 80 [↱] [%] 0.025 [÷] 1600 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 5.00x.

Modeling customer retention as a geometric survival series with monthly hazard rate \(c = 0.025\) gives an expected customer lifetime of \(1/c = 40\text{ months}\). Keying 250 [ENTER] 80 [↱] [%] isolates monthly gross margin contribution \((\$200.00/\text{mo})\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 250.00, X: 200.00)\), dividing by churn 0.025 [÷] capitalizes that stream into Customer Lifetime Value (\(\text{LTV} = \$8,000.00\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 250.00, X: 8000.00)\)), and dividing by 1600 [÷] yields the unit-economics multiple \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 250.00, X: \mathbf{5.00}\text{x})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.30: Operating Breakeven Volume (\(Q_{\text{BE}}\))
docs.text:
A manufacturing line carries annual fixed overhead of \(F = \$420,000.00\). Each unit sells for \(P = \$85.00\) with variable unit cost \(V = \$35.00\) (contribution margin \(\$50.00/\text{unit}\)): $\(Q_{\text{BE}} = \frac{F}{P - V} = \frac{420,000}{85 - 35}\)$ Keystrokes: 420000 [ENTER] 85 [ENTER] 35 [-] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 8,400 units.

In cost-volume-profit (CVP) accounting, each unit sold contributes \(P - V\) toward absorbing fixed overhead \(F\): staging 420000 [ENTER] \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 420000.00, X: 420000.00)\), forming the unit contribution margin 85 [ENTER] 35 [-] (\(\$50.00/\text{unit}\) in \(X\) while \(F\) waits in \(Y\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 420000.00, X: 50.00)\)), and dividing via [÷] determines the operating breakeven volume \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{8400}\text{ units})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 11.31: Commercial Real Estate Net Operating Income (NOI) & Cap Rate
docs.text:
An apartment building generates Gross Scheduled Rent of \(\$112,500.00/\text{year}\) with a \(28.0\%\) operating expense + vacancy ratio, offered at an asking price of \(\$1,250,000.00\): $\(\text{NOI} = 112,500 \times (1 - 0.28) = \$81,000.00, \qquad \text{Cap Rate} = \frac{\text{NOI}}{\text{Price}} \times 100\)$ Keystrokes: 112500 [ENTER] 28 [↱] [%] [-] 1250000 [÷] 100 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 6.48%.

Deducting the \(28\%\) vacancy and operating-expense reserve via 112500 [ENTER] 28 [↱] [%] \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 112500.00, X: 31500.00)\) followed by [-] isolates Net Operating Income (\(\text{NOI} = \$81,000.00\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 81000.00)\)); dividing by the \(\$1,250,000\) acquisition price (1250000 [÷] \(= 0.0648\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 0.0648)\)) and scaling by 100 [×] determines the unlevered capitalization rate \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{6.48}\%)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.1: Cubic Extrema & Root Guess Bracketing for Brent's Solver
docs.text:
Before executing Richard Brent's root finder ([↱] [SOLVE]), plot the polynomial in App Mode to visually bracket roots:

\[f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 = 0\]
  1. Program in [↱] [EQN]: X^3 - 3*X^2 - 9*X + 5
  2. Stage domain on the stack (\(x_{\min}\) in Register \(Y\), \(x_{\max}\) in Register \(X\)): 4 [+/-] [ENTER] 6

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.4: High-Pass RC Filter Frequency Response
docs.text:
The high-pass filter frequency response is given by:

$\(|H(f)| = \frac{f / f_c}{\sqrt{1 + (f / f_c)^2}}\)$ For cutoff frequency \(f_c = 1000\text{ Hz}\): 1. Program in [↱] [EQN]: (X/1000)/SQRT(1+(X/1000)^2) 2. Stage domain (\(x_{\min}\) in \(Y\), \(x_{\max}\) in \(X\)): 0 [ENTER] 5000 3. Press [↱] [PLOT]. The curve begins at \(0\) at DC (\(f=0\)), crosses \(0.707107\) at \(f = 1000\text{ Hz}\), and asymptotically approaches \(1.00\) at high frequencies. Octave-Above-Cutoff Check (\(f = 2000\text{ Hz}\)): 2000 [ENTER] 1000 [÷] [STO] A [↰] [x²] 1 [+] [√x] [RCL] A [x⇄y] [÷] \(\implies \mathbf{0.894427}\).

In a first-order RC high-pass section, the capacitor blocks DC (\(|H(0)| = 0\)) and passes high-frequency ac components above the corner frequency \(f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C} = 1000\text{ Hz}\). Evaluating the normalized frequency ratio at one octave above cutoff (2000 [ENTER] 1000 [÷] [STO] A \(\rightarrow f/f_c = 2.00\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 2.000000)\)), forming the impedance modulus \(\sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^2} = \sqrt{5}\) via [↰] [x²] 1 [+] [√x] \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 2.236068)\), and dividing via [RCL] A [x⇄y] [÷] establishes the octave-above-cutoff attenuation factor \(2/\sqrt{5}\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{0.894427}\), or \(-0.97\text{ dB})\). (Zero-Register Stack Alternative: Duplicating the normalized frequency ratio on the stack via 2000 [ENTER] 1000 [÷] [ENTER] [↰] [x²] 1 [+] [√x] [÷] keeps \(f/f_c = 2.00\) waiting in Register \(Y\) while \(\sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^2}\) forms in Register \(X\), resolving \(\mathbf{0.894427}\) without touching storage register A!)

Workbook Problem 12.8: Radioactive Exponential Decay Curve
docs.text:
Cobalt-60 activity decays according to \(A(t) = 100 \times e^{-0.1315 t}\) (\(t\) in years): Plot over \(t \in [0, 25\text{ years}]\): Trace at \(t = 5.27\text{ years}\) confirms \(A = 50.0\%\) (the half-life).

With decay constant \(\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = 0.1315\text{ yr}^{-1}\), evaluating the exponent at \(t = 5.27\text{ yr}\) (.1315 [+/-] 5.27 [×] \(= -0.693005 \approx -\ln 2\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: -0.693005)\)), exponentiating via [eˣ] (\(0.500072\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 0.500072)\)), and scaling by 100 [×] confirms the \(50\%\) half-life crossing \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{50.01}\%)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.9: Logistic Population Growth S-Curve (Sigmoidal)
docs.text:
Ecological population growth with carrying capacity \(K = 1000\), growth rate \(r = 0.5\), initial population \(P_0 = 50\):

$\(P(t) = \frac{K}{1 + \left(\frac{K - P_0}{P_0}\right) e^{-r t}} = \frac{1000}{1 + 19 e^{-0.5 t}}\)$ Plot over \(t \in [0, 20]\): curve shows initial exponential growth, an inflection point at \(P = 500\) (\(t = \ln(19)/0.5 \approx 5.89\)), and asymptotic approach to \(1000\).

Pierre-François Verhulst's logistic equation \(\frac{dP}{dt} = rP(1 - P/K)\) achieves its maximum absolute growth rate \(\frac{rK}{4}\) exactly at the half-saturation inflection time \(t_{\text{inf}} = \frac{\ln((K - P_0)/P_0)}{r} = \frac{\ln 19}{0.5} \approx 5.88894\): evaluating the damping term .5 [+/-] 5.88894 [×] [eˣ] 19 [×] yields \(19 e^{-r t_{\text{inf}}} = 1.000000\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 1.000000)\), adding 1 [+] forms the denominator \(2.000000\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 2.000000)\), and dividing into carrying capacity 1000 [x⇄y] [÷] confirms the inflection ordinate \(K/2\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{500.000000})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.10: Weber-Fechner Acoustic Decibel Curve
docs.text:
Sound pressure level \(L_p = 20 \log_{10}(P / P_0)\) where \(P_0 = 20\text{ }\mu\text{Pa}\): Logarithmic compression displays the human ear's vast dynamic range across acoustic pressures.

Because human auditory perception responds logarithmically to acoustic pressure amplitude, dividing a \(20,000\text{ }\mu\text{Pa}\) (\(0.02\text{ Pa}\)) sound wave by the \(20\text{ }\mu\text{Pa}\) hearing threshold via 20000 [ENTER] 20 [÷] isolates the amplitude ratio \(P/P_0 = 1000.00\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 1000.00)\), taking the base-10 logarithm [↰] [LOG] yields \(3.000000\text{ bels}\) of amplitude \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 3.000000)\), and scaling by 20 [×] converts to sound pressure level \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{60.00}\text{ dB})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.11: Statistical Residual Plot (\(y_i - \hat{y}_i\))
docs.text:
To verify that linear regression errors are normally distributed and homoscedastic, plot residuals:

$\(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}(x_i)\)$ * \(e_1 = 1.25 - 0.1245(10) = 1.25 - 1.245 = \mathbf{+0.005\text{ V}}\) * \(e_2 = 2.45 - 0.1245(20) = 2.45 - 2.490 = \mathbf{-0.040\text{ V}}\) * \(e_3 = 3.80 - 0.1245(30) = 3.80 - 3.735 = \mathbf{+0.065\text{ V}}\) * \(e_4 = 4.95 - 0.1245(40) = 4.95 - 4.980 = \mathbf{-0.030\text{ V}}\) Residual points scatter randomly above and below the zero-error axis, confirming absence of systematic non-linear bias.

Auditing regression residuals \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\) ensures that transducer non-linearity is not masquerading under a high correlation coefficient (\(r = 0.999565\)). Staging the first measured output 1.25 [ENTER] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1.250000, X: 1.250000)\), evaluating the fitted value 10 [ENTER] 0.1245 [×] (\(\hat{y}_1 = 1.245000\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.000000, Y: 1.250000, X: 1.245000)\)), and subtracting via [-] isolates \(e_1 = y_1 - \hat{y}_1\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{+0.005000}\text{ V})\), while 2.45 [ENTER] 20 [ENTER] 0.1245 [×] [-] yields \(e_2\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0050, X: \mathbf{-0.040000}\text{ V})\). (Zero-Re-Entry Residual & \(SS_{\text{res}}\) Choreography: Because the four calibration pairs from Textbook Showcase Problem 12.6 are already active in the statistical registers, you never need to re-type the slope 0.1245: keying 1.25 [ENTER] 10 [ŷ] [R↓] [-]—or parking the slope 0.1245 across the upper stack via 0.1245 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER]—evaluates each fitted voltage directly. Better still, squaring each residual in place ([↰] [x²]) as soon as it is formed accumulates the Residual Sum of Squares \(SS_{\text{res}} = \sum e_i^2 = 0.005^2 + (-0.040)^2 + 0.065^2 + (-0.030)^2 = \mathbf{0.006750\text{ V}^2}\) directly on the stack without re-entering a single residual!)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.12: Lissajous Figure 1:2 Harmonic Ratio
docs.text:
Signal frequencies \(f_x = 100\text{ Hz}, f_y = 200\text{ Hz}\):

$\(x(t) = \sin(t), \quad y(t) = \sin(2t)\)$ The parametric trajectory traces a figure-8 ("infinity" symbol \(\infty\)).

Jules Antoine Lissajous's 1:2 harmonic curve satisfies the algebraic lemniscate relation \(y^2 = 4x^2(1 - x^2)\), crossing the origin twice per fundamental cycle to form a figure-eight. In [RAD] mode, duplicating \(t = \pi/6\) via [↱] [π] 6 [÷] [ENTER] \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.523599, X: 0.523599)\), evaluating the second-harmonic ordinate [ENTER] 2 [×] [SIN] (\(y = \sin(\pi/3) = \sqrt{3}/2 \approx 0.866025\) in \(X\) while \(t\) waits in \(Y\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.523599, X: 0.866025)\)), and swapping [x⇄y] [SIN] resolves the fundamental abscissa \(x = \sin(\pi/6) = \mathbf{0.500000}\) in \(X\) while preserving \(y = 0.866025\) in \(Y\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.866025, X: 0.500000)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.13: Acoustic Cardioid Microphone Polar Pattern
docs.text:
In studio acoustics, a cardioid directional microphone exhibits polar sensitivity over \(\theta \in [0^\circ, 360^\circ]\):

\[r(\theta) = 2(1 - \cos\theta)\]

This profile produces a heart-shaped cardioid with a complete null (\(r = 0\)) at \(\theta = 0^\circ\), side sensitivity \(r = 2.0\) at \(\theta = \pm 90^\circ\), and peak rear sensitivity at \(\theta = 180^\circ\) (\(r = 4.0\)).

Polar-to-Rectangular Vector Check: To convert any \((x, y) = (1, 10)\) coordinate on a traced curve into polar magnitude \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\): 10 [↰] [x²] 1 [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] \(\implies \mathbf{10.049876}\).

Combining an omnidirectional pressure element with a figure-eight velocity-gradient element creates the uniaxial cardioid pattern \(r(\theta) = 2(1 - \cos\theta)\). Converting any traced Cartesian point \((x, y) = (1, 10)\) into radial distance via 10 [↰] [x²] (\(100.000000\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 100.000000)\)), 1 [↰] [x²] (\(1.000000\) in \(X\) with \(100.000000\) in \(Y\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 100.000000, X: 1.000000)\)), [+] (\(101.000000\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 101.000000)\)), and [√x] resolves the Euclidean radius \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{10.049876})\)—or in a single hardware operation via 10 [ENTER] 1 [↰] [▸θ,r]!

Workbook Problem 12.15: Gaussian Error Function (\(\text{erf}\)) Diffusion Profile
docs.text:
In Fickian heat and mass diffusion, concentration across a semi-infinite slab follows the Gaussian error function:

\[\text{erf}(x) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^x e^{-t^2} dt\]

The sigmoidal curve transitions smoothly from \(-1.0\) at \(-\infty\) to \(+1.0\) at \(+\infty\), passing through \((0, 0)\) with central inflection slope \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \approx \mathbf{1.128379}\) ([↱] [π] [√x] 2 [x⇄y] [÷]).

Solving Fick's second law \(\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} = D \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial z^2}\) via Boltzmann's similarity variable \(x = \frac{z}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\) yields the error-function profile whose steepest concentration gradient occurs at the interface \(x = 0\): evaluating [↱] [π] [√x] (\(\sqrt{\pi} \approx 1.772454\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 1.772454)\)), staging 2 [x⇄y] \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 2.000000, X: 1.772454)\), and dividing via [÷] establishes the Maclaurin leading-term slope \(2/\sqrt{\pi}\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{1.128379})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.16: Wien Displacement Blackbody Radiation Curve
docs.text:
Planck's spectral radiance for a tungsten filament at \(T = 3000\text{ K}\) obeys:

\[B(\lambda, T) \propto \frac{\lambda^{-5}}{e^{hc/(\lambda k_B T)} - 1}, \qquad \lambda_{\max} = \frac{b}{T}\]

The curve displays the steep short-wavelength ultraviolet cutoff (resolving the classical Rayleigh-Jeans catastrophe) and a peak spectral emission at \(\lambda_{\max} = \frac{2897.77\,\mu\text{m}\cdot\text{K}}{3000\text{ K}} = \mathbf{0.9659\,\mu\text{m}}\) in the near-infrared.

Differentiating Max Planck's spectral radiance distribution with respect to wavelength yields the transcendental root \(x = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{\max} k_B T} \approx 4.965114\), which defines Wilhelm Wien's displacement constant \(b = 2897.77\,\mu\text{m}\cdot\text{K}\): dividing 2897.77 [ENTER] \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 2897.770000, X: 2897.770000)\) by the filament temperature 3000 [÷] locates the emission peak in the near-infrared at \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{0.965923}\,\mu\text{m})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.17: Jakob Bernoulli's Lemniscate
docs.text:
In polar coordinates, the locus of points whose product of distances from two foci is constant follows:

\[r^2 = 4 \cos(2\theta)\]

This relation renders a symmetric figure-eight ribbon spanning \(r \in [0, 2.0]\) over \(\theta \in [-45^\circ, +45^\circ]\) and \([135^\circ, 225^\circ]\), while regions where \(\cos(2\theta) < 0\) are automatically clipped as imaginary branches by the vector plotter.

Jakob Bernoulli introduced the lemniscate ("decorated with ribbons") in Acta Eruditorum (1694) as the elastic curve of a bent rod and the locus of constant focal-distance product: evaluating at \(\theta = 30^\circ\) via 30 [ENTER] 2 [×] (\(2\theta = 60.0^\circ\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.000000, X: 60.000000)\)), [COS] (\(\cos 60^\circ = 0.500000\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 0.500000)\)), and [√x] 2 [×] determines the polar radius \(r = 2\sqrt{\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{2}\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{1.414214})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.18: Constant-Pitch Archimedean Spiral
docs.text:
In mechanical scroll compressors and vinyl groove geometry, the polar trajectory expands linearly with rotation angle \(\theta\) (in radians):

\[r(\theta) = 0.5\,\theta\]

Each full \(2\pi\) revolution increases the radius by a constant pitch \(\Delta r = 0.5(2\pi) = \pi \approx \mathbf{3.1416\text{ mm}}\). Verify linear spiral growth across multiple revolutions on the dot-matrix grid.

Unlike a logarithmic spiral whose turn spacing grows geometrically, Archimedes' spiral \(r(\theta) = a\theta\) maintains constant radial separation \(\Delta r = 2\pi a\) between adjacent involute wraps: evaluating one full revolution [↱] [π] 2 [×] (\(2\pi \approx 6.283185\text{ rad}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.000000, X: 6.283185)\)) and scaling by 0.5 [×] confirms the uniform scroll pitch \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{3.141593}\text{ mm})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.19: Supersonic Prandtl-Meyer & Mach Cone Angle Curve
docs.text:
The supersonic shock wave half-angle \(\mu(M)\) against Mach number \(M \in [1.0, 5.0]\) in Degrees mode (M [1/x] [↰] [ASIN]) follows:

\[\mu(M) = \arcsin\left(\frac{1}{M}\right)\]

The curve starts at a normal sonic wave \(\mu(1.0) = 90.0^\circ\), sweeps sharply through \(\mu(2.0) = \mathbf{30.0^\circ}\), and narrows to a slender hypersonic cone \(\mu(5.0) = \mathbf{11.537^\circ}\). Map compressible flow shock angle decay from sonic boom to hypersonic flight.

When a vehicle exceeds the speed of sound \(a\), spherical acoustic wavefronts coalesce along Ernst Mach's conical envelope of half-angle \(\sin\mu = a/v = 1/M\): at Mach 2, 2 [1/x] (\(0.500000\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 0.500000)\)) followed by [↰] [ASIN] yields \(\mu(2) = \mathbf{30.000000}^\circ\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{30.000000}^\circ)\), while at hypersonic Mach 5, 5 [1/x] (\(0.200000\) in \(X\) with \(30.0^\circ\) preserved in \(Y\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 30.000000, X: 0.200000)\)) followed by [↰] [ASIN] narrows the Mach cone to \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 30.000000, X: \mathbf{11.536959}^\circ)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.20: Thin-Airfoil Aerodynamic Lift Slope (\(C_L\) vs. \(\alpha\))
docs.text:
Classical thin-airfoil theory predicts section lift coefficient (for angle of attack \(\alpha\) in radians, or \(\frac{2\pi^2}{180}\alpha^\circ \approx 0.10966\,\alpha^\circ\)):

\[C_L(\alpha) = 2\pi \alpha\]

Plotting over \(\alpha \in [-5^\circ, +15^\circ]\) illustrates the linear inviscid lift regime up to \(C_L(10^\circ) \approx \mathbf{1.0966}\) prior to boundary-layer flow separation.

Max Munk and Hermann Glauert's thin-airfoil theory establishes that any symmetric cambered section in inviscid subsonic flow exhibits a universal lift-curve slope of \(\frac{dC_L}{d\alpha} = 2\pi\text{ rad}^{-1} = \frac{2\pi^2}{180}\text{ deg}^{-1} \approx 0.109662\text{ deg}^{-1}\): staging \(\alpha = 10^\circ\) via 10 [ENTER] \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 10.000000, X: 10.000000)\) and multiplying by 0.10966 [×] predicts the pre-stall section lift coefficient \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{1.096600})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.21: Van der Waals Real Gas Isotherms
docs.text:
Real gas pressure across molar volume \(V\) follows:

\[P(V) = \frac{R T}{V - b} - \frac{a}{V^2}\]

Isotherms below critical temperature \(T_c\) display characteristic van der Waals cubic loops, illustrating liquid-gas phase coexistence.

Johannes Diderik van der Waals corrected the ideal gas law for finite molecular excluded volume (\(b = 0.04\text{ m}^3/\text{mol}\)) and intermolecular London dispersion attraction (\(a = 0.36\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{m}^6/\text{mol}^2\)): evaluating kinetic thermal pressure 8.314 [ENTER] 300 [×] (\(RT = 2494.20\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.000, X: 2494.20)\)) divided by free molar volume .10 [ENTER] .04 [-] (\(V - b = 0.060000\) in \(X\) with \(2494.20\) in \(Y\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 2494.20, X: 0.060000)\)) via [÷] gives \(41570.00\text{ Pa}\) \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 41570.00)\); computing the cohesive pressure correction .36 [ENTER] .10 [↰] [x²] [÷] (\(36.00\text{ Pa}\) in \(X\) with \(41570.00\) in \(Y\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 41570.00, X: 36.00)\)) and subtracting via [-] yields the net real-gas pressure \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{41534.00}\text{ Pa})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.22: Bivariate Scatter Plot: Hooke's Law Spring Calibration
docs.text:
Accumulating four experimental force-displacement pairs \((1\text{ cm}, 4.8\text{ N})\), \((2\text{ cm}, 10.1\text{ N})\), \((3\text{ cm}, 14.9\text{ N})\), and \((4\text{ cm}, 20.2\text{ N})\) via [Σ+] (with no active equations in EQN) and pressing [↱] [PLOT] in App Mode renders the four \(2\times 2\) data markers alongside the least-squares regression line of slope \(k = \mathbf{5.10\text{ N/cm}}\) (\(510\text{ N/m}\)) and correlation \(r = \mathbf{0.9998}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.23: Automotive Kinetic Energy & Braking Distance Parabola
docs.text:
Plotting \(E_k(v) = \frac{1}{2} m v^2\) for a \(m = 1,200\text{ kg}\) vehicle over speed \(v \in [0, 40\text{ m/s}]\) (V [↰] [x²] 600 [×]) visually demonstrates why doubling highway speed from \(15\text{ m/s}\) to \(30\text{ m/s}\) quadruples kinetic energy from \(135\text{ kJ}\) to \(\mathbf{540\text{ kJ}}\).

By the work-energy theorem \(W = \mu m g d = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\), minimum stopping distance scales quadratically with entry speed: evaluating kinetic energy at \(15\text{ m/s}\) (15 [↰] [x²] 600 [×] \(\rightarrow E_{k,1} = 135,000\text{ J}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.000000, X: 135000.00)\)) and at \(30\text{ m/s}\) (30 [↰] [x²] 600 [×] \(\rightarrow E_{k,2} = 540,000\text{ J}\) in \(X\) while \(135,000\text{ J}\) lifts to \(Y\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.000000, Y: 135000.00, X: 540000.00)\)), then dividing via [x⇄y] [÷] confirms the \(2^2 = 4\times\) quadratic energy multiplier \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{4.000000}\text{x})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.25: Linear Thermal Dilatation Calibration Curve
docs.text:
Plotting \(\Delta L(T) = \alpha L_0 (T - T_0)\) for an aluminum metrology bar (\(\alpha = 23.1 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}\), \(L_0 = 1.0\text{ m}\)) over \(T \in [273\text{ K}, 373\text{ K}]\) provides a direct visual reference line of slope \(23.1\,\mu\text{m/K}\) (\(2.31\text{ mm}\) total expansion over \(100\text{ K}\)). Sweep temperature to plot linear expansion of precision metrology standards.

Across moderate temperature excursions between the ice point (\(273\text{ K}\)) and steam point (\(373\text{ K}\)), lattice anharmonicity produces linear thermal expansion: computing the temperature excursion 373 [ENTER] 273 [-] (\(\Delta T = 100.0\text{ K}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.000000, X: 100.000000)\)), multiplying by the linear expansion coefficient 23.1 [E] 6 [+/-] [×] (\(\Delta L = 0.002310\text{ m}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 0.002310)\)), and converting to millimeters via 1000 [×] yields the total gauge elongation \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{2.310000}\text{ mm})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.26: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiative Heat Emission
docs.text:
Power \(P(T) = \varepsilon \sigma A T^4\): Quartic curve demonstrates why radiative heat transfer dominates at high temperatures (\(T > 1000\text{ K}\)).

Integrating Planck's spectral distribution over all wavelengths and hemisphere solid angles yields the Josef Stefan and Ludwig Boltzmann \(T^4\) radiation law: raising billet temperature to the fourth power 1200 [ENTER] 4 [yˣ] (\(T^4 = 2.0736 \times 10^{12}\text{ K}^4\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 2.0736\text{E}12)\)), multiplying by \(\sigma = 5.67037 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\cdot\text{K}^{-4}\) (5.67037 [E] 8 [+/-] [×] \(\rightarrow 117580.8\text{ W/m}^2\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 117580.8)\)), and scaling by surface emissivity and area (.85 [×] .50 [×]) determines the radiative heat flux \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{49971.84}\text{ W} \approx 50.0\text{ kW})\)—note that 1200 [↰] [x²] [↰] [x²] computes \(T^4\) in two single-cycle squarings!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 12.27: Newton's Law of Cooling Exponential Asymptote
docs.text:
Plotting \(T(t) = T_{\text{env}} + (T_0 - T_{\text{env}}) e^{-k t}\) for a quenched steel billet (\(T_0 = 800\text{ K}\), \(T_{\text{env}} = 300\text{ K}\), \(k = 0.05\text{ s}^{-1}\)) over \(t \in [0, 100\text{ s}]\) (T 0.05 [×] [+/-] [eˣ] 500 [×] 300 [+]) illustrates rapid initial heat rejection followed by asymptotic approach to the \(300\text{ K}\) ambient floor.

When the Biot number \(\text{Bi} = \frac{h L_c}{k_{\text{solid}}} < 0.1\), internal thermal gradients are negligible and lumped-capacitance quenching decays exponentially with time constant \(\tau = 1/k = 20\text{ s}\): evaluating at \(t = 20\text{ s}\) (20 [ENTER] 0.05 [×] [+/-] \(\rightarrow -kt = -1.000000\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.000000, X: -1.000000)\)), exponentiating via [eˣ] (\(e^{-1} \approx 0.367879\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 0.367879)\)), scaling by the initial \(500\text{ K}\) thermal excess (500 [×] \(\rightarrow 183.939721\text{ K}\), \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: 183.939721)\)), and adding the \(300\text{ K}\) bath temperature (300 [+]) confirms the one-time-constant billet temperature \((T: 0.00, Z: 0.00, Y: 0.00, X: \mathbf{483.939721}\text{ K})\).
