docs.title: Part V: Four-Perspective Adversarial Audit & Architectural Hardening (Revision 5.0)
docs.text:
To ensure both volumes withstand scrutiny from domain experts, literary critics, and legal counsel, we subjected the entire 34-file manuscript corpus to an adversarial review from four demanding perspectives:

  1. The HP Calculator Purist (Corvallis RPN Historian):
  2. Findings: Flagged the Alpha register table (Q–Z) in SC-32 Appendix C where keys 9 (S) through 0 (Z) had shifted by one position (R appeared twice, S was omitted); asked for an explicit architectural explanation of how the SC-32's IEEE-754 binary64 (53-bit significand + 12-digit decimal guard rounding) engine compares to classic 1980s HP Saturn 12-digit / 15-digit Binary-Coded Decimal (BCD) microcode on decimal fractions like \(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3\).
  3. Resolution: Corrected the Alpha column (7=Q, 8=R, 9=S, 4=T, 5=U, 6=V, 1=W, 2=X, 3=Y, 0=Z) in sc32/appendix-c-keycap-directory.md to match the app's HP32KeyMap, and authored the IEEE-754 vs. Saturn BCD architectural analysis in sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md.

  4. Programmatic Prevention: Upgraded RPNCore/Sources/LaserLayoutExporter/main.swift in watch-calc-32 to export both physical key matrices and CalculatorMenu softkey menus directly to docs/assets/manuals/layout_data.json (SC-32) and layout_data_sc6.json (SC-6). Converted 10,915 keystroke references across all 34 manual files into {{key:NAME}} and {{keycap:NAME}} macros validated at build time by Tools/book_engine.py.

  5. Faceplate Theme Independence (Zero Shift Color Names):

  6. Findings: Because physical faceplates and the companion app support 7 distinct CMF themes (Pure Black, Retro Futurism, Pioneer, Stealth, Supernova, Voyager, and Arcade), shift key accent colors vary across editions.

  7. Resolution: Eliminated all color-dependent shift terminology ("Yellow Shift", "Gold Shift", "Blue Shift") across both books. All shift operations are now referenced strictly by their functional symbols exported from the app JSON: Left Shift [↰] and Right Shift [↱] on the SC-32, and [f] Shift and [g] Shift on the SC-6.

  8. The Practicing Scientist (Metrologist & Experimental Physicist):

  9. Findings: Noted that empirical CODATA physical constants (\(\alpha, \varepsilon_0, \mu_0, m_e, m_p, G\), etc.) are periodically revised by BIPM/CODATA task groups and should not be hardcoded in an evergreen textbook; requested the 2022 BIPM SI prefix additions (ronna, quetta, ronto, quecto) and a distinction between the Libby (\(5,568\text{ yr}\)) and Cambridge (\(5,730\text{ yr}\)) radiocarbon (\(^{14}\text{C}\)) half-lives.

  10. Resolution: Removed mutable CODATA physical constants from sc32/appendix-d-constants-and-equations.md (retaining only timeless mathematical constants \(\pi, e, \varphi, \gamma, \ln 2, \ln 10, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5}\), complete BIPM SI prefixes from quetta \(10^{30}\) to quecto \(10^{-30}\), exact defined unit conversions, and the 58 STEM equations), and added the Cambridge vs. Libby radiocarbon calibration convention note in Chapters 3 and 13.

  11. The New York Times Best Seller Judge (Literary Non-Fiction Critic):

  12. Findings: Flagged residual internal rubric headings ("The ... Persona"), CHAPTER BASELINE MODE banners appearing above opening narrative stories, unclosed ``` code fences, and manual section numbering collisions (## 10.6 appearing twice).

  13. Resolution: Replaced all "Persona" headings with natural editorial titles ("Perspectives from the Classroom, Studio & Bench", "For Educators & Classroom Mentors", "At the Kitchen Table: Guided Discovery", "From the Instrument Designer's Bench"), moved all CHAPTER BASELINE MODE banners below the opening narrative story, repaired all code fences and inline backticks, and implemented deterministic build-time section auto-numbering (## and ###) and cross-reference #anchor synchronization in Tools/book_engine.py.

  14. The IP & Product Liability Counsel:

  15. Findings: Identified mandatory federal safety and intellectual property disclosures required for commercial hardware/kit distribution and technical engineering handbooks.
  16. Resolution: Added statutory Reese's Law (16 CFR Part 1263 / P.L. 117-171) CR2032 lithium coin cell ingestion hazard warnings, CPSC Small Parts Choking Hazard (16 CFR § 1501 / ASTM F963) and 3D-printed FDM layer delamination inspection warnings, Trademark Attribution & Non-Affiliation Notices (Hewlett-Packard, Gridfinity, SwissMicros), and Engineering & Financial Limitation of Liability Disclaimers to both volumes.

docs.title: Part VIII: Canonical Chapter Architecture, Narrative Writing & Thematic Book Flow Rubric (Revision 8.0 — Mandatory Orchestrator & Auditor Standard)
8.1 Why Mechanical Checklists Are Not Enough
docs.text:
Earlier revisions of this rubric verified essential technical invariants (unit test coverage, {{res:ID}} accuracy, {{cite:ID}} bibliography macros, orthographic renders, and freedom from ASCII code boxes). However, a book can pass every regex and unit-test check while still failing a New York Times Bestseller judge or trade publisher if its internal chapter structure, narrative voice, and thematic flow feel stitched together from separate passes.

Specifically, the Orchestrator, Editorial Reviewer, and Forensic Auditor must actively inspect for and reject (REQUEST_CHANGES / FLAGGED) four structural anti-patterns: 1. "Frankenstein" Section Duplication: Prepended narrative tours followed later in the same chapter by older technical sections that explain the exact same concept, hardware feature, or demonstration equation a second time (e.g., explaining the 4-level stack twice and solving \((15-3)\times(4+2)\div 6 = 12\) twice in SC-6 Chapter 2; explaining the buttons, transflective screen, and \(15^\circ\) desk stand twice in SC-6 Chapter 1; or covering 1064nm laser micro-foaming and transflective LCD optics twice in SC-32 Chapter 1). 2. Point-of-View (POV) Whiplash in SC-6: Opening a chapter by speaking warmly to the young student ("you"), then abruptly switching mid-chapter to an adult curriculum syllabus talking about children in the third person ("In elementary mathematics, children are taught... which can feel counter-intuitive to a 7-year-old child", "When young learners skip the concrete and representational phases...", or placing unboxed ## Teaching Note: and ## Teacher Dialogue Scripts sections directly in the student's reading flow). 3. "Fake Umbrella" Expedition Headers Over Disconnected Worksheet Drills: Writing an exciting Mission Briefing paragraph for an Expedition (e.g., Expedition 1: The School Playground Construction Crew in SC-6 Ch 2 or Expedition 1: The Great Ancient Bazaar in SC-6 Ch 3), while the 8–10 problems underneath are still disconnected 1-line drills about squirrels finding acorns, birds on a wire, blueberry muffins, broken crayons, or naked numbers! 4. Abrupt Chapter Endings Without Thematic Bridges: Ending a chapter abruptly after the last problem table without a concluding synthesis that connects the chapter's discovery to the next chapter in the book's overarching narrative journey.

docs.title: 8.2 The Canonical 5-Act Chapter Blueprint (Required for Every Chapter in Both Volumes)
docs.text:
Every instructional chapter across Volume 1 (SC-6 Chapters 01–09) and Volume 2 (SC-32 Chapters 01–14) must follow a unified, non-repetitive 5-Act Narrative & Reference Architecture:

Act Structural Role Mandatory Narrative, Voice & Flow Standards Act I: The Opening Story & Intellectual Hook Why This Idea Matters Opens immediately after the # Chapter title with a gripping historical, human, or real-world narrative hook that poses a genuine puzzle before any mode banners or tables appear. Followed by the compact CHAPTER BASELINE MODE banner and (in SC-6) the Unlocked Keycaps Ribbon. Act II: The Core Mental Model & The Stack How to Think on the Stack Builds the chapter's core mathematical mental model and maps it directly onto The Number Stack (\(T, Z, Y, X\)). Strict Single-Source Rule: Every concept, hardware mechanism, and demonstration problem is taught once and only once in a single cohesive narrative arc—zero duplicate sections or repeated tables. Act III: Guided Studio Explorations Hands-On Blocks \(\to\) Stack Keys Walks the reader through 2–4 connected, story-driven explorations showing how physical manipulative blocks (SC-6 and geometric/algebraic chapters of SC-32) and RPN keystrokes work together step by step. Transition paragraphs between subsections must explain why each tool or key arises naturally from the previous one. Act IV: Cohesive Story-Driven Expeditions / Engineering Design Briefings Exhaustive Worked Examples in a Connected World Groups the chapter's worked problems into 3–5 themed Expeditions (SC-6) or Engineering Design Briefings (SC-32). Strict Thematic Cohesion Rule: Every single problem inside an Expedition must genuinely take place inside that Expedition's narrative setting (preserving 100% of verified numbers and {{res:ID}} macros) and be written in engaging, connected sentences rather than telegraphic worksheet fragments. Act V: Chapter Wrap-Up & "Looking Ahead" Bridge Thematic Closure & Book Continuity Concludes the chapter (after the final worked problem) with a brief, inspiring What You Mastered & Looking Ahead section (1–2 paragraphs) that synthesizes the chapter's big idea and bridges directly into the next chapter's question.

9.1 Why Revision 10.0–11.0 Is Required: Closing the Gap Between Surface Regex Checks and Domain-Expert Credibility
docs.text: An adversarial red-team audit from the vantage points of crusty hpmuseum.org HP-15C/32SII purists, skeptical K–8 classroom teachers, and viral trade publishers exposed seven deep structural, editorial, and technical defects that earlier regex gates missed: 1. Un-Simulated 4-Register \((T, Z, Y, X)\) Tables in SC-32: Several tables were synthesized without running the RPNCore stack state machine row-by-row, resulting in: - A broken \(T\)-register constant pipeline in sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md (Problem 2.4, where typing 1.125 × after 0.375 × lifts 9.5250 into \(Y\) and computes \(9.5250 \times 1.125\) instead of \(25.4 \times 1.125\) because × enables stack lift!). - Dyadic operators (x∥y, ×) falsely shown as pushing old answers up into \(Y, Z, T\) instead of consuming \(Y\) and \(X\) in a dyadic stack drop (sc32/02 Problem 2.2, sc32/06 Problem 6.12, sc32/09 Problem 9.8). - Small scientific constants like Planck's \(c_1 = 1.19104 \times 10^{-16}\) printed as $0.0000$ in fixed-point tables (sc32/03 Problem 3.9). 2. "Fake RPN" Anti-Idioms & Prose-vs-Table Contradictions in SC-32: - sc32/09 Problem 9.10 manually re-types ENTER 1.875 ÷ when \(V_{\max} = 0.5333\) is already sitting in Register \(Y\) and slope \(7.2381\) is in Register \(X\) (requiring only a single {{key:×}} keystroke!). - sc32/03 Problem 3.5 boasts of "Inside-Out Entry" while using an outside-in double-ENTER sequence. - sc32/03 Problem 3.3 contains tab-corrupted LaTeX ($[\text{HCO}_3^-]$), and sc32/14 Problems 14.9 & 14.12 have contradictions between prose headers and table rows. 3. Physical Kit Inventory Violations in SC-6 ("Count Out 185 Ten-Frames / 250 Tiles"): - Problems in sc6/04 (Problems 4.17, 4.21, etc.) tell students to model 185 items with 18 ten-frames or count out 250 tiles, violating the physical kit inventory (Ten-Frame Studio = 2 ten-frames / 20 counters; Counting Studio = 144 tiles) and missing the core pedagogical point: you model a small concrete case with your blocks (e.g., \(14 \div 12\)) to see how the operation works, and then scale up to big numbers (\(185 \div 12\)) on the SC-6 Stack Calculator! 4. SC-6 Chapter 8 Quiz Engine (≠ Inequality Key Misuse), Mode Keycap Contradictions & Split Geometry Examples: - All 48 drills in sc6/08-math-quiz-engine.md ask a question like 10 - 7 = ? (answer 3) in the heading, but show 10 ENTER ? - 3 x?y and tell 1st graders to tap {{key:7}} {{key:≠}} ("Test inequality \(X \neq Y\)")! - sc6/index.md maps the Number Rack to four different buttons (LINE, PV, ▦, COUNT). - sc6/06-geometry-surface-area.md (Triangular Prism, lines 428–450) mixes a \(3\text{-}4\text{-}5\) right prism (\(84\text{ cm}^2\)) in prose with a \(6 \times 4\) isosceles tent (\(120\text{ cm}^2\)) in the table directly between the paragraphs. 5. Repetitive Table Clones in SC-6 Ch 1 & Ch 3 and Missing Visual "Algebraic vs. StackCalc" Showdowns: - sc6/01 and sc6/03 pad dozens of problems by repeating 356 ENTER over and over with identical tables. - Both books need crisp, visual, screenshot-worthy "Algebraic Calculator Trap vs. StackCalc + Blocks Superpower" comparison tables in every chapter to drive viral word-of-mouth adoption. 6. End-of-Chapter "Table Wall" Dumps & Incomplete Chapter Audits: - In previous iterations, lines 400 to 1,800 of every chapter were generated as 40–50 consecutive identical 5-bullet blocks and markdown tables, degrading narrative momentum into a wall of spreadsheet grids. Furthermore, auditors and workers often sampled only the first 200 lines rather than reading every chapter from Line 1 to EOF. 7. Trite Design-Persona Bleed, Explicit Pedagogical Meta-Scaffolding & "AI Slop" Tell-Tales: - Earlier passes leaked internal review personas, pedagogical frameworks, rubric assertions, and script-injected filler directly into reader-facing prose—e.g., "Homeschooler Diagnostic Checkpoint:", "Calculator Enthusiast Note:", "Architectural Note for HP Purists", "For Parents & Teachers:", bulleted "CRA Pedagogical Sequence: *Concrete:* / *Representational:* / *Abstract:*", parenthetical kit-inventory rubric echoes ("($\le 24$ tiles)", "Model small with blocks...", "Scale Big on StackCalc..."), outline scaffolding labels ("Thematic Arc I —", "*Mission Briefing:*", "Hands-On Studio Proof"), script-injected filler sentences ("To evaluate <lowercased title> without nested parentheses...", "On the RPN stack, we evaluate this relationship..."), fake classroom roleplay scripts ("Teacher:" / "Student (Hannah (eyes wide)):") in student chapters, leaked internal identifiers (RPNCore, generatePlot, stackLiftEnabled, HP32SII Deviation Rubric), and self-congratulatory unit-test guarantees ("Automated Engine Reliability Guarantee", "100% Engine Grounding"). A great trade book or engineering manual shows these qualities organically in crisp, natural human prose without ever echoing the prompt or rubric on the page.

docs.title: Prologue: Writing Equations for Space, Solving Them in Time
docs.text:
In the autumn of 1924, in a quiet lecture hall at the University of Warsaw, the Polish logician and philosopher Jan Łukasiewicz stood before a blackboard covered in logic formulas and examined a curious habit of mathematical notation (Łukasiewicz, 1924): the ubiquity of parentheses.

Every high-school student who has ever stared at a page of Algebra II or Precalculus knows the feeling of parenthesis vertigo. You look at an equation on a printed page:

\[x = \sqrt{7 + \sqrt{13 + \sqrt{29 + \sqrt{41}}}} \tag{Eq. 0.1}\]

or a compound rational fraction from physics or chemistry:

\[Q = \frac{12.4 \times 8.6}{3.2 + 4.9} \tag{Eq. 0.2}\]

On paper, your eyes naturally read from left to right and from the outside in. In this radical pyramid, the first symbol you encounter on the left is the outer square-root radical \(\sqrt{\dots}\), followed by \(7 +\), followed by a second radical, a third radical, and finally, at the far right end of the line, the number \(41\).

The moment you sit down to solve that equation, the outer square root cannot be evaluated first because you cannot take the square root of a sum that has not been added yet. To find \(x\), evaluation must ignore the left-to-right order of the ink and travel straight to the innermost number, \(41\), extracting its square root first, adding \(29\), taking the next square root, adding \(13\), extracting that root, and finally adding \(7\) before one last square root completes the chain from right to left.

This mismatch—between equations printed from the outside in and calculations evaluated by every human mind and computer processor from the inside out—is a historical artifact of the printing press.

docs.title: The Typesetter's Bargain and the Inside-Out Mind
docs.text:
For thousands of years, from Babylonian clay scribes and Greek geometers to medieval Arab algebraists, mathematics was written out in spoken sentences: "Take forty-one, extract its root, add twenty-nine to what results..." Spoken language unfolds in time. Physical measurement and instrumentation follow the same chronological order, staging inputs first and triggering the operation second: an electrical engineer connects two test probes to an oscilloscope before triggering a differential sweep, and a chemist weighs two reagents on a balance before combining them in a beaker. In speech, measurement, and calculation alike, an operation cannot occur until its operands exist.

In the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, however, Renaissance mathematicians and European printers faced an economic problem. Movable lead type was expensive, and rag paper was costly. Printers wanted to pack an entire finished mathematical thought onto a single static horizontal line of type. To fit a multi-step timeline onto a flat two-dimensional line, they wedged action symbols (+, -, ×, ÷) between numbers in a convention called infix notation, and invented parentheses ( ), brackets [ ], and horizontal fraction bars as punctuation fences to warn the eye: "Do not read this line from left to right; jump inside the deepest fence first."

That 16th-century typesetter's bargain was well suited to static paper, where the eye can scan back and forth across a page. It became a cognitive obstacle the moment 20th-century engineers copied paper notation onto electronic calculator keyboards.

When you type an infix string like ( ( 12.4 × 8.6 ) ÷ ( 3.2 + 4.9 ) ) = into an algebraic pocket or smartphone calculator, you must feed the machine in the sequence of the printed ink, reversing the natural order of evaluation. Halfway through the formula, when you press ÷ (, the calculation stalls because the denominator (3.2 + 4.9) does not yet exist. Because human working memory holds only about four active items at once (Miller, 1956; Sweller, 1988), hiding intermediate numbers behind a single-line display while counting nested parentheses ( ( ... ) / ( ... ) ) diverts attention from the physical structure of the problem to clerical punctuation (Strogatz, 2012; Strogatz, 2019; Ellenberg, 2014).

docs.title: Jan Łukasiewicz's Breakthrough and the Four Visible Registers
docs.text:
In 1924, Jan Łukasiewicz proved a simple theorem (Łukasiewicz, 1924): if operators are placed consistently before or after their operands, parentheses disappear from mathematical notation. No matter how deeply an equation is nested, the order in which numbers combine is unambiguous without a single bracket or precedence rule.

Three decades later, Australian philosopher and computer scientist Charles Hamblin (1957) (Hamblin, 1957) paired the postfix (Reverse Polish) form of Łukasiewicz's parenthesis-free notation, in which operands precede their operator, with a last-in, first-out hardware memory structure: an operational stack.

On a four-register operational stack, four horizontal display lines are arranged from bottom to top as Registers \(X, Y, Z,\) and \(T\). Register \(X\) at the bottom of the screen is the active register where keyed digits appear and where every unary or binary operation writes its immediate result. When a first operand is completed in Register \(X\) and the central ENTER bar is pressed, that value copies upward into Register \(Y\), preparing Register \(X\) to receive the second operand. Whenever a calculation spans two or three separate branches—like the numerator and denominator of a rational expression—the completed subtotal from the first branch lifts into Register \(Z\) (and Register \(T\)) to remain visible while the second branch is evaluated across Registers \(Y\) and \(X\). As soon as that second branch reduces to a single value in Register \(X\), the waiting subtotal in Register \(Z\) drops back into Register \(Y\) so the two operands align for the final binary operation.

When equations are read from their innermost operands outward, expressions from disparate branches of science reveal shared algebraic skeletons (Horowitz & Hill, 2015). Wiring electrical resistors in parallel, focusing light through a thin optical lens, and averaging a round-trip velocity all follow the binary harmonic relation \(x \parallel y = (x^{-1} + y^{-1})^{-1}\), while nested expressions unfold in two-register steps from the deepest term out. In the four-level radical \(x = \sqrt{7 + \sqrt{13 + \sqrt{29 + \sqrt{41}}}}\), evaluation starts at the radicand \(41\): extracting \(\sqrt{41} \approx 6.403\) inside Register \(X\), adding \(29\) and taking the square root (\(\approx 5.95\)), and adding \(13\) and taking the square root (\(\approx 4.353\)) leaves one final addition of \(7\) and square root to yield \(x \approx \mathbf{3.369}\), while Registers \(Z\) and \(T\) remain at zero.

docs.title: From Warsaw to the Shirt Pocket: The Four-Register Lineage
docs.text:
Łukasiewicz's 1924 logic notation and Hamblin's 1957 hardware stack, formalized for digital computer evaluation by Arthur Burks, Don Warren, and Jesse Wright in 1954 (Burks et al., 1954), became the native operating language of scientific instruments through the engineering work of Hewlett-Packard in Palo Alto and Corvallis. Following Thomas Osborne's floating-point prototype and the desktop HP 9100A in 1968, William R. Hewlett challenged Osborne, David S. Cochran, and Thomas M. Whitney in 1971 to condense trigonometric, logarithmic, and exponential computation into a shirt-pocket instrument. Their work produced the 35-key HP-35 in January 1972 (Whitney, Rodé & Tung, 1972; Cochran, 1972), which replaced the slide rule with a four-register operational stack (\(X, Y, Z, T\)).

Over the next two decades, Hewlett-Packard's Corvallis Division and UC Berkeley numerical analyst William M. Kahan steadily expanded that four-register architecture (Hamrick, 1996). The HP-65 (1974) and HP-41C (1979) introduced magnetic program storage, alphanumeric displays, and an international community of engineers who shared algorithms through Richard J. Nelson's PPC Journal (Nelson, 1974; Musch, Wong & Conklin, 1980). Between 1979 and 1982, Kahan and the Corvallis engineering team led by Eric A. Evett, Paul J. McClellan, and Joseph P. Tanzini brought Richard Brent's hybrid root-finding algorithm (SOLVE), adaptive Romberg quadrature (∫), and split-stack complex arithmetic (CMPLX) into the HP-34C (1979) and the horizontal Voyager series—the HP-15C scientific, HP-12C financial, and HP-16C computer-scientist instruments (Kahan, 1979; HP, 1982; Evett et al., 1983).

In 1988 and 1991, the portrait-oriented Pioneer series—the HP-32S and HP-32SII (HP, 1991)—united one-handed vertical ergonomics with 26 named A–Z variables, a symbolic Equation List (EQN), mixed-fraction display, contextual function menus (PARTS, PROB, L.R., SUM, BASE, FLAGS), and metric–imperial unit conversions on the digit keys.

docs.title: Standing on the Shoulders of the HP-32SII and the RPN Tradition
docs.text: The StackCalc SC-32 continues the HP-32SII architecture and this four-decade lineage of parenthesis-free scientific instruments (Whitney, Rodé & Tung, 1972; Cochran, 1972; Kahan, 1979; HP, 1982; Evett et al., 1983; HP, 1991). Honoring the keyboard grammar, stack-lift rules, and numerical algorithms pioneered by Cochran, Kahan, and the Corvallis engineers, the SC-32 places all four stack registers (\(T, Z, Y, X\)) in full view on a 4-line transflective LCD above a dedicated 6-key dynamic softkey strip, while preserving the tactile one-handed portrait layout and four-register invariants (4-LVL, 8-LVL, and INF via FLAGS).
