To lay out the \(O = 6.0\text{ in.}\) I-beam offset at \(\theta = 30^\circ\) (\(48.0\text{ in.}\) from the splitter trough) and the subsequent \(6.0\text{ in.} \times 8.0\text{ in.}\) rolling offset into the MCC at \(30^\circ\), the electrician evaluates 6 [ENTER] 30 [OFS] (\(T = \mathbf{12.00\text{ in.}}\)), adds the \(1/4\text{ in/in}\) shrinkage (\(6 \times 0.25 = 1.50\text{ in.}\)) to \(48.0\text{ in.}\) to place the two bend marks at \(\mathbf{49.50\text{ in.}}\) and \(\mathbf{37.50\text{ in.}}\), and uses [g] [FIT] followed by [OFS] to compute the rolling offset travel \(T_{\text{roll}} = \mathbf{20.00\text{ in.}}\):

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X What Happens on the Stack 6 [ENTER] 30 [OFS] [C] \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(12\) Compute \(30^\circ\) I-beam offset travel \(T = 6 / \sin(30^\circ) = 12.00\text{ in.}\) 48 [ENTER] 6 [ENTER] 0.25 [×] [+] \(12\) \(12\) \(12\) \(49.5\) Add shrinkage \(S = 1.50\text{ in.}\) to \(48.0\text{ in.}\) for Mark 2 at \(49.50\text{ in.}\) [x⇄y] [-] \(12\) \(12\) \(12\) \(37.5\) Subtract travel \(T = 12.00\text{ in.}\) to locate Mark 1 at \(37.50\text{ in.}\) 6 [ENTER] 8 [g] [FIT] 30 [OFS] [C] \(12\) \(12\) \(37.5\) \(20\) Compute true rolling offset \(O_{\text{true}} = 10\text{ in.}\) ([g] [FIT]) and \(30^\circ\) travel \(T_{\text{roll}} = 20.00\text{ in.}\)

To evaluate the saddle bend clearances over a \(4\text{-in.}\) steam conduit using \(22.5^\circ\) bends (\(T = 4 / \sin(22.5^\circ) \approx \mathbf{10.45\text{ in.}}\)), compute total conductor area for twelve #10 AWG THHN wires (\(12 \times 0.0211 = 0.2532\text{ in}^2\)), and confirm raceway fill inside \(1\text{-in.}\) EMT (\(0.2532 / 0.864 \approx \mathbf{29.31\%} \le 40\%\)):

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X What Happens on the Stack 4 [ENTER] 22.5 [OFS] [C] \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(10.4525\) Compute outer \(22.5^\circ\) saddle leg travel \(T_{\text{saddle}} = 4/\sin(22.5^\circ) \approx 10.45\text{ in.}\) 12 [ENTER] 0.0211 [×] \(0\) \(0\) \(10.4525\) \(0.2532\) Compute total cross-sectional area of \(12\) #10 AWG THHN wires (\(0.2532\text{ in}^2\)) 0.864 [÷] 100 [×] \(0\) \(0\) \(10.4525\) \(29.3056\) Divide by \(1\text{-in.}\) EMT area (\(0.864\text{ in}^2\)) to confirm \(\text{Fill\%} \approx 29.31\% \le 40\%\) 0.3456 [ENTER] 0.0211 [÷] \(10.4525\) \(10.4525\) \(29.3056\) \(16.3791\) Divide \(40\%\) allowance (\(0.3456\text{ in}^2\)) by \(0.0211\text{ in}^2\) (\(\lfloor 16.38 \rfloor = 16\) max wires)

docs.title: Laying Out a Four-Bend Saddle Over a 12-Inch Steam Header and Checking Raceway Fill on the Stack
docs.text:
Stepping over to the conduit bench, Jimmy executes the complete layout and code audit of the four-bend saddle over the insulated steam main:

The route must clear an active steam header measuring \(6.0\text{ inches}\) high (\(O = 6.0\text{ in.}\)) and \(12.0\text{ inches}\) wide (\(W = 12.0\text{ in.}\)). Frank decides to use a four-bend saddle with \(30^\circ\) bends in \(1\text{-inch}\) EMT. The conduit will carry four #4 AWG THHN copper conductors.

Jimmy must determine: 1. The travel distance between marks for each \(30^\circ\) offset (\(T = O \csc 30^\circ = 12.00\text{ in.}\)). 2. The total shrink deduction for the entire four-bend saddle (\(S_{\text{total}} = 2 \times O \tan 15^\circ = 3.215\text{ in.}\)). 3. The exact tape-measure marks along the conduit pipe: - Mark 1: Starting bend (\(L_1 = \text{Centerline} - W/2 - T + S_{\text{total}}\)). - Mark 2: Second bend (\(L_2 = L_1 + T\)). - Mark 3: Third bend (\(L_3 = L_2 + W\)). - Mark 4: Fourth bend (\(L_4 = L_3 + T\)). 4. The NEC Chapter 9 raceway fill percentage for the four #4 conductors inside \(1\text{-inch}\) EMT.

Follow the kinetic stack execution:

Keystroke Sequence Reg T Reg Z Reg Y Reg X Electrical Trades Scenario Walkthrough 6 [ENTER] 30 [OFS] \(0\) \(0\) \(12.00\) \(1.61\) Compute single offset: \(T = 12.00\text{ in.}\) (\(Y\)), single shrink \(S_1 = 1.608\text{ in.}\) (\(X\)) 2 [×] \(0\) \(0\) \(12.00\) \(3.22\) Double shrink for 4-bend saddle: \(S_{\text{total}} = 2 \times 1.608 = \mathbf{3.215\text{ in.}}\) (\(3\text{-}3/16\text{ in.}\)) 48 [ENTER] 6 [-] 12 [-] [+] \(0\) \(12.00\) \(3.22\) \(33.22\) Obstacle center at \(48\text{ in.}\): Mark 1 is \(48 - 6 - 12 + 3.22 = \mathbf{33.22\text{ in.}}\) 12 [+] \(12.00\) \(3.22\) \(33.22\) \(45.22\) Add travel \(T = 12\text{ in.}\): Mark 2 is \(\mathbf{45.22\text{ in.}}\) 12 [+] \(3.22\) \(33.22\) \(45.22\) \(57.22\) Add bridge width \(W = 12\text{ in.}\): Mark 3 is \(\mathbf{57.22\text{ in.}}\) 12 [+] \(33.22\) \(45.22\) \(57.22\) \(69.22\) Add travel \(T = 12\text{ in.}\): Mark 4 is \(\mathbf{69.22\text{ in.}}\) 0.0824 [ENTER] 4 [×] 0.864 [÷] 100 [×] \(45.22\) \(57.22\) \(69.22\) \(38.15\) 4 wires \(\times 0.0824\text{ in.}^2 / 0.864\text{ in.}^2 \times 100\% = \mathbf{38.15\%}\) (compliant \(< 40\%\))

In seven operations, Jimmy computed every mark on the conduit pipe to a thirty-second of an inch and proved that the raceway fill satisfies NEC Chapter 9 limits. When bent and mounted, the saddle bridged the steam header with exactly one inch of thermal air clearance.

docs.title: Inverse Bend Angle Solving in [OFS] and Verifying NEC Conduit Fill
docs.text: When structural obstacles leave limited travel room between ceiling beams, electricians use the Bidirectional [OFS] Equation Solver Workspace ([XEQ] [OFS], T = O / SIN(A) with variable softkeys [T], [O], and [A]): - Inverse Bend Angle Solving in [OFS]: If the obstruction depth is \(O = 8.0\text{ in.}\) (8 [O]) but total allowable travel distance between two concrete beams is limited to \(T = 11.31\text{ in.}\) (11.31 [T]), pressing [XEQ] [A] solves backward for the required bend angle: $\(\theta = \arcsin\left(\frac{8.0}{11.31}\right) \approx \arcsin(0.7073) \approx \mathbf{45.00^\circ}\)$ - Verifying Conduit Fill: For three #6 AWG THHN copper conductors (\(0.0507\text{ in.}^2\) each, total \(0.1521\text{ in.}^2\)) inside a \(3/4\text{-inch}\) EMT conduit (\(A_{\text{internal}} = 0.533\text{ in.}^2, A_{40\%} = 0.213\text{ in.}^2\)), keying 0.0507 [ENTER] 3 [×] 0.533 [÷] 100 [×] yields a fill of \(\mathbf{28.54\%}\), safely below the \(40.0\%\) limit.

docs.title: Try It on the Stack
docs.text:
Work through these five field problems on your calculator. Step-by-step keystroke solutions and register walkthroughs are provided in Appendix C.

  1. Conduit Offset Travel and Shrinkage Deduction: An electrician must bend a \(30^\circ\) offset in a \(1\text{-inch}\) EMT conduit to clear a \(H = 9.50\text{ in.}\) obstruction. Calculate the center-to-center travel distance \(T\) between bend marks and determine the total shrinkage deduction \(S\).
  2. Compound Rolling Offset Spatial Travel: A raceway must navigate a compound rolling offset with a vertical rise of \(V = 14.0\text{ in.}\) and a horizontal roll of \(R = 18.0\text{ in.}\) using \(45^\circ\) bends. Calculate the true spatial offset depth \(D_{\text{spatial}}\), the center-to-center travel distance \(T\), and the shrinkage deduction \(S\).
  3. Three-Point Saddle Mark Layout and Shrink: A conduit run passes over a round steam pipe presenting an obstruction height of \(H = 4.00\text{ in.}\) using a three-point saddle (\(45^\circ\) center bend, \(22.5^\circ\) return bends). Determine the required outer mark spacing from center and calculate the overall shrinkage deduction.
  4. Four-Bend Saddle Over Rectangular Duct: A conduit crosses a rectangular ventilation duct measuring \(16.0\text{ in.}\) wide and \(H = 6.0\text{ in.}\) deep using two symmetrical \(30^\circ\) offsets. Calculate the travel distance along each incline, the total shrinkage across both offsets, and the overall spacing between the two inside bend marks.
  5. NEC Conduit Fill and Conductor Ampacity Derating: A \(1\text{-inch}\) EMT conduit has total internal cross-sectional area \(A = 0.864\text{ in.}^2\). Determine the maximum permitted \(40\%\) fill area for three or more conductors. Then, if nine #12 AWG THHN copper conductors are installed in the raceway (\(70\%\) derating factor per NEC Table 310.15(C)(1)), calculate the adjusted allowable ampacity from the \(30\text{ A}\) table baseline.

With the four EMT conduits bent and strapped to the ceiling slab, the chiller feeder cables were pulled without incident. In Chapter 6, the analysis turns from electrical raceways to the machine shop and process floor: dialing in CNC spindle speeds, eliminating chatter on a stainless-steel pump flange, and tuning noise-immune \(4\text{--}20\text{ mA}\) hydraulic process loops.

docs.title: Chapter 6: The Chattering Milling Cutter and the Drifting Pressure Loop
docs.text:
When a five-axis vertical machining center begins vibrating with an ear-splitting acoustic shriek, every experienced machinist recognizes the destructive onset of regenerative chatter. In Bay 4 of an industrial pump plant, a four-flute solid carbide end-mill cutting the sealing face of a \(316\text{L}\) stainless-steel centrifugal pump casing is carving jagged herringbone ripples across the gasket seat. Meanwhile, across the aisle, the hydraulic cooling loop feeding the spindle bearings is hunting in wild pressure surges because an erratic \(4\text{--}20\text{ mA}\) sensor signal is destabilizing the proportional relief valve.

In precision manufacturing, when metal is chattering and fluid loops are cavitating, you do not guess. CNC machinist Kurt Weber and instrumentation technician Sarah Lin meet at the control console with the SC-14 calculator: 1. Kurt must eliminate the destructive milling chatter by applying metal-cutting kinematics—recalculating Surface Feet per Minute (\(\text{SFM} = 240\text{ ft/min}\)), dialing in spindle speed \(N = 1{,}834\text{ RPM}\), and adjusting chip load per tooth (\(f_t = 0.002\text{ in/tooth}\)) to land in a stable cutting zone. 2. He must lay out a 12-hole flange bolt circle on a \(9.50\text{-inch}\) pitch diameter using chord spacing \(C = 2.459\text{ in.}\) to finish the pump casing. 3. Sarah must stabilize the hydraulic cooling loop by calculating valve flow coefficient \(C_v\) and pump brake horsepower (\(P_{\text{BHP}}\)) to eliminate fluid cavitation. 4. She must calibrate the \(4\text{--}20\text{ mA}\) pressure transmitter and \(\text{Pt100}\) RTD temperature sensor using the live zero standard to restore rock-solid spindle bearing pressure.

docs.title: Regenerative Machining Chatter, Valve Cavitation, and the Live Zero
docs.text: Before hitting the emergency stop button, the machinist identifies the source of the vibration. The high-pitched acoustic squeal from the CNC enclosure signals regenerative chatter—a destructive self-excited vibration between tool compliance and workpiece deflection that can destroy a carbide end-mill and ruin a precision stainless casting within seconds.

docs.title: Rotary Cutting Kinematics and the Physics of Metal Shearing
docs.text:
Metal cutting is not a process of slicing; it is a process of continuous plastic shear. As a rotating end-mill flute bites into \(316\text{L}\) stainless steel, it drives a localized shear zone ahead of the cutting edge, forcing atomic crystal planes of austenitic steel to slip, yield, and curl away as a metallic chip.

In 1906, after twenty-six years of rigorous experimentation during which he turned over eight hundred thousand pounds of steel into chips, Frederick Winslow Taylor presented his monumental treatise On the Art of Cutting Metals to the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME). Taylor established the fundamental empirical law of tool life:

\[V \cdot T^n = C\]

where \(V\) is cutting speed in Surface Feet per Minute (\(\text{SFM}\)), \(T\) is tool life in minutes, \(n\) is an empirical exponent governed by tool and workpiece material, and \(C\) is a constant.

Cutting velocity at the tool-workpiece interface is governed by tool diameter \(D\) (in inches) and spindle rotational speed \(N\) (in revolutions per minute, \(\text{RPM}\)):

\[\text{SFM} = \frac{\pi \cdot D \cdot N}{12}\]

Solving for spindle speed yields the classic machinist's rule:

\[N = \frac{12 \cdot \text{SFM}}{\pi \cdot D} \approx \frac{3.8197 \cdot \text{SFM}}{D} \approx \frac{3.82 \cdot \text{SFM}}{D}\]

Equally vital is the chip load per tooth (\(f_t\), in inches per tooth)—the physical thickness of the metal slice removed by each individual flute as it sweeps through the cut:

\[F_m = N \cdot f_t \cdot Z\]

where \(F_m\) is the table feed rate in inches per minute (\(\text{in/min}\)) and \(Z\) is the number of flutes on the cutter.

In austenitic stainless steels like \(316\text{L}\), chip load is exceptionally critical. Stainless steel work-hardens instantly under mechanical pressure. If the machinist feeds the tool too slowly (\(f_t < 0.001\text{ in/tooth}\)), the cutting edge does not shear the metal; it rubs across the work-hardened surface, generating intense friction heat that melts the carbide cutting edge. Conversely, if the feed is too fast (\(f_t > 0.004\text{ in/tooth}\)), cutting forces exceed the transverse rupture strength of the carbide, snapping the cutter flutes.

docs.title: The Dynamics of Regenerative Tool Chatter and Stability Lobe Tuning
docs.text:
What causes the deafening screech of tool chatter?

When an end-mill rotates, each cutting flute deflects slightly under the cutting force. As Flute 1 sweeps through the metal, that tiny mechanical deflection leaves an invisible wavy, scalloped surface on the workpiece.

When Flute 2 sweeps through the cut a fraction of a second later, it encounters that wavy surface. The chip thickness cut by Flute 2 is no longer constant; it oscillates thicker and thinner. This oscillating chip thickness produces an oscillating cutting force, which in turn excites the spindle structure to vibrate further.

This feedback loop is known across manufacturing engineering as regenerative chatter.

If the tooth-passing frequency (\(f_{\text{tooth}} = N \cdot Z / 60\)) coincides with a structural natural resonant frequency of the machine spindle, toolholder, or workpiece, the vibration grows exponentially. The tool hammers violently against the cut, destroying surface finish (leaving rough gouges \(> 250\ \mu\text{in}\) instead of a smooth \(32\ \mu\text{in}\) seal), work-hardening the stainless surface, and fracturing the carbide tool within seconds.

How does a master machinist eliminate chatter?

Inexperienced operators make the instinctive mistake of slowing down the spindle speed and feed rate. But in regenerative chatter, slowing down often moves the tool directly into a more severe resonance.

Transportation and manufacturing dynamicists J. Tlusty and S. A. Tobias proved that the boundary between stable cutting and violent chatter forms a series of scalloped peaks known as a Stability Lobe Diagram. By analyzing the relationship between spindle speed \(N\) and tooth count \(Z\), a machinist can find stability pockets at higher speeds where the tooth-passing frequency matches the structural phase lag, completely neutralizing the regeneration mechanism.

Kurt uses the SC-14 to retune the parameters: for a \(D = 0.500\text{ in.}\) 4-flute cutter cutting stainless at \(\text{SFM} = 240\text{ ft/min}\), exact spindle speed is \(N = (12 \times 240) / (\pi \times 0.500) \approx \mathbf{1{,}833.5\text{ RPM}}\), paired with a chip load of \(f_t = 0.002\text{ in/tooth}\) to yield a crisp table feed rate of \(F_m = 1833.5 \times 0.002 \times 4 \approx \mathbf{14.67\text{ in/min}}\).

docs.title: Fluid Cavitation, Valve \(C_v\), and Pump Suction Head
docs.text:
While Kurt prepares the milling pass, Sarah investigates the oscillating hydraulic test loop across the aisle.

In fluid power and industrial process systems, fluid flow through pipes, valves, and pumps is governed by the conservation of mass and energy: 1. Pipe Continuity: For an incompressible liquid flowing through a conduit of cross-sectional area \(A\) at velocity \(V\), volumetric flow \(Q\) is constant: $\(Q = A \times V\)$ 2. Control Valve Flow Coefficient (\(C_v\)): Developed in 1944 by the Fisher Governor Company, \(C_v\) is defined as the volume of water at \(60^\circ\text{F}\) (in US gallons per minute, \(\text{GPM}\)) that will flow through a wide-open valve with a pressure drop of exactly one pound per square inch (\(1.0\text{ PSI}\)): $\(Q = C_v \sqrt{\frac{\Delta P}{G}}\)$ where \(\Delta P\) is pressure drop across the valve in PSI, and \(G\) is the specific gravity of the fluid (\(G = 1.00\) for water, \(G \approx 0.88\) for hydraulic oil).

Sarah observes that the hydraulic relief valve is suffering from cavitation—the fluid-mechanical equivalent of tool chatter.

When fluid accelerates through the narrow restriction (the vena contracta) inside a control valve, Bernoulli's principle dictates that kinetic velocity surges while static pressure plummets. If static pressure drops below the vapor pressure of the liquid (\(P_{\text{vapor}}\)), the fluid literally boils at ambient temperature, forming millions of microscopic vapor bubbles.

As the fluid exits the restriction into the wider downstream pipe, velocity slows and static pressure recovers above vapor pressure. The vapor bubbles collapse instantaneously.

The collapse of a cavitation bubble is violent: liquid micro-jets slam inward at speeds exceeding supersonic velocities (\(> 1{,}000\text{ m/s}\)), generating localized impact pressures exceeding \(100{,}000\text{ PSI}\) and micro-temperatures of thousands of degrees. These shockwaves pit and excavate solid stainless-steel valve plugs, sounding like a shovel full of gravel being pumped through the line and destroying control valves within weeks.

To eliminate cavitation, Sarah must resize the valve coefficient \(C_v\) to ensure that localized pressure drop never pulls fluid below its cavitation threshold, while verifying that the pump delivers sufficient Net Positive Suction Head (NPSH) to prevent impeller erosion.

docs.title: The 4–20 mA Current Loop Standard and the Platinum RTD Live Zero
docs.text:
Finally, Sarah checks the electrical signaling between the hydraulic pressure transmitter and the programmable logic controller (PLC).

Why does the entire global industrial automation sector rely on \(4\text{--}20\text{ milliampere}\) current loops rather than \(0\text{--}10\text{ volt}\) signals or \(0\text{--}20\text{ mA}\) loops?

Two foundational engineering principles explain the dominance of \(4\text{--}20\text{ mA}\):

First, The Live Zero Principle: If an analog system used \(0\text{ to } 10\text{ volts}\) or \(0\text{ to } 20\text{ mA}\), what happens if a wire breaks, a terminal comes loose, or an instrument power supply fails? The reading at the controller drops to \(0.0\text{ V}\) or \(0.0\text{ mA}\). The control computer cannot distinguish between: - "The tank is completely empty (\(0.0\text{ PSI}\))" and - A severed sensor cable or disconnected terminal.

If the tank is actually at \(5{,}000\text{ PSI}\) and the wire breaks, the computer believes pressure is zero, drives the high-pressure pump to full power, and potentially over-pressurizing the vessel.

In a \(4\text{--}20\text{ mA}\) loop: - \(4.0\text{ mA}\) represents \(0\%\) measurement (Live Zero). - \(20.0\text{ mA}\) represents \(100\%\) measurement. - Current below \(3.6\text{ mA}\) or above \(21.0\text{ mA}\) triggers an immediate fault alarm (SENSOR OPEN / CABLE BREAK or SENSOR SHORT).

Second, Immunity to Cable Resistance and Electrical Noise: If an analog sensor sends a \(0\text{--}10\text{ V}\) signal across five hundred feet of copper wire, the wire's series resistance \(R_{\text{wire}}\) drops voltage (\(V_{\text{lost}} = I R\)). The voltage read at the PLC is lower than the voltage generated at the sensor. Furthermore, nearby \(480\text{V}\) motor starters and variable-frequency drives induce massive electromagnetic voltage spikes on signal cables.

A current loop is fundamentally different. A current transmitter behaves as an active constant-current sink. By Kirchhoff's Current Law, whatever current leaves the transmitter must return to the power supply—regardless of cable length or series resistance. A \(12.0\text{ mA}\) signal leaving a transmitter across a hundred ohms of wire resistance arrives at the PLC input resistor as exactly \(12.0\text{ mA}\).

For temperature measurement, Sarah uses a Platinum Resistance Temperature Detector (\(\text{Pt100}\) RTD). Platinum has an exceptionally linear and repeatable positive temperature coefficient of resistance (\(\alpha = 0.00385\ \Omega/\Omega/^\circ\text{C}\) under the DIN IEC 751 standard), where resistance at temperature \(T\) follows the Callendar-Van Dusen equation:

\[R(T) = R_0 \left(1 + A T + B T^2\right)\]

At \(0^\circ\text{C}\), the sensor measures exactly \(100.00\ \Omega\). At \(100^\circ\text{C}\), it measures \(138.51\ \Omega\). By exciting the platinum element with a stable \(1.0\text{ mA}\) sensing current, the transmitter reads temperature down to hundredths of a degree Celsius without thermocouple cold-junction drift.

docs.title: Rotary Cutting Kinematics, Thread Tapping, and Bolt Circle Trigonometry
docs.text: Machinists and toolmakers configure CNC feeds, speeds, and hole circles to maximize metal removal rates while preserving tool life and dimensional tolerances.

docs.title: Surface Feet per Minute, Spindle Speed, and Chip-Load Feed Rate
docs.text:
Cutting velocity measures the circumferential speed of the rotating tool edge across the workpiece (Surface Feet per Minute, \(\text{SFM}\), converted via [f] [SFM]). The rotational speed of the spindle \(N\) (in \(\text{RPM}\)) scales inversely with tool diameter \(D\) (in inches):

Eq. 6.1 — Spindle Rotational Speed and Table Feed Rate $\(N = \frac{12 \cdot \text{SFM}}{\pi \cdot D} \approx \frac{3.82 \cdot \text{SFM}}{D}\)$ $\(F_m = N \cdot f_t \cdot Z\)$

For a \(D = 0.500\text{ in.}\) four-flute carbide end-mill cutting \(316\text{L}\) stainless steel at \(\text{SFM} = 240\text{ ft/min}\) with a chip load of \(f_t = 0.002\text{ in/tooth}\) (\(Z = 4\text{ flutes}\)), pressing [f] [SFM] yields spindle speed \(N = \frac{3.8197 \times 240}{0.500} \approx \mathbf{1{,}833.5\text{ RPM}}\), producing a table feed rate of \(F_m = 1833.5 \times 0.002 \times 4 = \mathbf{14.67\text{ in/min}}\).

docs.title: Bolt Circle Chord Indexing and Right-Triangle Fixture Layout
docs.text:
To machine bolt-hole circles for pump flanges without rotary index tables, machinists calculate the straight-line chord distance \(C\) between adjacent holes on a pitch circle of diameter \(D_{\text{bolt}}\) with \(N_{\text{holes}}\) equally spaced holes ([g] [BC]):

Eq. 6.2 — Bolt Circle Chord Spacing $\(C = D_{\text{bolt}} \sin\!\left(\frac{180^\circ}{N_{\text{holes}}}\right)\)$

For the pump casing flange with \(N_{\text{holes}} = 12\) holes on a \(D_{\text{bolt}} = 9.50\text{ in.}\) pitch circle, pressing [g] [BC] yields the adjacent hole chord spacing \(C = 9.50 \sin(180^\circ / 12) = 9.50 \sin(15^\circ) \approx 9.50 \times 0.25882 = \mathbf{2.4588\text{ in.}}\) (\(2\text{-}15/32\text{ in.}\)).

docs.title: Pipe Flow Continuity, Valve Coefficient, Pump Power, and Process Loops
docs.text: Process engineers size valves, piping, and instrumentation loops to maintain hydraulic stability across industrial manufacturing plants.

docs.title: Pipe Continuity, Valve Flow Coefficient, Pump Power, and Suction Head
docs.text:
Volumetric liquid flow rate \(Q\) through a pipe of internal cross-sectional area \(A\) at mean velocity \(V\) is governed by continuity: \(Q = A \times V\) (evaluated directly on the stack via A [ENTER] V [×]). Sizing control valves across pressure drop \(\Delta P\) (in PSI) with fluid specific gravity \(G\) uses the valve flow coefficient \(C_v\) ([g] [Cᵥ]), while calculating hydraulic or brake horsepower \(P_{\text{HP}}\) for a pump delivering flow \(Q\) (in \(\text{GPM}\)) against total dynamic head \(H\) (in feet of liquid) evaluates the hydraulic work via \(P_{\text{HP}} = \frac{Q \cdot H}{3{,}960 \cdot \eta_{\text{pump}}}\):

Eq. 6.3 — Control Valve Volumetric Flow and Pump Power $\(Q = C_v \sqrt{\frac{\Delta P}{G}}\)$ $\(P_{\text{HP}} = \frac{Q \cdot H}{3{,}960 \cdot \eta_{\text{pump}}}\)$

For a coolant valve with flow coefficient \(C_v = 30.0\) operating across a pressure drop of \(\Delta P = 9.0\text{ psi}\) with water (\(G = 1.00\)), pressing [g] [Cᵥ] evaluates flow as \(Q = 30.0 \sqrt{9.0} = \mathbf{90.00\text{ GPM}}\), while a pump delivering that \(90\text{ GPM}\) against \(H = 88.0\text{ ft}\) of dynamic head at \(100\%\) efficiency requires \(P = (90 \times 88)/3960 = \mathbf{2.00\text{ HP}}\) (90 [ENTER] 88 [×] 3960 [÷]).

docs.title: Noise-Immune Four-to-Twenty Milliampere Loops and Platinum RTDs
docs.text:
Analog process sensors monitor temperature, pressure, flow, and level by converting physical variables into a standard direct-current signal spanning \(4.00\text{ mA}\) (\(0\%\) span, live zero) to \(20.00\text{ mA}\) (\(100\%\) span) ([mA]):

Eq. 6.4 — Four-to-Twenty Milliampere Current Scaling $\(I_{\text{mA}} = 4.00 + 16.00 \cdot \left(\frac{P - P_{\min}}{P_{\max} - P_{\min}}\right)\)$ $\(P = P_{\min} + \left(\frac{I_{\text{mA}} - 4.00}{16.00}\right) \cdot \left(P_{\max} - P_{\min}\right)\)$

For a hydraulic pressure transmitter calibrated from \(0.0\text{ PSI}\) to \(100.0\text{ PSI}\), a live signal of \(I_{\text{mA}} = 16.80\text{ mA}\) corresponds to operating pressure \(P = 0 + \frac{16.80 - 4.00}{16.00} \times 100.0 = \frac{12.80}{16.00} \times 100.0 = \mathbf{80.00\text{ PSI}}\).

docs.title: Flashing, Choked Flow, and Control Valve Cavitation Index
docs.text:
As Sarah inspects the cavitating hydraulic relief valve, she connects a differential pressure manometer across the inlet and outlet ports.

To rigorously predict and prevent cavitation damage in control valves, process instrumentation engineers analyze the non-dimensional Cavitation Index (\(\sigma_c\)):

\[\sigma_c = \frac{P_1 - P_v}{P_1 - P_2}\]

where \(P_1\) is valve upstream absolute pressure (in psia), \(P_2\) is valve downstream absolute pressure (in psia), and \(P_v\) is fluid absolute vapor pressure at operating temperature.

Under standard ISA-75 valve sizing criteria: - No Cavitation (\(\sigma_c > 2.0\)): Fluid velocities through the orifice remain sub-critical; pressure at the vena contracta remains safely above fluid vapor pressure. - Incipient Cavitation (\(1.5 < \sigma_c \le 2.0\)): Intermittent cavitation bubbles form and collapse, producing a faint sizzling sound like frying bacon. - Severe Cavitation (\(1.0 < \sigma_c \le 1.5\)): Continuous cavitation erupts inside the valve body, generating roaring gravel noise, severe pipe vibration, and rapid metal erosion. - Flashing and Choked Flow (\(\sigma_c \le 1.0\)): Downstream pressure \(P_2\) drops below vapor pressure \(P_v\). The vapor bubbles cannot collapse because downstream pressure is too low to re-condense the vapor. The fluid exits as a high-velocity two-phase mixture of vapor and liquid droplets that sandblasts downstream piping.

When flashing or cavitation occurs, the valve reaches Choked Flow. Further reducing downstream pressure \(P_2\) produces zero additional flow because sonic velocity (the speed of sound in the liquid-vapor froth) is reached at the vena contracta. The maximum allowable terminal pressure drop for sizing is governed by the Liquid Pressure Recovery Factor (\(F_L\)):

\[\Delta P_{\text{choked}} = F_L^2 \left( P_1 - F_F P_v \right)\]

where \(F_F \approx 0.96 - 0.28 \sqrt{P_v / P_c}\) is the critical pressure ratio factor and \(P_c\) is thermodynamic critical pressure. For a globe valve with \(F_L = 0.90\) operating with hydraulic oil at \(P_1 = 115\text{ psia}\) and low vapor pressure (\(P_v \approx 0\)), choked flow occurs at \(\Delta P_{\text{choked}} = (0.90)^2 \times 115 \approx \mathbf{93.15\text{ PSI}}\). Operating above this pressure drop produces choked flow and destructive cavitation.

docs.title: Cutting Heat Distribution, Unit Power, and Spindle Mechanical Deflection
docs.text:
Across the aisle, as Kurt dials in the finishing pass on the CNC mill, he explains the mechanical thermodynamics of metal removal.

When an end-mill shears metal chips, almost all mechanical work is converted directly into heat. Under the laws of metal cutting thermodynamics, total cutting heat is distributed across three zones: - \(80\%\) into the Chip: Carried away by the curling metallic chip as it flies into the machine basin. - \(10\%\) into the Workpiece: Conducted into the stainless casting, causing thermal expansion that can distort precision dimensional tolerances. - \(10\%\) into the Tool Edge: Concentrated in the tiny carbide tool radius, raising tool tip temperatures above \(800^\circ\text{C}\) (\(1{,}470^\circ\text{F}\)).

The total mechanical power required at the spindle is directly proportional to the Metal Removal Rate (MRR):

\[\text{MRR} = d \cdot w \cdot F_m\]

where \(d\) is depth of cut (inches), \(w\) is radial width of cut (inches), and \(F_m\) is table feed rate (in/min). Total cutting horsepower follows from the material's Unit Power (\(U_c\), in \(\text{HP}\cdot\text{min/in}^3\)):

\[P_{\text{cut}} = \text{MRR} \cdot U_c\]

For \(316\text{L}\) stainless steel, the unit power is approximately \(U_c \approx 1.10\ \text{HP}\cdot\text{min/in}^3\). Cutting a slot of depth \(d = 0.250\text{ in.}\), width \(w = 0.500\text{ in.}\), and feed rate \(F_m = 14.67\text{ in/min}\) produces:

\[\text{MRR} = 0.250 \times 0.500 \times 14.67 \approx \mathbf{1.8338\text{ in}^3/\text{min}}$$ $$P_{\text{cut}} = 1.8338 \times 1.10 \approx \mathbf{2.017\text{ HP}}\]

Accounting for spindle mechanical drive efficiency (\(\eta \approx 85\%\)), the spindle motor draws \(2.017 / 0.85 = \mathbf{2.37\text{ HP}}\), well within the machine's \(15\text{ HP}\) rating.

Finally, Kurt checks the physical cantilever deflection (\(y\)) of the end-mill under the radial cutting force \(F_r\):

\[y = \frac{F_r \cdot L_{\text{stickout}}^3}{3 \cdot E \cdot I_{\text{tool}}}\]

where \(L_{\text{stickout}}\) is tool overhang distance from the collet, \(E \approx 85 \times 10^6\text{ PSI}\) is the modulus of elasticity of solid tungsten carbide (more than three times stiffer than steel), and \(I_{\text{tool}} = \frac{\pi d_{\text{core}}^4}{64}\) is the second moment of area of the tool core.

Deflection scales with the third power of stickout length (\(L^3\)). If a machinist doubles tool stickout from \(1.5\text{ inches}\) to \(3.0\text{ inches}\), tool deflection multiplies by \(2^3 = \mathbf{8\text{ times}}\). That eightfold increase in compliance lowers the structural natural frequency into the chatter zone. Kurt minimizes stickout to \(1.25\text{ inches}\) in the hydraulic collet holder, increasing rigidity by a factor of four and eliminating chatter.

docs.title: Three-Wire and Four-Wire RTD Bridge Lead Resistance Cancellation
docs.text:
To ensure the \(\text{Pt100}\) RTD temperature sensor reports true hydraulic oil temperature without error, Sarah inspects the field wiring.

A \(\text{Pt100}\) sensor increases resistance by only \(0.385\ \Omega\) per degree Celsius. If a technician uses simple two-wire copper cable running two hundred feet from the sensor to the PLC, the copper wire's own series resistance (\(R_{\text{lead}} \approx 2.0\ \Omega\)) is in series with the sensor:

\[R_{\text{measured}} = R_{\text{sensor}} + 2 R_{\text{lead}} = 100.00 + 4.00 = 104.00\ \Omega\]

An extra \(4.00\ \Omega\) of wire resistance corrupts the temperature measurement by:

\[\Delta T = \frac{4.00\ \Omega}{0.385\ \Omega/^\circ\text{C}} \approx \mathbf{+10.39^\circ\text{C}}\]

The controller measures the oil over ten degrees Celsius above its true temperature.

To eliminate lead-wire error, Sarah rewires the circuit as a Three-Wire RTD Kelvin Bridge. In a 3-wire circuit: - Lead Wire 1 carries the sensing current to the platinum element. - Lead Wire 2 carries return current back to ground. - Lead Wire 3 connects to a high-impedance differential sensing terminal that carries zero current.

In the differential bridge circuit, the voltage drop across Lead 1 cancels the voltage drop across Lead 2 directly in the bridge equations (\(R_{\text{bridge}} = R_{\text{sensor}} + R_{\text{lead1}} - R_{\text{lead2}} = R_{\text{sensor}}\)). Lead resistance is completely neutralized, guaranteeing tenth-of-a-degree accuracy across the entire process operating range.

docs.title: HART Protocol FSK Modulation and Hydraulic Water Hammer Joukowsky Dynamics
docs.text:
As Sarah connects a handheld field communicator to the hydraulic transmitter terminals, she explains the hybrid digital-analog signaling of the HART (Highway Addressable Remote Transducer) Protocol.

Modern industrial facilities demand more than just a single raw analog value; they require remote sensor calibration, continuous diagnostic health monitoring, device temperature tracking, and secondary process variables without running new cables through the plant.

The HART protocol achieves this by superimposing high-frequency digital communications directly on top of the standard \(4\text{--}20\text{ mA}\) direct-current signal using the Bell 202 Frequency-Shift Keying (FSK) standard: - A digital binary 1 (mark) is represented by an alternating sinusoidal tone of frequency \(f_1 = \mathbf{1{,}200\text{ Hz}}\). - A digital binary 0 (space) is represented by an alternating sinusoidal tone of frequency \(f_0 = \mathbf{2{,}200\text{ Hz}}\). - The digital FSK signal has an amplitude of approximately \(\pm 0.5\text{ mA}\) peak-to-peak.

Why doesn't this digital AC ripple corrupt the analog \(4\text{--}20\text{ mA}\) measurement at the PLC?

Because the FSK waveform is purely symmetrical alternating current:

\[\int_0^{T_{\text{message}}} I_{\text{FSK}}(t) \, dt = 0\]

The average DC value of the high-frequency tone is identically zero. The low-pass filter on the analog input card of the PLC has an update response rate of \(10\text{ to } 50\text{ Hz}\). It strips out the \(1{,}200\text{ Hz}\) and \(2{,}200\text{ Hz}\) digital carrier frequencies, reading only the smooth \(4\text{--}20\text{ mA}\) DC process current. Meanwhile, a high-pass digital modem circuit in the controller decodes the digital FSK packets at 1,200 baud, reading transmitter diagnostics, sensor serial numbers, and calibration logs simultaneously across the exact same two wires.

Finally, Sarah checks the test loop for the most destructive transient phenomenon in fluid dynamics: Hydraulic Shock (Water Hammer).

When an electric solenoid valve or manual quarter-turn ball valve snaps shut abruptly while fluid is traveling through a pipe at velocity \(V\), the moving fluid column is suddenly brought to a dead stop. The kinetic energy of the moving liquid cannot disappear; it compresses the fluid and elastically expands the pipe walls, transforming into a violent acoustic shockwave traveling backward through the piping system.

In 1898, the Russian hydrodynamicist Nikolay Zhukovsky (Joukowsky) formulated the governing law of water hammer pressure rise:

\[\Delta P = \rho \cdot a \cdot \Delta V\]

where \(\Delta P\) is the instantaneous pressure surge (in Pascals or PSI), \(\rho\) is fluid mass density (\(\approx 880\text{ kg/m}^3\) for hydraulic oil), \(\Delta V\) is the change in fluid velocity (in \(\text{m/s}\) or \(\text{ft/s}\)), and \(a\) is the acoustic speed of sound in the fluid-pipe system:

\[a = \sqrt{\frac{K / \rho}{1 + \left(\frac{K}{E}\right) \left(\frac{D}{t}\right)}}\]

where \(K\) is the bulk modulus of elasticity of the liquid, \(E\) is the modulus of the steel pipe wall, \(D\) is pipe diameter, and \(t\) is wall thickness. In typical steel hydraulic lines, acoustic wave speed is approximately \(a \approx 4{,}000\text{ ft/s}\) (\(1{,}200\text{ m/s}\)).

If hydraulic oil flowing at \(V = 15.0\text{ ft/s}\) (\(4.57\text{ m/s}\)) is arrested instantaneously by an fast-closing solenoid valve, the resulting Joukowsky pressure surge is:

\[\Delta P = 880\text{ kg/m}^3 \times 1{,}200\text{ m/s} \times 4.57\text{ m/s} \approx 4{,}826{,}000\text{ Pa} \approx \mathbf{700.0\text{ PSI}}\]

This produces a seven-hundred-pound pressure transient on top of the existing \(1{,}500\text{ PSI}\) operating pressure. The total pressure surges to \(2{,}200\text{ PSI}\), stressing pipe hangers, degrading elastomeric O-ring seals, and risking pump casing fractures.

To suppress water hammer, Sarah installs a nitrogen-precharged bladder hydraulic accumulator immediately upstream of the valve. The compressible nitrogen gas behaves like a pneumatic spring, absorbing the kinetic pulse of the fluid and clamping transient shockwaves to safe levels.

docs.title: Operational Baton: Handing Off from Industrial Power to Embedded Silicon and Cyber Operations
docs.text:
With the alloy steel steam flange machined to mirror tolerance, the conduit raceways strapped to the hospital ceiling, and the hydraulic clamping loop holding rock-solid pressure, the physical heavy plant stands fully commissioned.

In Unit II, we have bridged the gap between theoretical electrical physics and the tactile reality of the industrial trades: 1. In Chapter 4, we diagnosed the heavy crane feeder on Pier 14, transforming Unit I's spatial vectors into rotating 60 Hz AC phasors, canceling reactive power slosh with shunt capacitors, and sizing conductors for continuous motor inrush currents. 2. In Chapter 5, we bent four parallel runs of electrical metallic tubing through a crowded boiler room, mastering tubular metallurgy, neutral axis mechanics, cosecant offset multipliers, axial shrink deductions, and NEC Chapter 9 raceway fill limits. 3. In Chapter 6, we stood at the CNC machining center and fluid test bench, tuning rotary kinematics to silence regenerative tool chatter, spacing bolt circles, sizing control valves against cavitation, and calibrating noise-immune \(4\text{--}20\text{ mA}\) loops.

Throughout Unit II, the governing theme has been heavy physical power: amperes, volts, kVAR, foot-pounds of cutting torque, and hydraulic pounds per square inch.

Yet heavy mechanical valves, induction motors, and CNC spindles are deaf, blind, and inert without digital control. Modern machines do not operate on mechanical flywheels or analog relays alone; their every motion is commanded by microcontrollers executing billions of instructions per second in embedded silicon.

In Unit III (SC-16 Digital Systems, Bitwise Logic & Cyber Operations), these principles scale into digital logic and microprocessor architecture. The 480-volt alternating current that powered Pier 14's crane transforms into 3.3-volt logic signals switching CMOS transistors in sub-nanosecond intervals. The 60-hertz grid gives way to 168-megahertz hardware timer prescalers; the continuous analog voltage drops become discrete 12-bit ADC quantization steps; and the physical wiring raceways transform into memory-mapped register buses, big-endian network packet streams, and cyclic redundancy checksums.

In Chapter 7, we step directly onto the circuit board of an ARM Cortex-M microcontroller governing a high-speed linear actuator, debugging stuck interrupt flags, mastering signed two's complement arithmetic, and isolating register bitfields on the RPN stack.

docs.title: Unit III: Digital Systems, Bitwise Logic & Embedded Timing
docs.text:
At a clock speed of one hundred megahertz, light travels barely three meters in a single instruction cycle. On a microchip, time is not an abstract dimension; it is physical distance etched in copper and silicon. In the winter of 1937, George Stibitz assembled two dry-cell batteries, two flashlight bulbs, a pair of telephone relays, and strips of tin cut from a tobacco can on the kitchen table of his Manhattan apartment. When he completed the circuit with a tin strip, the bulb glowed: the "Model K" adder was born, proving that Boolean algebra could execute in physical electronic circuits. In high-level software, computation is presented as an unconstrained world of infinite integers, frictionless floating-point types, and automatic garbage collection. But at the hardware boundary of embedded firmware, digital signal processing, and low-level kernel architecture, raw physical constraints govern every register: fixed word widths, finite propagation delays, and discrete voltage thresholds. Through George Boole's 1854 An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, Claude Shannon's 1937 master's thesis A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits, and John von Neumann's 1945 EDVAC architecture, computing hardware established binary logic—the physical presence or absence of a voltage potential (\(0\text{ V}\) vs. \(3.3\text{ V}\))—as the fundamental currency of modern civilization.

Because microprocessors store numbers in fixed-width physical registers of 8, 16, 32, or 64 flip-flops, arithmetic is fundamentally modular. Numbers do not stretch endlessly to infinity; they wrap around a finite mathematical ring (\(\mathbb{Z} / 2^n \mathbb{Z}\)). In signed arithmetic, the Two's Complement system maps the upper half of the unsigned integer range into negative values, permitting digital adders to execute subtraction using the exact same silicon logic gates as addition (\(A - B = A + (\sim B + 1)\)) with zero execution time penalty and zero ambiguity between \(+0\) and \(-0\). Meanwhile, peripheral control registers expose bare hardware pins directly into memory address space, demanding atomic bitwise masking (&= ~MASK, |= MASK) to toggle safety flags without overwriting neighboring bits.

Finite-precision arithmetic, endian byte alignment, and clock-drift truncation present subtle failure modes in automated control systems, as demonstrated on February 25, 1991, during Operation Desert Storm in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia. An American Patriot missile air-defense battery failed to track and intercept an incoming Iraqi Scud missile, which struck an army barracks, killing twenty-eight soldiers and injuring ninety-eight. The official Government Accountability Office (GAO) investigation revealed that the Patriot's radar tracking computer calculated time by multiplying an integer counter by \(0.1\) seconds. But in binary arithmetic, one-tenth (\(1/10\)) has an infinite repeating expansion:

\[0.1_{10} = 0.0001100110011001100110011..._2\]

The Patriot's 24-bit fixed-point register chopped this fraction at 24 bits, introducing an imperceptible timing error of \(0.000000095\) seconds per tick. Over one hundred hours of continuous operation without a system reboot, that tiny fractional truncation accumulated into an absolute clock drift of \(\mathbf{0.3433\text{ seconds}}\). At Mach 5 (\(1{,}676\text{ m/s}\)), the incoming Scud traveled more than \(575\text{ meters}\) during that fractional second. When the Patriot's radar opened its range gate to track the missile, the Scud was over half a kilometer outside the calculation window. The computer discarded the radar return as false clutter, failed to launch an interceptor, and the Scud hit the barracks. The Dhahran disaster stands as the ultimate cautionary monument in computer systems engineering: fixed-width binary arithmetic, floating-point truncation, and timer prescalers are matters of life and death.

Interfacing microcontrollers with real-world sensors, actuators, and communication buses demands tight coordination between register logic, network protocols, and sampling rates. Firmware engineers reverse endian byte ordering between big-endian network packet streams and little-endian ARM processors using single-cycle BSWAP primitives. Systems programmers unpack IEEE-754 floating-point bitfields, evaluate Galois-field cyclic redundancy checks (CRC-32) across noisy serial links, and synthesize ultrasonic pulse-width-modulated (PWM) motor frequencies using 16-bit hardware timer prescalers. Simultaneously, network architects partition Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) subnets and align direct memory access (DMA) buffers to natural cache-line boundaries.

At the interface between physical power and automated control, digital systems govern modern machinery through discrete logic, serialized telemetry, and network communication. The SC-16 Digital Systems, Bitwise Logic & Cyber Operations calculator brings multi-base hexadecimal arithmetic, signed modular rings, bitfield manipulation, and network subnetting directly to the engineer's fingertips. Three diagnostic case studies trace the boundary between embedded software and physical silicon:

In Chapter 7, we step into the cleanroom of a precision robotics laboratory to debug a stalled linear actuator, isolating stuck interrupt flags in memory-mapped timer registers, calculating signed two's complement velocities, and executing atomic bitmasking on the RPN stack.

In Chapter 8, we connect a protocol analyzer across an RS-485 serial telemetry bus to unpack corrupted sensor frames, reversing network byte order via BSWAP, decoding IEEE-754 floating-point temperatures, verifying reflected CRC-32 checksums, and calculating 16-times oversampled UART baud divisors.

In Chapter 9, we partition a factory floor industrial Ethernet network and configure mixed-signal sensor nodes, sizing CIDR subnet masks, calculating hardware timer PWM prescalers, determining 12-bit ADC quantization noise, and sizing passive RC anti-aliasing filters.

docs.title: Chapter 7: The Stuck Interrupt Flag in the Motor Controller
docs.text:
When an automated wafer-handling robotic arm in a semiconductor plant freezes midway through an eight-inch silicon transfer sweep, the failure occurs in total silence: an oscilloscope probe clipped to the PWM gate drive shows a constant, unmodulated high voltage. The motor windings are rapidly warming in stationary DC current, and the diagnostic LED on the ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller board is latched solid red.

Connecting a JTAG debugger reveals the processor trapped inside an infinite loop in the default HardFault_Handler. When firmware developers Maya Lin and Alex dump the peripheral registers, the core reveals a cascade of low-level digital bugs: 1. The hardware timer status register (TIM2->SR) has its interrupt flag locked high at bit 0 (UIF = 1), repeatedly re-triggering the timer interrupt service routine (ISR) before the processor can return to user-space code. 2. In the timer control register (TIM2->CR1), an engineer attempted to enable center-aligned PWM mode by assigning a raw decimal constant, inadvertently overwriting and clearing the critical auto-reload preload (ARPE) and clock division bits. 3. In the motor velocity loop, a signed negative shaft velocity read from the quadrature encoder interface was shifted right using a logical shift (LSR) instead of an arithmetic shift (ASR), stripping the sign bit and corrupting a backward velocity of \(-3{,}840\text{ counts/s}\) (0xF100) into a massive forward runaway command of \(+15{,}424\text{ counts/s}\) (0x3C40).

To resuscitate the robotic arm and prevent wafer contamination, Maya and Alex turn to the SC-16 Digital Systems, Bitwise Logic & Cyber Operations calculator: 1. Unpack positional radix notation across Hexadecimal (HEX), Decimal (DEC), Octal (OCT), and Binary (BIN) modes. 2. Master signed modular arithmetic and two's complement additive inversion (\(A - B = A + (\sim B + 1)\)) across 8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit, and 64-bit word boundaries. 3. Construct contiguous bitmasks to execute atomic read-modify-write peripheral updates (&= ~MASK, |= MASK). 4. Correct the signed velocity shift using sign-preserving arithmetic shifts (ASR) and fixed-point Q-format scaling.

docs.title: Silicon Transistor Switches, Two's Complement, and the Dhahran Clock Trap
docs.text: When moving from the 480-volt electrical switchgear of Unit II into embedded silicon, the governing scale shifts from macro-power to transistor states. A field-effect transistor has no intrinsic knowledge of mathematical signs or fractions; it is a physical switch saturated at \(3.3\text{ volts}\) (Boolean 1) or pulled down to ground at \(0.0\text{ volts}\) (Boolean 0). Every higher-level construct—from two's complement signed arithmetic to cryptographic checksums—is a mathematical abstraction mapped onto arrays of physical switches.

docs.title: From Heavy AC Power to 3.3V Silicon Transistor Switches
docs.text:
In Unit II, we explored polyphase alternating current: magnetic induction, rotating phasors, power triangles, and high-voltage feeder cables.

In Unit III, we cross the threshold into digital electronics. The physical principles do not vanish; they scale down into microscopic sub-micron silicon geometries: - A \(480\text{-volt}\) motor feeder carrying \(145\text{ A}\) through rigid steel conduit becomes a \(3.3\text{-volt}\) metal trace carrying microamperes on a printed circuit board. - The 60-hertz grid frequency gives way to high-frequency quartz crystal oscillators vibrating at \(168\text{ MHz}\) (\(168{,}000{,}000\text{ cycles per second}\)). - The continuous sinusoidal voltages of Steinmetz are replaced by discrete square pulses switching in hundreds of picoseconds.

Inside the ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller, over ten million complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) field-effect transistors switch on and off. Each transistor stores or transfers a single bit of information: charge trapped on a capacitive gate oxide. In modern 3.3V CMOS logic, these logic levels are defined by strict physical voltage thresholds: - \(V_{\text{IL}}\) (Input Low Maximum): Typically \(0.3 \times V_{\text{DD}} \approx 0.99\text{ V}\). Any input voltage below this threshold is reliably detected as Boolean 0. - \(V_{\text{IH}}\) (Input High Minimum): Typically \(0.7 \times V_{\text{DD}} \approx 2.31\text{ V}\). Any input voltage above this threshold is reliably detected as Boolean 1. - \(V_{\text{OL}}\) (Output Low Maximum): Typically \(0.4\text{ V}\). Guaranteed maximum output voltage when asserting logic 0. - \(V_{\text{OH}}\) (Output High Minimum): Typically \(V_{\text{DD}} - 0.4\text{ V} \approx 2.9\text{ V}\). Guaranteed minimum output voltage when asserting logic 1.

The difference between \(V_{\text{IL}}\) and \(V_{\text{OL}}\) (\(0.99\text{ V} - 0.40\text{ V} = 0.59\text{ V}\)) represents the low-state noise margin (\(NM_{\text{L}}\)), while the difference between \(V_{\text{OH}}\) and \(V_{\text{IH}}\) (\(2.90\text{ V} - 2.31\text{ V} = 0.59\text{ V}\)) represents the high-state noise margin (\(NM_{\text{H}}\)). Within these noise margins, physical transistors operate deterministically despite thermal fluctuations and power rail ripple.

Because physical registers are built from finite arrays of silicon flip-flops (8 bits in a uint8_t, 16 bits in a half-word, 32 bits in a standard ARM word, 64 bits in a quad-word), arithmetic in digital hardware is fundamentally modular. Numbers do not stretch endlessly to infinity; they wrap around a finite integer ring (\(\mathbb{Z} / 2^N \mathbb{Z}\)).

docs.title: Why Two's Complement Won: Zero Logic Gate Overhead and the Elimination of Minus Zero
docs.text:
In the dawn of modern digital computing during the 1940s and 1950s, computer architects experimented with multiple methods to represent signed negative numbers in binary:

  1. Sign-and-Magnitude: The most significant bit (MSB) serves as a sign flag (\(0 = \text{positive}, 1 = \text{negative}\)), while the remaining \(N-1\) bits store the absolute magnitude of the number.
  2. For an 8-bit byte: $\(+5_{10} = \text{00000101}_2 = \text{0x05}\)$ $\(-5_{10} = \text{10000101}_2 = \text{0x85}\)$
  3. One's Complement (Diminished Radix Complement): Negative numbers are generated by flipping every bit in the positive binary representation (bitwise NOT):
  4. For an 8-bit byte: $\(+5_{10} = \text{00000101}_2 = \text{0x05}\)$ $\(-5_{10} = \sim(\text{00000101}_2) = \text{11111010}_2 = \text{0xFA}\)$

Why did both Sign-and-Magnitude and One's Complement fail, disappearing from modern microprocessor architectures?

Because both systems contain two catastrophic hardware and software flaws:

First, The Dual-Zero Ambiguity Bug (\(+0\) vs. \(-0\)): In Sign-and-Magnitude, there are two distinct physical bit patterns for zero: - Positive Zero: \(\text{00000000}_2 = \text{0x00} = +0\) - Negative Zero: \(\text{10000000}_2 = \text{0x80} = -0\)

In One's Complement, there are likewise two zeros: - Positive Zero: \(\text{00000000}_2 = \text{0x00} = +0\) - Negative Zero: \(\text{11111111}_2 = \text{0xFF} = -0\)

Having two representations of zero creates severe hazards in real-time control. A conditional branch like if (velocity == 0) fails if the compiler tests only for 0x00 while an arithmetic operation produces 0x80 or 0xFF. Testing for zero requires multiple logic gates and extra clock cycles, introducing race conditions in interrupt service routines.

Second, The Requirement for Dual Silicon Adders and Subtractors: In Sign-and-Magnitude, you cannot add a positive number and a negative number using a standard binary adder. The CPU must first compare the magnitudes of both numbers, determine which one is larger, subtract the smaller magnitude from the larger magnitude using a dedicated subtractor circuit, and conditionally assign the sign bit. This required massive amounts of redundant silicon circuitry and introduced severe propagation delays.

The solution that triumphed across all modern computer architectures was Two's Complement, formalized by John von Neumann and early computer pioneers.

In Two's Complement, the negative of an integer \(X\) is defined as its additive inverse in the modular ring \(\mathbb{Z} / 2^N \mathbb{Z}\):

\[X^* = 2^N - X = \left((2^N - 1) - X\right) + 1 = \sim X + 1\]

To negate a number in two's complement, you simply: 1. Invert all bits (bitwise NOT, \(\sim X\)). 2. Add one (\(+1\)).

Analyze the practical consequences of this definition:

  1. Zero Silicon Overhead Between Addition and Subtraction: Subtracting \(B\) from \(A\) is mathematically identical to adding the two's complement of \(B\): $\(A - B = A + (\sim B + 1)\)$ The central processing unit requires no dedicated subtraction hardware. The exact same binary adder circuit (ripple-carry or carry-lookahead adder) that adds two positive numbers executes subtraction with zero silicon overhead. The CPU simply inverts the \(B\) input bits through XOR gates and asserts the adder's carry-in bit (\(C_{\text{in}} = 1\)).
  2. Exactly One Zero: In two's complement, negating zero yields: $\(\sim(\text{00000000}_2) + 1 = \text{11111111}_2 + 1 = \text{100000000}_2\)$ The 9th bit overflows and is discarded by the 8-bit register, leaving only \(\text{00000000}_2\). There is no negative zero; zero is unique, unambiguous, and testable with a single NOR gate.
  3. Asymmetric Range: Because zero uses one of the positive bit patterns (starting with MSB = \(0\)), an \(N\)-bit two's complement integer has an asymmetric range: $\(\left[-2^{N-1}, \; 2^{N-1} - 1\right]\)$
  4. 8-bit (BYTE): \([-128, \; +127]\)
  5. 16-bit (WORD): \([-32{,}768, \; +32{,}767]\)
  6. 32-bit (DWORD): \([-2{,}147{,}483{,}648, \; +2{,}147{,}483{,}647]\)
  7. 64-bit (QWORD): \([-9{,}223{,}372{,}036{,}854{,}775{,}808, \; +9{,}223{,}372{,}036{,}854{,}775{,}807]\)

The most negative number (such as \(-128\) in 8-bit mode, 0x80) has no positive counterpart. Attempting to negate \(-128\) produces: $\(\sim(\text{10000000}_2) + 1 = \text{01111111}_2 + 1 = \text{10000000}_2 = -128\)$ It overflows back to itself. This asymmetry is a mathematical property of modular rings that every systems programmer must account for.

docs.title: The Dhahran Patriot Missile Failure: Binary Truncation in Real-Time Systems
docs.text:
Consider the decimal number \(0.1\) (\(1/10\)) represented in base 2. In base 10, \(0.1\) is a single-digit terminating fraction. But converting \(1/10\) to base 2 reveals an infinite repeating expansion: - \(0.1 \times 2 = 0.2 \to 0\) - \(0.2 \times 2 = 0.4 \to 0\) - \(0.4 \times 2 = 0.8 \to 0\) - \(0.8 \times 2 = 1.6 \to 1\) - \(0.6 \times 2 = 1.2 \to 1\) - \(0.2 \times 2 = 0.4 \to 0\) (the sequence repeats indefinitely).

In binary, \(0.1_{10}\) is an infinite repeating fraction:

\[0.1_{10} = 0.00011001100110011001100110011..._2\]

Just as \(1/3 = 0.333333...\) cannot be represented with a terminating decimal fraction, \(1/10\) cannot be represented with a terminating binary fraction.

This mathematical reality triggered a well-documented military software failure on February 25, 1991, during Operation Desert Storm in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia. An American Patriot missile air-defense battery failed to track and intercept an incoming Iraqi Scud missile, which struck an army barracks.

The Patriot radar tracking computer measured system time by incrementing an integer counter by one every tenth of a second (\(0.1\text{ s}\)). To calculate time in seconds for radar velocity tracking, the software multiplied this integer count by a fixed-point binary representation of \(1/10\).

The Patriot used a 24-bit fixed-point register. Truncating the infinite binary expansion of \(1/10\) at 24 bits resulted in:

\[0.1_{10} \approx 0.00011001100110011001100_2 = \frac{1{,}677{,}721}{16{,}777{,}216} \approx 0.099999904632568359375\text{ s}\]

The error per tick was small:

\[\Delta t_{\text{tick}} = 0.1 - 0.099999904632568359375 \approx 0.000000095367\text{ seconds}\]

This error is less than one ten-millionth of a second per tick. In a system intended to run for a few hours before rebooting, this drift was negligible. But at Dhahran, the battery had been running continuously for 100 hours:

\[\text{Total Ticks} = 100\text{ hours} \times 3{,}600\text{ s/hr} \times 10\text{ ticks/s} = 3{,}600{,}000\text{ ticks}\]

Multiplying the total ticks by the tiny 24-bit truncation error:

\[\Delta t_{\text{total}} = 3{,}600{,}000 \times 0.000000095367\text{ s} \approx \mathbf{0.3433\text{ seconds}}\]

This accumulated into a timing drift of over a third of a second. When an incoming Al-Hussein Scud missile approached at Mach 5 (\(v \approx 1{,}676\text{ m/s}\)), the Patriot radar predicted where the missile should be by searching a spatial range gate. Due to the \(0.3433\text{ s}\) clock drift, the radar searched a volume of sky displaced by:

\[\Delta x = v \times \Delta t_{\text{total}} = 1{,}676\text{ m/s} \times 0.3433\text{ s} \approx \mathbf{575.43\text{ meters}}\]

The Scud was more than half a kilometer away from the predicted range gate. The radar declared the target a false track, dropped lock, and never launched an interceptor. The Dhahran failure stands as an enduring lesson in computer systems engineering: fixed-width binary arithmetic, floating-point truncation, and timer prescalers are matters of life and death.

docs.title: Memory-Mapped I/O and Peripheral Register Assignment
docs.text:
In ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers, peripherals (timers, UARTs, SPI, GPIO) do not use dedicated I/O instructions; they use Memory-Mapped Input/Output (MMIO). Every hardware control register is mapped to a physical 32-bit address on the peripheral bus: - TIM2->CR1 (Timer 2 Control Register 1) resides at address 0x40000000. - TIM2->SR (Timer 2 Status Register) resides at address 0x40000010.

Consider an attempt to configure center-aligned PWM mode via raw assignment: 

TIM2->CR1 = 0x0020; // Attempting to set CMS bits [6:5]

Raw assignment (=) overwrites every bit in the 32-bit register. By writing 0x0020, software sets bit 5, but simultaneously clears bits 0, 7, 8, and 9 to zero. Clearing bit 0 halts the timer counter; clearing bit 7 disables the preload buffer, causing motor PWM duty cycles to glitch; and clearing bits 8-9 alters the dead-time clock prescaler, causing both the high-side and low-side MOSFETs in the H-bridge inverter to turn on simultaneously—a dead short across the DC bus known as shoot-through.

Furthermore, on high-performance microcontrollers equipped with an Advanced High-Performance Bus (AHB) and Advanced Peripheral Bus (APB), peripheral writes are buffered. If software writes to a register and immediately proceeds without verifying bus completion, pipeline latency can cause subsequent instructions to execute before the hardware state has settled. In critical sections, systems programmers insert memory barriers (__DSB(), Data Synchronization Barrier) and declare register pointers as volatile to prevent the C compiler from optimizing out repeated register reads or reordering bus transactions.

To safely manipulate peripheral registers, an embedded engineer must use Bitwise Boolean Masking: 1. Setting Bits (Atomic OR): 

TIM2->CR1 |= (1 << 0); // Sets CEN (bit 0) without modifying any other bit
2. Clearing Bits (Atomic Inverted AND): 
TIM2->CR1 &= ~(1 << 0); // Clears CEN (bit 0) while leaving all other bits intact
3. Modifying Multi-Bit Fields (Read-Modify-Write): To update a multi-bit field (such as bits 6:5), you must first clear the field using the inverted mask, and then OR in the new value: 
#define CMS_MASK (0x3 << 5) // Bits [6:5] mask = 0x0060
TIM2->CR1 = (TIM2->CR1 & ~CMS_MASK) | (0x1 << 5); // Clears [6:5] then sets to 01
4. Write-1-to-Clear (W1C) Status Registers: In many peripherals, status flags (like UIF, bit 0 of TIM2->SR) are cleared by writing a 0 or a 1 depending on the silicon architecture. In standard STM32/ARM timers, writing 0 to a status bit clears it, while writing 1 has no effect: 
TIM2->SR = ~(1 << 0); // Writes 0 to bit 0, preserving other pending hardware flags
Executing TIM2->SR = 0; clears capture-compare interrupt flags that occurred simultaneously, dropping encoder counts.

docs.title: Hardware Memory-Mapped Bit-Banding in ARM Cortex-M Architectures
docs.text:
Even a standard read-modify-write operation (TIM2->CR1 |= MASK) has a subtle flaw in preemptive real-time systems: it is not atomic at the machine-code level.

When the CPU executes TIM2->CR1 |= (1 << 0);, the compiler generates three distinct assembly instructions: 

LDR  R0, =0x40000000   ; Load register address
LDR  R1, [R0]          ; Read: fetch current 32-bit register value into R1
ORR  R1, R1, #0x01     ; Modify: set bit 0
STR  R1, [R0]          ; Write: store updated 32-bit value back to peripheral

Suppose a high-priority hardware interrupt fires between the LDR and the STR. The interrupt service routine modifies bit 4 of TIM2->CR1 and returns. When the interrupted main thread resumes, its stale value in R1 is written back via STR, overwriting the change made by the ISR. This is the classic read-modify-write race condition in multi-threaded firmware.

To solve this without the severe execution penalty of disabling global interrupts (__disable_irq()), ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M4 processors implement an ingenious hardware feature: Bit-Banding.

Bit-banding maps individual bits within memory-mapped peripheral and SRAM regions into an entirely separate, expanded 32-megabyte address space known as the bit-band alias region: 1. Peripheral Bit-Band Region: Physical addresses 0x40000000 through 0x400FFFFF (\(1\text{ MB}\)) map to alias addresses 0x42000000 through 0x43FFFFFF (\(32\text{ MB}\)). 2. SRAM Bit-Band Region: Physical addresses 0x20000000 through 0x200FFFFF (\(1\text{ MB}\)) map to alias addresses 0x22000000 through 0x23FFFFFF (\(32\text{ MB}\)).

In this alias region, every single bit of the original memory space is assigned its own dedicated 32-bit word address. When the CPU writes a 1 or 0 to an alias word address, the internal bus matrix hardware automatically performs an atomic read-modify-write transaction directly on the target peripheral register in a single cycle.

The mathematical formula to compute the 32-bit alias word address from a byte address and bit number is:

\[\text{Bit\_Band\_Address} = \text{Alias\_Base} + (\text{Byte\_Offset} \times 32) + (\text{Bit\_Number} \times 4)\]

Where: - \(\text{Alias\_Base}\) is 0x42000000 for peripherals or 0x22000000 for SRAM. - \(\text{Byte\_Offset}\) is the byte distance from the start of the bit-band region (\(\text{Target\_Address} - \text{Base\_Address}\)). - \(\text{Bit\_Number}\) is the target bit position (\(0 \le \text{Bit\_Number} \le 7\) within that byte, or \(0 \le \text{Bit\_Number} \le 31\) within a 32-bit word).

Consider clearing bit 0 of the Timer 2 Status Register (TIM2->SR) located at physical address 0x40000010. 1. Peripheral base is 0x40000000, so \(\text{Byte\_Offset} = \text{0x40000010} - \text{0x40000000} = \text{0x10} = 16_{10}\). 2. Bit number is \(0\). 3. Evaluating the alias formula: $\(\text{Bit\_Band\_Address} = \text{0x42000000} + (16 \times 32) + (0 \times 4) = \text{0x42000000} + 512 + 0 = \text{0x42000200}\)$

By simply executing a single store instruction: 

*((volatile uint32_t *)0x42000200) = 0;
The processor clears bit 0 of TIM2->SR with hardware atomicity. No interrupts can preempt it, no temporary registers are corrupted, and zero race conditions can occur.

docs.title: Positional Radix Compression and Fixed-Width Two's Complement Rings
docs.text: The SC-16 provides dedicated hardware modes for four positional number bases: Hexadecimal (base 16), Decimal (base 10), Octal (base 8), and Binary (base 2).

docs.title: Binary Nibbles, Octal Triads, and Hexadecimal Register Notation
docs.text:
In any positional number system of radix \(b\), a number is represented by a sequence of digits \((d_{n-1} d_{n-2} \dots d_1 d_0)_b\) whose magnitude evaluates the polynomial expansion:

Eq. 7.1 — Positional Number Base Radix Expansion $\(V = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_i \cdot b^i = d_{n-1} b^{n-1} + d_{n-2} b^{n-2} + \dots + d_1 b^1 + d_0 b^0\)$

Where each digit is bounded by \(0 \le d_i < b\).

Why do engineers switch between bases? 1. Binary (\(b = 2\), digits \(0, 1\)): Direct reflection of physical CMOS voltage levels. Every digit is one bit. However, a 32-bit register requires 32 digits, making human visual inspection exhausting and error-prone. 2. Octal (\(b = 8\), digits \(0\text{–}7\)): Groups bits into groups of 3 (\(2^3 = 8\)), known as triads. Historically dominant in 12-bit, 18-bit, and 36-bit minicomputer architectures such as the PDP-8 and PDP-11, where instruction opcodes were partitioned into 3-bit fields. Octal is still used in Unix file system permissions (chmod 755). However, because 8 bits, 16 bits, and 32 bits do not divide evenly by 3, octal produces awkward split boundaries in modern byte-oriented architectures. 3. Hexadecimal (\(b = 16\), digits \(0\text{–}9, \text{A–F}\)): The universal language of embedded systems. Because \(2^4 = 16\), exactly four binary bits compress into a single hexadecimal digit (a nibble). - An 8-bit byte is exactly 2 hex digits (0x00 to 0xFF). - A 16-bit word is exactly 4 hex digits (0x0000 to 0xFFFF). - A 32-bit double-word is exactly 8 hex digits (0x00000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF). - A 64-bit quad-word is exactly 16 hex digits.

Hexadecimal aligns perfectly with byte boundaries. Converting between binary and hexadecimal requires zero arithmetic calculation; it is pure visual pattern matching: - 0x42964000: - 4 = 0100 - 2 = 0010 - 9 = 1001 - 6 = 0110 - 4 = 0100 - 0 = 0000 - 0 = 0000 - 0 = 0000

Summing powers of two evaluates the decimal equivalent: \(V = 1{,}117{,}143{,}040_{10}\).

docs.title: Modular Integer Rings, Two's Complement Negation, and Signed Overflow
docs.text:
In an \(N\)-bit processor register, arithmetic operations occur within the finite ring of integers modulo \(2^N\) (\(\mathbb{Z} / 2^N \mathbb{Z}\)).

When a positive number exceeds the maximum representable integer, it does not stop; it wraps around to zero (in unsigned arithmetic) or wraps into negative values (in signed two's complement arithmetic).

The two's complement additive inverse equation is:

Eq. 7.2 — Two's Complement Additive Inversion $\(X^* = 2^N - X = \sim X + 1\)$

Where \(\sim X\) is the bitwise NOT operation (inverting all \(N\) bits), and \(+1\) completes the additive inverse in modulo \(2^N\).

       Unsigned Byte (0 to 255)                  Signed Byte (-128 to +127)
               0x00 (0)                                  0x00 (0)
        0xFF              0x01                    0xFF              0x01
        (255)              (1)                    (-1)              (+1)
    0xFE                      0x02            0xFE                      0x02
    (254)                      (2)            (-2)                      (+2)
   0x80                        0x7F          0x80                        0x7F
   (128)                      (127)         (-128)                      (+127)

Look at the boundary at 0x7F (\(+127\)) transitioning to 0x80: - In unsigned arithmetic, 0x7F + 1 = 0x80 (\(127 + 1 = 128\)). - In signed arithmetic, 0x7F + 1 = 0x80 (\(+127 + 1 = \mathbf{-128}\)).

This sudden sign inversion is Signed Integer Overflow.

docs.title: The Silicon Arithmetic Logic Unit: Carry (\(C\)), Overflow (\(V\)), and Condition Codes
docs.text:
To detect arithmetic boundaries, every microprocessor ALU sets condition flags inside the status register (e.g., APSR in ARM, EFLAGS in x86): 1. Zero Flag (\(Z\)): Set to \(1\) if the result of an operation is exactly zero; \(0\) otherwise. 2. Negative Flag (\(N\) or \(S\)): Matches the most significant bit (MSB) of the result (\(1\) if negative, \(0\) if positive). 3. Carry Flag (\(C\)): Set when an unsigned addition produces a carry out of the MSB (\(> 2^N - 1\)), or when an unsigned subtraction requires a borrow. (Note: in ARM processors, \(C=1\) on subtraction indicates "no borrow", whereas in x86 \(C=1\) indicates "borrow"). 4. Overflow Flag (\(V\)): Set when a signed operation produces a result that exceeds the representable signed range \(\left[-2^{N-1}, 2^{N-1}-1\right]\).

In physical silicon, the Overflow Flag is generated by a simple, elegant logic gate: the exclusive-OR of the carry into the MSB (\(C_{\text{in}}\)) and the carry out of the MSB (\(C_{\text{out}}\)):

\[V = C_{\text{in}} \oplus C_{\text{out}}\]

Equivalently, signed overflow occurs if and only if two positive numbers yield a negative sum, or two negative numbers yield a positive sum:

\[V = (A_{\text{MSB}} \land B_{\text{MSB}} \land \overline{R_{\text{MSB}}}) \lor (\overline{A_{\text{MSB}}} \land \overline{B_{\text{MSB}}} \land R_{\text{MSB}})\]

For an 8-bit signed byte, adding \(+120\) (0x78) and \(+15\) (0x0F) yields \(+135\), which exceeds \(+127\). The bit result is 0x87, which interprets in two's complement as \(-121\). The positive sum overflowed into a negative representation, asserting the processor's Overflow Flag (\(V = 1\)).

This distinction between \(C\) and \(V\) dictates how processors evaluate conditional branch instructions:

Comparison Instruction Evaluated Flags Condition Name Arithmetic Domain BEQ (Branch Equal) \(Z = 1\) Equal Both Signed and Unsigned BNE (Branch Not Equal) \(Z = 0\) Not Equal Both Signed and Unsigned BHI (Branch Higher) \(C = 1 \land Z = 0\) Greater Than Unsigned BLS (Branch Lower or Same) \(C = 0 \lor Z = 1\) Less Than or Equal Unsigned BGT (Branch Greater Than) \(Z = 0 \land (N = V)\) Greater Than Signed BLT (Branch Less Than) \(N \ne V\) Less Than Signed BGE (Branch Greater or Equal) \(N = V\) Greater Than or Equal Signed BLE (Branch Less or Equal) \(Z = 1 \lor (N \ne V)\) Less Than or Equal Signed

If a developer compiles a boundary check with unsigned types (unsigned int len), the compiler emits unsigned comparisons (BHI/BLS). If the developer compares signed variables with unsigned bounds, catastrophic cyber vulnerabilities occur (such as the classic negative-index heap overwrite, where \(-1\) treated as unsigned evaluates to \(4{,}294{,}967{,}295\), bypassing length limits).

docs.title: Sign Extension Across Register Boundaries: CBW, SXTB, and MOVSX
docs.text:
When a microprocessor loads an 8-bit or 16-bit signed integer into a 32-bit or 64-bit general-purpose register, how does it preserve its mathematical value?

Suppose an 8-bit temperature reading is \(-5_{10}\), stored in memory as byte 0xFB (11111011_2). If the CPU loads this byte into a 32-bit register without sign extension (zero-extension, MOVZX in x86): $\(\text{Register} = \text{0x000000FB} = +251_{10}\)$ The temperature reading wraps from \(-5^\circ\text{C}\) to \(+251^\circ\text{C}\), corrupting downstream process control.

To preserve the negative signed value, the processor must perform Sign Extension: it replicates the most significant bit of the smaller type across all upper bit positions of the larger register: - Positive number (0x05, MSB = 0) \(\to\) 0x00000005 (+5). - Negative number (0xFB, MSB = 1) \(\to\) 0xFFFFFFFB (-5).

Modern assembly architectures provide dedicated instructions for this operation: - x86: CBW (Convert Byte to Word), CWDE (Convert Word to Doubleword Extended), CDQ (Convert Doubleword to Quadword), and MOVSX (Move with Sign Extension). - ARM: SXTB (Signed Extend Byte), SXTH (Signed Extend Halfword), and SBFX (Signed Bit Field Extract).

On the SC-16 calculator, changing the active word size with [g] [WSZ] while in signed mode automatically enforces correct sign extension and truncation rules, allowing engineers to audit register widening bugs directly on the stack.

docs.title: Bitwise Boolean Masking, Shifts, and Fixed/Floating-Point Encoding
Boolean Logic Gates and Peripheral Control Register Masking
docs.text:
Silicon microcontrollers do not modify physical pins directly; they modify bits inside peripheral registers. The fundamental Boolean logic operations are:

  1. Bitwise AND (&, [&]): Output is \(1\) if and only if both inputs are \(1\). Used to mask and isolate specific bits, clearing all others to \(0\).
  2. \(X \ \& \ 1 = X\) (preserves bit)
  3. \(X \ \& \ 0 = 0\) (forces bit to zero)
  4. Bitwise OR (|, [|]): Output is \(1\) if either input is \(1\). Used to set specific bits without disturbing adjacent bits.
  5. \(X \mid 0 = X\) (preserves bit)
  6. \(X \mid 1 = 1\) (forces bit to one)
  7. Bitwise XOR (^, [⊕]): Output is \(1\) if inputs are different; \(0\) if identical. Used to toggle/invert bits and calculate parity.
  8. \(X \oplus 0 = X\) (preserves bit)
  9. \(X \oplus 1 = \sim X\) (toggles bit)
  10. \(X \oplus X = 0\) (clears register to zero in a single cycle)
  11. Bitwise NOT (~, [g] [~]): Inverts every bit (one's complement).

To manipulate a specific bitfield of width \(W\) starting at bit position \(P\), we generate a contiguous bitmask:

Eq. 7.3 — Contiguous Bitfield Mask Generation $\(\text{Mask} = (2^W - 1) \ll P\)$

Where \(W\) is the field bit-width, \(P\) is the starting bit position (offset), and \(\ll\) is the logical shift-left operator.

For example, to isolate or update a 4-bit configuration field (\(W = 4\)) at bit position \(P = 8\) (bits [11:8]): $\(\text{Mask} = (2^4 - 1) \ll 8 = (16 - 1) \ll 8 = 15 \ll 8 = \text{0x0F} \ll 8 = \mathbf{\text{0x0F00}}\)$

To update bits [11:8] in register REG containing 0xA528 to new value 0x5 (0x0500): 1. Clear the field: REG & ~0x0F00 = 0xA528 & 0xF0FF = 0xA028. 2. OR in the new value: 0xA028 | 0x0500 = 0xA528.

In modern ARM Cortex microcontrollers, dedicated bitfield instructions accelerate these operations: - UBFX Rd, Rn, #lsb, #width (Unsigned Bit Field Extract): Extracts \(W\) bits starting at position \(P\) into register Rd, zero-extending the result. - SBFX Rd, Rn, #lsb, #width (Signed Bit Field Extract): Extracts \(W\) bits and sign-extends the highest extracted bit across the destination register. - BFI Rd, Rn, #lsb, #width (Bit Field Insert): Copies \(W\) bits from the low-order bits of Rn into Rd starting at position \(P\), leaving all other bits of Rd intact.

docs.title: Logical Shifts, Sign-Preserving Arithmetic Shifts, Rotations, and Fixed-Point Scaling
docs.text:
Bit shifts move all bits inside a register to the left or right by \(k\) positions:

  1. Logical Shift Left (LSL, <<, [≪]): Shifts bits left, discarding bits that fall off the MSB, and shifting in zeros (0) at the LSB.
  2. Mathematically equivalent to multiplying by \(2^k\): $\(X \ll k = X \cdot 2^k \pmod{2^N}\)$
  3. Logical Shift Right (LSR, >>, [≫]): Shifts bits right, discarding bits that fall off the LSB, and shifting in zeros (0) at the MSB.
  4. Correct for unsigned integer division by \(2^k\): $\(X \gg_{\text{logical}} k = \lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor\)$
  5. Arithmetic Shift Right (ASR, >>, [f] [ASR]): Shifts bits right, discarding bits that fall off the LSB, but replicates the sign bit (MSB) into the vacated high-order bit positions.
  6. Mandatory for signed two's complement division by \(2^k\): $\(X \gg_{\text{arithmetic}} k = \lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor\)$
  7. Rotate Right (ROR, [g] [ROR]) and Rotate Left (ROL, [g] [ROR]): Circular shifts where bits shifted out of one end wrap around and enter the opposite end. Zero bits are lost. Essential in cryptographic hashing algorithms (MD5, SHA-256) to achieve the avalanche effect.

docs.title: Fixed-Point Q-Format Arithmetic Architectures
docs.text:
In resource-constrained microcontrollers lacking a floating-point unit (FPU), or in ultra-low-latency motor control loops where FPU cycles are too slow, engineers use Fixed-Point Arithmetic.

In Q-format notation, a signed \(N\)-bit integer is partitioned into: - \(1\) sign bit (implicitly part of the integer bits). - \(M\) integer bits. - \(F\) fractional bits, where \(M + F = N - 1\) (or \(N\) total bits). - Notation: \(\text{Q}M.F\) or simply \(\text{Q}F\) when total word size \(N\) is known.

Common industrial Q formats: - Q16.16 (32-bit word): 1 sign bit, 15 integer bits, 16 fractional bits. - Range: \([-32{,}768.0, \; +32{,}767.9999847]\) - Resolution: \(\epsilon = 2^{-16} = \frac{1}{65{,}536} \approx 0.0000152588\) - Q8.8 (16-bit word): 1 sign bit, 7 integer bits, 8 fractional bits. - Range: \([-128.0, \; +127.99609375]\) - Resolution: \(\epsilon = 2^{-8} = \frac{1}{256} \approx 0.00390625\) - Q1.15 or Q15 (16-bit DSP format): 1 sign bit, 0 integer bits, 15 fractional bits. Widely used for normalized audio waveforms in \([-1.0, +0.999969]\).

To convert a real number \(V_{\text{real}}\) into fixed-point integer representation \(X_{\text{fixed}}\): $\(X_{\text{fixed}} = \text{round}(V_{\text{real}} \times 2^F)\)$

To convert back to real floating-point: $\(V_{\text{real}} = \frac{X_{\text{fixed}}}{2^F}\)$

Fixed-point arithmetic rules: 1. Addition and Subtraction: Direct integer operations, provided both operands share the exact same Q format: $\(Z_{\text{fixed}} = X_{\text{fixed}} \pm Y_{\text{fixed}}\)$ 2. Multiplication: Multiplying two Q\(M.F\) numbers produces an intermediate product with \(2F\) fractional bits: $\(P_{\text{raw}} = X_{\text{fixed}} \times Y_{\text{fixed}} \implies Z_{\text{fixed}} = (X_{\text{fixed}} \times Y_{\text{fixed}}) \gg F\)$ To prevent intermediate overflow, 32-bit Q16.16 multiplication must store the product in a 64-bit integer before shifting right by 16 bits. 3. Division: Dividing two Q\(M.F\) numbers drops the fractional scaling: $\(Z_{\text{fixed}} = \frac{X_{\text{fixed}} \ll F}{Y_{\text{fixed}}}\)$ The dividend must be pre-shifted left by \(F\) bits (using a wider 64-bit integer) prior to division to retain precision.
