  5. Two-Asset Portfolio Variance and Volatility Diversification: Asset 1 has volatility \(\sigma_1 = 15.0\%\) and Asset 2 has volatility \(\sigma_2 = 25.0\%\). The two assets are held in equal weights (\(w_1 = 0.50, w_2 = 0.50\)) with correlation coefficient \(\rho_{12} = 0.20\). Calculate the combined portfolio variance and portfolio volatility \(\sigma_p\).

Having priced debt capital, mastered duration-convexity dynamics, and hedged market volatility via options, the enterprise turns inward to physical operations. In Chapter 27, the manual enters the manufacturing shop floor: auditing machine tool wear, evaluating bivariate regressions, resolving volatility drag, and calculating Six Sigma process capability indices.

docs.title: Chapter 27: Catching the Drifting Grinding Spindle Before Scrap Happens
docs.text:
In precision aerospace manufacturing, a series of machined parts that fall within blueprint tolerances can still conceal the onset of severe scrap. When an automated CNC cylindrical grinder finishes case-hardened steel turbine shafts with a journal diameter specified at \(25.000\text{ mm}\) (\(\text{USL} = 25.020\text{ mm}, \text{LSL} = 24.980\text{ mm}\), total tolerance band \(40.0\ \mu\text{m}\)), measuring five consecutive hourly samples that pass inspection (\(25.002, 25.005, 25.007, 25.011, 25.014\text{ mm}\)) offers false comfort.

Behind those acceptable measurements lies a steady upward trend driven by grinding wheel breakdown, spindle bearing thermal expansion, and coolant degradation. Left uncorrected, systematic drift combined with random variation will breach the Upper Specification Limit within hours, scrapping expensive aerospace shafts. Quality engineering is the discipline of distinguishing common-cause noise from assignable-cause drift.

Applying Ordinary Least-Squares (OLS) Bivariate Linear Regression quantifies the hourly drift rate \(\beta_1\) and forecasts the exact hour of out-of-tolerance failure. Furthermore, evaluating a baseline lot (\(N = 100\), \(\mu = 25.008\text{ mm}\), \(\sigma = 0.003\text{ mm}\)) reveals the true Six Sigma process capability: potential capability \(C_p\), off-center capability \(C_{pk}\), mean shift factor \(k\), and predicted defect rates in Defects Per Million Opportunities (DPMO) under the \(1.5\sigma\) long-term mean drift.

To preserve manufacturing quality and eliminate production scrap, the engineer turns to the SC-95 Quantitative Finance, Fixed-Income Valuation & Six Sigma Quality calculator:

docs.title: Sample Regression, Sampling Distributions, and Statistical Inference
docs.text: In high-precision manufacturing, zero variation is a physical impossibility. Every mechanical process experiences common-cause random fluctuations (vibrations, thermal gradients, electrical noise) and assignable-cause systematic drift (tool wear, bearing play, metallurgical variation).

docs.title: The Quality Engineer's Dilemma: The Illusion of Zero-Defect Samples
docs.text:
Consider the fundamental trap of sampling inspection:

[Small Sample of 5 Parts Inspected]
All 5 Parts Fall Within Blueprint Tolerances (24.980 to 25.020 mm)
           |
           +---> Static Inspection: "Zero defects observed in sample"
           |
           +---> Statistical Engineer: Audits Drift Velocity (3.0 µm/hr)
                 Forecasts Out-of-Specification Breach by Hour 7

An untrained technician inspecting a small sample of five machined parts sees that every single part falls cleanly between \(24.980\text{ mm}\) and \(25.020\text{ mm}\). Relying solely on discrete pass/fail inspection, the technician certifies the machine and walks away.

Two hours later, the manufacturing line begins churning out hundreds of non-conforming, oversized shafts. Why? Because the technician evaluated static positions rather than dynamic vector trajectories.

Tool wear is continuous. If a grinding spindle drifts upward at \(3.0\ \mu\text{m}\) per hour, the fact that a part measured at Hour 5 is \(25.014\text{ mm}\) (\(6\ \mu\text{m}\) below the ceiling) guarantees that by Hour 7, parts will cross \(25.020\text{ mm}\) into scrap. To prevent waste, statistical process control must model rates of change using linear regression and project probability distributions across tolerance limits.

docs.title: Sample Mean, Dispersion, and Ordinary Least-Squares Linear Regression ([Σ+], [x̄,ȳ], [g] [s,σ], [g] [L.R.])
docs.text:
When analyzing a bivariate dataset of paired observations \((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \dots, (x_n, y_n)\), the SC-95 statistical accumulator registers ([Σ+]) aggregate six running statistical summations: $\(\sum x, \quad \sum y, \quad \sum x^2, \quad \sum y^2, \quad \sum xy, \quad n\)$

From these six fundamental sums, the arithmetic sample means are evaluated directly:

\[\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n y_i\]

docs.title: Bessel's Correction and Unbiased Sample Variance
docs.text:
In finite sample statistics, dividing the sum of squared deviations by the sample size \(n\) systematically underestimates the true population dispersion because sample deviations are measured relative to the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) rather than the true population mean \(\mu\).

In 1815, Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel established Bessel's Correction: dividing by the degrees of freedom (\(n - 1\)) eliminates this downward bias, yielding the unique minimum-variance unbiased estimator of population variance:

Eq. 27.1 — Sample Variance and Ordinary Least-Squares Linear Regression $\(s_x^2 = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(x_i - \bar{x}\right)^2 = \frac{\sum x^2 - \frac{(\sum x)^2}{n}}{n - 1}\)$

\[s_y^2 = \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \bar{y}\right)^2 = \frac{\sum y^2 - \frac{(\sum y)^2}{n}}{n - 1}\]

docs.title: Ordinary Least-Squares (OLS) Regression
docs.text:
To model the linear trend \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\), Carl Friedrich Gauss and Adrien-Marie Legendre formulated the method of least squares: minimizing the sum of squared vertical residuals \(\sum e_i^2 = \sum (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i))^2\). Setting partial derivatives to zero yields the closed-form normal equations:

\[\beta_1 = \frac{SS_{xy}}{SS_{xx}} = \frac{\sum xy - \frac{(\sum x)(\sum y)}{n}}{\sum x^2 - \frac{(\sum x)^2}{n}}\] \[\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1 \bar{x}\]

The Pearson Product-Moment Correlation Coefficient (\(r\)) quantifies the strength and direction of linear association:

\[r = \frac{SS_{xy}}{\sqrt{SS_{xx} \cdot SS_{yy}}}\]

where \(r^2\) is the Coefficient of Determination, representing the exact percentage of total variation in diameter \(y\) explained by elapsed machining time \(x\).

For our grinding spindle data (\(x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]\), \(y = [25.002, 25.005, 25.007, 25.011, 25.014]\)): - \(n = 5\) - \(\sum x = 15.0 \implies \bar{x} = 3.0\text{ hours}\) - \(\sum y = 125.039 \implies \bar{y} = 25.00780\text{ mm}\) - \(\sum x^2 = 55.0 \implies SS_{xx} = 55.0 - (15.0)^2 / 5 = 55.0 - 45.0 = 10.0\) - \(SS_{xy} = 0.03000\) - \(SS_{yy} = 0.0000908\)

Evaluating the regression parameters via the SC-95 [g] [L.R.] function:

\[\beta_1 = \frac{0.03000}{10.0} = \mathbf{0.003000\text{ mm/hr}} \quad (\mathbf{3.0\ \mu\text{m/hr}})\] \[\beta_0 = 25.00780 - 0.003000(3.0) = 25.00780 - 0.00900 = \mathbf{24.998800\text{ mm}}\] \[r = \frac{0.03000}{\sqrt{10.0 \times 0.0000908}} = \frac{0.03000}{0.030133} = \mathbf{0.99558} \implies r^2 = \mathbf{0.99119} \quad (\mathbf{99.12\%})\]

The correlation is extraordinarily strong (\(r = 0.9956\)); over \(99.1\%\) of the diameter variation is directly driven by predictable linear tool wear.

docs.title: Forecasting the Scrap Horizon
docs.text:
Using the calibrated regression line:

\[\hat{y}(x) = 24.998800 + 0.003000 \cdot x\]

Forecasting diameter at Hour 8 (\(x = 8.0\)):

\[\hat{y}(8) = 24.998800 + 0.003000(8) = 24.998800 + 0.024000 = \mathbf{25.02280\text{ mm}}\]

Because \(\hat{y}(8) = 25.0228\text{ mm} > \text{USL} = 25.0200\text{ mm}\), parts produced at Hour 8 will exceed tolerance by \(2.8\ \mu\text{m}\).

Solving backward for the exact Scrap Horizon \(x_{\text{breach}}\) where diameter crosses USL:

\[25.020000 = 24.998800 + 0.003000 \cdot x \implies x_{\text{breach}} = \frac{25.020000 - 24.998800}{0.003000} = \frac{0.021200}{0.003000} = \mathbf{7.067\text{ hours}}\]

The process will breach upper tolerance at exactly 7 hours and 4 minutes of operation. The quality engineer schedules mandatory tool wear offset compensation at Hour 6.5, eliminating scrap before it occurs.

docs.title: Shewhart Control Charts, Western Electric Rules, and Student's t Inference
docs.text: Statistical process control separates random common-cause variation from assignable mechanical failure through control charting and hypothesis testing.

docs.title: Shewhart \(\bar{X}\) and \(R\) Control Charts
docs.text:
On May 16, 1924, Walter A. Shewhart drafted his historic memorandum at Bell Telephone Laboratories, introducing the statistical control chart. For subgroups of size \(n\) sampled periodically from a machining line: 1. The Center Line (\(\text{CL}\)): Represents the grand process average \(\bar{\bar{x}} = \frac{1}{k} \sum \bar{x}_i\). 2. Control Limits (\(\text{UCL}\) and \(\text{LCL}\)): Set at three standard errors (\(3\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 3\sigma / \sqrt{n}\)) from the center line: $\(\text{UCL}_{\bar{x}} = \bar{\bar{x}} + A_2 \bar{R} \qquad \text{LCL}_{\bar{x}} = \bar{\bar{x}} - A_2 \bar{R}\)$ where \(\bar{R}\) is the average subgroup range, and \(A_2\) is a tabulated factor based on subgroup size \(n\) (for \(n = 5\), \(A_2 = 0.577\)).

Unlike blueprint engineering specifications (\(\text{USL}\) and \(\text{LSL}\)), which represent customer desires, control limits represent the voice of the process—the physical boundaries of natural variation.

docs.title: The Western Electric Rules for Assignable Cause Detection
docs.text:
To detect subtle mechanical drift before parts exceed control limits, the Western Electric Company (1956) codified four empirical alarm rules: - Rule 1 (Outlier): Any single data point falls beyond the \(3\sigma\) control limit. - Rule 2 (Zone A Run): Two out of three consecutive points fall beyond the \(2\sigma\) warning limit on the same side of the center line. - Rule 3 (Zone B Run): Four out of five consecutive points fall beyond the \(1\sigma\) band on the same side of the center line. - Rule 4 (Trend / Bias): Eight or nine consecutive points fall on the same side of the center line, or six consecutive points steadily increase or decrease.

Any violation of these rules signals an assignable mechanical disturbance requiring immediate intervention.

docs.title: Student's \(t\)-Distribution and Small-Sample Confidence Intervals
docs.text:
When sample size \(n\) is small (\(n < 30\)) and the true population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, substituting the sample standard deviation \(s\) into the standard normal statistic introduces additional stochastic uncertainty.

In 1908, William Sealy Gosset—publishing under the pseudonym "Student" while serving as Head Brewer at Arthur Guinness & Son in Dublin—derived the exact probability density function for the ratio:

\[t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}}\]

The Student's \(t\)-distribution possesses heavier tails than the Gaussian normal distribution, reflecting the extra sampling variability of \(s\). As degrees of freedom \(\nu = n - 1 \to \infty\), the \(t\)-distribution converges asymptotically to the standard normal \(Z\)-distribution.

The two-sided \(100(1 - \alpha)\%\) confidence interval for the true population mean is:

\[\bar{x} - t_{\alpha/2, \, n-1} \left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \le \mu \le \bar{x} + t_{\alpha/2, \, n-1} \left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]

For our five spindle measurements (\(\bar{y} = 25.00780\text{ mm}\), \(s = 0.004764\text{ mm}\), \(n = 5 \implies \nu = 4\)), the critical two-tailed \(t\)-value at \(95\%\) confidence (\(\alpha = 0.05\)) is \(t_{0.025, \, 4} = 2.776\) (compared to \(Z = 1.960\)). The true process mean lies within:

\[\mu = 25.00780 \pm 2.776 \left(\frac{0.004764}{\sqrt{5}}\right) = 25.00780 \pm 2.776 (0.002131) = 25.00780 \pm 0.00592\text{ mm}\] \[\mu \in [25.00188\text{ mm}, \, 25.01372\text{ mm}]\]

The statistical engineer proves with \(95\%\) confidence that the true underlying process mean has shifted significantly above the nominal \(25.000\text{ mm}\) target.

docs.title: Memory-Based Control Charts: CUSUM and EWMA for Subtle Drift Detection
docs.text:
While classical Shewhart control charts are outstanding at catching large mechanical disruptions (\(> 2.5\sigma\)), they suffer from a major operational limitation: Shewhart charts evaluate only the current sample, possessing zero historical memory.

If a grinding spindle begins drifting slowly at \(0.5\sigma\) to \(1.0\sigma\) per hour, individual hourly samples will fluctuate within the \(3\sigma\) control limits for dozens of hours, producing out-of-tolerance scrap before a Shewhart rule triggers. To catch subtle micro-drifts, statistical quality engineering uses memory-based control charts:

docs.title: Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) Control Charts
docs.text:
In 1954, E. S. Page introduced the CUSUM Chart, which directly integrates historical deviations from the target nominal mean \(\mu_0\). The tabular CUSUM tracks two one-sided running cumulative sums:

\[C_i^+ = \max\left(0, \, x_i - \left(\mu_0 + K\right) + C_{i-1}^+\right)\] \[C_i^- = \max\left(0, \, \left(\mu_0 - K\right) - x_i + C_{i-1}^-\right)\]

where: - \(C_0^+ = C_0^- = 0\) is the initial state. - \(K = \frac{1}{2} \delta \sigma\) is the Reference Value (slack value), chosen to detect a target mean shift of magnitude \(\delta\) (typically \(\delta = 1.0\sigma \implies K = 0.5\sigma\)). - If either \(C_i^+\) or \(C_i^-\) exceeds the Decision Interval \(H = 5\sigma\) (or \(H = 4\sigma\)), the chart signals an out-of-control alarm.

Unlike Shewhart charts, where a \(1.0\sigma\) shift requires an Average Run Length (ARL) of over \(44\) samples to detect, CUSUM detects the exact same shift in fewer than \(8\) samples—catching tool wear hours before scrap is produced.

docs.title: Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) Charts
docs.text:
In 1959, J. Stuart Hunter formulated the EWMA Chart, which computes a recursive, geometrically weighted moving average of all past and current observations:

\[z_i = \lambda x_i + \left(1 - \lambda\right) z_{i-1}\]

where \(\lambda \in (0, 1]\) is the smoothing constant (typically \(\lambda = 0.10\text{ to }0.20\)), and \(z_0 = \mu_0\). The variance of \(z_i\) increases over time, stabilizing to:

\[\sigma_{z_i}^2 = \sigma^2 \left(\frac{\lambda}{2 - \lambda}\right) \left[1 - \left(1 - \lambda\right)^{2i}\right] \xrightarrow{i \to \infty} \sigma^2 \left(\frac{\lambda}{2 - \lambda}\right)\]

The time-varying control limits are:

\[\text{UCL}_i, \, \text{LCL}_i = \mu_0 \pm L \, \sigma \sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2 - \lambda} \left[1 - \left(1 - \lambda\right)^{2i}\right]}\]

Setting \(\lambda = 0.10\) and \(L = 2.7\) provides optimal sensitivity for detecting \(0.5\sigma\) to \(1.5\sigma\) process shifts, functioning as a high-precision digital low-pass filter that separates thermal machine drift from high-frequency measurement noise.

docs.title: Six Sigma Process Capability and Defect Rate Prediction
docs.text: While regression captures dynamic mechanical drift, Process Capability Analysis evaluates whether a centered, stable manufacturing process has the statistical precision to operate consistently within customer blueprint specifications.

docs.title: Process Potential Versus Centered Process Capability ([g] [Cpk])
docs.text: Engineering blueprints define allowable variation through specification limits (\(\text{USL}\) and \(\text{LSL}\)). The manufacturing process exhibits natural variation described by its standard deviation \(\sigma\). In statistical quality control, the natural spread of a process is defined as six standard deviations (\(6\sigma\), spanning \(\pm 3\sigma\) from the mean, enclosing \(99.73\%\) of output).

docs.title: Potential Process Capability (\(C_p\))
docs.text:
The Process Potential Index (\(C_p\)) compares the total allowable tolerance bandwidth to the natural process spread, assuming the process mean is perfectly centered between specification limits:

\[C_p = \frac{\text{Tolerance Width}}{\text{Process Width}} = \frac{\text{USL} - \text{LSL}}{6\sigma}\]
  • If \(C_p < 1.0\): The process is fundamentally incapable of meeting specifications; even if perfectly centered, the process will produce scrap.
  • If \(C_p = 1.0\): The process spread exactly matches the tolerance window (\(3\sigma\) quality).
  • If \(C_p \ge 1.33\): The process is capable (4-sigma quality).
  • If \(C_p \ge 2.00\): World-Class Six Sigma Process Potential.

docs.title: Actual Process Capability (\(C_{pk}\))
docs.text:
In reality, manufacturing processes are rarely centered perfectly at the nominal midpoint. Thermal expansion, clamping pressure, and tool offsets push the process mean \(\mu\) toward one specification limit.

The Actual Process Capability Index (\(C_{pk}\)) measures the distance from the process mean to the nearest specification limit in units of \(3\sigma\):

Eq. 27.2 — Centered and Asymmetric Process Capability Indices $\(C_{pk} = \min\left(CPU, \, CPL\right) = \min\left(\frac{\text{USL} - \mu}{3\sigma}, \, \frac{\mu - \text{LSL}}{3\sigma}\right)\)$

where: $\(CPU = \frac{\text{USL} - \mu}{3\sigma} \qquad CPL = \frac{\mu - \text{LSL}}{3\sigma}\)$

The index relates to potential capability via the Off-Center Shift Factor \(k\):

\[k = \frac{|\mu - \text{Target}|}{\frac{1}{2}(\text{USL} - \text{LSL})} \qquad C_{pk} = C_p (1 - k)\]

For our baseline turbine shaft production (\(USL = 25.020\text{ mm}\), \(LSL = 24.980\text{ mm}\), Target \(= 25.000\text{ mm}\), process mean \(\mu = 25.008\text{ mm}\), process standard deviation \(\sigma = 0.003\text{ mm}\)):

\[C_p = \frac{25.020 - 24.980}{6(0.003)} = \frac{0.040}{0.018} = \mathbf{2.2222}\]

The process has outstanding potential capability (\(C_p = 2.22 > 2.0\)), qualifying for Six Sigma capability if centered.

Now evaluating actual centered capability:

\[CPU = \frac{25.020 - 25.008}{3(0.003)} = \frac{0.012}{0.009} = \mathbf{1.3333}\] \[CPL = \frac{25.008 - 24.980}{3(0.003)} = \frac{0.028}{0.009} = \mathbf{3.1111}\] \[C_{pk} = \min(1.3333, 3.1111) = \mathbf{1.3333}\] \[k = \frac{|25.008 - 25.000|}{0.020} = \frac{0.008}{0.020} = \mathbf{0.4000} \quad (40\% \text{ off-center})\] \[C_{pk} = 2.2222 \times (1 - 0.4000) = 2.2222 \times 0.6000 = \mathbf{1.3333}\]

Because the mean is shifted \(8.0\ \mu\text{m}\) toward the upper specification limit, the actual capability drops from \(2.22\) down to \(1.3333\).

docs.title: Gaussian Tail Integration and Defects Per Million Opportunities
docs.text: To calculate expected scrap rates, the engineer translates capability indices into cumulative standard normal probabilities.

docs.title: Standardized \(Z\) Scores
docs.text:
The standardized distance to each specification limit in units of standard deviations is:

\[Z_{\text{USL}} = \frac{\text{USL} - \mu}{\sigma} = 3 \cdot CPU \qquad Z_{\text{LSL}} = \frac{\mu - \text{LSL}}{\sigma} = 3 \cdot CPL\]

For our shaft production: - \(Z_{\text{USL}} = 3 \times 1.3333 = \mathbf{4.00}\) (\(4.0\sigma\) clearance to upper limit). - \(Z_{\text{LSL}} = 3 \times 3.1111 = \mathbf{9.33}\) (\(9.33\sigma\) clearance to lower limit).

docs.title: Gaussian Tail Probability
docs.text:
The total probability of producing a non-conforming part (\(p_{\text{scrap}}\)) is the sum of the upper and lower tail integrals:

Eq. 27.3 — Gaussian Tail Scrap Rate and Defect Density $\(p_{\text{scrap}} = \left[1 - N(Z_{\text{USL}})\right] + \left[1 - N(Z_{\text{LSL}})\right] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{Z_{\text{USL}}}^\infty e^{-u^2/2} du + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{Z_{\text{LSL}}}^\infty e^{-u^2/2} du\)$

Evaluating the tail integrals via the SC-95 [g] [pN] function: - At \(Z_{\text{USL}} = 4.00\): $\(p_{\text{upper}} = 1 - N(4.00) = 1 - 0.99996833 = \mathbf{0.000031671} \quad (3.167 \times 10^{-5})\)$ - At \(Z_{\text{LSL}} = 9.33\): $\(p_{\text{lower}} = 1 - N(9.33) \approx \mathbf{0.000000000}\)$

Total scrap probability:

\[p_{\text{scrap}} = 3.1671 \times 10^{-5}\]

Multiplying by one million yields Defects Per Million Opportunities (DPMO):

\[\text{DPMO} = p_{\text{scrap}} \times 10^6 = 3.1671 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^6 = \mathbf{31.67\text{ DPMO}}\]

Out of every one million turbine shafts manufactured, exactly \(31.67\) parts will be oversized scrap.

docs.title: Motorola's \(1.5\sigma\) Mean Drift Hypothesis
docs.text:
In the mid-1980s, Motorola engineers Bill Smith and Mikel Harry analyzed decades of manufacturing data across mechanical, electrical, and chemical assembly lines. They discovered a universal empirical law: over long operational horizons, process means drift by approximately \(1.5\) standard deviations (\(1.5\sigma\)) due to tool wear, ambient temperature shifts, raw material batch variation, and operator fatigue.

Therefore, a process designed with short-term Six Sigma potential (\(C_p = 2.0\), with specifications set at \(\pm 6\sigma\)) will experience long-term drift that pushes the mean \(1.5\sigma\) closer to one specification limit.

The effective long-term clearance is not \(6.0\sigma\), but:

\[Z_{\text{long-term}} = 6.0\sigma - 1.5\sigma = \mathbf{4.5\sigma}\]

Integrating the Gaussian tail at \(Z = 4.50\):

\[p = 1 - N(4.50) = \mathbf{3.39767 \times 10^{-6}}\]

Multiplying by one million:

\[\text{DPMO}_{\text{Six Sigma}} = 3.39767 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^6 = \mathbf{3.40\text{ DPMO}}\]

This derivation unmasks one of modern engineering's most celebrated numbers: the global benchmark of "Six Sigma Quality" is not zero defects, but precisely \(3.4\text{ defects per million opportunities}\), representing a \(6\sigma\) potential process undergoing realistic \(1.5\sigma\) long-term drift.

docs.title: The Taguchi Loss Function and Measurement Systems Analysis (Gauge R&R)
docs.text: Two advanced principles separate modern Six Sigma engineering from archaic manufacturing practices:

docs.title: Genichi Taguchi's Quadratic Loss Function
docs.text:
Traditional manufacturing views quality through a binary "goalpost" mentality: any part that falls inside specification limits is considered completely acceptable (\(0\%\text{ loss}\)), while any part falling \(0.1\ \mu\text{m}\) outside is classified as total scrap.

In the 1960s, Japanese engineer Genichi Taguchi demonstrated that this binary step-function is an economic fiction. Customer dissatisfaction, mechanical friction, warranty failures, and energy losses do not begin abruptly at the blueprint line; they begin the moment a dimension deviates from the nominal target \(m\). Taguchi modeled this customer cost through the Quadratic Loss Function:

\[L(y) = k \left(y - m\right)^2\]

where \(k\) is the financial loss coefficient determined by the cost to scrap or repair a part at the specification limit:

\[k = \frac{\text{Cost of Scrap}}{\Delta_{\text{spec}}^2} = \frac{C_{\text{scrap}}}{(\text{USL} - m)^2}\]

For an ongoing production run with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), the expected loss per unit produced is:

\[E[L(y)] = k \left[(\mu - m)^2 + \sigma^2\right]\]

Taguchi's equation reveals an essential management insight: loss is driven by both off-center bias \((\mu - m)^2\) and process variance \(\sigma^2\). Centering the process and shrinking dispersion directly minimizes societal and commercial economic loss.

docs.title: Measurement Systems Analysis (MSA) and Gauge R&R
docs.text:
Before analyzing process capability, the quality engineer must verify that the measuring instrument itself is not confounding the data. In Gauge Repeatability and Reproducibility (Gauge R&R), the total observed variance in inspection measurements (\(\sigma_{\text{total}}^2\)) is partitioned into two independent components:

\[\sigma_{\text{total}}^2 = \sigma_{\text{part}}^2 + \sigma_{\text{measurement}}^2\]

where measurement variance is further decomposed:

\[\sigma_{\text{measurement}}^2 = \sigma_{\text{repeatability}}^2 + \sigma_{\text{reproducibility}}^2\]
  1. Repeatability (Equipment Variation): The variation observed when the same operator measures the exact same part multiple times using the same gauge.
  2. Reproducibility (Appraiser Variation): The variation observed between different operators measuring the same part with the same gauge.

The percentage of process tolerance consumed by measurement error (%GRR) is:

\[\%GRR = \frac{6 \cdot \sigma_{\text{measurement}}}{\text{USL} - \text{LSL}} \times 100\%\]

Under AIAG (Automotive Industry Action Group) standards: - \(\%GRR < 10\%\): The measurement system is acceptable. - \(10\% \le \%GRR \le 30\%\): The system is marginally acceptable depending on application criticality. - \(\%GRR > 30\%\): The measurement system is unacceptable; instrument noise and operator technique overwhelm true process dimensions.

docs.title: Design of Experiments (DOE) and Non-Normal Process Capability
docs.text: In modern quality engineering, resolving the root causes of process variability requires factorial experimentation and transformations for non-normal metrology data:

docs.title: Factorial Design of Experiments (DOE)
docs.text:
Rather than altering one machine parameter at a time (an unscientific approach that fails to detect interaction effects), Ronald A. Fisher and George E. P. Box developed Factorial Design of Experiments (DOE).

In a \(2^k\) full factorial design, \(k\) factors are simultaneously evaluated at two levels (low '\(-\)' and high '\(+\)'). For our CNC grinding operation: - Factor A: Spindle Speed (\(1500\text{ RPM}\) vs. \(2200\text{ RPM}\)) - Factor B: Feed Rate (\(0.05\text{ mm/rev}\) vs. \(0.12\text{ mm/rev}\)) - Factor C: Coolant Concentration (\(5\%\) vs. \(12\%\))

Evaluating all \(2^3 = 8\) experimental runs allows the engineer to calculate main effects \(\beta_A, \beta_B, \beta_C\) and two-factor interaction terms (\(AB, AC, BC\)). If the interaction between feed rate and coolant concentration is significant (\(p < 0.01\)), increasing feed rate without adequate coolant concentration accelerates thermal spindle growth—identifying the exact thermodynamic mechanism driving the drift.

docs.title: Non-Normal Process Capability and the Box–Cox Transformation
docs.text:
Classical capability indices (\(C_p, C_{pk}\)) strictly assume that process data follows a Gaussian normal distribution. However, many critical quality characteristics—such as surface roughness (\(R_a\)), circularity runout, flatness, and chemical impurity concentrations—are physically bounded by zero and exhibit severe positive skewness.

Calculating \(C_{pk}\) on skewed data using normal formulas yields wildly incorrect defect predictions. To resolve non-normality, George Box and David Cox (1964) formulated the Box–Cox Power Transformation:

\[y^{(\lambda)} = \begin{cases} \frac{y^\lambda - 1}{\lambda} & \text{if } \lambda \ne 0 \\ \ln(y) & \text{if } \lambda = 0 \end{cases}\]

The parameter \(\lambda\) is chosen by maximum likelihood estimation to transform skewed observations into a Gaussian distribution. Once normalized, the engineer evaluates capability indices and maps probability tails back to original engineering blueprint units, preserving statistical rigor across all manufacturing domains.

docs.title: Multivariate Process Capability and Hotelling's T-Squared Metrology
docs.text: In advanced aerospace and automotive manufacturing, parts are rarely characterized by a single independent dimension. A CNC turbine shaft possesses multiple interrelated geometric features: journal bearing outer diameter (\(y_1\)), internal bore diameter (\(y_2\)), and concentricity runout (\(y_3\)).

docs.title: The Fallacy of Univariate Inspection
docs.text: Evaluating correlated dimensions through separate univariate control charts (\(\bar{X}_1\) and \(\bar{X}_2\)) creates dangerous inspection distortions: 1. The Rectangular Tolerance Fiction: Univariate limits define a rectangular acceptance boundary \([\text{LSL}_1, \text{USL}_1] \times [\text{LSL}_2, \text{USL}_2]\). However, if the two dimensions are positively correlated (\(\rho > 0.80\), because the same grinding wheel forms both surfaces), the true physical distribution of acceptable parts forms an inclined Bivariate Normal Tolerance Ellipse. 2. False Acceptance and False Rejection: A machined shaft can fall inside both individual univariate tolerance intervals, yet lie far outside the joint bivariate ellipse—functioning as an unbalance defect that will vibrate and destroy high-speed turbine bearings.

docs.title: Hotelling's \(T^2\) Statistic
docs.text:
In 1947, Harold Hotelling generalized the Student's \(t\) statistic to multivariate datasets. For a vector of \(p\) correlated quality characteristics \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2, \dots, x_p]^T\) with sample mean vector \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\) and sample covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}\):

\[T^2 = n \left(\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}\right)^T \mathbf{S}^{-1} \left(\mathbf{x} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}\right)\]

where \(\mathbf{S}^{-1}\) is the inverse of the sample covariance matrix, weighting deviations inversely by their variance and covariance. The \(T^2\) statistic is a scalar metric representing the standardized Mahalanobis distance from the multivariate process centroid.

The upper control limit for \(T^2\) monitoring in Phase II production is governed by the Snedecor \(F\)-distribution:

\[\text{UCL}_{T^2} = \frac{p(m + 1)(n - 1)}{m n - m - p + 1} \, F_{\alpha, \, p, \, m n - m - p + 1}\]

where \(m\) is the number of historical baseline subgroups and \(n\) is subgroup size. If \(T^2 > \text{UCL}\), the metrology system signals an immediate multivariate out-of-control condition, triggering automated robotic part quarantine.

docs.title: Precision Dimensional Metrology, Abbe's Principle, and Thermal Expansion
docs.text: In high-precision manufacturing, statistical process control depends upon the physical integrity of measurement metrology. When inspecting tolerances at the micron scale (\(1.0\ \mu\text{m} = 0.001\text{ mm} = 0.000039\text{ inches}\)), two physical laws govern measurement fidelity:

docs.title: Ernst Abbe's Principle (1890)
docs.text:
In 1890, German physicist and optical pioneer Ernst Abbe formulated the foundational law of dimensional metrology:

The measuring reference instrument and the physical dimension being measured must be arranged collinearly along the exact same measurement axis.

If the measuring scale is offset from the component axis by an offset distance \(d\), any slight angular pitch or yaw tilt \(\theta\) (in radians) in the mechanical carriage or caliper jaw produces a first-order Abbe Error:

\[\Delta L_{\text{Abbe}} = d \cdot \tan(\theta) \approx d \cdot \theta\]

Consider a standard vernier caliper where the measuring jaws are offset from the internal scale by \(d = 40.0\text{ mm}\). A minuscule angular play of only \(\theta = 0.05^\circ = 0.000873\text{ radians}\) in the sliding jaw introduces an Abbe measurement error of:

\[\Delta L_{\text{Abbe}} = 40.0\text{ mm} \times 0.000873 = \mathbf{0.0349\text{ mm}} \quad (\mathbf{34.9\ \mu\text{m}})\]

An Abbe error of \(34.9\ \mu\text{m}\) consumes nearly the entire \(40.0\ \mu\text{m}\) tolerance band of our turbine shaft. This explains why high-precision metrology prohibits handheld calipers for final inspection, mandating collinear micrometers, air gauges, and laser interferometers where Abbe offset \(d = 0\).

docs.title: Thermal Expansion Compensation and ISO 1 Standard Reference Temperature
docs.text:
Under International Organization for Standardization standard ISO 1, the global reference temperature for industrial dimensional measurements is legally defined as:

\[T_{\text{ref}} = \mathbf{20.0^\circ\text{C}} \quad (\mathbf{68.0^\circ\text{F}})\]

All metals expand and contract with temperature according to their Coefficient of Linear Thermal Expansion (\(\alpha\), in \(\mu\text{m/m/}^\circ\text{C}\) or \(10^{-6}/^\circ\text{C}\)). For alloyed carbon steel, \(\alpha \approx 11.5 \times 10^{-6}/^\circ\text{C}\).

Thermal length expansion follows:

\[\Delta L = L_0 \cdot \alpha \cdot \left(T - 20.0^\circ\text{C}\right)\]

If our \(25.000\text{ mm}\) turbine shaft is measured immediately after grinding while warm from friction at \(T = 32.0^\circ\text{C}\) (\(\Delta T = +12.0^\circ\text{C}\)):

\[\Delta L = 25.000\text{ mm} \times (11.5 \times 10^{-6}) \times 12.0 = \mathbf{0.00345\text{ mm}} \quad (\mathbf{3.45\ \mu\text{m}})\]

The warm shaft will measure \(3.45\ \mu\text{m}\) oversized. If the machine operator compensates by grinding off an additional \(3.5\ \mu\text{m}\), once the shaft cools to the \(20^\circ\text{C}\) inspection room temperature, it will shrink by \(3.5\ \mu\text{m}\)—plunging below the Lower Specification Limit into undersized scrap.

In precision metrology laboratories, parts and reference gauges must undergo thermal soaking in climate-controlled cleanrooms (\(\pm 0.5^\circ\text{C}\)) before inspection to ensure that thermal drift does not corrupt the statistical process control records.

docs.title: A/B Testing Conversion Significance and Two-Sample Student's t-Testing on the Stack
docs.text: In contemporary digital product engineering, quantitative marketing, and clinical trials, decision-makers cannot rely on subjective intuition. When evaluating product redesigns or promotional pricing, organizations deploy randomized controlled experiments (A/B tests). Evaluating the statistical significance of observed differences protects teams from celebrating random noise or missing genuine breakthroughs.

docs.title: 1. E-Commerce Checkout Funnel A/B Conversion Test ([g] [A/B] / PROP)
docs.text:
A digital commerce platform tests a streamlined one-page checkout against the legacy multi-step checkout flow across \(50{,}000\) randomized sessions (\(N = 25{,}000\) visitors per variant): - Variant A (Control): \(n_A = 25{,}000\), completed purchases \(x_A = 1{,}875 \implies p_A = \frac{1{,}875}{25{,}000} = \mathbf{7.50\%} = 0.0750\). - Variant B (Redesign): \(n_B = 25{,}000\), completed purchases \(x_B = 2{,}150 \implies p_B = \frac{2{,}150}{25{,}000} = \mathbf{8.60\%} = 0.0860\).

The absolute conversion rate lift is \(\Delta p = 8.60\% - 7.50\% = \mathbf{+1.10\%\text{ points}}\), representing a relative lift of: $\(\text{Relative Lift} = \frac{8.60\% - 7.50\%}{7.50\%} \times 100\% = \mathbf{+14.67\%}\)$

To determine whether this \(+14.67\%\) lift is statistically significant or merely sampling noise, the team tests the null hypothesis \(H_0: p_B = p_A\) against \(H_1: p_B > p_A\).

Under \(H_0\), the pooled conversion proportion across all \(50{,}000\) visitors is: $\(\bar{p} = \frac{x_A + x_B}{n_A + n_B} = \frac{1{,}875 + 2{,}150}{50{,}000} = \frac{4{,}025}{50{,}000} = \mathbf{0.0805} \quad (8.05\%)\)$

The standard error of the difference between the two proportions is: $\(SE_{\Delta p} = \sqrt{\bar{p}(1 - \bar{p}) \left( \frac{1}{n_A} + \frac{1}{n_B} \right)} = \sqrt{0.0805 \times 0.9195 \times \left( \frac{2}{25{,}000} \right)} = \sqrt{0.07402 \times 8.0 \times 10^{-5}} = \mathbf{0.002433}\)$

The two-proportion \(Z\)-test statistic is: $\(Z = \frac{p_B - p_A}{SE_{\Delta p}} = \frac{0.0860 - 0.0750}{0.002433} = \mathbf{4.52}\)$

On the SC-95, this test can be executed directly on the stack or in the dedicated PROP: PROP TEST solver workspace (Z = (P - Q) / √(Q(1 - Q)/N) via [g] [A/B]). At a 99% significance level (\(\alpha = 0.01\), two-tailed critical value \(Z_{\text{crit}} = 2.576\)), the observed \(Z = 4.52\) yields a \(p\)-value \(p < 0.00001\). The conversion lift is overwhelmingly statistically significant, giving management total confidence to roll out Variant B globally.

docs.title: 2. Customer Spend Lift and the Two-Sample Student's \(t\)-Test ([f] [t₂] / TTEST)
docs.text:
Next, the executive committee investigates whether an AI-driven product recommendation engine increases average order value (AOV) among purchasing customers. They sample \(n = 50\) transactions from each cohort: - Cohort 1 (Control / Standard Recommendations): \(\bar{X}_1 = \$64.50\), sample standard deviation \(s_1 = \$14.20\), \(n_1 = 50\). - Cohort 2 (Treatment / Personalized Engine): \(\bar{X}_2 = \$71.80\), sample standard deviation \(s_2 = \$15.10\), \(n_2 = 50\).

The observed lift in average spend is \(\Delta \bar{X} = \$71.80 - \$64.50 = \mathbf{+\$7.30}\) per order (\(+11.32\%\)).

To verify statistical significance with unknown population variance, Gosset's two-sample Student's \(t\)-test pools the sample variances: $\(s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}} = \sqrt{\frac{49(14.20^2) + 49(15.10^2)}{98}} = \sqrt{\frac{201.64 + 228.01}{2}} = \sqrt{214.825} = \mathbf{\$14.657}\)$

The standard error of the difference in sample means is: $\(SE_{\Delta \bar{X}} = s_p \sqrt{\frac{2}{n}} = 14.657 \times \sqrt{\frac{2}{50}} = 14.657 \times 0.200 = \mathbf{\$2.9314}\)$

The Student's \(t\)-statistic is: $\(t = \frac{\bar{X}_2 - \bar{X}_1}{SE_{\Delta \bar{X}}} = \frac{\$7.30}{\$2.9314} = \mathbf{2.490}\)$

With degrees of freedom \(df = n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 98\), the two-tailed critical \(t\)-value at \(\alpha = 0.05\) is \(t_{0.025, \, 98} = \mathbf{1.984}\). Because the calculated test statistic \(t = 2.490 > 1.984\) (\(p = 0.0145 < 0.05\)), the null hypothesis of equal average spend is decisively rejected. The personalized recommendation engine delivers a proven, statistically verified lift in customer spending.

docs.title: Grand Epilogue Coda: The Architecture of Human Reason
docs.text:
Across twenty-seven chapters, nine specialized units, and three comprehensive volumes, this work has examined the universal mathematical grammar that governs the physical and built world: civil geodesy, structural mechanics, fluid dynamics, orbital ballistics, nuclear physics, digital architectures, cinema photometry, radio-frequency propagation, chemical stoichiometry, zymurgical thermodynamics, clinical pharmacokinetics, and quantitative finance.

Through every domain, across every physical discipline and industrial frontier, a singular instrument has accompanied the practitioner: the Reverse Polish Notation calculator.

docs.title: The Cognitive Ergonomics of the Operational Stack
docs.text:
The RPN stack is not merely an alternative input format; it is an operational architecture designed to mirror the natural forward flow of physical reasoning.

In traditional algebraic notation, calculations are encumbered by arbitrary syntactical rules: operator precedence hierarchies (\(PEMDAS\)), nested parentheses, and hidden internal state registers. To evaluate a compound fraction:

\[\frac{A + B}{C + D}\]

an algebraic calculator forces the human mind to halt, anticipate future operations, insert artificial left parentheses, evaluate the numerator, close the parentheses, press divide, insert a second set of parentheses, evaluate the denominator, and finally close the expression. If the user makes an error on the tenth nested term, the entire expression collapses into an opaque SYNTAX ERROR, forcing the practitioner to begin anew.

Reverse Polish Notation eliminates this cognitive burden entirely. Formulated in 1924 by the Polish logician Jan Łukasiewicz to simplify formal mathematical logic, and adapted for computer architectures by Australian philosopher and computer scientist Charles Hamblin in 1957, postfix notation operates strictly from operands to operators.

On the operational RPN stack—with its immediate visible registers and the steadfast preservation of \(\text{Last } X\): 1. Every calculation proceeds in the exact chronological order in which physical reality unfolds: from causes to effects, from empirical measurements to intermediate invariants, and from invariants to final decisions. 2. Intermediate results are immediately visible in the active registers, never hidden behind an un-evaluated algebraic tree. 3. The human working memory—which cognitive psychologists George A. Miller (1956) and Nelson Cowan (2001) established as operating optimally on chunks of immediate information (\(4 \pm 1\))—aligns naturally with the operational stack. Direct visibility of active registers provides immediate operational depth to hold intermediate invariants of a complex differential or algebraic equation without overwhelming the engineer's visual field.

Furthermore, the dedicated \(\text{Last } X\) register acts as an instantaneous undo mechanism and a conversational partner. When an engineer divides by an incorrect constant, or needs to reuse an input variable in the subsequent line of a multi-step calculation, pressing [f] [LASTX] instantly recalls the preceding argument into Register \(X\) without requiring paper scratchpads or re-entry.

docs.title: Bidirectional Solvers as Scientific Collaborators
docs.text:
When closed-form analytical solutions reach their mathematical boundaries—whether balancing the implicit Colebrook friction factor in turbulent pipes, isolating the internal rate of return across irregular capital flows, solving for supratherapeutic pharmacokinetic hold times, or determining Six Sigma audit sample sizes—the calculator's Bidirectional Equation Solver Workspaces transform numerical root-finding into a transparent partnership.

Equations are declared once, in their pure physical and physiological beauty: - \(Q = \dot{m} / C_{\text{drug}}\) in critical care infusions. - \(P = C [1 - (1+y)^{-N}]/y + M(1+y)^{-N}\) in fixed-income bond valuation. - \(B = \sqrt{H \cdot W / 3600}\) in anthropometric surface area. - \(T_{\text{min}} = (P_{\text{psi}} - 200) \times 0.28 / F\) in medevac flight oxygen budgeting.

The underlying Secant–Brent and Newton–Raphson numerical engines invert these expressions backward and forward, isolating any unknown parameter while preserving physical boundary constraints. The engineer, physician, brewer, or financial analyst is liberated from tedious, error-prone symbolic manipulations in the field, focusing human intellect entirely on physical interpretation and ethical decision-making.

docs.title: The Tactile Instrument as an Anchor of Reality
docs.text:
Beyond mathematical algorithms and stack mechanics, the physical calculator embodies an irreplaceable tactile relationship between the human engineer and the physical universe.

In the long lineage of scientific instrumentation—stretching from the astrolabes of Islamic golden-age astronomers and Galileo Galilei's proportional compass, through John Napier's calculating bones, William Oughtred's logarithmic slide rule, to the pioneering Hewlett-Packard HP-35 that rode aboard Apollo missions into lunar orbit—the tool has always served as an extension of the practitioner's senses.

The modern StackCalc32 hardware instrument honors this legacy: - Mechanical Tactile Micro-Switches: The distinct mechanical click of a dome switch provides immediate somatosensory confirmation of data entry. In high-vibration environments—aboard a turboprop aeromedical evacuation flight, inside the acoustic roar of a steam turbine hall, or beside a stamping press—the engineer's fingers know with certainty when an entry has registered, without requiring visual gaze shifts from the physical workpiece. - Reflective Monochromatic Metrology Displays: Unlike emissive smartphone displays that wash out under direct equatorial sunlight and cause pupillary fatigue in darkened cockpits, a high-contrast reflective liquid crystal display leverages ambient light, remaining perfectly legible from bright midday desert civil surveys to dim red-lit night-vision emergency medical stations. - Independence from the Ephemeral Cloud: A dedicated calculating instrument requires no wireless network connectivity, incurs no software subscription renewals, demands no operating system security patches, and uploads no private patient or proprietary corporate telemetry to remote commercial cloud servers. It functions as an autonomous, self-contained mathematical island—instantly operational the moment power is switched on, whether in an underground mine shaft, an offshore oil platform, or a spaceflight capsule.

By anchoring high-level mathematics in a rugged physical chassis, the calculator preserves the craftsman's direct connection to physical reality.

docs.title: Notation, Verification, and the Engineering Ethos
docs.text:
In 1979, Turing Award laureate Kenneth E. Iverson delivered his landmark lecture Notation as a Tool of Thought. Iverson observed that a concise, transparent mathematical notation does not simply record thought; it actively directs the course of reasoning, freeing the mind to focus on essential relationships while shielding it from incidental complexity.

Reverse Polish Notation is such a notation. By organizing calculations into an open operational stack, it eliminates the artificial scaffolding of nested parentheses and operator-precedence hierarchies, mirroring the chronological unfolding of physical laws from initial measurements to final decisions.

In mission-critical engineering, clinical medicine, and industrial production, calculating tools are not neutral accessories; they shape how practitioners conceptualize problems. When a flight nurse calculates an emergency oxygen reserve over mountainous terrain, a structural engineer verifies maximum shear stress on an aged bridge girder, or an intensivist titrates a vasoactive infusion for a hemodynamically unstable patient, the calculation is an ethical act. Professional responsibility cannot be outsourced to opaque, unverified systems whose intermediate reasoning cannot be audited in real time.

The capacity of a practitioner to stand before a complex physical system—grounded in first principles, working through an operational stack, and verifying physical truth step by step—remains the foundation of technical craftsmanship. Tools will continue to evolve, but as long as matter and energy obey invariant conservation laws, the need for deterministic mathematical clarity remains absolute.

docs.title: Unit I: Geomatics, Land Surveying, and Flight Navigation
docs.text: The SC-35 provides dedicated faceplate keys and bidirectional Equation Solver workspaces to execute the governing laws of this domain. Each equation is indexed below with its physical motivation, governing formula, and operational calculator softkeys.

docs.title: Eq. 1.1 — Sexagesimal Angular Polynomial
docs.text:
A sexagesimal angle read from a theodolite glass circle or historic deed plat consists of integer degrees \(D^\circ\), integer arcminutes \(M' \in [0, 59]\), and arcseconds \(S'' \in [0, 60)\). Because one degree contains \(60\) arcminutes and \(60 \times 60 = 3{,}600\) arcseconds, converting between packed sexagesimal notation DDD.MMSS (where the first two digits after the decimal point store arcminutes MM and the next two store arcseconds SS, converted directly via [f] [▸DEG] / [▸HR] and [f] [▸HMS]) and decimal degrees \(\theta_{\text{dec}}\) evaluates a base-\(60\) polynomial:

\[\theta_{\text{dec}} = D + \frac{M}{60} + \frac{S}{3600}\]

In this expression, \(D\) is the whole-degree component, \(M\) is the arcminute count divided by \(60\text{ min/deg}\), and \(S\) is the arcsecond count divided by \(3{,}600\text{ sec/deg}\). For a historic deed azimuth of \(47^\circ 22' 30''\) (written in packed field notation as 47.2230), dividing the \(22\) arcminutes by \(60\) yields \(0.366667^\circ\), dividing the \(30\) arcseconds by \(3{,}600\) yields \(0.008333^\circ\), and summing with \(47^\circ\) via [f] [▸DEG] produces \(\theta_{\text{dec}} = \mathbf{47.375^\circ}\). Reversing the conversion via [f] [▸HMS] on \(47.375^\circ\) extracts the integer part \(D = 47^\circ\), multiplies the fractional remainder \(0.375 \times 60 = 22.5'\) to isolate \(M = 22'\), and multiplies the remaining \(0.5' \times 60 = 30''\) to recover 47.2230 (\(47^\circ 22' 30''\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [▸HR] / [f] [▸HMS] • Expression / Workspace: Direct stack conversion • Softkeys: [▸HR] [▸HMS]

docs.title: Eq. 1.2 — Ravine Slope Reduction
docs.text:
When the total station on the north rim of the Pine Barrens ravine sights a prism across an inclined slope distance \(S\) at a vertical slope angle \( u\) (measured above \(+\) or below \(-\) the horizontal horizon), legal property boundaries and map projections depend on the flat horizontal ground distance \(D_H\) and the vertical elevation difference \(\Delta V\) (operational shorthand [SLP]). In this right triangle, the slant laser range forms the hypotenuse; multiplying by the cosine projects the slope down onto the flat horizon, while multiplying by the sine projects the vertical elevation climb:

\[D_H = S \cos( u)\]

In this reduction, \(S\) is the slant range in Register \(Y\), \( u\) is the vertical inclination angle in Register \(X\), \(D_H\) is the reduced horizontal distance placed into Register \(X\), and \(\Delta V\) is the vertical elevation difference placed into Register \(Y\). Sighting across the cedar ravine over a slope distance of \(S = 412.68 ext{ ft}\) at a vertical angle of \( u = 6^\circ 15' 00''\) (6.15 in DDD.MMSS, or \(6.25^\circ\) via [f] [▸DEG]) projects a horizontal ground distance of \(D_H = \mathbf{410.10 ext{ ft}}\) in Register \(X\) and a vertical elevation difference of \(\Delta V = \mathbf{44.92 ext{ ft}}\) in Register \(Y\). Across regional surveys, field crews further scale horizontal ground distance to state-plane grid coordinates using the combined factor \(k_{ ext{comb}} = k_{ ext{grid}} imes k_{ ext{elev}}\), where elevation factor \(k_{ ext{elev}} = R_E / (R_E + H + N)\) accounts for mean Earth radius \(R_E\), orthometric station elevation \(H\), and geoid undulation \(N\), linking GPS ellipsoidal heights (\(h\)) to gravity-based drainage elevation (\(H = h - N\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [SLP] • Expression / Workspace: Stack: S in Y, ν in X • Softkeys: [SLP]

docs.title: Eq. 1.3 — Forward Coordinate Traverse Projection
docs.text:
In plane surveying, every boundary station is indexed by an ordered pair of orthogonal coordinates \((N, E)\), where Northing (\(N\)) measures distance north of a reference origin and Easting (\(E\)) measures distance east of the origin, while directions are measured as a full-circle Azimuth \(\alpha \in [0^\circ, 360^\circ)\) clockwise from True North (\(0^\circ\)). Projecting a known horizontal ground distance \(D_H\) along a known clockwise azimuth \(\alpha\) from a starting station \(A(N_A, E_A)\) to determine the North change (\(\Delta N\), Latitude), the East change (\(\Delta E\), Departure), and the target coordinates \(B(N_B, E_B)\) constitutes the Forward Coordinate Geometry Problem ([TRV]). Because azimuth rotates clockwise from the vertical North axis, the trigonometric projections swap roles: cosine governs North-South displacement, while sine governs East-West displacement:

\[\Delta N = D_H \cos(\alpha)\]

The updated station coordinates follow directly by addition: \(N_B = N_A + \Delta N\) and \(E_B = E_A + \Delta E\). Because \(\cos\alpha\) is positive in the northern quadrants (\(270^\circ < \alpha < 90^\circ\)) and negative in the southern quadrants (\(90^\circ < \alpha < 270^\circ\)), while \(\sin\alpha\) is positive in the eastern quadrants (\(0^\circ < \alpha < 180^\circ\)) and negative in the western quadrants (\(180^\circ < \alpha < 360^\circ\)), these North-clockwise projection identities assign the correct algebraic signs in all four compass quadrants without manual lookup tables.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [TRV] • Expression / Workspace: Stack: α in Y, D in X • Softkeys: [TRV]

docs.title: Eq. 1.4 — Inverse Coordinate Geometry
docs.text:
Running the Forward projection in reverse—starting from two known monument coordinates \((N_A, E_A)\) and \((N_B, E_B)\) and recovering the straight-line horizontal distance \(D\) and clockwise North azimuth \(\alpha \in [0^\circ, 360^\circ)\) between them—is the Inverse Coordinate Geometry Problem ([INV]). From the coordinate displacements \(\Delta N = N_B - N_A\) and \(\Delta E = E_B - E_A\), the Euclidean hypotenuse gives the ground distance \(D\). To find the compass heading, the two-argument arctangent—or \(\operatorname{atan2}\)—asks what direction on the full circle produces that specific ratio of Easting departure to Northing latitude, resolving the quadrant automatically without sign ambiguity:

\[D = \sqrt{(\Delta N)^2 + (\Delta E)^2}\]

Whereas geodetic computations use \(0^\circ\text{--}360^\circ\) clockwise azimuths, colonial and modern metes-and-bounds property deeds record directions as Quadrant Bearings ([BRG]). A quadrant bearing begins on either the North (N) or South (S) meridian and turns an acute angle \(\theta \in [0^\circ, 90^\circ]\) toward either the East (E) or West (W):

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [INV] • Expression / Workspace: Stack: ΔN in Y, ΔE in X • Softkeys: [INV] [BRG]

docs.title: Eq. 1.5 — Bowditch Compass Rule Closure
docs.text:
In an exact closed polygon of \(n\) sides, the vector sum of all North latitudes \(\Sigma_{\Delta N} = \sum_{i=1}^n \Delta N_i\) and the vector sum of all East departures \(\Sigma_{\Delta E} = \sum_{i=1}^n \Delta E_i\) both equal zero. Because field measurements contain small random optical and atmospheric errors, the accumulated traverse returns to a coordinate slightly displaced from the POB. The hypotenuse of that residual gap is the Linear Error of Closure \(E_c\) ([g] [CLS]), and dividing total perimeter \(P = \sum_{i=1}^n D_i\) by \(E_c\) defines the Relative Precision Ratio. Once closure meets statutory standards, Nathaniel Bowditch's 1807 Compass Rule distributes the misclosure across each leg in proportion to its length fraction:

\[E_c = \sqrt{\left(\Sigma_{\Delta N}\right)^2 + \left(\Sigma_{\Delta E}\right)^2}\]

For a four-leg rectangular boundary loop of total perimeter \(P = 3{,}200.00\text{ ft}\) whose field measurements return with net latitude misclosure \(\Sigma_{\Delta N} = -0.12\text{ ft}\) and net departure misclosure \(\Sigma_{\Delta E} = +0.16\text{ ft}\), the linear error of closure is \(E_c = \sqrt{(-0.12)^2 + 0.16^2} = \mathbf{0.20\text{ ft}}\) ([g] [CLS]), yielding a relative precision ratio of \(1 : (3200 / 0.20) = \mathbf{1 : 16{,}000}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [CLS] • Expression / Workspace: Traverse ledger closure in [g] [▦] • Softkeys: [CLS] [PT+]

docs.title: Eq. 1.6 — Gauss Shoelace Parcel Area
docs.text:
The additive coordinate corrections for each leg \(i\) are \(\delta N_i = -\Sigma_{\Delta N}(D_i / P)\) and \(\delta E_i = -\Sigma_{\Delta E}(D_i / P)\). From the sequential vertex coordinates \((N_1, E_1), (N_2, E_2), \dots, (N_n, E_n)\) of a closed simple polygon (with \((N_{n+1}, E_{n+1}) = (N_1, E_1)\)), Gauss's Shoelace Formula crosses adjacent coordinates around the perimeter to evaluate the enclosed planar area \(A\) (displayed live alongside [g] [CLS] inside the @COGO reference table [g] [▦] via softkey [AREA]), which converts to statutory acreage (\(43{,}560\text{ ft}^2/\text{acre}\)) and metric hectares (\(10{,}000\text{ m}^2/\text{ha}\)):

\[A = \frac{1}{2} \left\lvert \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( E_i N_{i+1} - E_{i+1} N_i \right) \right\rvert\]

For a four-leg rectangular boundary loop of total perimeter \(P = 3{,}200.00\text{ ft}\) (spanning \(600.00\text{ ft}\) North-South by \(1{,}000.00\text{ ft}\) East-West) whose field measurements return with net latitude misclosure \(\Sigma_{\Delta N} = -0.12\text{ ft}\) and net departure misclosure \(\Sigma_{\Delta E} = +0.16\text{ ft}\), the linear error of closure is \(E_c = \sqrt{(-0.12)^2 + 0.16^2} = \mathbf{0.20\text{ ft}}\) ([g] [CLS]), yielding a relative precision ratio of \(1 : (3200 / 0.20) = \mathbf{1 : 16{,}000}\), and Gauss's shoelace sum across the adjusted corners in [g] [▦] gives an enclosed area of \(A = \mathbf{600{,}000\text{ ft}^2}\), or \(600{,}000 / 43{,}560 \approx \mathbf{13.7741\text{ acres}}\) (\(5.5742\text{ ha}\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [CLS] / [g] [▦] • Expression / Workspace: Gauss Shoelace area in [g] [▦] • Softkeys: [AREA] [CLOS]

docs.title: Eq. 1.7 — Bearing-Bearing Coordinate Intersection
docs.text:
When sighting an inaccessible boundary mark or monument \(P(N, E)\) from two known baseline control stations \(A(N_1, E_1)\) and \(B(N_2, E_2)\) along forward azimuths \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\), the lines of sight define simultaneous linear vector equations. Equating coordinates and isolating the distance \(d_1\) from Station 1 yields:

\[d_1 = \frac{(E_2 - E_1)\cos\alpha_2 - (N_2 - N_1)\sin\alpha_2}{\sin(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2)}\]

In terms of coordinate differences \(\Delta N = N_2 - N_1\) and \(\Delta E = E_2 - E_1\) and tangent slopes \(T_1 = \tan\alpha_1\) and \(T_2 = \tan\alpha_2\), the intersection Northing evaluates directly via the classic surveying formula:

\[N = \frac{N_1 T_2 - N_2 T_1 + \Delta E}{T_2 - T_1}\]

On the SC-35, staging azimuth \(\alpha_1\) in Register \(Y\) and \(\alpha_2\) in Register \(X\) before pressing [f] [ISC] computes the intersection Northing \(N\) into Register \(X\) and Easting \(E\) into Register \(Y\) (with distance \(d_1\) in Register \(Z\)). In the bidirectional Equation Solver Workspace ([g] [SOLVE] [f] [ISC]), the calculator displays ISC: INTERSECT with governing equation N = (N1·T2 - N2·T1 + ΔE) / ΔT and softkeys [N], [D], and [A].

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [ISC] • Expression / Workspace: ISC: N = (N1·T2 - N2·T1 + ΔE) / ΔT • Softkeys: [N] [D] [A]

docs.title: Eq. 2.1 — Circular Curve Tangent and Arc Length
docs.text:
Bisecting the central angle \(\Delta\) with the radial line from \(O\) through the mid-arc apex to PI partitions the layout into two congruent right triangles of half-angle \(\Delta / 2\). The tangent setback distance \(T\) uses the half-angle tangent to measure how far back along the straight approach road the crew must begin curving, while the circular arc length \(L\) scales the central deflection angle in radians by the radius to measure the actual curved centerline pavement:

\[T = R \tan\!\left(\frac{\Delta}{2}\right)\]

In these expressions, \(R\) is the centerline radius of curvature in feet, \(\Delta\) is the exterior deflection angle in decimal degrees, \(T\) is the opposite leg of the right triangle of angle \(\Delta / 2\) and adjacent side \(R\), \(L\) scales the radian measure \(\Delta(\pi / 180^\circ)\) by \(R\), and the straight-line long chord connecting PC directly to PT doubles the half-chord: \(LC = 2 R \sin(\Delta / 2)\). For the Granite Gorge highway curve of radius \(R = 1{,}200.00\text{ ft}\) in Register \(Y\) and deflection angle \(\Delta = 28.5^\circ\) in Register \(X\) (half-angle \(\Delta / 2 = 14.25^\circ\)), pressing [CRV] yields the tangent setback distance \(T = 1200\tan(14.25^\circ) = \mathbf{304.77\text{ ft}}\) in Register \(Y\) and the centerline paving arc length \(L = 1200 \times 28.5^\circ \times (\pi / 180^\circ) = \mathbf{596.90\text{ ft}}\) in Register \(X\), while the straight-line long chord is \(LC = 2400\sin(14.25^\circ) = \mathbf{590.80\text{ ft}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [CRV] • Expression / Workspace: CRV: L = R × D × π / 180 • Softkeys: [L] [R] [D]

docs.title: Eq. 2.2 — Parabolic Vertical Curve Elevation
docs.text:
At the canyon crest, transitioning from an entry grade \(g_1\) (in percent grade) at the Point of Vertical Curvature (\(\text{PVC}\)) to an exit grade \(g_2\) over a vertical curve of length \(L\) stations ([f] [VCV]) traces a second-degree vertical parabola. Because a parabola has a constant second derivative, the rate of vertical curvature remains constant across the entire span, eliminating sudden vertical jolts for traveling vehicles. The elevation at any station \(x\) combines the starting elevation, the initial slope, and a quadratic sag-or-crest curvature correction driven by the grade difference:

\[\text{Elev}(x) = \text{PVC} + g_1 x + \left(\frac{g_2 - g_1}{2 L}\right) x^2\]

For a vertical crest curve starting at elevation \(\text{PVC} = 425.00\text{ ft}\) with entry grade \(g_1 = +2.50\%\), exit grade \(g_2 = -1.75\%\), and curve length \(L = 8\text{ stations}\) (\(800\text{ ft}\)), the midpoint elevation at \(x = L / 2 = 4\text{ stations}\) is \(\text{Elev}(4) = 425.00 + 2.5(4) + \frac{-1.75 - 2.5}{2(8)}(4)^2 = 425.00 + 10.00 - 4.25 = \mathbf{430.75\text{ ft}}\) (and at the end of the curve \(x = 8\text{ stations}\), \(\text{PVT} = 425.00 + 2.5(8) - 17.00 = \mathbf{428.00\text{ ft}}\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [VCV] • Expression / Workspace: VCV: Parabolic elevation workspace • Softkeys: PVC g1 g2 L

docs.title: Eq. 2.3 — Average End-Area Cut Volume
docs.text:
To determine the volume of earth and rock that must be blasted out of the granite hillside, highway engineers approximate the cut as a series of trapezoidal prisms. The average end-area method ([g] [CUT]) averages the cross-sectional cut areas \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) (in square feet) at the beginning and end of each station, multiplying by the interval length \(L_{\text{cut}}\) and dividing by \(27\text{ ft}^3/\text{yd}^3\) to yield bank volume in cubic yards:

\[V_{\text{cut}} = \frac{A_1 + A_2}{2} \cdot \frac{L_{\text{cut}}}{27}\]

For a vertical crest curve starting at elevation \(\text{PVC} = 425.00\text{ ft}\) with entry grade \(g_1 = +2.50\%\), exit grade \(g_2 = -1.75\%\), and curve length \(L = 8\text{ stations}\) (\(800\text{ ft}\)), the midpoint elevation at \(x = L / 2 = 4\text{ stations}\) is \(\text{Elev}(4) = 425.00 + 2.5(4) + \frac{-1.75 - 2.5}{2(8)}(4)^2 = 425.00 + 10.00 - 4.25 = \mathbf{430.75\text{ ft}}\) (and at the end of the curve \(x = 8\text{ stations}\), \(\text{PVT} = 425.00 + 2.5(8) - 17.00 = \mathbf{428.00\text{ ft}}\)). Across a \(L_{\text{cut}} = 150.0\text{ ft}\) granite bench cut between end areas \(A_1 = 320.0\text{ ft}^2\) and \(A_2 = 400.0\text{ ft}^2\), [g] [CUT] evaluates \(V_{\text{cut}} = \frac{320 + 400}{2} \times \frac{150}{27} = \mathbf{2{,}000.00\text{ yd}^3}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [CUT] • Expression / Workspace: Prism earthwork volume • Softkeys: [CUT] [STA]

docs.title: Eq. 2.4 — Three-Wire Differential Spirit Leveling
docs.text:
To carry a vertical elevation from a Benchmark (BM) of known elevation \(H = E_{\text{BM}}\) to an uphill Turning Point (TP) or construction stake, a surveyor sets up a compensated optical level midway between the two stations ([f] [LVL]). Sighting backward along the horizontal optical plane to a graduated leveling rod held plumb on the benchmark yields the Backsight reading \(B\), which adds to \(H\) to establish the optical Height of Instrument (\(\text{HI} = H + B\)). Turning the telescope forward to a rod held on the new station yields the Foresight reading \(F\), which subtracts from \(\text{HI}\) to determine the new station Elevation \(E\):

\[\text{HI} = H + B\]

In this differential leveling chain, \(H\) is the starting benchmark elevation above mean sea level, \(\text{HI}\) is the elevation of the telescope's horizontal line of sight, and \(B - F\) is the net vertical rise (\(+\)) or fall (\(-\)) between the two rod positions. Setting up above canyon-floor benchmark BM-1 (\(H = 4{,}812.40\text{ ft}\)) and reading a backsight of \(B = 6.85\text{ ft}\) establishes the optical plane at \(\text{HI} = 4812.40 + 6.85 = \mathbf{4{,}819.25\text{ ft}}\). Sighting forward to the curve entry stake at PC (Station 124+50.00 via [g] [STA]) with a center-wire foresight of \(F = 5.42\text{ ft}\) determines the PC pavement elevation as \(E = 4819.25 - 5.42 = \mathbf{4{,}813.83\text{ ft}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [LVL] • Expression / Workspace: LVL: E = H + B - F • Softkeys: [E] [H] [B] [F]

docs.title: Eq. 2.5 — Earth Curvature and Atmospheric Refraction
docs.text:
Because the Earth is an oblate spheroid of mean radius \(R_E \approx 20{,}906{,}000\text{ ft}\) (\(6{,}371{,}000\text{ m}\)), the true level surface curves downward away from the instrument's flat tangent plane by \(h_c = D^2 / (2 R_E) \approx 0.667 \cdot D_{\text{miles}}^2\text{ ft}\). Simultaneously, terrestrial atmospheric refraction bends the optical sightline downward toward denser air near the ground, refracting the apparent line of sight upward by approximately one-seventh of curvature (\(r \approx 0.093 \cdot D_{\text{miles}}^2\text{ ft}\)). Combining physical curvature with atmospheric refraction yields the net vertical drop:

\[h_{cr} = 0.574 \cdot D_{\text{miles}}^2\text{ ft}\] \[h_{cr} = 0.0675 \cdot D_{\text{km}}^2\text{ m}\]

Carlos points across the canyon reservoir: over an extended 2-mile shot across the lake (\(D = 2.0\text{ miles}\)), the line of sight dips by \(h_{cr} = 0.574 \times (2.0)^2 = 2.296 \approx \mathbf{2.3\text{ ft}}\). Over that single two-mile sightline, the uncorrected rod reading overstates the true elevation by nearly two and a half feet. Sighting across water bodies where balancing backsight and foresight distances is precluded demands subtracting \(h_{cr}\) (\(E = \text{HI} - (F - h_{cr})\)) before staking grade stakes into the subbase.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: Basic Arithmetic on Stack (x², ×) • Expression / Workspace: Stack: D in X, square and multiply by 0.574 (miles) or 0.0675 (km) • Softkeys: [x²] [×]

docs.title: Eq. 3.1 — Orthogonal Wind Vector Decomposition
docs.text:
When an aircraft aligns with a runway or flies a cross-country course of heading \(\psi_{\text{course}}\), a wind of speed \(V_w\) (in knots, with statute miles converted via [f] [▸NM]) blowing from direction \(\psi_{\text{wind}}\) forms a relative wind angle \(\theta = \psi_{\text{wind}} - \psi_{\text{course}}\) with the flight path. Staging wind speed \(V_w\) in Register \(Y\) and relative wind angle \(\theta\) in Register \(X\) and pressing [f] [WND] decomposes the wind vector into orthogonal components: the cosine projection governs the longitudinal headwind along the fuselage, while the sine projection governs the lateral crosswind pushing the wings sideways:

\[V_{\text{hw}} = V_w \cos(\theta)\]

With a \(V_w = 28\text{ kt}\) wind blowing at \(\theta = 40^\circ\) off the course (28 [ENTER] 40 [f] [WND]), the instrument places the headwind component \(V_{\text{hw}} = 28\cos(40^\circ) = \mathbf{21.45\text{ kt}}\) into Register \(Y\) and the crosswind component \(V_{\text{xw}} = 28\sin(40^\circ) = \mathbf{18.00\text{ kt}}\) into Register \(X\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [WND] • Expression / Workspace: WND: X = V × SIN(A) • Softkeys: [X] [V] [A]

docs.title: Eq. 3.2 — Aeronautical Wind Correction Angle
docs.text:
To prevent the crosswind from drifting the aircraft off course, the pilot points the aircraft's nose slightly into the wind. The required crab angle uses the inverse sine—or \(\arcsin\)—to ask the fundamental question of the unit circle: what crab angle into the wind produces a sideways velocity component that exactly counteracts the crosswind drift? Because the sine of an angle is the perpendicular projection of a unit vector, taking the arcsin of the crosswind-to-airspeed ratio finds the precise nose heading required to keep the aircraft's track pinned to the centerline:

\[\text{WCA} = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{V_{\text{xw}}}{V_{\text{TAS}}}\right)\]

Crabbing into the wind at \(V_{\text{TAS}} = 145\text{ kt}\) with \(V_{\text{xw}} = 18.00\text{ kt}\) requires \(\text{WCA} = \arcsin(18.00 / 145) \approx \mathbf{7.13^\circ}\) ([f] [ASIN]), pinning the aircraft's track to the runway centerline.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [XWC] • Expression / Workspace: WCA = arcsin(V_xw / V_TAS) • Softkeys: [XWC] [ASIN]

docs.title: Eq. 3.3 — Effective Flight Groundspeed
docs.text:
Once the aircraft crabs into the wind, its forward progress along the desired geographic track is the cosine projection of its true airspeed minus the opposing headwind component:

\[\text{GS} = V_{\text{TAS}} \cos(\text{WCA}) - V_{\text{hw}}\]

With a \(V_w = 28\text{ kt}\) wind blowing at \(\theta = 40^\circ\) off the course (28 [ENTER] 40 [f] [WND]), the instrument places the headwind component \(V_{\text{hw}} = 28\cos(40^\circ) = \mathbf{21.45\text{ kt}}\) into Register \(Y\) and the crosswind component \(V_{\text{xw}} = 28\sin(40^\circ) = \mathbf{18.00\text{ kt}}\) into Register \(X\). Crabbing into the wind at \(V_{\text{TAS}} = 145\text{ kt}\) by \(\text{WCA} = \arcsin(18.00 / 145) \approx \mathbf{7.13^\circ}\) ([f] [ASIN]) holds the desired track over the ridge at a net ground speed of \(\text{GS} = 145\cos(7.13^\circ) - 21.45 \approx 143.88 - 21.45 = \mathbf{122.43\text{ kt}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [TSD] • Expression / Workspace: TSD: D = S × T • Softkeys: [D] [S] [T]

docs.title: Eq. 3.4 — Barometric Density Altitude
docs.text:
By the ideal gas law (\(\rho = P / (R_{\text{specific}} T)\)), heating an air parcel at constant pressure causes it to expand and become less dense. Each \(1^\circ\text{C}\) of warming above the standard altitude temperature \(T_{\text{ISA}}(P) = 15 - 0.002 P\) thins the air by the equivalent of \(+120\text{ ft}\) of altitude gain, defining the Density Altitude ([g] [ALT]) from Pressure Altitude \(P\) (in feet) in Register \(Y\) and Outside Air Temperature \(T\) (in \(^\circ\text{C}\)) in Register \(X\):

\[\text{DA} = P + 120 \times \left(T - T_{\text{ISA}}(P)\right)\]

At the high-desert strip where Pressure Altitude is \(P = 6{,}200\text{ ft}\) (\(T_{\text{ISA}} = 2.6^\circ\text{C}\)) and the afternoon Outside Air Temperature is \(T = 28^\circ\text{C}\), the \(+25.4^\circ\text{C}\) thermal deviation above standard temperature adds \(120 \times 25.4 = +3{,}048\text{ ft}\), raising the true Density Altitude via 6200 [ENTER] 28 [g] [ALT] to \(\text{DA} = 6200 + 3048 = \mathbf{9{,}248\text{ ft}}\) and warning the crew to use high-altitude landing flare speeds and full reverse thrust.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [ALT] • Expression / Workspace: ALT: D = P + 120 × (T - 15) • Softkeys: [D] [P] [T]

docs.title: Unit II: Industrial Trades, Electrical, and Mechanical
docs.text: The SC-14 provides dedicated faceplate keys and bidirectional Equation Solver workspaces to execute the governing laws of this domain. Each equation is indexed below with its physical motivation, governing formula, and operational calculator softkeys.

docs.title: Eq. 4.1 — Conductor Circular Mil Area and DC Resistance
docs.text:
In Euclidean geometry, a cylindrical wire of diameter \(d\) has cross-sectional area \(A = \frac{\pi}{4}d^2\). To eliminate the transcendental factor \(\pi/4\) from field cable tables, North American electrical engineering defines the Circular Mil (\(\text{CM}\)) as the area of a circle whose diameter is exactly one mil (\(1\text{ mil} = 0.001\text{ in}\)), so area in circular mils equals the square of the diameter in mils:

\[\text{CM} = d_{\text{mils}}^2 = \left(1000 \cdot d_{\text{inches}}\right)^2\]

In these expressions, \(d_{\text{mils}}\) is the conductor diameter in thousandths of an inch, \(L\) is the conductor length in feet, and \(K\) is the material's specific resistance constant (in \(\Omega\cdot\text{cmil/ft}\) at \(75^\circ\text{C}\) operating temperature), equal to \(K_{\text{Cu}} = 12.9\ \Omega\cdot\text{cmil/ft}\) for uncoated copper and \(K_{\text{Al}} = 21.2\ \Omega\cdot\text{cmil/ft}\) for aluminum (both listed in the [g] [▦] NEC reference table). Solid and stranded building conductors are indexed on the logarithmic American Wire Gauge ([AWG]) scale, in which smaller gauge numbers designate thicker conductors that double in cross-sectional area every three gauge steps down. NEC Chapter 9, Table 8 tabulates the direct-current resistance \(R_{1000}\) in ohms per thousand feet (\(\Omega/\text{kft}\) at \(75^\circ\text{C}\)) alongside NEC Table 310.16 \(75^\circ\text{C}\) copper ampacities:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [AWG] • Expression / Workspace: NEC Table 8 wire circular mils and resistance • Softkeys: [AWG] [Ω]

docs.title: Eq. 4.2 — Single-Phase and Three-Phase Feeder Voltage Drop
docs.text:
When current flows through a long feeder run, the conductor's ohmic resistance converts voltage into waste heat. In a single-phase circuit, current travels out and back, creating a round-trip path of twice the one-way distance. In a balanced three-phase circuit, the three alternating currents are separated by 120 degrees and partially cancel in their return paths, replacing the two-wire factor of two with the geometric ratio \(\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\):

\[V_{\text{drop},1\phi} = \frac{2 \cdot K \cdot L \cdot I}{\text{CM}}\]

On a \(480\text{ V}\) three-phase feeder supplying \(45\text{ kVA}\) over \(L = 220\text{ ft}\) of #6 AWG copper wire (\(R_{1000} = 0.491\ \Omega/\text{kft}\), \(I_L = 54.13\text{ A}\)), [AWG] evaluates \(V_{\text{drop},3\phi} = \frac{\sqrt{3} \times 0.491 \times 220 \times 54.13}{1000} \approx \mathbf{10.13\text{ V}}\) (\(2.11\% \le 3.0\%\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [AWG] • Expression / Workspace: AWG: D = 2 × R × L × I / 1000 • Softkeys: [D] [R] [L] [I]

docs.title: Eq. 4.3 — Harmonic Parallel Resistance
docs.text:
When two parallel conductors or loads share the current path, total conductance is the sum of their individual conductances. Inverting that sum gives the harmonic mean—the product over the sum:

\[R_1 \parallel R_2 = \frac{R_1 \cdot R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\]

Here \(R_{1000}\) is the NEC Table 8 conductor resistance in \(\Omega/\text{kft}\), \(L\) is the one-way run length in feet, \(I\) is the line current in amperes, and \(R_1 \parallel R_2 = (R_1^{-1} + R_2^{-1})^{-1}\) is the harmonic-mean parallel operator. On Pier 14's three-phase \(480\text{ V}\) crane feeder carrying \(I = 90.211\text{ A}\) over \(L = 450\text{ ft}\) of #2 AWG copper (\(R_{1000} = 0.194\ \Omega/\text{kft}\)), the single-phase equivalent drop is \(V_{\text{drop},1\phi} = \frac{2 \times 450 \times 90.211 \times 0.194}{1000} \approx 15.75\text{ V}\) and the balanced three-phase line voltage drop is \(V_{\text{drop},3\phi} = \frac{\sqrt{3} \times 450 \times 90.211 \times 0.194}{1000} \approx \mathbf{13.64\text{ V}}\) (\(2.84\%\) at rated steady current), which spikes to \(\mathbf{20.46\text{ V}}\) (\(4.26\%\), starving the crane terminals down to \(459.5\text{ V}\)) during a \(150\%\) hoist starting surge. Paralleling two #1/0 AWG conductors per phase (\(R_1 = R_2 = 0.122\ \Omega/\text{kft}\), so \(0.122 \parallel 0.122 = \mathbf{0.061\ \Omega/\text{kft}}\) via [x∥y]) cuts the steady three-phase voltage drop to \(\frac{\sqrt{3} \times 450 \times 90.211 \times 0.061}{1000} \approx \mathbf{4.29\text{ V}}\) (\(0.89\%\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [x∥y] • Expression / Workspace: Harmonic parallel resistance shortcut • Softkeys: [x∥y]

docs.title: Eq. 4.4 — NEC Continuous Load Feeder Ampacity
docs.text:
Under National Electrical Code Article 215.2(A)(1) (and Article 210.19(A)(1) for branch circuits), a continuous load is defined as any load where maximum current continues for three hours or longer. Standard overcurrent protective devices and terminal distribution blocks are rated to carry continuous load at only \(80\%\) of their nominal nameplate rating (\(1 / 0.80 = 1.25\)). Sizing conductors for only \(100\%\) of continuous load exposes terminal lugs to chronic thermal fatigue and setscrew loosening from differential thermal expansion. To prevent terminal lug burnout and maintain switchgear within its rated thermal dissipation envelope, feeder conductors must be sized to carry at least \(125\%\) of continuous load plus \(100\%\) of non-continuous load:

\[I_{\text{min}} = 1.25 \cdot I_{\text{continuous}} + I_{\text{non-continuous}}\]

For Pier 14's crane hoist hydraulic pump drawing \(I_{\text{continuous}} = 72.0\text{ A}\) alongside an auxiliary non-continuous service lighting load of \(I_{\text{non-continuous}} = 18.0\text{ A}\), the minimum allowable feeder conductor ampacity prior to raceway derating is \(I_{\text{min}} = 1.25 \times 72.0 + 18.0 = 90.0 + 18.0 = \mathbf{108.0\text{ A}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: Continuous Load Scaling on Stack (1.25 × +) • Expression / Workspace: Stack: I_cont in Y, 1.25 in X, multiply and add I_noncont • Softkeys: [×] [+]

docs.title: Eq. 4.5 — Alternating Current Power Triangle
docs.text:
In a resistive load such as an immersion heater, alternating current rises and falls in phase with alternating voltage. In an inductive load such as the Pier 14 gantry crane hoist motor, the alternating magnetic field stores and returns reactive energy every quarter-cycle, causing the RMS line current \(I\) to lag behind the RMS supply voltage \(V\) by a phase angle \(\phi\). Because only the current component in phase with voltage (\(I\cos\phi\)) performs real mechanical or thermal work, AC power forms a right triangle governed by the dimensionless Power Factor \(\text{PF} = \cos\phi \in [0, 1]\) ([PF]), linking Real Working Power \(P\) (in watts, \(\text{W}\), or kilowatts, \(\text{kW}\), converted via [f] [▸kW] and [g] [▸HP]), Reactive Magnetizing Power \(Q\) (in volt-amperes reactive, \(\text{VAR}\), or \(\text{kVAR}\)), and Apparent Power \(S\) (in volt-amperes, \(\text{VA}\), or \(\text{kVA}\)):

\[P = S \cos(\phi)\]

In this power triangle, \(S\) is the hypotenuse that sizes transformers, switchgear, and feeder conductors, \(P\) is the adjacent horizontal leg converted into shaft work and heat, and \(Q\) is the opposite vertical leg oscillating between the source and the motor's magnetic field. On Pier 14's crane rated at apparent power \(S = 75.0\text{ kVA}\) and lagging power factor \(\text{PF} = 0.80\) (\(\phi = \arccos(0.80) \approx 36.87^\circ\), \(\sin\phi = 0.60\)), the real working power is \(P = 75.0 \times 0.80 = \mathbf{60.0\text{ kW}}\) (\(80.46\text{ HP}\) via [g] [▸HP]) and the reactive magnetizing demand is \(Q = 75.0 \times 0.60 = \mathbf{45.0\text{ kVAR}}\). Installing a parallel \(25.0\text{ kVAR}\) capacitor bank at the crane disconnect supplies \(25.0\text{ kVAR}\) locally, reducing net reactive draw from the feeder to \(Q_{\text{new}} = 45.0 - 25.0 = 20.0\text{ kVAR}\), shrinking apparent feeder demand to \(S_{\text{new}} = \sqrt{60.0^2 + 20.0^2} \approx \mathbf{63.25\text{ kVA}}\), and raising the corrected power factor to \(\text{PF}_{\text{new}} = 60.0 / 63.2456 \approx \mathbf{0.9487}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [PF] • Expression / Workspace: PF: P = V × I × F • Softkeys: [P] [V] [I] [F]

docs.title: Eq. 4.6 — Three-Phase Motor Full-Load Current
docs.text:
This geometric ratio \(\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73205\) produces the two standard commercial voltage systems in North America: multiplying \(V_{LN} = 120\text{ V}\) by \(\sqrt{3}\) gives \(207.85\text{ V}\) (\(208\text{Y}/120\text{ V}\)), and multiplying \(V_{LN} = 277\text{ V}\) by \(\sqrt{3}\) gives \(479.78\text{ V}\) (\(480\text{Y}/277\text{ V}\)). Because each of the three phases delivers apparent power \(V_{LN} I_L = (V_{LL}/\sqrt{3})I_L\), total three-phase apparent power across all three phases is \(3(V_{LL}/\sqrt{3})I_L = \sqrt{3}\,V_{LL}I_L\). Expressing three-phase apparent power \(S_{\text{kVA}}\) in kilovolt-amperes ([g] [kVA]) to solve for per-phase line current \(I_L\), or converting rated mechanical output horsepower \(\text{HP}\) (\(1\text{ HP} = 746\text{ W}\)) and fractional efficiency \(\eta \in (0, 1]\) into three-phase motor Full-Load Amps \(I_{\text{FLA}}\) ([g] [FLA]), gives:

\[I_{\text{FLA}} = \frac{\text{HP} \times 746}{\sqrt{3} \cdot V_{LL} \cdot \eta}\]
