For a \(30\text{ HP}\) induction motor operating at \(480\text{ V}\) with efficiency \(\eta = 0.90\) and power factor \(0.86\), [g] [FLA] evaluates \(I_{\text{FLA}} = \frac{30 \times 746}{\sqrt{3} \times 480 \times 0.90 \times 0.86} \approx \mathbf{34.78\text{ A}}\), requiring \(125\%\) continuous-duty feeder ampacity of \(\mathbf{43.47\text{ A}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [FLA] • Expression / Workspace: Three-phase motor full-load amperes • Softkeys: [I] [P] [V] [E]

docs.title: Eq. 5.1 — Conduit Offset Travel and Half-Angle Shrinkage
docs.text:
In the right triangle formed by the perpendicular offset depth \(O\) (opposite side) and the bend angle \(\theta\) (denoted \(A\) in the [OFS] solver workspace T = O / SIN(A) opened via [OFS]), the center-to-center Travel Distance \(T\) along the diagonal pipe between the two bend marks ([OFS]) is the cosecant hypotenuse \(O\csc\theta\). Because the conduit previously spanned the full length \(T\) along the wall but now projects horizontally across only the adjacent side \(O\cot\theta\), bending the offset pulls the far end of the pipe backward toward the starting coupling by the axial Conduit Shrinkage \(S_{\text{shrink}}\), which simplifies by the trigonometric half-angle identity \(\csc\theta - \cot\theta = \frac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \tan(\theta / 2)\):

\[T = \frac{O}{\sin(\theta)} = O \csc(\theta)\]

In these expressions, \(O\) is the perpendicular offset depth in inches, \(\theta\) is the bender shoe angle in degrees, \(T\) is the distance measured along the tubing between the two bend marks, and \(S_{\text{shrink}}\) is the length added to the obstruction setback when placing the Obstruction-Approach mark first (while a 3-argument [OFS] call with offset \(O\) in Register \(Z\), angle \(\theta\) in Register \(Y\), and bender deduct \(D\) in Register \(X\) returns net travel \(T - D\)). Standard conduit bender shoes engrave five primary bend angles, each with its cosecant travel multiplier and half-angle tangent shrinkage per inch of offset depth:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [OFS] • Expression / Workspace: OFS: T = O / SIN(A) • Softkeys: [T] [O] [A]

docs.title: Eq. 5.2 — Compound Rolling Offset Travel
docs.text:
When a conduit run must simultaneously shift vertically by a Rise \(R_{\text{vert}}\) and horizontally by a lateral Roll \(R_{\text{horiz}}\) to enter a misaligned cabinet, the two perpendicular displacements form a right triangle in the cross-sectional plane perpendicular to the conduit axis. By the Pythagorean theorem, rotating the conduit bender in that plane aligns the shoe with the True Offset Depth \(O_{\text{true}}\) ([g] [FIT] or [f] [MIT]), which then scales by \(\csc\theta\) via [OFS] to yield the rolling travel distance \(T_{\text{roll}}\):

\[O_{\text{true}} = \sqrt{R_{\text{vert}}^2 + R_{\text{horiz}}^2}\]

Here \(R_{\text{vert}}\) and \(R_{\text{horiz}}\) are the orthogonal vertical and horizontal shifts in inches, \(O_{\text{true}}\) is the diagonal offset depth in the rotated bending plane evaluated via [g] [FIT] or [f] [MIT], and \(T_{\text{roll}}\) is the center-to-center distance between bend marks along the conduit evaluated via [OFS]. Where the boiler-room rack rises \(R_{\text{vert}} = 6.0\text{ in.}\) and rolls laterally \(R_{\text{horiz}} = 8.0\text{ in.}\) into the MCC knockouts, keying 6 [ENTER] 8 [g] [FIT] returns the true diagonal offset \(O_{\text{true}} = \sqrt{6.0^2 + 8.0^2} = \mathbf{10.00\text{ in.}}\), and keying 30 [OFS] bends that compound offset at \(\theta = 30^\circ\) with a travel distance of \(T_{\text{roll}} = 10.00 / \sin(30^\circ) = \mathbf{20.00\text{ in.}}\) between marks.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [FIT] • Expression / Workspace: FIT: Rolling compound offset • Softkeys: [FIT] [MIT]

docs.title: Eq. 5.3 — Three-Point Saddle Outer Leg Travel
docs.text:
When a conduit strapped flat against a wall must step over a single cylindrical pipe of height \(O\) and return to the same mounting surface, electricians form a Three-Point Saddle consisting of a center crown bend of angle \(\theta_{\text{center}} = 45^\circ\) placed directly over the obstruction centerline, flanked by two symmetric outer return bends of \(\theta_{\text{outer}} = \theta_{\text{center}} / 2 = 22.5^\circ\):

\[T_{\text{saddle}} = \frac{O}{\sin(22.5^\circ)} = O \csc(22.5^\circ) \approx 2.6131 \cdot O\]

Total axial shrinkage across both sloped legs adds \(S_{\text{saddle}} = 2 \cdot O \tan(11.25^\circ) \approx \frac{3}{16}\text{ in.} \times O\) to the center mark distance. Over the boiler room's \(O = 4.0\text{ in.}\) steam pipe centered \(120.0\text{ in.}\) (\(10\text{ ft } 0\text{ in.}\)) down the wall, total saddle shrinkage is \(4 \times (3/16\text{ in.}) = \mathbf{0.75\text{ in.}}\) (\(3/4\text{ in.}\)), placing the center \(45^\circ\) mark at \(120.75\text{ in.}\) and the two outer \(22.5^\circ\) return marks at \(T_{\text{saddle}} = 4.0 / \sin(22.5^\circ) \approx \mathbf{10.45\text{ in.}}\) (\(10\text{-}7/16\text{ in.}\) via [f] [f-i], or \(10.0\text{ in.}\) by the \(2.5\times\) field rule) on either side of the center mark.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [OFS] • Expression / Workspace: Three-point saddle 45°/22.5° outer travel • Softkeys: [OFS] [f-i]

docs.title: Eq. 5.4 — National Electrical Code Cross-Sectional Raceway Fill
docs.text:
Once a conduit run is installed, pulling insulated conductors around multiple bends generates capstan friction proportional to \(e^{\mu \Sigma\theta}\) and traps \(I^2 R\) heat inside the tube. To prevent insulation abrasion during pulling and ensure adequate air space for heat dissipation, NEC Chapter 9, Table 1 (accessible directly via [g] [▦] on the SC-14: 1W FILL = 53% MAX, 2W FILL = 31% MAX, 3+W FIL = 40% MAX) limits the cross-sectional Conduit Fill Ratio to \(53\%\) for \(1\) conductor, \(31\%\) for \(2\) conductors, and \(\mathbf{40\%}\) for \(3\) or more conductors:

\[\text{Fill\%} = \left(\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{N} A_{\text{wire},k}}{A_{\text{conduit}}}\right) \times 100\% \le 40\%\]

Here \(A_{\text{conduit}}\) is the total internal cross-sectional area of the raceway from NEC Chapter 9, Table 4 (with raceway and conductor dimensions referenced from NEC tables or caliper readings), \(A_{\text{wire}}\) is the insulated conductor area from NEC Chapter 9, Table 5, and \(N_{\max}\) is the maximum whole number of identical conductors permitted at the \(40\%\) ceiling:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [AWG] • Expression / Workspace: NEC Chapter 9 Table 1 40% raceway fill • Softkeys: [AWG] [▦]

docs.title: Eq. 6.1 — Spindle Rotational Speed and Table Feed Rate
docs.text:
When a lathe turns a cylindrical bar of diameter \(D\) (in inches) or a milling machine spins an end-mill of diameter \(D\) at spindle rotational speed \(N\) (in Revolutions Per Minute, \(\text{RPM}\)), each revolution carries a cutting tooth around the outer circumference \(\pi D\text{ inches} = \frac{\pi D}{12}\text{ feet}\). Multiplying by \(N\text{ rev/min}\) defines the tangential cutting velocity in Surface Feet per Minute ([f] [SFM]), and inverting that relation determines the required Spindle Speed \(N\) ([f] [SFM] / [g] [RPM]), the linear table Feed Rate \(F_m\) (in \(\text{in/min}\)) for a cutter with \(Z\) flutes and chip load \(f_t\) (in \(\text{in/tooth}\)), and the \(75\%\)-thread Tap Drill Diameter \(D_{\text{tap}}\) ([f] [TAP]) for a screw of major diameter \(D_{\text{major}}\) and pitch \(P_{\text{tpi}}\) (threads per inch, or metric/decimal pitch \(p\) when \(X \le 3\)):

\[N = \frac{12 \cdot \text{SFM}}{\pi \cdot D} \approx \frac{3.8197 \cdot \text{SFM}}{D}\]

The \(75\%\) tap drill diameter subtracts one thread pitch from major diameter: \(D_{\text{tap}} = D_{\text{major}} - 1/P_{\text{tpi}}\). In these machining equations, \(D\) is the cutter or workpiece diameter in inches, \(12 / \pi \approx 3.8197186\) (\(3.82\) in the [f] [SFM] workspace N = 3.82 × S / D with softkeys [N], [S], [D]) converts feet per minute into inches per revolution, \(f_t \cdot Z\) is the linear advance per spindle revolution, and subtracting one pitch length \(1 / P_{\text{tpi}}\) from the major diameter \(D_{\text{major}}\) yields the standard \(75\%\) unified national thread tap drill diameter. While an aluminum roughing pass at \(\text{SFM} = 400\text{ ft/min}\) on a \(D = 0.500\text{ in.}\) cutter runs at 400 [ENTER] 0.5 [f] [SFM] \(\to \mathbf{3{,}055.77\text{ RPM}}\), milling 4140 steel rated at \(\text{SFM} = 100\text{ ft/min}\) with a \(D = 0.500\text{ in.}\) 4-flute end-mill and a chip load of \(f_t = 0.003\text{ in/tooth}\) requires reducing the spindle speed via 100 [ENTER] 0.5 [f] [SFM] to \(N = \frac{12 \times 100}{\pi \times 0.500} \approx \mathbf{763.94\text{ RPM}}\) and setting the table feed rate to \(F_m = 763.9437 \times 0.003 \times 4 \approx \mathbf{9.17\text{ in/min}}\). When taking light radial finishing cuts where radial engagement is under half the cutter diameter (\(A_e < D/2\)), machinists apply radial chip thinning (\(f_{\text{actual}} = f_t / \sqrt{A_e/D}\)) to maintain effective chip thickness and prevent tool rubbing and work hardening. Tapping the 1/2-13 UNC flange holes (\(D_{\text{major}} = 0.500\text{ in.}\), \(P_{\text{tpi}} = 13\text{ TPI}\)) via 0.5 [ENTER] 13 [f] [TAP] requires a tap drill diameter of \(D_{\text{tap}} = 0.500 - 1/13 \approx \mathbf{0.4231\text{ in.}}\) (\(27/64\text{ in.} = 0.4219\text{ in.}\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [SFM] • Expression / Workspace: SFM: N = 3.82 × S / D • Softkeys: [N] [S] [D]

docs.title: Eq. 6.2 — Bolt Circle Chord Spacing
docs.text:
When drilling \(N\) equally spaced bolt holes around a pitch circle of diameter \(D_{\text{bolt}}\) (radius \(R = D_{\text{bolt}}/2\)), the central angle between adjacent holes is \(\Delta\theta = 360^\circ / N\). Bisecting the isosceles triangle formed by the circle center and two adjacent holes yields two right triangles with half-angle \(\frac{\Delta\theta}{2} = \frac{180^\circ}{N}\) and hypotenuse \(R = D_{\text{bolt}}/2\):

\[C = 2 R \sin\!\left(\frac{180^\circ}{N}\right) = D_{\text{bolt}} \sin\!\left(\frac{180^\circ}{N}\right)\]

Cartesian hole coordinates follow as \(X_k = \frac{D_{\text{bolt}}}{2}\cos(\theta_0 + k \cdot \frac{360^\circ}{N})\) and \(Y_k = \frac{D_{\text{bolt}}}{2}\sin(\theta_0 + k \cdot \frac{360^\circ}{N})\). Here \(C\) is the straight-line center-to-center Chord Distance ([g] [BC], which also opens the [g] [BC] workspace C = D × SIN(180 / N) with softkeys [C], [D], [N]) between adjacent holes used for caliper verification, and \((X_k, Y_k)\) are the Cartesian CNC table coordinates of hole \(k \in \{0, 1, \dots, N-1\}\) starting from reference angle \(\theta_0\). On an \(N = 8\text{-bolt}\) hub with a \(D_{\text{bolt}} = 6.00\text{ in.}\) pitch circle (\(\frac{180^\circ}{8} = 22.5^\circ\)), keying 6 [ENTER] 8 [g] [BC] returns \(C = 6.00\sin(22.5^\circ) \approx \mathbf{2.2961\text{ in.}}\), while on the outer \(D_{\text{bolt}} = 10.00\text{ in.}\) steam flange (10 [ENTER] 8 [g] [BC]), the chord spacing is \(C = 10.00\sin(22.5^\circ) \approx \mathbf{3.8268\text{ in.}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [BC] • Expression / Workspace: BC: C = D × SIN(180 / N) • Softkeys: [C] [D] [N]

docs.title: Eq. 6.3 — Control Valve Volumetric Flow and Pump Power
docs.text:
In the cooling header supplying the machining center, incompressible fluid of cross-sectional pipe area \(A\) moving at velocity \(V\) obeys the Pipe Flow Continuity Law \(Q = A \times V\) (evaluated on the stack via \(A \times V\)). Downstream, a control valve of Flow Coefficient \(C_v\) ([g] [Cᵥ]) passes \(Q\text{ GPM}\) ([f] [▸GPM]) of fluid of specific gravity \(G = \rho / \rho_w\) ([g] [ρw]) across pressure drop \(\Delta P\) (in \(\text{psi}\), [f] [▸PSI]), lifting \(Q\text{ GPM}\) against \(H\text{ feet}\) of total dynamic head requires hydraulic Pump Power \(P_{\text{BHP}} = (Q \times H) / 3960\) (where \(33{,}000\text{ ft}\cdot\text{lb/min} \div 8.333\text{ lb/gal} = 3{,}960\)), and preventing cavitation at the pump impeller eye requires maintaining Available Net Positive Suction Head \(\text{NPSH}_a\) ([g] [NPH]) above the pump's required threshold:

\[Q = C_v \sqrt{\frac{\Delta P}{G}}\]

Continuity dictates \(Q = A \cdot V\), while suction margin follows as \(\text{NPSH}_a = P_{\text{atm}} - P_{\text{vap}} \pm z_s - h_f\). In these fluid-power relations, \(Q\) scales with pipe area and velocity and with the square root of valve pressure drop \(\Delta P\) in [g] [Cᵥ] ([g] [Cᵥ] workspace softkeys [Q], [C], [P], [G]), \(P_{\text{BHP}}\) measures the water horsepower delivered by the pump, and [g] [NPH] evaluates available suction head margin so vapor bubbles do not implode against the impeller vanes. Meanwhile, with the fixture's \(\varnothing\,2.00\text{ in.}\) hydraulic clamping cylinder (\(A_{\text{piston}} = \frac{\pi}{4}(2.00)^2 = \pi \approx 3.1416\text{ in}^2\)) pressurized to \(P_{\text{psi}} = 1{,}875\text{ psi}\), the clamping force holding the 4140 flange is \(F_{\text{clamp}} = 1875 \times \pi \approx \mathbf{5{,}890.49\text{ lbf}}\) ([g] [▸lbf]). A coolant control valve with \(C_v = 25\) at \(\Delta P = 16\text{ psi}\) (\(G = 1.0\)) delivers \(Q = 25\sqrt{16} = \mathbf{100.0\text{ GPM}}\) via 25 [ENTER] 16 [g] [Cᵥ], and pumping \(Q = 198\text{ GPM}\) against \(H = 100\text{ ft}\) of head requires \(P_{\text{BHP}} = (198 \times 100)/3960 = \mathbf{5.00\text{ HP}}\) via 198 [ENTER] 100 [×] 3960 [÷].

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [Cᵥ] • Expression / Workspace: CV: Q = C × √(P / G) • Softkeys: [Q] [C] [P] [G]

docs.title: Eq. 6.4 — Four-to-Twenty Milliampere Current Scaling
docs.text:
Across the \(16.0\text{ mA}\) active span between \(4.0\text{ mA}\) (\(0\%\)) and \(20.0\text{ mA}\) (\(100\%\)), loop current \(I_{\text{mA}}\) scales linearly with process percentage \(\text{Pct} \in [0, 100]\) via [mA], while an industrial \(\text{Pt100}\) Resistance Temperature Detector ([f] [RTD])—standardized to ice-point resistance \(R_0 = 100.0\ \Omega\) at \(0^\circ\text{C}\) with IEC 60751 platinum temperature coefficient \(\alpha = 0.00385\ \Omega/(\Omega\cdot^\circ\text{C})\)—follows the linear Callendar–Van Dusen relation at temperature \(T\) (in \(^\circ\text{C}\)):

\[I_{\text{mA}} = 4.0 + 16.0 \times \left(\frac{\text{Pct}}{100}\right)\]

Here \(\text{Pct}\) is the percentage of calibrated transmitter span, \(I_{\text{mA}}\) is the loop current in milliamperes evaluated via [mA], and \(R(T)\) is the \(\text{Pt100}\) sensor resistance in ohms evaluated via [f] [RTD]. When the fixture's \(0\text{--}3{,}000\text{ psi}\) hydraulic transmitter is pressurized to \(1{,}875\text{ psi}\) (\(\text{Pct} = (1875 / 3000) \times 100\% = 62.5\%\)), keying 62.5 [mA] gives the calibrated loop current \(I_{\text{mA}} = 4.0 + 16.0(0.625) = \mathbf{14.00\text{ mA}}\) (developing \(14.0\text{ mA} \times 250\ \Omega = 3.50\text{ V}\) across the PLC's \(250\ \Omega\) sense resistor), confirming that the transmitter is accurate and the intermittent alarm was caused by a loose terminal screw rather than hydraulic pressure loss.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [mA] • Expression / Workspace: Four-to-twenty milliampere loop scaling • Softkeys: [mA] [RTD]

docs.title: Unit III: Systems Programming, Embedded, and Cyber Operations
docs.text: The SC-16 provides dedicated faceplate keys and bidirectional Equation Solver workspaces to execute the governing laws of this domain. Each equation is indexed below with its physical motivation, governing formula, and operational calculator softkeys.

docs.title: Eq. 7.1 — Positional Number Base Radix Expansion
docs.text:
In any positional number system of integer radix \(b \ge 2\)—where \(b = 16\) for Hexadecimal ([HEX]), \(b = 10\) for Decimal ([f] [DEC]), \(b = 8\) for Octal ([f] [OCT]), and \(b = 2\) for Binary ([g] [BIN])—a \(k\)-digit word \((d_{k-1} d_{k-2} \dots d_1 d_0)_b\) with digits \(d_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, b-1\}\) represents the scalar integer \(V\) obtained by summing each digit weighted by its positional power \(b^i\):

\[V = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} d_i \cdot b^i\]

When [HEX] mode is active on the SC-16, the six top-row softkeys automatically bind to the hexadecimal digits [A], [B], [C], [D], [E], and [F] for rapid single-keystroke entry of 16-, 32-, and 64-bit register words. Because \(16 = 2^4\), partitioning a binary string into blocks of four bits (nibbles) from the least significant bit (\(i = 0\)) upward maps each 4-bit block \((b_{4m+3} b_{4m+2} b_{4m+1} b_{4m})_2\) with internal weights \((8, 4, 2, 1)\) onto a single hexadecimal digit \(H_m \in [0, 15]\) (0–9, [A]–[F]), while \(8 = 2^3\) maps each 3-bit triad onto a single octal digit (0–7).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [HEX] / [f] [DEC] • Expression / Workspace: Radix base switching • Softkeys: [HEX] [DEC] [OCT] [BIN]

docs.title: Eq. 7.2 — Two's Complement Additive Inversion
docs.text:
In a fixed \(W\)-bit register ([g] [WSZ]), an Unsigned Integer ([g] [UNS]) assigns positive weight \(+2^i\) to every bit \(b_i\) from \(i = 0\) through \(W - 1\). To encode negative numbers without building separate subtraction circuitry, digital processors use Two's Complement ([f] [NEG]) representation, in which the most significant bit \(b_{W-1}\) carries negative weight \(-2^{W-1}\) while the lower \(W - 1\) bits retain positive weights \(+2^i\). Adding any \(W\)-bit word \(X\) to its bitwise one's complement \(\sim X\) ([g] [~], where every 0 flips to 1 and every 1 flips to 0) produces a word of \(W\) ones equal to \(2^W - 1\). Adding \(1\) yields \(X + ((\sim X) + 1) = 2^W \equiv 0 \pmod{2^W}\). Consequently, the additive inverse \(-X\) in \(W\)-bit two's complement ([f] [NEG]) is formed by inverting all \(W\) bits and adding \(1\):

\[-X \equiv 2^W - X \equiv (\sim X) + 1 \pmod{2^W}\]

Because zero (0x00) consumes one of the \(2^{W-1}\) non-negative bit patterns, every signed \(W\)-bit two's complement range is asymmetric by one count, extending from \(-2^{W-1}\) (0x80...0) to \(+2^{W-1} - 1\) (0x7F...F):

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [NEG] • Expression / Workspace: Two's complement additive negation • Softkeys: [NEG] [WSZ] [UNS]

docs.title: Eq. 7.3 — Contiguous Bitfield Mask Generation
docs.text:
To isolate or modify a multi-bit hardware field of width \(w\) bits starting at bit offset \(s\), the Bitfield Mask Generator ([f] [MSK]) shifts \(2^w - 1\) (\(w\) contiguous 1 bits) left by \(s\) positions:

\[\text{MSK}(s, w) = \left((1 \ll w) - 1\right) \ll s\]

The updated register is synthesized via read-modify-write: \(R_{\text{updated}} = (R \ \& \ \sim\text{MSK}(s, w)) \mid ((V_{\text{field}} \ll s) \ \& \ \text{MSK}(s, w))\). In this identity, \(R\) is the initial control register value, \(\text{MSK}(s, w)\) is the positive mask covering bits \([s+w-1 : s]\), \(\sim\text{MSK}(s, w)\) is the inverted clear mask with 0s across the target field and 1s everywhere else, and \(V_{\text{field}} \ll s\) aligns the new setting into position. For our motor controller's 4-bit clock-divider field (\(w = 4\)) at bit offset \(s = 8\) (bits [11:8]), the mask is \(\text{MSK}(8, 4) = ((1 \ll 4) - 1) \ll 8 = 15 \times 256 = \mathbf{\text{0x0F00}}\) (\(3{,}840\)). Clearing bits [11:8] of 0x00240505 with \(\sim\text{0x0F00}\) leaves 0x00240005, and merging 0xA shifted left by \(8\) (0x0A00) via [|] yields 0x00240A05 (or \(\mathbf{\text{0xA05}}\) on the low 16-bit halfword).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [MSK] • Expression / Workspace: Contiguous bitfield mask synthesis • Softkeys: [MSK] [SB] [CB] [B?]

docs.title: Eq. 8.1 — IEEE 754 Floating-Point Real Decoding
docs.text:
Once the 32-bit word is in native host order, the IEEE 754 Single-Precision (binary32) standard ([FLT], alongside half-precision [f] [F16] and double-precision [g] [F64]) partitions bits [31:0] into a 1-bit sign \(S \in \{0, 1\}\) at bit 31, an 8-bit unsigned biased exponent \(E \in [1, 254]\) at bits [30:23] (with bias \(127\), so the true binary exponent is \(e = E - 127\)), and a 23-bit fractional mantissa \(M \in [0, 2^{23}-1]\) at bits [22:0] with an implicit leading \(1\) before the binary point:

\[V_{\text{float}} = (-1)^S \times \left(1 + \frac{M}{2^{23}}\right) \times 2^{E - 127}\]

On microcontrollers without floating-point hardware, \(Q_{m.n}\) Fixed-Point Scaling ([f] [Q.n] and [g] [FXP]) instead converts between a real value and an integer scaled by \(2^n\): \(Q_{\text{int}} = \operatorname{round}(V_{\text{real}} \cdot 2^n)\) and \(V_{\text{real}} = Q_{\text{int}} / 2^n\). When the biased exponent bits in an IEEE 754 word are all zero (\(E = 0\)), the representation shifts into subnormal gradual underflow with an implicit leading zero bit (\(v = (-1)^S \times 2^{-126} \times 0.m\)), avoiding sudden precision cliffs when subtracting nearly equal quantities. In the byte-swapped 32-bit telemetry word 0x41440000 (0100 0001 0100 0100 0000 0000 0000 0000), sign bit \(S = 0\) indicates a positive value, biased exponent \(E = \text{1000 0010}_2 = 130\) gives true exponent \(e = 130 - 127 = +3\), and the fractional mantissa bits .1000100..._2 evaluate to \(2^{-1} + 2^{-5} = 0.5 + 0.03125 = 0.53125\), yielding \(V_{\text{float}} = +1.53125 \times 2^3 = \mathbf{+12.25^\circ\text{C}}\) (while 0x41480000 \(= 1{,}095{,}237{,}632\) decodes via [FLT] to \(+1.5625 \times 2^3 = \mathbf{+12.50^\circ\text{C}}\), and pressing [FLT] on 12.5 encodes back to 1095237632 \(= \text{0x41480000}\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [FLT] • Expression / Workspace: IEEE 754 binary32 encode/decode • Softkeys: [FLT] [F16] [F64]

docs.title: Eq. 8.2 — Reflected CRC-32 LFSR Step
docs.text:
To detect burst noise on serial sensor buses and Ethernet links, a Cyclic Redundancy Check ([f] [CRC]) treats a binary message frame as a polynomial over the two-element Galois field \(\text{GF}(2)\), where addition and subtraction are both carry-free [⊕] (\(\oplus\)), and computes the remainder modulo a generator polynomial: - 8-Bit Sensor Bus CRC8/CCITT (\(G(x) = x^8 + x^2 + x + 1\), Polynomial 0x07): For compact 1-wire and RS-485 sensor headers, each bit shift tests the MSB (\(b_7\)) of the 8-bit accumulator and XORs with 0x07 when \(b_7 = 1\). - 32-Bit Frame CRC-32 (\(G_{\text{ref}} = \text{0xEDB88320}\)): For IEEE 802.3 Ethernet and telemetry frames, starting from \(C_0 = \text{0xFFFFFFFF} \oplus X\), the reflected Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) shifts right and XORs with 0xEDB88320 whenever the LSB is 1, followed by final bitwise inversion \(\sim C\):

\[C_{i+1} = \begin{cases} (C_i \ggg 1) \oplus G_{\text{poly}} & \text{if } (C_i \ \& \ 1) = 1 \\ C_i \ggg 1 & \text{if } (C_i \ \& \ 1) = 0 \end{cases}\]

Routing telemetry frames from the RS-485 gateway onto the plant Ethernet backbone requires synthesizing CIDR netmasks and host capacities ([NET]) and verifying that the \(16\times\) oversampled UART baud clock ([g] [BPS]) remains within framing tolerance.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [CRC] • Expression / Workspace: Reflected CRC-32 LFSR polynomial step • Softkeys: [CRC] [SWP]

docs.title: Eq. 8.3 — CIDR Netmask and Usable Host Capacity
docs.text:
In Classless Inter-Domain Routing ([NET]), an IPv4 subnet prefix [NET] (\(P \in [0, 32]\)) assigns the upper \(P\) bits of a 32-bit IPv4 word to the network mask and leaves \(32 - P\) bits for host addresses. Pressing [NET] with prefix \(P\) in Register \(X\) evaluates both the 32-bit Netmask in Register \(Y\) and the Usable Host Count \(N_{\text{hosts}}\) in Register \(X\):

\[\text{Netmask}(P) = \left(2^{32} - 2^{32 - P}\right) = \text{0xFFFFFFFF} \ll (32 - P)\]

For a standard /24 industrial VLAN (24 [NET]), the 32-bit netmask pushed to Register \(Y\) is 4294967040 (\(\mathbf{\text{0xFFFFFF00}}\), or 255.255.255.0) and the usable host count in Register \(X\) is \(2^{32-24} - 2 = \mathbf{254\text{ hosts}}\) (excluding the .0 network address and .255 broadcast address).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [NET] • Expression / Workspace: IPv4 netmask and host capacity • Softkeys: [NET] [MOD]

docs.title: Eq. 8.4 — Sixteen-Times Oversampled UART Baud Divisor
docs.text:
Because a Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter ([g] [BPS]) transmits data without a shared clock wire, the receiver oversamples the incoming line at \(16\) times the target symbol rate \(B\) (in \(\text{bits/s}\)) so it can align its sample point with the center (\(8\text{th}\) tick) of each bit cell. Dividing the peripheral clock \(f_{\text{clk}}\) (in Register \(Y\)) by \(16 \cdot B\) (\(B\) in Register \(X\)) and rounding to the nearest integer yields the hardware baud divisor \(D\):

\[D = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{f_{\text{clk}}}{16 \cdot B}\right)\]

where \(B_{\text{actual}} = f_{\text{clk}} / (16 \cdot D)\). Here \(D\) is the integer value written to the baud-rate register via [g] [BPS], \(B_{\text{actual}}\) is the synthesized bit rate, and \(\text{Err\%}\) is the fractional clock skew (which must remain within \(\pm 2.0\%\) over a 10-bit start-data-stop frame to prevent stop-bit framing errors). On our \(f_{\text{clk}} = 48\text{ MHz}\) bus targeting \(B = 115{,}200\text{ bps}\), keying 48000000 [ENTER] 115200 [g] [BPS] evaluates \(\frac{48{,}000{,}000}{16 \times 115{,}200} = 26.0417\) and rounds to \(D = \mathbf{26}\). The actual baud rate is \(\frac{48{,}000{,}000}{16 \times 26} \approx \mathbf{115{,}384.6\text{ bps}}\), a clock drift of \(+0.16\%\)—proving that the UART timing is well within tolerance and the CRC errors were caused by an un-terminated RS-485 bus end rather than baud-rate skew.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [BPS] • Expression / Workspace: BPS: D = C / (16 × B) • Softkeys: [D] [C] [B]

docs.title: Eq. 9.1 — Pulse-Width Modulation Carrier Frequency
docs.text:
A hardware timer divides the peripheral bus clock \(f_{\text{clk}}\) ([C], in \(\text{Hz}\)) through an integer Prescaler \(P\) ([P]) to produce a counter tick clock \(f_{\text{tick}} = f_{\text{clk}} / P\), which then counts up to an integer Auto-Reload Period \(\text{ARR}\) ([A]) to synthesize a Pulse-Width Modulation ([g] [PWM]) carrier of frequency \(f_{\text{PWM}}\) ([F]):

\[f_{\text{PWM}} = \frac{f_{\text{clk}}}{P \cdot \text{ARR}} \iff \text{ARR} = \frac{f_{\text{clk}}}{P \cdot f_{\text{PWM}}}\]

Duty cycle percentage is governed by the capture-compare threshold: \(\text{Duty\%} = (\text{CCR} / \text{ARR}) \times 100\%\). On the immediate RPN stack, pressing [g] [PWM] with \(f_{\text{clk}}\) in Register \(Z\), prescaler \(P\) in Register \(Y\), and auto-reload period \(\text{ARR}\) in Register \(X\) computes \(f_{\text{PWM}} = f_{\text{clk}} / (P \times \text{ARR})\) and opens the [g] [PWM] Equation Solver Workspace (F = C / (P × A)) with variable softkeys [F], [C], [P], and [A]. Driven by a \(f_{\text{clk}} = 48\text{ MHz}\) (\(48{,}000{,}000\text{ Hz}\)) bus clock with prescaler \(P = 48\) and auto-reload period \(\text{ARR} = 1{,}000\), keying 48000000 [ENTER] 48 [ENTER] 1000 [g] [PWM] generates \(f_{\text{PWM}} = \mathbf{1{,}000.0\text{ Hz}}\) (\(1.0\text{ kHz}\)). Conversely, when upgrading the servo stage to an ultrasonic \(F = 20{,}000\text{ Hz}\) (\(20\text{ kHz}\)) switching frequency on a \(C = 168{,}000{,}000\text{ Hz}\) (\(168\text{ MHz}\)) timer bus with prescaler \(P = 4\), solving F = C / (P × A) backward for [A] via [g] [SOLVE] [A] yields \(\text{ARR} = \frac{168{,}000{,}000}{4 \times 20{,}000} = \mathbf{2{,}100\text{ counts}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [PWM] • Expression / Workspace: PWM: F = C / (P × A) • Softkeys: [F] [C] [P] [A]

docs.title: Eq. 9.2 — Successive-Approximation ADC Quantization
docs.text:
An \(N\)-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter ([f] [ADC]) partitions its full-scale reference voltage \(V_{\text{ref}}\) into \(2^N\) uniform quantization steps of width \(V_{\text{LSB}}\) (the Least Significant Bit voltage), mapping a continuous analog input voltage \(V_{\text{in}} \in [0, V_{\text{ref}})\) to the integer digital code \(D \in [0, 2^N - 1]\) (while [g] [DAC] reconstructs \(V_{\text{out}}\) from a 12-bit code):

\[V_{\text{LSB}} = \frac{V_{\text{ref}}}{2^N}\]

In these quantization equations, \(N\) is the converter resolution in bits, \(2^N\) is the total number of discrete code bins (\(4{,}096\) for a 12-bit converter or \(65{,}536\) for a 16-bit converter), and \(V_{\text{LSB}}\) is the smallest voltage change that increments \(D\) by \(1\). Because ideal uniform quantization introduces a sawtooth error bounded by \(\pm\frac{1}{2} V_{\text{LSB}}\) with root-mean-square noise \(V_{q,\text{rms}} = V_{\text{LSB}} / \sqrt{12}\), a full-scale sine wave of RMS amplitude \(V_{\text{ref}} / (2\sqrt{2})\) achieves a theoretical Signal-to-Noise-and-Distortion ratio \(\text{SINAD}_{\text{dB}} = 6.0206 N + 1.7609\text{ dB}\), defining the converter's Effective Number of Bits: \(\text{ENOB} = (\text{SINAD}_{\text{dB}} - 1.7609) / 6.0206\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [ADC] • Expression / Workspace: ADC: D = V / R × 2^N • Softkeys: [D] [V] [R] [N]

docs.title: Eq. 9.3 — Resistor-Capacitor Filter Cutoff and Exponential Settling
docs.text:
To prevent front-end charge-injection droop from degrading \(\text{ENOB}\), the external RC anti-aliasing and sample-and-hold network ([f] [τ]) of time constant \(\tau = R C\) and \(-3\text{ dB}\) cutoff frequency \(f_c\) must settle following an input step until tracking error falls below half an LSB:

\[\tau = R \cdot C\]

Full settling requires \(t_{\text{acq}} \ge (N + 1)\ln(2)\,\tau\), or at least \(9.01\) time constants for a 12-bit converter. On our vibration node's 12-bit [f] [ADC] with reference \(V_{\text{ref}} = 3.30\text{ V}\), the step size is \(V_{\text{LSB}} = 3.30 / 4096 \approx \mathbf{0.80566\text{ mV/LSB}}\) (\(805.66\ \mu\text{V}\)), a DC bias input of \(V_{\text{in}} = 1.65\text{ V}\) maps to mid-scale code \(D = \lfloor (1.65 / 3.30) \times 4096 \rfloor = \mathbf{2{,}048}\) (0x800), and a live DMA register sample \(D = 2{,}894\) (0xB4E) inverts in the [f] [ADC] workspace (D = V / R × 2^N, softkeys [D], [V], [R], [N]) to \(V_{\text{in}} = 2894 \times 3.30 / 4096 = \mathbf{2.3316\text{ V}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [τ] • Expression / Workspace: RC anti-aliasing cutoff and settling • Softkeys: [τ] [fc]

docs.title: Eq. 9.4 — Classless Inter-Domain Routing Host Capacity
docs.text:
In Classless Inter-Domain Routing ([NET]), a 32-bit IPv4 address written with prefix length [NET] (\(P \in [0, 32]\)) allocates the upper \(P\) bits to the fixed Network Prefix (where the subnet mask pushed to Register \(Y\) has [f] [#B] \(= P\) leading 1 bits) and leaves \(H = 32 - P\) bits for Host Addresses:

\[\text{Block Size} = 2^{32 - P}\]

Because the all-zeros host pattern (\(0\)) is reserved for the Subnet Network ID and the all-ones host pattern (\(2^{32-P} - 1\)) is reserved for the Subnet Broadcast Address, pressing [NET] on a [NET] prefix pushes the 32-bit netmask to Register \(Y\) and \(N_{\text{hosts}} = 2^{32 - P} - 2\) usable Host Addresses to Register \(X\). For our factory floor /26 subnet (26 [NET], leaving \(H = 6\) host bits and fourth-octet mask \(256 - 2^6 = 192\), or 255.255.255.192 \(= \text{0xFFFFFFC0}\)), the total block size is \(2^6 = 64\) addresses and the usable capacity is \(N_{\text{hosts}} = 64 - 2 = \mathbf{62\text{ usable hosts}}\)—accommodating all \(54\) vibration nodes and the .200 gateway with \(7\) addresses to spare. Because \(\lfloor 200 / 64 \rfloor \times 64 = 3 \times 64 = 192\), the 192.168.10.200/26 block starts at Network ID 192.168.10.192, spans usable hosts 192.168.10.193 through 192.168.10.254, and terminates at Broadcast Address 192.168.10.255.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [NET] • Expression / Workspace: CIDR subnet host block sizing • Softkeys: [NET] [#B] [CLZ]

docs.title: Eq. 9.5 — Natural Power-of-Two Memory Bus Alignment
docs.text:
Inside system memory, CPU load/store units and DMA engines require packet descriptors to begin at byte addresses \(A\) divisible by a power-of-two Alignment Boundary \(B \in \{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 4096\}\) ([g] [ALN]), or round a minimum ring-buffer size \(S\) up to the next power of two \(S_{\text{pow2}}\), with binary storage keys ([f] [▸B], [g] [▸bit], [f] [▸KiB], [g] [▸MiB], [f] [▸GiB], [g] [▸TiB]) converting between raw bit counts and IEC power-of-two byte capacities (\(1\text{ KiB} = 2^{10} = 1{,}024\text{ B}\)):

\[A_{\text{aligned}} = \left\lceil \frac{A}{B} \right\rceil \times B = (A + B - 1) \ \& \ \sim(B - 1)\]

Here \((A + B - 1) \ \& \ \sim(B - 1)\) clears the lower \(\log_2 B\) address bits to round \(A\) up to the next multiple of \(B\). Aligning our vibration node's raw 53-byte packet descriptor (\(A = 53\)) up to a \(B = 16\text{-byte}\) DMA burst boundary via 53 [ENTER] 16 [g] [ALN] yields \(A_{\text{aligned}} = \lceil 53 / 16 \rceil \times 16 = 4 \times 16 = \mathbf{64\text{ bytes}}\), while rounding a \(300\text{-byte}\) circular sample queue up to the next power of two via 0 [ENTER] 300 [g] [ALN] yields \(S_{\text{pow2}} = 2^9 = \mathbf{512\text{ bytes}}\) (\(0.5\text{ KiB}\) via [f] [▸KiB]).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [ALN] • Expression / Workspace: Power-of-two memory address alignment • Softkeys: [ALN] [▸KiB]

docs.title: Eq. 9.6 — High-Speed Synchronous Bus Timing Margins
docs.text:
In high-speed synchronous serial interfaces such as SPI buses, data transfer is referenced to a master clock of period \(T_{\text{clk}} = 1 / f_{\text{clk}}\). To guarantee that the receiving flip-flop latches transmitted bits without entering metastability, two timing margins must remain strictly non-negative across worst-case thermal and supply voltage variations:

\[t_{\text{margin,setup}} = T_{\text{clk}} - t_{\text{co,\max}} - t_{\text{prop,\max}} - t_{su} \ge 0\] \[t_{\text{margin,hold}} = t_{\text{co,\min}} + t_{\text{prop,\min}} - t_h - \Delta t_{\text{skew}} \ge 0\]

Here \(t_{su}\) is the required data setup time, \(t_h\) is the required data hold time, \(t_{\text{co}}\) is the transmitter clock-to-output propagation delay, \(t_{\text{prop}}\) is the PCB trace flight time (roughly \(160\text{ ps/in}\) on FR-4), and \(\Delta t_{\text{skew}}\) is the clock skew. Crucially, hold time violations cannot be cured by reducing clock frequency, demanding careful matching of trace lengths and series damping resistance.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: Bus Margin Evaluation on Stack (-, +) • Expression / Workspace: Stack: T_clk in Z, delays in Y, subtract to find margin • Softkeys: [-] [+]

docs.title: Unit IV: Cinema Optics, Broadcast Timecode, and Sound
docs.text: The SC-24 provides dedicated faceplate keys and bidirectional Equation Solver workspaces to execute the governing laws of this domain. Each equation is indexed below with its physical motivation, governing formula, and operational calculator softkeys.

docs.title: Eq. 10.1 — Sexagesimal Timecode Expansion and Integer Frame Accumulation
docs.text:
To translate between human clock-face notation and raw discrete frame counts, the time address is decomposed hierarchically. Hours are multiplied by thirty-six hundred seconds, minutes by sixty seconds, and whole seconds are added directly, while the trailing frame counter is divided by the project frame rate \(R\) to represent the fractional second. Multiplying that continuous time duration by the frame rate accumulates the exact total number of discrete frames exposed since midnight:

\[S = 3600 \cdot \text{HH} + 60 \cdot \text{MM} + \text{SS} + \frac{\text{FF}}{R}\]

Here \(S\) is the elapsed duration in seconds (\(\text{s}\)), \(R\) is the frame rate in frames per second (\(\text{fps}\)), and \(F\) is the exact count of frames since 00:00:00:00. When adding ([g] [+TC]) or subtracting ([g] [-TC]) two packed timecode durations \(A\) and \(B\), arithmetic proceeds from right to left across the four radices, carrying \(+1\text{ second}\) whenever the frame sum reaches or exceeds \(R\), carrying \(+1\text{ minute}\) whenever seconds reach \(60\), and carrying \(+1\text{ hour}\) whenever minutes reach \(60\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [▸TC] / [f] [▸FRM] • Expression / Workspace: SMPTE timecode frame conversion • Softkeys: [▸TC] [▸FRM]

docs.title: Eq. 10.2 — Overcrank Speed Magnification and Shutter Exposure Deficit
docs.text:
Because every captured frame must be displayed during playback, the total frame count \(F_{\text{total}}\) is conserved across timebases. The speed ramp magnification factor is simply the ratio of acquisition frame rate to projection frame rate: capturing at five times the playback rate stretches physical time fivefold on screen. Because higher frame rates force each individual frame shutter to open for a shorter fraction of a second, the camera sensor receives fewer photons per frame. In photographic exposure, each factor-of-two reduction in integration time represents one full stop of exposure loss; taking the base-two logarithm of the speed ratio yields the exact exposure deficit in Exposure Value stops that must be compensated on set:

\[M_{\text{ramp}} = \frac{R_{\text{shoot}}}{R_{\text{play}}}\]

In these relations, \(R_{\text{play}}\) is the base delivery timeline frame rate staged in Register \(Y\) (such as \(24\text{ fps}\)), \(R_{\text{shoot}}\) is the camera sensor acquisition rate staged in Register \(X\) (such as \(60\text{ fps}\) or \(120\text{ fps}\)), \(M_{\text{ramp}}\) is the dimensionless slow-motion playback factor deposited in Register \(X\) by [FPS], and \(\Delta\text{EV}_{\text{fps}}\) is the exposure stop loss deposited in Register \(Y\) by [FPS] (because raising the frame rate at a fixed rotary shutter angle shortens each frame's integration time proportionally).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [FPS] • Expression / Workspace: Overcrank speed ramp magnification • Softkeys: [FPS] [SHT]

docs.title: Eq. 10.3 — NTSC Color Pulldown and Wall-Clock Drift Rate
docs.text:
Because the video frame rate is dialed back by exactly one part in a thousand, each broadcast second takes one thousand and one thousandths of a physical second to pass. A counter that increments thirty whole frames per second therefore lags behind atomic wall-clock time by exactly one tenth of a percent: one second of drift every thousand seconds, accumulating \(3.6\text{ seconds}\) of wall-clock lag across every nominal broadcast hour:

\[R_{\text{NTSC}} = \frac{30}{1.001} = \frac{30{,}000}{1001} \approx 29.97003\text{ fps}\]

In this pulldown relationship, \(t_{\text{nominal}} = F / 30\) is the apparent duration indicated by a Non-Drop-Frame (NDF) counter that increments one second every \(30\) frames, \(t_{\text{real}} = F / R_{\text{NTSC}}\) is the true wall-clock elapsed time in seconds ([f] [DF]), and \(\Delta t_{\text{drift}} = t_{\text{real}} - t_{\text{nominal}}\) is the cumulative clock error. Similarly, when theatrical \(24\text{ fps}\) cinema masters are transferred to NTSC video via \(2:3\) telecine pulldown (scaled by \(1.001\)), the cinema frame rate is pulled down by \(1000/1001\) to \(24 / 1.001 \approx 23.976024\text{ fps}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [DF] • Expression / Workspace: NTSC 29.97 color pulldown clock drift • Softkeys: [DF] [FPS]

docs.title: Eq. 10.4 — SMPTE Drop-Frame Label Skip and Physical Frame Index
docs.text:
To maintain perfect synchronization without discarding recorded footage, the display skips frame label numbers rather than physical images. Skipping two numbers on nine minutes out of ten, while retaining every number on decade minutes (zero, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, and fifty), drops exactly one hundred eight labels an hour. The physical frame index is evaluated by accumulating one hundred seven thousand eight hundred ninety-two frames per hour, seventeen hundred ninety-eight frames per minute, and adding back two frames for every decade minute boundary:

\[N_{\text{dropped}} = 2 \times \left(M_{\text{total}} - \left\lfloor \frac{M_{\text{total}}}{10} \right\rfloor\right)\]

Here \(M_{\text{total}} = 60 \cdot \text{HH} + \text{MM}\) is the total number of elapsed minute boundaries, \(N_{\text{dropped}}\) is the cumulative count of skipped frame numbers (labels :00 and :01 omitted at the start of every minute except minutes 00, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50), and \(F_{\text{DF}}\) is the exact physical frame index corresponding to a Drop-Frame address HH:MM:SS;FF (written by convention with a semicolon before the frame field).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [DF] • Expression / Workspace: SMPTE drop-frame label skip compensation • Softkeys: [DF] [+TC] [-TC]

docs.title: Eq. 11.1 — Rectilinear Field of View and Scene Coverage
docs.text:
The optical axis bisects the horizontal width \(W\) (in \(\text{mm}\)) of the active sensor or film aperture into two congruent right triangles, each having an opposite leg of half-width \(W / 2\) and an adjacent leg of focal length \(F\). The ratio of half the sensor width to the focal length forms the tangent of half the angular field of view. The inverse tangent asks what angle produces that specific geometric ratio; doubling that angle yields the full horizontal field of view across the scene:

\[A = 2 \arctan\left(\frac{W}{2F}\right)\]

In these expressions, \(W\) is the active horizontal sensor width in \(\text{mm}\), \(F\) is the lens focal length in \(\text{mm}\), \(A\) is the horizontal coverage angle in degrees, \(s\) is the subject distance along the optical axis, and \(K_{\text{crop}}\) scales focal length to its \(35\text{ mm}\) Full-Frame ([f] [▸35], \(K_{\text{crop}} \approx 1.5\times\) from Super 35) or Super 16 ([g] [▸16], \(K_{\text{crop}} \approx 2.88\times\)) equivalent angle of view (\(F_{\text{equiv}} = F \times K_{\text{crop}}\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [FOV] • Expression / Workspace: FOV: A = 2 × ATAN(W / (2 × F)) • Softkeys: [A] [W] [F]

docs.title: Eq. 11.2 — Hyperfocal Distance and Conjugate Depth-of-Field Boundaries
docs.text:
Because human visual acuity is finite when viewing a theater screen from a standard seating distance, any blur disk smaller than a critical diameter \(C\) (standardized at \(C = 0.029\text{ mm}\)–\(0.030\text{ mm}\) for \(35\text{ mm}\) Full-Frame reference gates and \(C = 0.025\text{ mm}\) for Super 35 cinema work) appears indistinguishable from a sharp point. The hyperfocal distance is the focus setting that extends acceptable sharpness all the way to optical infinity. It scales with the square of focal length and inversely with the aperture f-number and the permissible Circle of Confusion. Once the hyperfocal distance is known, the near and far limits of acceptable focus form harmonic conjugates around the subject distance. The near limit divides the product of hyperfocal distance and subject distance by their sum, while the far limit divides their product by their difference. When the subject distance reaches the hyperfocal mark, the difference in the denominator becomes zero, pushing the far focus limit out to infinity:

\[H = \frac{F^2}{N \cdot C}\]

Here \(F\) is the focal length in \(\text{mm}\), \(N\) is the f-stop number, \(C\) is the Circle of Confusion diameter in \(\text{mm}\), \(H\) is the hyperfocal distance (in \(\text{mm}\) in the [DOF] solver workspace, or divided by \(1000\) in meters on the immediate stack), and \(s\) is the focus distance in the same length units as \(H\). When the focus ring is set directly to the hyperfocal mark (\(s = H\)), the denominator of \(D_{\text{far}}\) vanishes (\(H - H = 0 \implies D_{\text{far}} \to \infty\)) while \(D_{\text{near}}\) reduces to \(H^2 / (2H) = H / 2\), rendering everything from half the hyperfocal distance to the horizon acceptably sharp.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [DOF] • Expression / Workspace: DOF: H = F² / (N × C) • Softkeys: [H] [F] [N] [C]

docs.title: Eq. 11.3 — Exposure Value, Rotary Shutter Integration, and Neutral Density
docs.text:
In photography, Exposure Value unifies aperture and shutter time onto a base-two scale. The square of the lens f-number measures the geometric light constriction of the iris. Dividing that squared f-number by the exposure time in seconds gives the relative light demand; taking the base-two logarithm measures this demand in discrete exposure stops. For a cinema camera with a spinning rotary disk shutter, the open shutter angle represents the fraction of a complete three-hundred-sixty-degree circle during which the sensor is exposed. For neutral-density filters, each optical density step of zero point three corresponds to a factor-of-two reduction in transmitted light—one full exposure stop—matching the base-ten logarithm of two:

\[E = \log_2\left(\frac{N^2}{T}\right)\]

In these photometric equations, \(N\) is the lens f-number, \(T\) is the exposure integration time in seconds, \(E\) is the Exposure Value (\(\text{EV}_{100}\)), \(\theta_{\text{shutter}} \in (0^\circ, 360^\circ]\) is the rotary shutter angle, \(D\) is the dimensionless neutral-density filter rating ([g] [▸ND] converts stops \(s\) in Register \(X\) into optical density \(D = 0.3 \times s\) in Register \(X\) and filter factor \(2^s\) in Register \(Y\)), and \(T_{\text{trans}} = 2^{-\text{stops}} = 10^{-D}\) is the fractional light transmittance. In cinematography optics, depth of field depends on geometric aperture (\(f\)-stop \(N = f/D\)), whereas exposure irradiance depends on photometric transmittance (\(T\)-stop \(T_{\text{stop}} = N / \sqrt{\tau_{\text{trans}}}\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [EV] • Expression / Workspace: EV: N² = T × 2^E • Softkeys: [E] [N] [T] [▸ND]

docs.title: Eq. 11.4 — Flicker-Free Shutter Angle and Integration Period
docs.text:
When filming under alternating-current discharge lamps or LED drivers operating at line frequency \(f_{\text{line}}\) (\(60\text{ Hz}\) in North America or \(50\text{ Hz}\) in Europe), the lamp intensity pulses at twice the utility line frequency (\(2 f_{\text{line}}\): \(120\text{ Hz}\) or \(100\text{ Hz}\)). Avoiding rolling exposure bands across the frame requires choosing a shutter integration time \(T\) that integrates an integer number \(k \in \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}\) of half-cycles:

\[T_{\text{flicker-free}} = \frac{k}{2 f_{\text{line}}}\] \[\theta_{\text{flicker-free}} = 360^\circ \cdot \text{FPS} \cdot \left(\frac{k}{2 f_{\text{line}}}\right)\]

Under North American \(60\text{ Hz}\) mains (\(120\text{ Hz}\) pulses), shooting at \(24\text{ fps}\) with \(k = 2\) half-cycles sets \(T = 1/60\text{ s}\) (\(\theta_{\text{shutter}} = 144^\circ\)). Under European \(50\text{ Hz}\) mains (\(100\text{ Hz}\) pulses), shooting at \(24\text{ fps}\) requires an exact integration time of \(T = 1/50\text{ s} = 20.0\text{ ms}\), corresponding to the classic European flicker-free rotary shutter angle of \(\theta_{\text{shutter}} = \mathbf{172.8^\circ}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [SHT] • Expression / Workspace: SHT: T = θ / (360 × FPS) • Softkeys: [SHT] [FPS]

docs.title: Eq. 11.5 — Inverse-Square Illuminance and Micro-Reciprocal Degree Gel Shift
docs.text:
As light radiates from a fixture, its radiant power spreads across an expanding spherical wavefront whose surface area grows with the square of distance. Consequently, illuminance in lux falls off inversely with the square of throw distance. For color temperature, human perception does not see equal Kelvin differences equally: a five-hundred Kelvin shift at warm tungsten temperatures creates a dramatic visual amber cast, whereas the same shift at high daylight temperatures is barely noticeable. Converting absolute Kelvin temperature into its reciprocal multiplied by one million—termed micro-reciprocal degrees or Mireds (\(M = 10^6 / T_K\))—makes color filtration additive across the spectrum. Subtracting the source Mired value from the target Mired value specifies the exact corrective gel shift:

\[E_{\text{lx}} = \frac{I}{D^2}\]

Here a positive shift (\(\Delta M > 0\)) calls for an amber Color Temperature Orange (CTO) gel to warm a daylight source toward tungsten, whereas a negative shift (\(\Delta M < 0\)) calls for a blue Color Temperature Blue (CTB) gel to cool a \(T_{\text{source}} = 3200\text{ K}\) tungsten lamp (\(M_{\text{source}} = 10^6 / 3200 = 312.50\text{ Mireds}\)) up to \(T_{\text{target}} = 5600\text{ K}\) daylight (\(M_{\text{target}} = 10^6 / 5600 = 178.57\text{ Mireds}\)), yielding \(\Delta M = 178.57 - 312.50 = \mathbf{-133.93\text{ Mireds}}\) (a Full CTB gel).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [LUX] • Expression / Workspace: LUX: E = I / D² • Softkeys: [E] [I] [D] [▸fc]

docs.title: Eq. 12.1 — Thermal Speed of Sound and Acoustic Propagation Delay
docs.text:
Sound is a mechanical pressure wave passed from air molecule to air molecule. Because higher temperatures increase the thermal speed of gas molecules, the speed of sound rises linearly with temperature, starting at \(331.3\text{ m/s}\) at freezing and adding roughly \(0.606\text{ m/s}\) for every degree Celsius of warmth. The acoustic transit time across a venue is simply distance divided by velocity; multiplying by one thousand converts seconds into milliseconds. Dividing sound speed by the acoustic frequency yields the physical wavelength—the spatial distance between adjacent compression peaks:

\[v_s(T_C) = 331.3 + 0.606 \cdot T_C \quad \left[\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}\right]\]

In these expressions, \(T_C\) is the ambient air temperature in degrees Celsius (\(^\circ\text{C}\)), \(v_s\) is the acoustic phase velocity in \(\text{m/s}\) (evaluating to \(343.42\text{ m/s} \approx 343\text{ m/s}\) at the standard \(20^\circ\text{C}\) room reference recalled by [f] [vₛ]), \(d\) is the physical distance from the main stage array to the delay tower in meters, \(\Delta t_{\text{ms}}\) is the acoustic transit delay in milliseconds (\(\text{ms}\)), and \(\lambda\) is the physical wavelength in meters.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [vₛ] • Expression / Workspace: Thermal speed of sound and DSP delay • Softkeys: [vₛ] [DLY]

docs.title: Eq. 12.2 — Sabine Reverberation Time
docs.text:
In an enclosed room, sound bounces repeatedly between boundaries, creating a decaying reverberant field. Wallace Clement Sabine's 1898 architectural law states that the time needed for reverberant sound energy to drop by sixty decibels—one millionth of its original power—is directly proportional to the total enclosed air volume and inversely proportional to the total acoustic absorption in metric sabins:

\[RT_{60} = \frac{0.161 \cdot V}{A} = \frac{0.161 \cdot V}{\sum_{i} S_i \alpha_i}\]

For a broadcast studio of volume \(V = 2400\text{ m}^3\) treated with acoustic baffles providing \(A = 480\text{ metric sabins}\) of absorption, Sabine's formula predicts a tight decay time of \(RT_{60} = (0.161 \times 2400) / 480 = \mathbf{0.805\text{ s}}\), while an \(f = 68.6\text{ Hz}\) bass note at \(v_s = 343\text{ m/s}\) has an acoustic wavelength of \(\lambda = 343 / 68.6 = \mathbf{5.00\text{ m}}\) (68.6 [g] [λ]).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [EQN] • Expression / Workspace: Sabine reverberation decay time • Softkeys: V A

docs.title: Eq. 12.3 — Spherical Spreading Attenuation and Acoustic Reach
docs.text:
On the logarithmic decibel scale, the attenuation equals twenty times the base-ten logarithm of the distance ratio. Every doubling of distance reduces sound pressure level by six decibels:

\[L_2 = L_1 - 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)\]

Here \(L_1\) is the known Sound Pressure Level in \(\text{dBSPL}\) at reference distance \(D_1\), and \(L_2\) is the Sound Pressure Level at distance \(D_2\) (when called with two arguments \(D_1\) in \(Y\) and \(D_2\) in \(X\), [f] [SPL] returns the relative decibel attenuation \(\Delta L = -20\log_{10}(D_2 / D_1)\)). Every doubling of distance (\(D_2 / D_1 = 2\)) reduces sound pressure level by \(20\log_{10}(2) \approx \mathbf{6.0206\text{ dB}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [SPL] • Expression / Workspace: Spherical acoustic inverse-square decay • Softkeys: [SPL] [dB]

docs.title: Eq. 12.4 — Incoherent Acoustic Decibel Addition and Studio Voltage Levels
docs.text:
When independent sound sources radiate into the same space, their pressure waves do not interfere coherently; instead, their acoustic energies add together. To sum two decibel levels, each is divided by ten and raised as a power of ten to recover its linear acoustic power. These powers are added together, and taking ten times the base-ten logarithm yields the combined decibel level. Combining two identical uncorrelated sources always produces a three-decibel increase, reflecting a doubling of total radiated power:

\[L_{\Sigma,\text{incoherent}} = 10 \log_{10}\left(10^{L_1 / 10} + 10^{L_2 / 10}\right)\]

In broadcast audio transmission, electrical peak decibels are monitored alongside integrated Loudness Units relative to Full Scale (LUFS / LKFS under ITU-R BS.1770 and EBU R128), applying K-weighting acoustic filters and gating algorithms to target \(-24\text{ LUFS}\) for television broadcast and \(-14\text{ LUFS}\) for commercial streaming.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [dB] • Expression / Workspace: Incoherent acoustic decibel power summation • Softkeys: [dB] [SPL]

docs.title: Unit V: RF Spectrum, Transmission Lines, and Microwave
docs.text: The SC-50 provides dedicated faceplate keys and bidirectional Equation Solver workspaces to execute the governing laws of this domain. Each equation is indexed below with its physical motivation, governing formula, and operational calculator softkeys.

docs.title: Eq. 13.1 — Decibel-Milliwatt Power Scaling and Root-Mean-Square Line Voltage
docs.text:
Because radio signal powers range across many orders of magnitude, power is expressed logarithmically relative to one milliwatt. Taking ten times the base-ten logarithm of milliwatt power converts linear watts into decibel-milliwatts. Across a transmission line of characteristic impedance \(Z_0\), root-mean-square radio-frequency voltage follows Ohm's law, equaling the square root of the power in watts multiplied by the impedance:

\[P_{\text{dBm}} = 10 \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_{\text{mW}}}{1\text{ mW}}\right) = 10 \log_{10}(P_{\text{W}}) + 30\]

In these expressions, \(P_{\text{dBm}}\) is the absolute power level in \(\text{dBm}\), \(P_{\text{mW}}\) is linear power in milliwatts, \(P_{\text{W}} = P_{\text{mW}} / 1000\) is linear power in watts, and \(Z_0\) is the transmission-line characteristic impedance in ohms (\(\Omega\), standardized at \(50\ \Omega\) for transmitters and \(75\ \Omega\) for video/broadcast coax).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [dBm] • Expression / Workspace: Decibel-milliwatt logarithmic power • Softkeys: [dBm] [▸dBm] [▸dBW]

docs.title: Eq. 13.2 — Complex Voltage Reflection Coefficient and Standing Wave Ratio
docs.text:
When a guided electromagnetic wave encounters an antenna whose complex impedance differs from the line's characteristic impedance, the boundary conditions of electromagnetism demand that a fraction of the voltage reflect backward. The complex reflection coefficient divides the difference between load impedance and characteristic impedance by their sum. Its magnitude measures the fraction of voltage reflected, while its angle reveals the phase shift:

\[\Gamma = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0} = |\Gamma| \angle \theta\]

For a load impedance \(Z_L = 75 + j50\ \Omega\) on a \(Z_0 = 50\ \Omega\) line, [Γ] computes \(\Gamma = \frac{25 + j50}{125 + j50} \approx 0.3846 + j0.2462\) with magnitude \(|\Gamma| = \mathbf{0.4564}\), yielding standing wave ratio \(\text{VSWR} = \frac{1 + 0.4564}{1 - 0.4564} \approx \mathbf{2.68\text{ : } 1}\) via [SWR].

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [Γ] • Expression / Workspace: Complex reflection coefficient and VSWR • Softkeys: [Γ] [SWR] [Z₀]

docs.title: Eq. 13.3 — Return Loss and Mismatch Loss
docs.text:
As the reflected voltage wave \(V^-\) travels backward and superposes with the incident wave \(V^+\), constructive interference produces stationary voltage peaks while destructive interference produces voltage troughs. The ratio of peak to trough voltage is the VSWR. Expressing the fraction of power reflected in decibels yields the Return Loss: twenty times the negative base-ten logarithm of reflection magnitude. Higher return loss means less reflected power and a better match. The reduction in forward power delivered into the antenna is Mismatch Loss, evaluated from ten times the negative base-ten logarithm of one minus the reflected power fraction:

\[\text{RL}_{\text{dB}} = -20 \log_{10}|\Gamma|\]

On real high-frequency transmission lines, distributed series conductor resistance from the radio-frequency skin effect and shunt dielectric conductance attenuate traveling waves exponentially as \(e^{-\alpha z}\). In the complex plane, the Smith chart maps reflection coefficient \(\Gamma = |\Gamma|e^{j\theta}\) directly to normalized impedance, where line attenuation causes impedance trajectories to spiral inward toward the \(50\ \Omega\) center as reflected power diminishes.

  • Calculator Interface: Complex Menu Softkey: [RL] in [f] [CMPLX] (or [SWR]) • Expression / Workspace: Return loss and mismatch loss • Softkeys: [RL] [SWR]

docs.title: Eq. 13.4 — High-Frequency Conductor Skin Depth
docs.text:
In alternating-current circuits at radio and microwave frequencies, oscillating magnetic fields induce localized eddy currents that oppose current flow in the conductor interior, crowding the alternating current toward the outer perimeter. The characteristic depth at which current density drops to \(1/e\) (\(\approx 36.8\%\)) of its surface value is the Skin Depth (\(\delta\)):

\[\delta = \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\pi f \mu}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi f \sigma \mu_0 \mu_r}}\]

At \(f = 6\text{ GHz}\) (\(6 \times 10^9\text{ Hz}\)), the skin depth in copper (\(\rho \approx 1.68 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot\text{m}\)) contracts to \(\delta \approx \mathbf{0.85\ \mu\text{m}}\). Because over \(98\%\) of the RF current travels within \(4\delta \approx 3.4\ \mu\text{m}\), microwave waveguides and coaxial center conductors utilize micro-inch silver electroplating (\(50\text{--}100\ \mu\text{in}\)) over lightweight structural brass or aluminum rather than solid precious metal.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: Conductor Skin Depth on Stack (√, ÷, ×) • Expression / Workspace: Stack: f in Y, resistivity in X, solve for δ • Softkeys: [√x] [÷] [×]

docs.title: Eq. 13.5 — Quarter-Wave Matching Transformer and Physical Stub Length
docs.text:
To match a source impedance to a load resistance, a quarter-wave section's characteristic impedance must equal the geometric mean of the two port impedances. The physical length of the stub equals one quarter of the free-space wavelength scaled by the cable's velocity factor:

\[\ell_{\lambda/4} = \frac{\lambda}{4} \cdot \text{VF} = \frac{c}{4 f} \cdot \text{VF}\]

Here \(f_{\text{MHz}}\) is the operating frequency in megahertz, \(\lambda = c/f = 299.792458 / f_{\text{MHz}}\text{ m}\) is the free-space wavelength in meters, \(\text{VF} = 1 / \sqrt{\varepsilon_r}\) is the coaxial cable velocity factor, and \(Z_{\text{match}}\) is the geometric-mean characteristic impedance in ohms. At the repeater frequency of \(f = 146.0\text{ MHz}\), the free-space wavelength is \(\lambda = 299.792458 / 146.0 \approx \mathbf{2.0534\text{ m}}\) and a free-space quarter-wave whip measures \(\ell_{\lambda/4} = 2.0534 / 4 \approx \mathbf{0.5133\text{ m}}\) (\(51.33\text{ cm}\)). Cut from foam-dielectric coaxial cable with velocity factor \(\text{VF} = 0.82\), the physical quarter-wave stub length is \(0.5133 \times 0.82 \approx \mathbf{0.4209\text{ m}}\) (\(42.1\text{ cm}\)). To match a \(Z_S = 50\ \Omega\) line to a \(Z_L = 112.5\ \Omega\) antenna resistance, the required quarter-wave section impedance is \(Z_{\text{match}} = \sqrt{50 \times 112.5} = \sqrt{5625} = \mathbf{75.0\ \Omega}\), allowing standard \(75\ \Omega\) video coax to serve as an exact quarter-wave transformer.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [TLN] • Expression / Workspace: Quarter-wave transformer stub length • Softkeys: [TLN] [λ/L]

docs.title: Eq. 13.6 — L-Network Matching Reactances and LC Resonance
docs.text:
The circuit's operating quality factor \(Q\) is the square root of the ratio of high resistance to low resistance minus one. The required series reactance equals the quality factor times the lower resistance, while the shunt reactance equals the higher resistance divided by the quality factor. In resonant LC circuits, inductive and capacitive reactances cancel at the resonant frequency \(f_0\):

\[Q = \sqrt{\frac{R_{\text{high}}}{R_{\text{low}}} - 1}\]

Consider matching our repeater's resistive component \(R_{\text{low}} = 35\ \Omega\) up to \(R_{\text{high}} = 50\ \Omega\) at \(f = 146.0\text{ MHz}\). The required nodal quality factor is \(Q = \sqrt{(50 / 35) - 1} = \sqrt{0.42857} \approx \mathbf{0.6547}\), which specifies a net series inductive reactance of \(|X_{\text{series}}| = 0.6547 \times 35 \approx \mathbf{22.91\ \Omega}\) and a shunt capacitive reactance of \(|X_{\text{shunt}}| = 50 / 0.6547 \approx \mathbf{76.38\ \Omega}\). Because the iced antenna already exhibits \(-j25\ \Omega\) of series capacitive reactance, the series inductor must simultaneously cancel that \(-25\ \Omega\) reactance and supply \(+22.91\ \Omega\) of net inductive reactance, requiring a total inductive reactance of \(X_L = 25 + 22.91 = \mathbf{47.91\ \Omega}\) (\(L = 47.91 / (2\pi \times 146 \times 10^6) \approx \mathbf{52.23\text{ nH}}\)) paired with a shunt capacitor of \(C = 1 / (2\pi \times 146 \times 10^6 \times 76.38) \approx \mathbf{14.27\text{ pF}}\). Similarly, when stepping a \(R_{\text{low}} = 10\ \Omega\) power-transistor collector up to \(R_{\text{high}} = 50\ \Omega\), the nodal quality factor is \(Q = \sqrt{(50/10) - 1} = \mathbf{2.00}\), giving \(|X_{\text{series}}| = \mathbf{20.0\ \Omega}\) and \(|X_{\text{shunt}}| = \mathbf{25.0\ \Omega}\).

docs.title: Eq. 14.1 — Friis Free-Space Path Loss
docs.text:
In free space, an isotropic antenna radiates power over an expanding sphere of area four pi times distance squared. Because the receiving antenna's effective capture area shrinks with the square of wavelength, the received power fraction falls with the square of distance and the square of frequency. Expressed in decibels with distance in kilometers and frequency in megahertz, Friis's free-space path loss formula adds twenty times the base-ten logarithm of distance, twenty times the logarithm of frequency, and thirty-two point forty-four decibels:

\[\text{FSPL}_{\text{dB}} = 20 \log_{10}(d_{\text{km}}) + 20 \log_{10}(f_{\text{MHz}}) + 32.44\]

In this expression, \(d_{\text{km}}\) is the line-of-sight hop distance in kilometers, \(f_{\text{MHz}}\) is the carrier frequency in megahertz, and \(\text{FSPL}_{\text{dB}}\) is the positive isotropic path attenuation in decibels. Doubling either the hop distance \(d_{\text{km}}\) or the carrier frequency \(f_{\text{MHz}}\) adds \(20\log_{10}(2) \approx \mathbf{6.02\text{ dB}}\) of path loss.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [FSL] • Expression / Workspace: FSL: L = 20LOG(D×F) + 32.4 • Softkeys: [L] [D] [F]

docs.title: Eq. 14.2 — Logarithmic RF Link Budget and Fade Margin
docs.text:
A logarithmic link budget sums all power gains and subtracts all transmission losses along the path. Starting with transmitter output power in decibel-milliwatts, net antenna and amplifier gains in decibels are added, and total path and cable losses in decibels are subtracted. The difference between the resulting received power and the receiver's minimum sensitivity threshold establishes the fade margin against rain attenuation and atmospheric multipath fading:

\[P_{\text{rx,dBm}} = P_{\text{tx,dBm}} + G_{\text{dB}} - L_{\text{dB}}\]

Here \(P_{\text{rx,dBm}}\) is the unfaded received signal power in \(\text{dBm}\), \(S_{\text{min,dBm}}\) is the receiver's minimum sensitivity threshold for a target modulation scheme and bit-error rate, and \(M_{\text{fade}}\) is the link's Fade Margin in \(\text{dB}\) against heavy rain, snow, or atmospheric multipath ducting. Along terrestrial paths, microwave engineers also verify that intervening terrain obstacles maintain at least \(60\%\) clearance of the First Fresnel Zone (\(r_1 \approx 13.14\sqrt{d_{\text{km}}/(4 f_{\text{GHz}})}\text{ m}\)) to prevent destructive diffraction fading.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [LNK] • Expression / Workspace: LNK: R = P + G - L • Softkeys: [R] [P] [G] [L]

docs.title: Eq. 14.3 — First Fresnel Zone Midpoint Radius and Clearance Criterion
docs.text:
Radio waves do not travel along a hairline ray; they expand through an ellipsoid of constructive phase coherence known as the First Fresnel Zone. Waves passing through the outer boundary of this ellipsoid travel exactly half a wavelength farther than the central ray. At the midpoint of a microwave hop, the radius of this zone scales with the square root of distance divided by carrier frequency. To prevent diffraction fading, the optical sightline must clear all terrain and obstacles by at least sixty percent of the First Fresnel Zone radius:

\[r_1 = \sqrt{\frac{\lambda \cdot d}{4}} = 8.656 \sqrt{\frac{d_{\text{km}}}{f_{\text{GHz}}}}\quad [\text{m}]\]

In this expression, \(d_{\text{km}}\) is the total hop length in kilometers, \(f_{\text{GHz}}\) is the carrier frequency in gigahertz, \(r_1\) is the midpoint cross-sectional radius in meters of the first phase-coherent ellipsoid, and \(h_{\text{clear,min}}\) is the required obstacle-free clearance.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [F₁] • Expression / Workspace: First Fresnel zone clearance radius • Softkeys: [F₁] [LNK]

docs.title: Eq. 15.1 — Johnson–Nyquist Thermal Noise Floor
docs.text:
Thermal agitation of electrons sets the ultimate physical limit on radio reception. At standard room temperature, thermal noise delivers an available power density of roughly minus one hundred seventy-four decibel-milliwatts per hertz of bandwidth. Integrating across the receiver channel bandwidth adds ten times the base-ten logarithm of bandwidth in hertz, establishing the thermal noise floor:

\[N_{\text{floor,dBm}} = 10 \log_{10}(k_B T_0 \cdot 1000) + 10 \log_{10}(B_{\text{Hz}}) \approx -173.977 + 10 \log_{10}(B_{\text{Hz}})\]

Across a \(B = 20\text{ MHz}\) channel at reference temperature \(T_0 = 290\text{ K}\), [g] [Pₙ] evaluates the thermal noise floor as \(P_n = -174 + 10\log_{10}(20 \times 10^6) = -174 + 73.01 = \mathbf{-100.99\text{ dBm}}\) (or \(\mathbf{-101.0\text{ dBm}}\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [Pₙ] • Expression / Workspace: Johnson–Nyquist thermal noise floor • Softkeys: [Pₙ] [T₀] [kB]

docs.title: Eq. 15.2 — Friis Cascaded Noise Factor
docs.text:
In a cascaded receiver chain, each successive stage adds noise. Harald Friis's 1944 cascade law demonstrates that the total noise factor is dominated by the very first amplifier. The first stage's noise factor is transferred directly, while each subsequent stage's excess noise is divided by the linear power gains of all preceding stages. Placing a high-gain, low-noise amplifier at the masthead suppresses downstream cable and receiver noise:

\[F_{\text{tot}} = F_1 + \frac{F_2 - 1}{G_1} + \frac{F_3 - 1}{G_1 G_2} + \dots\]

In this equation, \(F_1\) and \(G_1\) are the linear noise factor and linear power gain of the very first component following the antenna, and each subsequent stage's excess noise \((F_k - 1)\) is divided by the product of all preceding linear gains \(G_1 G_2 \cdots G_{k-1}\). In addition, a passive lossy component (such as a coaxial cable of insertion loss \(L_{\text{dB}}\) at \(290\text{ K}\)) has linear gain \(G_{\text{cable}} = 10^{-L_{\text{dB}} / 10} < 1\) and linear noise factor \(F_{\text{cable}} = 1 / G_{\text{cable}} = 10^{+L_{\text{dB}} / 10}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [NF] • Expression / Workspace: NF: F = A + (B - 1) / G • Softkeys: [F] [A] [B] [G]

docs.title: Eq. 15.3 — Spurious-Free Dynamic Range
docs.text:
When strong interfering signals pass through non-linear receiver components, third-order intermodulation distortion rises three times faster in decibels than the fundamental signal. The input third-order intercept point extrapolates where these distortion products would equal the fundamental. Spurious-Free Dynamic Range measures the usable window between the noise floor and the point where distortion products emerge from the noise, spanning exactly two thirds of the difference between the third-order intercept point and the noise floor:

\[\text{SFDR}_{\text{dB}} = \frac{2}{3}\left(\text{IIP3}_{\text{dBm}} - N_{\text{floor,dBm}}\right)\]

For a receiver front-end with \(\text{IIP3} = +5.0\text{ dBm}\) and an effective noise floor of \(N_{\text{floor}} = -100.0\text{ dBm}\), the spurious-free dynamic range spans \(\text{SFDR} = \frac{2}{3}(5.0 - (-100.0)) = \mathbf{70.0\text{ dB}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [IP3] • Expression / Workspace: Spurious-free dynamic range and IP3 • Softkeys: [IP3] [FDR]

docs.title: Eq. 15.4 — Shannon–Hartley Channel Capacity and Spectral Efficiency
docs.text:
The channel capacity in bits per second equals the bandwidth in hertz multiplied by the base-two logarithm of one plus the linear signal-to-noise ratio. The base-two logarithm asks how many bits of information can be reliably encoded into each hertz of channel bandwidth:

\[C = B \log_2\left(1 + \text{SNR}\right) \quad [\text{bps}]\]

Here \(B\) is the channel bandwidth in hertz, \(\text{SNR}\) is the dimensionless linear signal-to-noise power ratio, \(C\) is the maximum theoretical error-free data rate in \(\text{bps}\), and \(\eta = C / B\) is the spectral efficiency in \(\text{bits/s/Hz}\). At high signal-to-noise ratios (\(\text{SNR} \gg 1\)), spectral efficiency grows as \(\eta \approx \log_2(\text{SNR}) = \text{SNR}_{\text{dB}} / (10\log_{10} 2) = \text{SNR}_{\text{dB}} / 3.0103\text{ bits/s/Hz}\) per power ratio (or \(\text{SNR}_{\text{dB}} / 6.0206\) amplitude bits per sample).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [C/B] • Expression / Workspace: C/B: C = B × LOG2(1 + S) • Softkeys: [C] [B] [S]

docs.title: Eq. 15.5 — Doppler Velocity Shift and Fourth-Power Radar Echo
docs.text:
When a radio wave is received from a moving transmitter, wave crests are compressed or stretched, shifting the carrier frequency by the ratio of closing velocity to the speed of light. In a monostatic radar, the wave travels out to the target and reflects back, doubling the Doppler frequency shift. Because the wave spreads spherically on both the outbound and return paths, echo power drops inversely with the fourth power of target range:

\[\Delta f_{\text{1-way}} = \frac{f_0 \cdot v}{c}\]

For our CubeSat transmitting at \(f_0 = 437.0\text{ MHz}\) (\(4.37 \times 10^8\text{ Hz}\)) with a radial closure speed of \(v = 7500\text{ m/s}\) (437 [ENTER] 7500 [g] [Δf]), the one-way telemetry downlink shift in Register \(X\) is \(\Delta f_{\text{1-way}} = (4.37 \times 10^8 \times 7500) / 299{,}792{,}458 \approx \mathbf{10{,}932.6\text{ Hz}}\) (\(10.93\text{ kHz}\)), and the two-way monostatic radar shift in Register \(Y\) is \(\Delta f_{\text{2-way}} \approx \mathbf{21{,}865.1\text{ Hz}}\) (\(21.87\text{ kHz}\)). Because two-way radar return scales with \(\sigma / ((4\pi)^3 R^4)\) ([f] [RCS] with range \(R\) in Register \(Y\) and cross-section \(\sigma\) in Register \(X\)), doubling a radar's maximum detection range \(R_{\max}\) requires increasing transmitter power sixteen-fold (\(2^4 = 16\), or \(+12.04\text{ dB}\)).
