docs.title: Unit VI: Wet-Lab Chemistry, Stoichiometry, and Spectroscopy
docs.text: The SC-60 provides dedicated faceplate keys and bidirectional Equation Solver workspaces to execute the governing laws of this domain. Each equation is indexed below with its physical motivation, governing formula, and operational calculator softkeys.

docs.title: Eq. 16.1 — Gravimetric Solute Mass and Molar Mass Summation
docs.text:
Because chemical reactions occur between individual molecules, chemical amounts are measured in moles. The molar mass of a substance sums the atomic weights of all constituent atoms in its chemical formula. To find the macroscopic mass in grams needed on an analytical balance, the chemical amount in moles is multiplied by the molar mass in grams per mole:

\[M = \sum_{i} \nu_i A_i \quad \left[\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mol}}\right]\]

In these expressions, \(\nu_i\) is the integer stoichiometric subscript of element \(i\) in the chemical formula, \(M\) is the molar mass in \(\text{g/mol}\), \(n\) is the chemical amount in moles (\(\text{mol}\)), and \(W\) is the physical mass in grams (\(\text{g}\)) weighed on the balance pan.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [MW] • Expression / Workspace: MW: W = N × M • Softkeys: [W] [N] [M] [Z]

docs.title: Eq. 16.2 — Elemental Mass Percentage and Hydrate Molar Mass
docs.text:
When verifying elemental purity by combustion analysis or preparing trace-metal media, chemists evaluate the Elemental Mass Percentage \(\text{WT\%}_i\) ([f] [w/w])—the percentage of one mole's total mass contributed by element \(i\). Furthermore, when an inorganic salt crystallizes from water as a hydrate (\(\text{Salt} \cdot k\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)) containing \(k\) stoichiometric molecules of water (\(M(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 18.015\text{ g/mol}\)) locked inside its solid crystal lattice, those water molecules contribute directly to the gravimetric molar mass:

\[\text{WT\%}_i = \frac{\nu_i A_i}{M} \times 100\%\] \[M_{\text{hydrate}} = M_{\text{anhydrous}} + k \cdot M(\text{H}_2\text{O})\]

In sulfuric acid (\(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\), \(M = 98.072\text{ g/mol}\)), hydrogen accounts for \(2.056\%\), sulfur for \(32.690\%\), and oxygen for \(65.254\%\). For hydrates such as sodium phosphate heptahydrate (\(\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}\)), the seven water molecules add \(126.105\text{ g/mol}\) to the anhydrous mass (\(141.958\text{ g/mol}\)), bringing the total crystalline mass to \(268.063\text{ g/mol}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [w/w] / [MW] • Expression / Workspace: Stack: component in Y, total M in X • Softkeys: [w/w] [MW]

docs.title: Eq. 16.3 — Volumetric Solution Molarity and Solute Mass
docs.text:
Molarity measures solution concentration as the chemical amount of dissolved solute divided by the total solution volume in liters. To prepare a solution of target molarity, the required dry solute mass is the product of target molarity, final volume, and solute molar mass:

\[C = \frac{n}{V} = \frac{W}{M \cdot V}\]

Here \(C\) is the target molar concentration in \(\text{mol/L}\) (\(\text{M}\)), \(V\) is the final solution volume in liters (\(\text{L}\), where \(1\text{ mL} = 10^{-3}\text{ L}\)), \(n\) is the dissolved solute amount in moles, \(M\) is the reagent molar mass in \(\text{g/mol}\), and \(W\) is the dry mass in grams.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [RXN] • Expression / Workspace: RXN: N = C × V • Softkeys: [N] [C] [V]

docs.title: Eq. 16.4 — Conservation of Solute Moles in Stock Dilution
docs.text:
Because adding pure water introduces zero additional solute molecules, the total number of solute moles \(n_{\text{solute}}\) aspirated in the stock aliquot \(V_1\) equals the total number of solute moles present in the final diluted volume \(V_2\). Multiplying stock concentration by aliquot volume equals final concentration multiplied by final volume:

\[C_1 V_1 = C_2 V_2 \iff V_1 = \frac{C_2 V_2}{C_1}\]

In this bilateral conservation equation, \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) may be expressed in any matching concentration unit (\(\text{M}, \text{mM}, \mu\text{M}\), or \(\text{mg/mL}\)) and \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) in any matching volume unit (\(\text{L}, \text{mL}\), or \(\mu\text{L}\)), while \(V_{\text{solvent}}\) is the volume of pure diluent added to bring the aliquot \(V_1\) up to the mark \(V_2\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [C₁V₁] • Expression / Workspace: C1V1: C × V = D × U • Softkeys: [C] [V] [D] [U]

docs.title: Eq. 16.5 — Serial Pipetting Error Propagation
docs.text:
When a technician executes \(k\) sequential dilutions using a micropipette whose relative volume delivery uncertainty at each transfer is \(\sigma_V / V\), independent random pipetting errors add in quadrature, causing the cumulative relative concentration uncertainty \(\sigma_{C_k} / C_k\) after \(k\) steps to grow as the square root of the step count:

\[\frac{\sigma_{C_k}}{C_k} \approx \sqrt{k}\,\left(\frac{\sigma_V}{V}\right)\]

A six-step serial dilution (\(k = 6\)) with a \(\pm 1.5\%\) micropipette inflates random concentration error to \(\sqrt{6} \times 1.5\% \approx \pm 3.67\%\) (plus six times any systematic calibration bias), demonstrating why analytical chemists prefer single-cut aliquots ([C₁V₁]) from primary standards ([MW]) whenever possible.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: Stack calculation • Expression / Workspace: Stack: k in X, SQRT, error in Y, × • Softkeys: [√x] [×]

docs.title: Eq. 16.6 — Colligative Freezing Point Depression
docs.text:
Colligative properties depend strictly on the ratio of dissolved solute particles to solvent molecules, independent of solute chemical identity. Dissolved non-volatile solute particles lower the chemical potential of the liquid phase, depressing the equilibrium freezing point according to Sir Charles Blagden's 1788 cryoscopic law:

\[\Delta T_f = i \cdot K_f \cdot m\]

Here \(\Delta T_f\) is the freezing point depression in degrees Celsius (\(^\circ\text{C}\) or \(\text{K}\)), \(i\) is the dimensionless van 't Hoff dissociation factor (\(i=1\) for non-electrolytes, \(i \approx 2\) for \(\text{NaCl}\), \(i \approx 3\) for \(\text{CaCl}_2\)), \(K_f\) is the molal freezing point depression constant (\(1.853\ ^\circ\text{C}\cdot\text{kg/mol} \approx 1.86\ ^\circ\text{C}\cdot\text{kg/mol}\) for pure water), and \(m\) is solute molality (\(\text{mol/kg}\)). Analytical chemists use this relation to formulate sub-zero eutectic salt reaction baths (depressing ice baths to \(-10^\circ\text{C}\) or down to \(-21.1^\circ\text{C}\) with eutectic \(\text{NaCl}\)) and audit reagent solute purity and molecular weight through precision freezing point osmometry.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: Cryoscopic Depression on Stack (×, [MW]) • Expression / Workspace: Stack: i in Z, Kf in Y, m in X, multiply • Softkeys: [MW] [×]

docs.title: Eq. 17.1 — Sørensen Logarithmic Acidity and Acid Dissociation Constant
docs.text:
Because aqueous proton concentrations span fourteen orders of magnitude, Sørensen introduced the pH scale using the negative base-ten logarithm. Taking the negative base-ten logarithm asks what power of ten represents the hydrogen-ion concentration; each one-unit decrease in pH represents a tenfold surge in free proton activity:

\[\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+] \iff [\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}\]

In these equations, \([\text{H}^+]\) is the molar hydrogen-ion concentration in \(\text{mol/L}\), \(K_a\) is the equilibrium acid dissociation constant, and \(\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14.00\) at \(25^\circ\text{C}\). A strong acid solution at \([\text{H}^+] = 0.0010\text{ M}\) (\(10^{-3}\text{ M}\)) has \(\text{pH} = \mathbf{3.00}\), while acetic acid with \(K_a = 1.75 \times 10^{-5}\) has \(\text{p}K_a = -\log_{10}(1.75 \times 10^{-5}) \approx \mathbf{4.757}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [pH] • Expression / Workspace: Sørensen logarithmic acidity • Softkeys: [pH] [pKₐ]

docs.title: Eq. 17.2 — Henderson–Hasselbalch Buffer Equilibrium
docs.text:
The solution pH equals the weak acid's pKa plus the base-ten logarithm of the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid. When base and acid are present in equal amounts, the ratio is one, the logarithm is zero, and pH equals pKa:

\[\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log_{10}\left(\frac{[\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}\right)\]

Here \([\text{A}^-]\) is the molar concentration of the proton-accepting conjugate base, \([\text{HA}]\) is the molar concentration of the proton-donating weak acid, and \(r = [\text{A}^-] / [\text{HA}]\) is the dimensionless conjugate base-to-acid ratio. This reflects structural unity across physical science: just as the Nernst equation shifts electrochemical cell voltage by \((2.3026 R T / n_e F) \log_{10}([\text{Ox}]/[\text{Red}])\) (\(59.16\text{ mV}\) per decade at \(25^\circ\text{C}\)) and decibels measure \(10\log_{10}(P_2/P_1)\), the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation shifts chemical proton potential by \(1.00\text{ pH unit}\) per decade change in the conjugate ratio \([\text{A}^-]/[\text{HA}]\). Furthermore, because dissociation constants depend on temperature—most notably in amine buffers such as Tris, where a large temperature coefficient of \(\Delta \text{p}K_a / \Delta T \approx -0.028 / ^\circ\text{C}\) shifts a benchtop solution from \(\text{pH } 7.40\) at \(25^\circ\text{C}\) to nearly \(\text{pH } 8.0\) in a \(4^\circ\text{C}\) cold room—chemists calibrate electrodes and prepare buffers at the intended assay temperature.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [BUF] • Expression / Workspace: BUF: P = K + LOG(A/H) • Softkeys: [P] [K] [A] [H]

docs.title: Eq. 17.3 — Van Slyke Buffer Capacity and Species Partitioning
docs.text:
The resistance of a conjugate buffer solution to \(\text{pH}\) shifts upon addition of strong acid or base is quantified by the Van Slyke Buffer Capacity (\(\beta\)). Buffer capacity reaches its theoretical maximum \(\beta_{\max} \approx 0.576 \cdot C_{\text{total}}\) when weak acid and conjugate base concentrations are exactly equal (\([\text{HA}] = [\text{A}^-]\)), which occurs precisely at \(\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a\):

\[\beta = 2.303 \cdot C_{\text{total}} \cdot \frac{[\text{HA}][\text{A}^-]}{([\text{HA}] + [\text{A}^-])^2} \le 0.576 \cdot C_{\text{total}}\] \[[\text{HA}] = \frac{C_{\text{total}}}{1 + 10^{\text{pH} - \text{p}K_a}} \iff [\text{A}^-] = \frac{r \cdot C_{\text{total}}}{1 + r}\]

When solution \(\text{pH}\) deviates from \(\text{p}K_a\) by more than one full unit (where the base-to-acid ratio exceeds \(10:1\) or falls below \(1:10\)), buffer capacity collapses below \(33\%\) of its peak value, defining the practical buffering window as \(\text{pH} \in [\text{p}K_a - 1, \text{p}K_a + 1]\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [BUF] • Expression / Workspace: BUF: P = K + LOG(A/H) • Softkeys: [P] [K] [A] [H]

docs.title: Eq. 17.4 — Buffer Acid-Spike Shift and Neutralization
docs.text:
The buffer's post-spike pH is evaluated by subtracting the added proton concentration from the initial conjugate base and adding it to the weak acid:

\[\text{pH}_{\text{after acid}} = \text{p}K_a + \log_{10}\left(\frac{[\text{A}^-]_0 - \Delta C_{\text{H}^+}}{[\text{HA}]_0 + \Delta C_{\text{H}^+}}\right)\]

Substituting our initial phosphate concentrations (\([\text{A}^-]_0 = 61.31\text{ mM}\) and \([\text{HA}]_0 = 38.69\text{ mM}\)) and the \(\Delta C_{\text{H}^+} = 5.0\text{ mM}\) acid spike gives the new concentrations \([\text{A}^-] = 61.31 - 5.0 = 56.31\text{ mM}\) (\(0.05631\text{ M}\)) and \([\text{HA}] = 38.69 + 5.0 = 43.69\text{ mM}\) (\(0.04369\text{ M}\)). The new base-to-acid ratio is \(r_{\text{new}} = 56.31 / 43.69 \approx \mathbf{1.2889}\), and the resulting solution \(\text{pH}\) is:

docs.title: Eq. 17.5 — Volumetric Titration Equivalence Point
docs.text:
When an analytical chemist standardizes an acid or base by Volumetric Titration ([f] [EQV]), a burette dispenses a measured volume \(V_A\) of titrant of known molarity \(C_A\) (producing \( u_A\) moles of \( ext{H}^+\) or \( ext{OH}^-\) per formula unit) into a sample volume \(V_B\) of unknown molarity \(C_B\) (accepting or donating \( u_B\) equivalents per formula unit). At the stoichiometric equivalence point, total acid equivalents equal total base equivalents:

\[ u_A \cdot C_A \cdot V_A = u_B \cdot C_B \cdot V_B \iff C_B = \left( rac{ u_A}{ u_B} ight) rac{C_A \cdot V_A}{V_B}\]

For a monoprotic neutralization (\( u_A = u_B = 1\), such as \( ext{HCl} + ext{NaOH} \longrightarrow ext{NaCl} + ext{H}_2 ext{O}\)), equivalence simplifies to \(C_A V_A = C_B V_B\): if \(V_A = 24.50 ext{ mL}\) of \(C_A = 0.1000 ext{ M}\) standard \( ext{NaOH}\) neutralizes a \(V_B = 25.00 ext{ mL}\) monoprotic acid sample, the acid molarity is \(C_B = (0.1000 imes 24.50) / 25.00 = \mathbf{0.0980 ext{ M}}\).

docs.title: Eq. 18.1 — Beer–Lambert Spectrophotometric Absorbance
docs.text:
Integrating \(dI / I = -\alpha c\,dx\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = b\) shows that the emergent intensity \(I\) and fractional Transmittance \(T = I / I_0 \in (0, 1]\) decay exponentially with both path length \(b\) and concentration \(c\). The negative base-ten logarithm transforms this multiplicative attenuation into an additive, linear metric where each unit of absorbance represents one order of magnitude of photon extinction. This gives the Beer–Lambert Law ([εbc]):

\[A = -\log_{10}(T) = \varepsilon \cdot b \cdot c\]

Inverting the relationship yields the unknown molar concentration directly from the spectrophotometer's optical absorbance reading:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [εbc] • Expression / Workspace: EBC: A = E × B × C • Softkeys: [A] [E] [B] [C] [%T]

docs.title: Eq. 18.2 — Arrhenius Thermal Reaction Kinetics and Acceleration
docs.text:
The natural exponential function evaluates the Boltzmann fraction of molecular collisions possessing sufficient thermal energy to surmount the reaction barrier \(E_a\). The fundamental rate equation is:

\[k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R \cdot T}\right)\]

Comparing reaction velocity constants \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) between two absolute temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) yields the Arrhenius Acceleration Ratio:

\[\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \exp\left[\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1} - \frac{1}{T_2}\right)\right]\]

On the SC-60, pressing [↱] [SOLVE] [g] [Eₐ] (or [g] [Eₐ] with empty stack) launches the bidirectional Arrhenius Kinetics Equation Solver Workspace (ARR: ARRHENIUS), rendering K = A × EXP(-E / (R × T)) across Line 1 with softkeys [K], [A], [E], and [T] (with \(R = 8.314462618\text{ J}/(\text{mol}\cdot\text{K})\) built into the solver kernel). Immediate stack execution with \(E_a\) in Register \(Y\) and \(T\) in Register \(X\) evaluates the Boltzmann exponential factor \(\exp(-E_a / (RT))\) directly into Register \(X\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [Eₐ] • Expression / Workspace: ARR: K = A × EXP(-E / (R × T)) • Softkeys: [K] [A] [E] [T]

docs.title: Eq. 18.3 — Relative Centrifugal Force and Rotor Speed
docs.text:
When a centrifuge spins a sample tube at angular velocity \(\omega = 2\pi \cdot \text{RPM} / 60\) (in radians per second) at radial distance \(r\) from the central spindle axis, the outward centripetal acceleration is \(a_c = \omega^2 r\). Dividing this acceleration by standard Earth gravity (\(g = 9.80665\text{ m/s}^2 = 980.665\text{ cm/s}^2\)) defines the dimensionless Relative Centrifugal Force (expressed in multiples of Earth gravity, \(\times g\), evaluated on the stack via \(1.1182 \times 10^{-5} \cdot r \cdot \text{RPM}^2\)):

\[\text{RCF} \approx 1.118 \times 10^{-5} \cdot r_{\text{cm}} \cdot \text{RPM}^2\]

Because centripetal acceleration scales quadratically with angular velocity, solving for the required spindle revolutions per minute takes the square root:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: Stack Arithmetic ([↰] [x²], [×], [√x]) • Expression / Workspace: RCF = 1.1182e-5 × r × RPM² • Softkeys: [x²] [√x]

docs.title: Unit VII: Commercial Bakery, Fermentation Science, and Brewing
docs.text: The SC-78 provides dedicated faceplate keys and bidirectional Equation Solver workspaces to execute the governing laws of this domain. Each equation is indexed below with its physical motivation, governing formula, and operational calculator softkeys.

docs.title: Eq. 19.1 — Baker's Percentage Mass Ratio and Ingredient Weight
docs.text:
In the Baker's Percentage ([BK%]) coordinate system, the combined mass of all milled grain flours introduced into the mixer—high-protein bread flour, stoneground whole wheat, rye, or Khorasan—is defined as the reference flour mass \(F\) and assigned \(100.0\%\). Each ingredient percentage \(P_i\) expresses its weight \(I_i\) as a proportion of total flour mass rather than total dough mass, allowing individual ingredient ratios to be modified without perturbing the rest of the formula:

\[P_i = \left(\frac{I_i}{F}\right) \times 100\]

Multiplying the reference flour mass by that percentage yields the required ingredient scaling weight:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [BK%] • Expression / Workspace: BK%: P = I / F × 100 • Softkeys: [P] [I] [F] [ΣW]

docs.title: Eq. 19.2 — Desired Dough Water Temperature and Friction Balance
docs.text:
To maintain a repeatable four-hour bulk fermentation schedule, mixed sourdough must exit the bowl at a target Desired Dough Temperature (\(D\), typically \(24.0^\circ\text{C}\) for country hearth loaves). Under the commercial Three-Factor Rule ([Tw]), final dough temperature is governed by an energy balance among ambient room air temperature \(R\), stored flour temperature \(F\), strike water temperature \(W\), and the mechanical friction heat \(M\) imparted by mixer shear. Multiplying the target Desired Dough Temperature \(D\) by three and subtracting room, flour, and friction temperatures yields the required strike-water temperature:

\[W = 3 D - R - F - M\]

Rearranging the balance enables backward calibration of the mixer's empirical friction factor from measured test-batch temperatures:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [Tw] • Expression / Workspace: TW: W = 3×D - R - F - M • Softkeys: [W] [D] [R] [F] [M]

docs.title: Eq. 19.3 — Latent-Heat Flake Ice Mass Substitution
docs.text:
When the required strike-water temperature \(T_{\text{target}} = W\) falls below the temperature of municipal tap water (\(T_{\text{tap}} = 21.0^\circ\text{C}\)) and the bakery lacks a refrigerated water chiller, the baker substitutes crushed or flake ice for part of the liquid water mass \(W_{\text{water}}\). Liquid water cools sensibly by one kilocalorie per kilogram for each degree Celsius dropped. Solid ice at \(0^\circ\text{C}\), by contrast, absorbs approximately eighty kilocalories per kilogram in latent heat (recalled via [g] [ΔHf]) solely to undergo the solid-to-liquid phase transition. Dividing the sensible cooling deficit by eighty determines the required flake-ice mass:

\[W_{\text{ice}} = \frac{W_{\text{water}} \cdot \left(T_{\text{tap}} - W\right)}{80}\]

The remaining liquid tap-water addition is then simply the difference between total water and ice mass:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [Tw] / [g] [ΔHf] • Expression / Workspace: Stack: W × ΔT / 80 • Softkeys: [Tw] [ΔHf]

docs.title: Eq. 20.1 — Specific Gravity and Extract Conversion
docs.text:
Degrees Brix and Plato measure the mass percentage of sucrose-equivalent extract in aqueous solution. Because dissolved sugars increase liquid density nonlinearly, converting between refractometric extract and hydrometer Specific Gravity uses the American Society of Brewing Chemists (ASBC) rational relation:

\[\text{SG} = 1 + \frac{B}{258.6 - \left(\frac{B}{258.2}\right) \times 227.1}\]

Inverting the mapping yields the cubic ASBC extract polynomial:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [▸SG] • Expression / Workspace: ASBC specific gravity and extract Plato • Softkeys: [▸SG] [▸Brx] [▸°P]

docs.title: Eq. 20.2 — Apparent Attenuation and Alcohol by Volume
docs.text:
As yeast ferments the sweet wort from Original Gravity (\(O\)) down to Final Gravity (\(F\)), the percentage of gravity points consumed defines Apparent Attenuation (\(\text{ATT}_{\%}\)):

\[\text{ATT}_{\%} = \left(\frac{O - F}{O - 1.000}\right) \times 100\]

Multiplying that density drop by the stoichiometric fermentation constant \(131.25\) determines finished Alcohol by Volume ([ABV], \(A\)) and distilled spirit proof ([g] [▸PRF], \(\text{Proof} = 2 \times \text{ABV}_{\%}\)):

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [ABV] • Expression / Workspace: ABV: A = (O - F) × 131.25 • Softkeys: [A] [O] [F]

docs.title: Eq. 20.3 — Tinseth Hop Bitterness and Utilization Kinetics
docs.text:
One International Bitterness Unit ([IBU], \(I\)) is defined analytically as \(1.0\text{ mg}\) of isomerized alpha acids per liter of beer (\(1\text{ mg/L}\)). Glenn Tinseth's utilization function models the biochemical efficiency of the boil: the exponential gravity factor accounts for the reduced solubility of alpha acids in dense wort, while the time factor captures first-order thermal isomerization asymptotically approaching a practical extraction limit:

\[I = \frac{W_{\text{g}} \cdot A \cdot U \cdot 1000}{V_{\text{L}}}\]

In U.S. customary units (\(W_{\text{oz}}\) in ounces, percentage alpha acid \(A_{\%}\), and batch volume \(V_{\text{gal}}\) in gallons), the conversion factor is \(74.89\):

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [IBU] • Expression / Workspace: IBU: I = W × A × U × 74.89 / V • Softkeys: [I] [W] [A] [U] [V]

docs.title: Eq. 21.1 — Compounding Fabrication Yield and Edible Mass
docs.text:
In culinary cost accounting, the gross weight of an untrimmed commodity as delivered by the supplier is the As-Purchased Mass (\(W_{\text{AP}}\)), whereas the net weight of fabricated, cooked food ready for service is the Edible Portion Mass (\(W_{\text{EP}}\)). When a product undergoes \(m\) sequential processing stages with individual decimal stage yields \(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_m \in (0, 1]\) (where \(y_k = 1 - \ell_k\) for stage fractional loss \(\ell_k\)), mass conservation dictates that the stage yields multiply geometrically rather than subtracting linearly:

\[y_{\text{cum}} = \prod_{k=1}^{m} y_k = \prod_{k=1}^{m} \left(1 - \ell_k\right)\]

The resulting cumulative yield decimal \(y_{\text{cum}} = Y_{\%} / 100\) determines the edible finished mass \(W_{\text{EP}}\) from the gross delivery weight \(W_{\text{AP}}\):

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [%] / Stack Arithmetic • Expression / Workspace: Stack: EP / AP × 100 • Softkeys: [%] [SCL]

docs.title: Eq. 21.2 — Yield-Adjusted Edible Portion Unit Cost
docs.text:
When an untrimmed commodity is purchased at an As-Purchased Unit Cost of \(C_{\text{AP}}\) (in dollars per pound or kilogram) and yields a cumulative decimal fraction \(y_{\text{cum}} = Y_{\%} / 100 = \prod_{k=1}^m y_k\) of edible product after fabrication and cooking, the entire invoice expenditure must be recovered across the smaller edible mass \(W_{\text{EP}}\). Dividing \(C_{\text{AP}}\) by \(y_{\text{cum}}\) gives the true Edible Portion Unit Cost (\(C_{\text{EP}}\)):

\[C_{\text{EP}} = \frac{C_{\text{AP}}}{y_{\text{cum}}} = \frac{C_{\text{AP}}}{\prod_{k=1}^{m} y_k}\]

Multiplying that edible unit cost by portion serving weight \(w_{\text{portion}}\) yields the raw plate protein cost:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [CST] • Expression / Workspace: CST: P = C / (F / 100) • Softkeys: [P] [C] [F]

docs.title: Eq. 21.3 — Food Cost to Gross Margin Hyperbolic Mapping
docs.text:
Food cost fraction \(f\) and gross margin \(m\) normalize profit against selling price \(P\), whereas markup \(u\) normalizes that same profit against kitchen cost \(C\). Because margin divides by price and markup divides by cost, their relationship forms a hyperbolic curve with a vertical asymptote as gross margin approaches one hundred percent:

\[f = \frac{C}{P} \iff P = \frac{C}{f} = \frac{C}{1 - m} = C \left(1 + u\right)\]

The inverse transformations convert bidirectionally between gross margin \(m\) and markup on cost \(u\):

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [PRC] • Expression / Workspace: Food cost to gross margin hyperbolic mapping • Softkeys: [PRC] [CST]

docs.title: Unit VIII: Clinical Nursing, Hospital Pharmacy, and Infusions
docs.text: The SC-80 provides dedicated faceplate keys and bidirectional Equation Solver workspaces to execute the governing laws of this domain. Each equation is indexed below with its physical motivation, governing formula, and operational calculator softkeys.

docs.title: Eq. 22.1 — Mosteller Body Surface Area and Inversion
docs.text:
Two patients who each weigh \(88.0\text{ kg}\) can possess markedly different internal drug distribution volumes. A tall, muscular patient has an expansive vascular bed, high cardiac output, and large hepatic and renal parenchymal mass, whereas a shorter, sedentary patient of the same \(88.0\text{ kg}\) weight carries a substantial fraction of mass as poorly perfused adipose tissue. Because extracellular fluid volume, glomerular filtration, and basal metabolic rate correlate closely with external Body Surface Area ([BSA], \(B\)) in square meters (\(\text{m}^2\), averaging \(1.73\text{ m}^2\) in a reference adult), Robert D. Mosteller (1987) formulated [BSA] from patient height \(H\) (in \(\text{cm}\)) and total body weight \(W\) (in \(\text{kg}\)) using the dimensional normalization constant \(3600 = 60^2\text{ cm}\cdot\text{kg/m}^4\):

\[B = \sqrt{\frac{H \cdot W}{3600}}\]

Inverting the square root yields the patient mass required to achieve a specified target surface area:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [BSA] • Expression / Workspace: BSA: B = √(H × W / 3600) • Softkeys: [B] [H] [W] [PAT]

docs.title: Eq. 22.2 — Devine Ideal Body Weight and Adipose Adjustment
docs.text:
When dosing hydrophilic medications that remain inside lean tissue and extracellular water, using raw total body weight (\(\text{TBW} = W\)) in an overweight patient causes systematic over-dosing. To estimate lean metabolically active mass from skeletal stature alone, Ben Devine (1974) established the Ideal Body Weight ([f] [IBW], in \(\text{kg}\)) equations for adults at least \(60\text{ inches}\) (\(152.4\text{ cm}\), or \(5\text{ feet}\)) tall, where \(H_{\text{in}} = H / 2.54\) is height in inches, \(50.0\text{ kg}\) (male) and \(45.5\text{ kg}\) (female) are the baseline lean weights at \(60\text{ inches}\), and \(2.3\text{ kg/in}\) (\(0.9055\text{ kg/cm}\)) is the linear lean-mass increment per inch above five feet:

\[\text{IBW}_{\text{male}} = 50.0 + 2.3\left(\frac{H}{2.54} - 60\right)\]

When a patient's total body weight \(\text{TBW}\) exceeds \(\text{IBW}\) by more than \(20\%\), polar antibiotics such as aminoglycosides penetrate roughly \(40\%\) into excess adipose extracellular water, which clinical pharmacists capture via Adjusted Body Weight ([g] [ABW], in \(\text{kg}\)) using the empirical adipose distribution factor \(0.40\):

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [IBW] • Expression / Workspace: Devine ideal and adjusted body weight • Softkeys: [IBW] [ABW] [BMI]

docs.title: Eq. 22.3 — Cockcroft–Gault Creatinine Clearance Estimation
docs.text:
Creatinine is a nitrogenous breakdown product of creatine phosphate in skeletal muscle, released into blood plasma at a steady daily rate proportional to muscle mass and filtered freely by the renal glomeruli into the urine. At steady state, urinary creatinine excretion matches muscle creatinine production, making Creatinine Clearance ([GFR], \(C\))—the volume of plasma cleared of creatinine per minute (\(\text{mL/min}\))—inversely proportional to steady-state serum creatinine (\(S\), in \(\text{mg/dL}\)). Because skeletal muscle mass and nephron count decline linearly with adult age (\(A\), in years), Donald Cockcroft and Henry Gault (1976) formulated bedside [GFR] from dosing weight \(W\), using the empirical constant \(72\) in the denominator and a \(0.85\) factor in biological females ([FEM] in [PAT]) to reflect lower average skeletal muscle mass per kilogram:

\[C_{\text{male}} = \frac{\left(140 - A\right) \cdot W}{72 \cdot S}\]

A fifteen percent reduction accounts for lower average muscular mass in biological females:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [GFR] • Expression / Workspace: GFR: C = (140 - A) × W / (72 × S) • Softkeys: [C] [A] [W] [S]

docs.title: Eq. 22.4 — Holliday–Segar Pediatric 4-2-1 Fluid Maintenance
docs.text:
To replace daily insensible (respiratory and cutaneous) and urinary water losses in hospitalized children and adults, Malcolm Holliday and William Segar (1957) tied basal water requirements to metabolic caloric expenditure across three body-mass tiers, establishing the 4-2-1 Maintenance Fluid Rule ([g] [421]):

\[R_{\text{maint,mL/hr}} = \begin{cases} 4 \cdot W & \text{if } W \le 10 \\ 40 + 2\left(W - 10\right) & \text{if } 10 < W \le 20 \\ 60 + 1\left(W - 20\right) & \text{if } W > 20 \end{cases}\]

Across clinical nutrition ([f] [REE]) and veterinary medicine ([g] [VET]), basal caloric demand follows Max Kleiber's \(3/4\)-power allometric Resting Energy Expenditure (in \(\text{kcal/day}\)):

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [IV] • Expression / Workspace: Holliday–Segar pediatric 4-2-1 fluid rate • Softkeys: [IV] [DOS]

docs.title: Eq. 23.1 — Continuous Vasoactive Mass Flux to Volumetric Pump Rate
docs.text:
When a physician orders a continuous weight-based dose \(D\) (in \(\mu\text{g}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}\cdot\text{min}^{-1}\)) for a patient of body mass \(W\) (in \(\text{kg}\), pre-populated from [PAT]), multiplying \(D \cdot W\) gives the microgram delivery rate per minute (\(\mu\text{g/min}\)), and multiplying by \(60\text{ min/hr}\) yields the hourly microgram flux \(\dot{m}_{\text{mcg/hr}} = 60 D W\) (or dividing by \(1000\ \mu\text{g/mg}\) via the immediate [DRP] stack operator gives the hourly milligram flux \(\dot{m}_{\text{mg/hr}} = 0.060 D W\)). Dividing the hourly microgram flux by the pharmacy bag's microgram concentration \(C = 1000 \cdot (M_{\text{bag,mg}} / V_{\text{bag,mL}})\) (in \(\mu\text{g/mL}\)) yields the Volumetric Infusion Pump Rate \(R\) (in \(\text{mL/hr}\)), while algebraic inversion in the [DRP] Solver Workspace solves backward via [XEQ] for the Delivered Dose Rate \(D\) from an observed pump rate \(R\):

\[R = \frac{D \cdot W \cdot 60}{C} \iff D = \frac{R \cdot C}{60 \cdot W}\]

The active drug concentration \(C\) in micrograms per milliliter reflects the pharmacy bag reconstitution:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [DRP] • Expression / Workspace: DRP: R = D × W × 60 / C • Softkeys: [R] [D] [W] [C]

docs.title: Eq. 23.2 — Gravity Drop Frequency from Volumetric Flow
docs.text:
Every manual intravenous administration set manufactures its drip-chamber orifice to form drops of a fixed volumetric size, specified by the tubing Drop Factor (\(DF_{\text{gtt/mL}}\), in drops per milliliter, \(\text{gtt/mL}\)). Standard adult macro-drip sets deliver \(10\), \(15\), or \(20\text{ gtt/mL}\), whereas pediatric and critical-care micro-drip sets use a fine stainless-steel needle orifice that delivers \(60\text{ gtt/mL}\). Multiplying the hourly volumetric flow rate \(R_{\text{mL/hr}}\) by \(DF_{\text{gtt/mL}}\) gives drops per hour, and dividing by \(60\text{ min/hr}\) yields the Gravity Drip Rate ([gtt], \(R_{\text{gtt/min}}\), in drops per minute):

\[R_{\text{gtt/min}} = \frac{R_{\text{mL/hr}} \cdot DF_{\text{gtt/mL}}}{60}\]

In a \(60\text{ gtt/mL}\) micro-drip chamber: when \(DF_{\text{gtt/mL}} = 60\), the ratio \(60 / 60\) equals unity, so \(R_{\text{gtt/min}} = R_{\text{mL/hr}}\) numerically. For our ICU transport running at \(R_{\text{mL/hr}} = 15.00\text{ mL/hr}\), a macro-drip set with \(DF = 15\text{ gtt/mL}\) produces a drip rate via [gtt] of \(R_{\text{gtt/min}} = (15.00 \times 15) / 60 = \mathbf{3.75\text{ gtt/min}}\), whereas switching to a \(60\text{ gtt/mL}\) micro-drip chamber raises the drip frequency to \(\mathbf{15.00\text{ gtt/min}}\) (one drop every \(4.0\text{ seconds}\)).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [gtt] • Expression / Workspace: Gravity drop frequency from flow rate • Softkeys: [gtt] [DRP]

docs.title: Eq. 23.3 — Mean Arterial Pressure and Parkland Resuscitation
docs.text:
Vasoactive infusions are titrated to restore organ perfusion pressure and cardiac output, while severe thermal burns require high-volume crystalloid infusions to replace capillary plasma leakage. At resting heart rates, the cardiac ventricles spend roughly one-third of each cardiac cycle in systolic ejection (\(\text{SBP}\), in \(\text{mmHg}\)) and two-thirds in diastolic relaxation (\(\text{DBP}\), in \(\text{mmHg}\)), defining Mean Arterial Pressure ([f] [MAP], in \(\text{mmHg}\)):

\[\text{MAP} = \text{DBP} + \frac{1}{3}\left(\text{SBP} - \text{DBP}\right) = \frac{\text{SBP} + 2 \cdot \text{DBP}}{3}\]

Multiplying heart rate \(H\) (\(\text{bpm}\)) by stroke volume \(S\) (\(\text{mL/beat}\)) and dividing by \(1000\text{ mL/L}\) gives Cardiac Output ([ICU], \(Q = H \cdot S / 1000\text{ L/min}\)). Simultaneously, Charles Baxter's 1968 Parkland Formula ([g] [BRN]) sizes the total \(24\text{-hour}\) Lactated Ringer's crystalloid resuscitation volume \(V\) (in \(\text{mL}\)) from patient weight \(W\) (pre-populated from [PAT]) and the percentage of Total Body Surface Area burned (\(B = \%\,\text{TBSA}\), entered as a whole number such as \(35\) for \(35\%\)):

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [ICU] • Expression / Workspace: Mean arterial pressure and Parkland resuscitation • Softkeys: [ICU] [BRN]

docs.title: Eq. 24.1 — One-Compartment First-Order Elimination Kinetics
docs.text:
When an intravenous bolus dose of mass \(D\) (in \(\text{mg}\)) mixes across the Apparent Volume of Distribution (\(V\), in liters \(\text{L}\)) cleared at volumetric Systemic Clearance rate \(C_{\text{CL}}\) (in \(\text{L/hr}\)), it establishes an initial peak concentration \(C_0 = D / V\) (in \(\text{mg/L}\)). Because the rate of drug elimination \(-dM/dt = C_{\text{CL}} \cdot C(t)\) is proportional to instantaneous concentration \(C(t)\), plasma concentration decays exponentially according to the first-order Elimination Rate Constant (\(K\), in \(\text{hr}^{-1}\)) and Elimination Half-Life (\(T_{1/2}\), in hours), where \(\ln(2) \approx 0.693147\) ([PK]):

\[C(t) = C_0 \, e^{-K t}\]

The biological half-life divides the natural logarithm of two by the elimination rate constant:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [PK] • Expression / Workspace: PK: T = .69315 × V / C • Softkeys: [T] [V] [C]

docs.title: Eq. 24.2 — Multi-Dose Steady-State Accumulation Factor
docs.text:
When the same maintenance dose \(D\) is repeated at a fixed dosing interval \(\tau\) (in hours), each new dose adds \(C_0 = D / V\) on top of the residual trough remaining from all prior doses. After \(n\) doses, the finite geometric series \(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} r^j = (1 - r^n)/(1 - r)\) with per-interval survival ratio \(r = e^{-K \tau} = 2^{-\tau / T_{1/2}}\) converges as \(n \to \infty\) to the Steady-State Accumulation Factor \(R_{\text{acc}}\), determining the Steady-State Peak (\(C_{\text{ss,max}}\)), Steady-State Trough (\(C_{\text{ss,min}}\)), and Average Steady-State Concentration (\(C_{\text{ss,avg}}\), which equals \(\text{AUC}_{0\to\tau} / \tau\)):

\[R_{\text{acc}} = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} e^{-j K \tau} = \frac{1}{1 - e^{-K \tau}}\]

Multiplying the single-dose peak increment \(C_0\) by \(R_{\text{acc}}\) gives the steady-state maximum and minimum concentrations:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [PK] • Expression / Workspace: Multi-dose steady-state drug accumulation • Softkeys: [PK] [DOS]

docs.title: Eq. 24.3 — Bazett Heart Rate-Corrected QT Interval
docs.text:
Alongside blood gas analysis, Henry Cuthbert Bazett's (1920) Corrected QT Interval ([f] [QTc], in \(\text{ms}\)) normalizes ventricular repolarization time \(\text{QT}_{\text{ms}}\) to a \(60\text{ bpm}\) (\(RR = 1.0\text{ s}\)) reference by dividing by the square root of the cardiac RR cycle length in seconds:

\[\text{QT}_c = \frac{\text{QT}_{\text{ms}}}{\sqrt{60 / \text{HR}}}\]

With a measured interval \(\text{QT} = 380\text{ ms}\) at heart rate \(88\text{ bpm}\) (\(RR = 60 / 88 \approx 0.6818\text{ s}\)), Bazett's formula evaluated via [f] [QTc] yields \(\text{QT}_c = \frac{380}{\sqrt{0.6818}} \approx \mathbf{460.2\text{ ms}}\), flagging borderline prolongation.

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [QTc] • Expression / Workspace: Bazett heart rate-corrected QT interval • Softkeys: [QTc]

docs.title: Eq. 24.4 — Compressed Medical Oxygen Cylinder Remaining Duration
docs.text:
The Compressed Oxygen Cylinder Law ([f] [O₂]) relates remaining tank pressure \(P_{\text{psi}}\) (above the \(200\text{ psi}\) safe residual cushion) and cylinder conversion factor \(k_{\text{tank}}\) (\(0.28\text{ L/psi}\) for a portable E-cylinder; \(3.14\text{ L/psi}\) for a bulk H-cylinder) to delivery flow rate \(F\) (\(\text{L/min}\)) and transport duration \(T\) (\(\text{min}\)):

\[T_{\text{min}} = \frac{\left(P_{\text{psi}} - 200\right) \times 0.28}{F}\]

At \(F_i\text{O}_2 = 0.40\), \(P_a\text{CO}_2 = 28\text{ mmHg}\), and \(P_a\text{O}_2 = 110\text{ mmHg}\), pressing 110 [ENTER] 0.40 [÷] gives a Horowitz \(P/F\) ratio of \(\mathbf{275.0\text{ mmHg}}\), while alveolar oxygen is \(P_A\text{O}_2 = 0.40(713) - 28/0.8 = 285.2 - 35.0 = 250.2\text{ mmHg}\), giving \(\Delta P_{A-a}\text{O}_2 = 250.2 - 110 = \mathbf{140.2\text{ mmHg}}\). On the ECG monitor (\(\text{QT} = 420\text{ ms}\) at \(\text{HR} = 96\text{ bpm}\), so \(RR = 60/96 = 0.625\text{ s}\)), pressing 420 [ENTER] 96 [f] [QTc] gives \(\text{QT}_c = 420 / \sqrt{0.625} = \mathbf{531.26\text{ ms}}\) (alerting the team to pause QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics). Finally, because \(T\) and \(F\) are reciprocally symmetric in \(T \cdot F = (P_{\text{psi}} - 200) \times 0.28\), for the \(T = 70.0\text{-minute}\) helicopter transfer with an E-cylinder at \(P_{\text{psi}} = 1950\text{ psi}\), pressing 1950 [ENTER] 70 [f] [O₂] directly yields the maximum safe oxygen flow rate \(F = (1950 - 200) \times 0.28 / 70.0 = 490.0 / 70.0 = \mathbf{7.00\text{ L/min}}\).

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [O₂] • Expression / Workspace: Compressed oxygen cylinder remaining time • Softkeys: [O₂]

docs.title: Eq. 24.5 — Radiopharmaceutical Exponential Half-Life Decay
docs.text:
In nuclear pharmacy and hospital radiochemistry, therapeutic and diagnostic radioisotopes (such as Technetium-\(99\text{m}\), Fluorine-\(18\), and Iodine-\(131\)) disintegrate via first-order nuclear decay. The instantaneous radioactivity \(A(t)\) after elapsed transit or preparation time \(T\) depends on the initial calibrated activity \(A_0\) and the physical half-life \(H = t_{1/2}\):

\[A = A_0 \cdot 2^{-T / H} = A_0 \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\ln 2}{H} \cdot T\right)\]

Inverting the relationship solves for the required compounding pre-calibration activity \(A_0 = A \cdot 2^{T/H}\) needed to deliver a target patient dose at injection time, or evaluates the decay time \(T = -H \frac{\ln(A / A_0)}{\ln 2}\).

On the SC-80, staging initial activity \(A_0\) in Register \(Y\) and elapsed time \(T\) in Register \(X\) before pressing [f] [VIL] calculates the remaining activity \(A\) (using isotope half-life \(H\) stored in variable H, defaulting to \(6.0\text{ hours}\) for Technetium-\(99\text{m}\)). In the bidirectional Equation Solver Workspace ([XEQ] [f] [VIL]), the calculator displays RAD: DECAY / HL with governing equation A = A0 × 2^(-T / H) and softkeys [A], [O], [T], and [H].

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [f] [VIL] • Expression / Workspace: RAD: A = A0 × 2^(-T / H) • Softkeys: [A] [O] [T] [H]

docs.title: Unit IX: Quantitative Finance, Actuarial Science, and Six Sigma
docs.text: The SC-95 provides dedicated faceplate keys and bidirectional Equation Solver workspaces to execute the governing laws of this domain. Each equation is indexed below with its physical motivation, governing formula, and operational calculator softkeys.

docs.title: Eq. 25.1 — Five-Variable Time Value of Money Governing Equation
docs.text:
Across any level-payment financial contract in the [TVM] workspace, five parameters are coupled together on softkeys [N], [I%], [PV], [PMT], and [FV] (alongside payment timing [END]/[BEG]): the total number of compounding or payment periods \(N\) ([N]), the periodic interest rate [I%] expressed as a percentage per period where the decimal rate is \(i = (\text{I\%})/100\) (obtained from the nominal annual rate by dividing by \(M\) compounding periods per year), the initial Present Value \(\text{PV}\) ([PV]) at \(t = 0\), the level periodic Payment \(\text{PMT}\) ([PMT]) at the end of each period \(t = 1, 2, \dots, N\), and the terminal Future Value or balloon balance \(\text{FV}\) ([FV]) at horizon \(t = N\). Discounting each cash flow back to \(t = 0\) and summing the finite geometric series \(\sum_{t=1}^{N} (1+i)^{-t} = (1 - (1+i)^{-N})/i\) yields the Time Value of Money Balance Equation:

\[\text{PV} + \text{PMT}\left(\frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i}\right) + \text{FV}(1 + i)^{-N} = 0\]

Compounded forward to future horizon \(t = N\), the terminal balance is:

  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [TVM] • Expression / Workspace: TVM: Five-variable financial balance • Softkeys: [N] [I%] [PV] [PMT] [FV]

docs.title: Eq. 25.2 — Uniform Series Net Present Value and Internal Rate of Return
docs.text:
When a capital project requires an initial investment \(I_0\) at \(t = 0\) and generates a uniform net operating cash inflow \(C\) across \(N\) periods discounted at the firm's opportunity cost of capital (hurdle rate) \(r = R / 100\), Net Present Value ([g] [CF], opening the [g] [CF] Solver Workspace) subtracts \(I_0\) from the present value of the cash-flow annuity. A positive \(\text{NPV} > 0\) certifies that the asset earns more than the hurdle rate \(r\):

\[\text{NPV} = C\left(\frac{1 - (1 + r)^{-N}}{r}\right) - I_0\]

The break-even discount rate \(r^*\) at which \(\text{NPV}(r^*) = 0\) defines the Internal Rate of Return (\(\text{IRR}\)):

docs.title: Eq. 25.3 — Breakeven Production Volume and Economic Order Quantity
docs.text:

\[Q_{\text{BEP}}^* = \frac{F_{\text{fixed}}}{P - V}\]

docs.title: Eq. 25.4 — Calendar Day Count and Settlement Date Mathematics
docs.text:
In fixed-income bond valuation, syndicated loan syndication, commercial paper settlement, and interest rate swaps, cash flow payments depend on exact calendar schedules. The SC-95 provides dedicated calendar arithmetic based on Gregorian Julian Day Number (\(\text{JDN}\)) algorithms:

  1. Days Between Dates ([g] [ΔD]): With settlement date \(\text{Date}_1\) in Register \(Y\) and maturity date \(\text{Date}_2\) in Register \(X\) (entered in either standard financial notation MM.DDYYYY or international ISO YYYY.MMDD), pressing [g] [ΔD] evaluates the exact integer elapsed days:
\[\Delta\text{Days} = \text{JDN}(\text{Date}_2) - \text{JDN}(\text{Date}_1)\]
  1. Date Addition ([f] [DT+]): With a start date \(\text{Date}_1\) in Register \(Y\) and elapsed integer days \(n\) in Register \(X\) (or vice versa), pressing [f] [DT+] projects the forward or backward calendar settlement date, accounting for varying month lengths and leap years:
\[\text{Date}_{\text{target}} = \text{Gregorian}(\text{JDN}(\text{Date}_1) + n)\]

  1. Date Format Conversion ([g] [▸YMD]): Converts a calendar date in Register \(X\) between American financial notation MM.DDYYYY and ISO standard notation YYYY.MMDD.

  2. Calculator Interface: Primary Keys: [g] [ΔD] / [f] [DT+] / [g] [▸YMD] • Expression / Workspace: Calendar day count and settlement date math • Softkeys: [ΔD] [DT+] [▸YMD]

docs.title: Eq. 26.1 — Fixed-Coupon Bond Present Value Pricing
docs.text:
For a bond with par redemption value \(F = 100\), periodic coupon payment \(C\), and \(N\) remaining periods to maturity discounted at periodic Yield to Maturity (\(y = Y/100\)), the fair market Bond Price ([g] [BND], \(P_{\text{bond}}\)) is the sum of the present value of the coupon stream and the discounted par redemption:

\[P_{\text{bond}} = C\left(\frac{1 - (1 + y)^{-N}}{y}\right) + F(1 + y)^{-N}\]

In the United States corporate and Treasury bond markets, a \(10\text{-year}\) bond paying a \(5.00\%\) annual coupon rate distributes \(C_{\text{semi}} = 2.50\) every six months across \(N_{\text{semi}} = 20\) semiannual periods at a periodic yield of \(Y_{\text{semi}} = Y_{\text{nom}} / 2 = 3.00\%\) (\(y = 0.030\)), whereas Eurobonds pay \(C_{\text{ann}} = 5.00\) once per year across \(N_{\text{ann}} = 10\) annual periods at \(Y_{\text{ann}} = 6.00\%\) (\(y = 0.060\)). When the market yield equals the coupon rate (\(y = C/F\)), \(P_{\text{bond}} = 100.00\) (par). When \(y > C/F\), \(P_{\text{bond}} < 100.00\) (discount). And when \(y < C/F\), \(P_{\text{bond}} > 100.00\) (premium).

docs.title: Eq. 26.2 — Macaulay Duration, Modified Duration, and Price Sensitivity
docs.text:
In 1938, Frederick Macaulay defined the effective time horizon of a bond—Macaulay Duration (\(D_{\text{Mac}}\))—as the present-value-weighted average arrival time of its cash flows, which admits a closed-form algebraic expression in terms of periodic coupon rate \(c = C/F\), periodic yield \(y\), and period count \(N\):

\[D_{\text{Mac,periods}} = \frac{1 + y}{y} - \frac{1 + y + N(c - y)}{c\left[(1 + y)^N - 1\right] + y}\]

Dividing Macaulay Duration (in years) by \((1 + y)\) yields the first-derivative price sensitivity with respect to yield, known as Modified Duration (\(D_{\text{Mod}}\)). For large yield shocks (\(\Delta y\)), incorporating the second-order Convexity Adjustment (\(C\)) restores exact pricing curvature:

\[\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D_{\text{Mod}} \cdot \Delta y + \frac{1}{2} C (\Delta y)^2\]
  • Calculator Interface: Primary Key: [g] [BND] • Expression / Workspace: Macaulay duration, convexity, and price sensitivity • Softkeys: [BND] [TVM]

docs.title: Eq. 26.3 — Black–Scholes European Option Pricing Model
docs.text:
Assuming the underlying asset price \(S_t\) follows geometric Brownian motion \(dS_t = \mu S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t\) with annualized volatility \(\sigma\) and continuous risk-free interest rate \(r\), Fischer Black, Myron Scholes, and Robert Merton proved in 1973 that the drift rate \(\mu\) cancels out of a continuously delta-hedged portfolio. The arbitrage-free price of a European Call Option (\(C_{\text{call}}\)) on a non-dividend-paying asset of spot price \(S_0\) with strike price \(K\) and time to expiration \(T\) (in years) is governed by the standard normal cumulative distribution function \(\Phi(z) = \text{pnorm}(z)\) ([g] [pN]):

\[C_{\text{call}} = S_0 \, \Phi(d_1) - K e^{-rT} \Phi(d_2)\]

docs.title: Eq. 26.4 — Put–Call Parity and European Put Valuation

\[P_{\text{put}} = C_{\text{call}} - S_0 + K e^{-rT}\]

docs.title: Eq. 27.2 — Centered and Asymmetric Process Capability Indices
docs.text:
For a manufacturing process with mean \(\mu\) and short-term standard deviation \(\sigma\) operating between Lower Specification Limit \(\text{LSL}\) and Upper Specification Limit \(\text{USL}\), Process Potential (\(C_p\)) divides the blueprint tolerance width \((\text{USL} - \text{LSL})\) by the natural \(6\sigma\) process spread (\(\pm 3\sigma\)). Because \(C_p\) ignores where the mean \(\mu\) is located, Centered Process Capability (\(C_{pk}\)) evaluates the upper capability \(C_{pu}\) and lower capability \(C_{pl}\) separately and takes the minimum—measuring the distance from \(\mu\) to the nearer specification wall in units of \(3\sigma\):

\[C_p = \frac{\text{USL} - \text{LSL}}{6\sigma}\]

docs.text:

\[z_{\text{USL}} = \frac{\text{USL} - \mu}{\sigma} = 3 \cdot C_{pu}\]

docs.title: Appendix B: Domain Instrument Keycap & Workspace Directory
docs.text: This directory catalogs the physical keycaps, Row 0 domain softkeys, yellow ([↰]) and blue ([↱]) shift layers, bidirectional Equation Solver Workspaces ([g] [SOLVE] / [XEQ]), and register input-output signatures across all nine instruments in the StackCalc Domain Series (SC-35 through SC-95). Each table lists the pre-execution stack arguments consumed from Register T, Register Z, Register Y, and Register X alongside the post-execution results returned to Register X' and Register Y' and the softkey variable bindings inside each instrument's Equation Solver Workspace.

docs.title: Shared Core Keys and Architecture Across All Nine Instruments
docs.text:
Every calculator in the StackCalc Domain Series provides configurable RPN stack depth ([4-LV], [8-LV], or [INF] cycled on Flag 5 5:DEP inside [↱] [FLAGS]), dual-mode domain keys that combine one-key RPN stack evaluation with a bidirectional Equation Solver Workspace ([g] [SOLVE] / [XEQ]), and non-destructive Live Reference Ledgers ([g] [▦]) paired with ten general-purpose memory registers (R₀–R₉):
